source: Wildland Fire Lessons Learned Center, Spatial Incident Review Database

incidents.name: Timber Canyon Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Alfredo de la Riva was entrapped while attempting to evacuate a miner in the Topatopa mountains of Ventura County, California. De la Riva was an early employee of the Santa Barbara Forest Reserve (which later became the Los Padres National Forest). De la Riva assisted the elderly man in attempting to escape a wind-driven fire. The miner was overcome by fire at the scene and perished, and de la Riva suffered burn injuries.

incidents.name: Tammany Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 2, 1910, William Polleys, a 27-year-old lumberman in Western Montana, was killed by a falling tree while hiking off a forest fire with his crew near Tammany, Montana.
incidents.quote: Polleys reportedly pushed the man next to him out of the way of the falling tree and warned the other men.

incidents.name: Worcester County Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: George Dodge, a farmer in Wilkinsville, Massachusetts, was killed when he was overcome by fire on April 26, 1911. Dodge had gone missing during fire suppression on the 1,000 acre wildfire, and was found deceased and burned in the black.

incidents.name: Waterman Canyon Fire Firefighter Fatality
incidents.summary: An unidentified deceased firefighter was found during a patrol of the fireline on the Waterman Canyon Fire that was burning near Big Bear, California, on the San Bernardino National Forest. Reports indicate that numerous firefighters assigned to this fire were injured and were without supplies or assistance.

incidents.name: Snow Creek Canyon Fire Fall Fatality
incidents.summary: C. B. Hyde was fatally injured on February 26, 1911, when he fell and struck his head while assigned to the Snow Creek Canyon Fire located above Whitewater, California. Fire-loosened rocks were a hazard on this fire. Hyde was either struck by a rock or lost his footing to avoid a rock and fell down a steep slope. He was treated by a fellow firefighter while another went for help at Whitewater down at the base of the mountains. A group of responders mobilized, but arrived at the accident scene after Hyde had died from his injuries.

incidents.name: Bell Rock Road Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Frederick Sheppard, a farmer in Fall River, Massachusetts, was found deceased after he had gone missing while fighting fire in the woods near his farm. A group of locals mobilized to fight the fire, and at some point noticed that Sheppard was no longer with them. A group searched the burnt forest and found Sheppard's burned body. It was thought he had become overcome by smoke or heat and his body subsequently burned.

incidents.name: Curry County Hit by Tree Fatality 1914
incidents.summary: Thomas Winfield, an employee at Harris Tie Camp (constructing railroad ties), was killed by a falling tree on a forest fire located near the Rogue River in Curry County, Oregon. Winfield, a brand-new employee at the mill, went with rest of the workers to assist suppressing this fire that ignited near the camp. While Winfield was working alone, a tree fell on him, crushing his chest and pinning him to the ground. Nearby colleagues ran to the scene after hearing the tree fall. They were able to cut the tree off of him. Even so, Winfield succumbed to his injuries. Ultimately, this fire burned a small area and did not cause significant damage. Very little information is readily available about Thomas Winfield. He was believed to have been 50 years old.

incidents.name: Wounded Buck Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: James Barden, a firefighter employed by the Flathead National Forest, was killed September 3, 1914, by a falling tree while assigned to a fire on Wounded Buck Creek south of Hungry Horse, Montana. It is believed the tree that struck Barden had burned out at the base and fell without warning, striking him on the head.

incidents.name: Santa Clara County Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Carl Stagen, a ranch hand working on one of the ranches near California's Santa Clara-San Mateo County border, was entrapped and killed while suppressing a fire in the Santa Cruz Mountains in the vicinity of Page Mill Road. Stagen was assigned by his employer to hold a stretch of road to prevent the fire crossing it and threatening a summer home owned by the mayor of San Francisco. Pushed by wind, the fire ran down slope. Stagen attempted to swat the flames out when he was overcome and perished.
incidents.quote: This man had been a sailor aboard a German ship which was detained in the harbor when World War I began.

incidents.name: Clallam County Entrapment Burn Injuries 1916
incidents.summary: Fifty firefighters were entrapped while attempting to suppress a fire and keep it from destroying structures at an Olympic Peninsula logging camp located west of Port Angeles, Washington. The men loaded onto a logging locomotive and rode through the burning forest, crossing a burning bridge, until they reached safety. During this escape, some of the men received burn injuries to their backs and faces as well as smoke inhalation. The smoke inhalation was most severe to the two men who ran through the smoke to throw a railroad switch. They had suppressed fire for 36 hours straight. Despite their efforts, 18 buildings at Puget Sound Timber Company's Camp 5 burned.

incidents.name: Knappa Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: When the firefighters were instructed to run to safety, the crew broke into two groups. Some went down a trail and the others escaped via a railroad right of way. Of the railroad group, three escaped. But two firefighters, Stit Kulik and Alex Aushiki, were overcome and perished. These two men were natives of Grodno, a region that is now in Belarus. However, at that time, it was part of Russia.
incidents.quote: At some time around August 24, 1917, two firefighters were entrapped and fatally injured on a forest fire near Astoria, Oregon. These firefighters were both described as "Russians"--immigrants working for the Big Creek Logging Company at the time of their deaths. Their crew of loggers was working as firefighters on this fire when they were entrapped by a fire run burning in a clearcut.

incidents.name: Kneeland Prairie Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Andrew Erickson was one of a group of firefighters assigned to suppress a fire located east of Eureka, California. They had been on this fire several days when he was struck by a tree limb and killed. Erickson was reportedly on the fireline for multiple days when he had laid down to sleep at the base of a large tree. A limb from that tree fell while he was asleep, causing his fatal injury.

incidents.name: Clearwater National Forest Hit by Tree Fatality 1918
incidents.summary: Elias Tanner was employed by the U.S. Forest Service on the Clearwater National Forest in Idaho when he was struck by a falling tree and killed instantly. Tanner was felling a tree and was hit when he attempted to escape the tree as it fell. His fire crew was assigned to one of the many fires burning at that time in the Clearwater, Nez Perce, Pend Oreille and Kaniksu national forests.

incidents.name: Skagit County Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 11, 1919, George Charles, an employee of the Lyman Timber & Lumber Company was struck on the arm by a tree while helping suppress a fire on the company's timber land near Hamilton, east of Sedro-Woolley, Washington. The tree drove Charles' arm violently into his chest. He was taken to the hospital in Sedro-Woolley, where he remained for approximately 24 hours before passing away on the next evening.

incidents.name: Cold Creek Fire Medical Emergency Fatality 1919
incidents.summary: C. Lewis, who had recently come to Montana to assist the U.S. Forest Service in suppressing forest fires died suddenly on the Cold Creek Fire near St. Regis on the Lolo National Forest. Lewis had been working on this fire for a few days when he suffered an apparent heart attack while conversing with the crew foreman. Lewis' full name or any other information regarding his death is not readily available.

incidents.name: Deer Creek Fire Hit by Tree Accidents 1919
incidents.summary: On August 19, 1919: William Johnson was struck and killed by a falling tree on the Deer Creek Fire on the Lewis and Clark National Forest along Deer Creek, a tributary of Sun River in central Montana. It was believed that Johnson died instantly. His injuries were described as two broken thighs and contusions over his head and body. On August 29, 1919: William Smith was hit by a falling lodgepole pine. The tree caused a fracture at the base of Smith's skull. He was unconscious for at least a week afterwards. A local doctor rode five hours on horseback to tend to Smith at the scene of the fire. Smith remained in the hospital for three weeks before he was released--successfully recovering from an injury that had initially been believed to be fatal.

incidents.name: San Dimas Canyon Fire Entrapment Burn Injury
incidents.summary: A firefighter helping suppress a fire located in San Dimas Canyon on the Angeles National Forest, was entrapped and burned. He is quoted in the Ontario Daily Report newspaper: "We were all working like mad and suddenly the flames began to surround us. The other men saw the danger in time and were able to get out without being burned. I was working a little to one side. Before I realized what had happened, the wind sent a tongue of flame behind me and I found myself surrounded. There was nothing for me to do but to make a dash for it."
incidents.quote: At the time (in 1919), 160,000 acres on the Angeles NF had already burned.

incidents.name: Trinity River Firefighter Drowning Fatality
incidents.summary: Paul Regnier drowned while swimming to cool down from several days' work on a forest fire at Taylor Flat (near French Bar by Del Loma) outside of Helena, California. Regnier was one of three surveyors working in this area when the nearby fire was discovered.
incidents.quote: Cramps seized him and he sank. He was 26.

incidents.name: Waptus Trail Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: An Austrian immigrant coal miner whose name is reported as Bles Cheferin was killed by a falling tree on the Waptus Trail Fire on the Wenatchee National Forest in Washington. The tree fell without warning when a group of three firefighters was suppressing a spot fire along the trail. Cheferin suffered severe head and leg injuries. He was carried to the main group of firefighters, and, with their help, down to Roslyn. Cheferin had responded to the Forest Service's call for additional firefighting help issued several days before the accident.

incidents.name: Watson Mountain Fire Hit by Tree Injury
incidents.summary: John Burk, a firefighter with the U.S. Forest Service in Idaho, was hit by a falling tree and injured on the Watson Mountain Fire in the Kaniksu National Forest, near Priest Lake, Washington. The tree strike caused what was described as a "severe scalp wound." Documentation indicates that Burk recovered following treatment at Sacred Heart Hospital in Spokane, Washington.

incidents.name: Cherry Valley Fire Hit By Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Leo McDonald, a 19-year-old logger from Canada, was killed by a falling tree while helping suppress a fire east of Seattle near the town of Stillwater, Washington. McDonald was an employee of the Cherry Valley Lumber Company. He and other company employees had responded to this fire. According to McDonald's death certificate, the falling tree fractured his spine. His death apparently occurred shortly after this tree strike accident.

incidents.name: Verdugo Hills Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Clarence Edwards and Joseph McGahan, plumbers by trade, volunteered to help suppress a rapidly developing brush fire located in the Verdugo Hills in Los Angeles County when they were entrapped and perished. Some time later, their bodies were found by other firefighters. Whether the men were part of a larger crew or were working independently and without direction is unclear from existing reports. Thirty firefighters received minor injuries.
incidents.quote: They attempted to escape by the only remaining route available to them: farther upslope.

incidents.name: Truckee River Fire Hit by Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: Karl Rosel, a Canadian citizen working as a superintendent at a paper mill in Floriston, California, was killed by a falling rock while directing firefighting forces on a fire located along the Truckee River. This unnamed fire ultimately burned 15,000 acres in California and an unknown area in Nevada, as the fire burned directly adjacent to the state border. Rosel was struck on the head by a large rock. His skull was fractured. Soon after, he succumbed to his injuries at the scene of the accident.

incidents.name: Beaver Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Robert "Bud" Clyburn, 22, was killed by a falling snag while working with a crew to suppress a fire on Beaver Creek, a tributary of the Klamath River in far northern California. The snag burned out at the base and fell as Clyburn was improving handline. Clyburn had been working the fire for many hours and fatigue may have been a factor in not identifying the hazard tree. Clyburn's body was carried six miles out on a mule, accompanied by a group of fellow firefighters.

incidents.name: Tangle Blue Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Lyle Ritz, a 25-year-old World War I veteran, was killed by a falling snag while hiking in to suppress a 100-acre fire near Tangle Blue Creek on the Shasta National Forest in California. Ritz was struck by the snag around midnight as he and five other firefighters hiked along a trail toward the fire. Ritz's injuries included a shattered femur and broken back. His companions placed Ritz on a stretcher and began to carry him back toward the nearest road for evacuation to medical care. A few minutes later, while still enroute, Ritz passed away.

incidents.name: Lamb Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: John Gleason and Ole Jackson were killed while assigned to a fire crew on the Lamb Creek Fire on the Kaniksu National Forest, in the Lamb Creek Valley near Priest Lake, Idaho. The men were found more than 24 hours after they went missing on the fire. Two survivors of this same entrapment, Emil Lambert and Luke Krikor, suffered burn injuries and had to walk 18 miles from the fire scene to receive help. Attempts to find relatives of either of these deceased two men were unsuccessful. They were buried next to each other in a Newport, Washington cemetery for poor or unclaimed decedents.
incidents.quote: John Gleason and Ole Jackson were caught in an area of heavy blow-down timber and unable to escape a fire behavior flare-up on the fireline caused by a sudden wind shift.

incidents.name: Siskiyou County Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Two fires burning in the mountains southwest of Yreka, California, merged into one blaze under the influence of strong winds and entrapped two firefighters.
incidents.quote: One firefighter dug out an area to lie in to partially protect himself. He survived the burnover with unspecified burn injuries. The other firefighter was found deceased.

incidents.name: Tehama County Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Llewellyn Foster, a 57-year-old businessman from Red Bluff, California, died suddenly while attempting to suppress a vegetation fire that was threatening ranches in the rural area west of Red Bluff. Foster had joined a group of volunteers assisting in suppressing the fire and protecting ranch houses and buildings. His death was believed to be the result of an existing heart condition.

incidents.name: Laureldale Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Robert "Bliss" Keys and Richard Cornett were part of a 15-person fire crew assigned to the 600-acre Laureldale Fire on the Unaka National Forest in Virginia. Following a sudden increase in fire behaviour the Forest Guard running the crew called to the crew and directed their escape, paying special attention to four 16-year-old boys who carried drinking water for the crew. As Keys and Cornett ran to escape the fire, they were cut off and tried to find another way to safety. Their bodies were found hours later some distance away from where they were last seen alive. The Unaka National Forest was later divided into the Pisgah National Forest (in North Carolina) and the Jefferson National Forest (in Virginia).
incidents.quote: Significant progress had been made on the fire when a sudden wind shift followed by a "whirlwind" (possibly a firewhirl) caused a sudden increase in fire behavior.

incidents.name: Yaksum Canyon Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: When seeing the seemingly controlled fire roaring up the canyon again, Doelle and Coon engaged, evidently with some plan in mind to check its advance.
incidents.quote: This was in a section of grass and greasewood, not timber, that burned like gasoline, fanned by 35-mile winds--so that the men did not have a chance after getting into the path of the fire.

incidents.name: Vernonia Fire Response Railroad Accident
incidents.summary: Logger Robert S. Vetter was traveling to the scene of a fire in a small railroad "speeder" on August 8, 1929, when the speeder collided with a railroad locomotive near Vernonia, Oregon. Vetter received serious injuries and passed away the next day in a Portland hospital.

incidents.name: Dollar Mountain Fire Multiple Incidents 1929
incidents.summary: On August 15, 1929, Vasiliy P. Makeiff (sometimes erroneously recorded as William Mikaryoff), a Doukhobor firefighter, was hit by a tree and received a fatal skull fracture. The injured firefighter was taken to Mt. Carmel Hospital in Colville, where he died from his injuries.
incidents.quote: One of the largest fires of the 1929 fire season, the Dollar Mountain Fire on the Colville National Forest in Washington, was contained at 98,000 acres after burning for a month. Among the firefighters mobilized were 300 Russian-Canadians from a religious group, the Doukhobors. On August 8, 1929, a crew of 65 of these firefighters was entrapped and spent the night in the black before all of them returned safely to camp the next morning. In the vicinity of this entrapment the waterway was named Doukhobor Creek to honor these firefighters. On August 12, strong winds pushed the Dollar Mountain Fire toward two fire camps with 150 personnel each. Both of these fire camps were moved minutes before burnovers occurred. While equipment was lost in both camp burnovers, no injuries or fatalities were reported.

incidents.name: Lake Samish Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Clarence Hutton and Frank Arnold were struck when the top of a snag broke and fell while they helped to suppress the Lake Samish Fire near Bellingham, Washington. This fire had been burning in logging slash on private timber land for multiple days. Hutton received a spinal and leg fracture and was killed instantly. Arnold received deep leg contusions and was hospitalized after a difficult and extended carry-out over slash and downed logs.
incidents.quote: The snag that hit Hutton and Arnold had been identified and was noticed to be burned, but was believed to be sound and capable of standing for some time. Suddenly, on August 13 at 0300 hours, the snag broke 40 feet up and fell and hit these two men.

incidents.name: Camas Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Their bodies were recovered two weeks later between McFarland and Squaw creeks on the Chelan National Forest
incidents.quote: On August 13, 1929, Regional Range Manager Douglas Ingram and firefighter Ernani St. Luise were entrapped and killed on the Camas Creek Fire in Washington.

incidents.name: Canyon Creek Fire Entrapment 1929
incidents.summary: Richard Gell, approximately 60 years old, a Canadian-American World War I veteran, wasmobilized to the Canyon Creek Fire on the Trinity National Forest in California from his homein Eureka. The fire was located near Derrick, California. On August 23, 1929, a burned andunidentifiable body was discovered in the vicinity of Fisher Gulch on Canyon Creek.Employment rolls indicated that only Richard Gell was unaccounted for. At the time of Gell'sdeath, no family members in Canada or the United States could be located. He was buried inWeaverville, California. The Canyon Creek Fire was contained at 1,500 acres.

incidents.name: Camas Creek Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 24, 1929, firefighter John F. Martin collapsed and died while assigned to the Camas Creek Fire. An autopsy determined cause of death was pulmonary infarction during fire suppression duties on the Chelan National Forest.

incidents.name: Lost Horse Fire Drowning Fatality
incidents.summary: Thomas Gorman, a miner living in Butte, Montana, was assigned for 19 days to the Lost Horse Fire on the Bitterroot National Forest south of Hamilton. On August 28, 1929, after the work day ended at 1600 hours, Gorman left camp, likely to bathe in the nearby creek in a swimming hole created by a beaver dam. That is where Gorman's body was discovered. Evidently, he was a victim of accidental drowning. Gorman's body was retrieved with great difficulty and carried by stretcher more than nine miles to a road where it was received by Ranger Shockley in a truck.

incidents.name: Sullivan Creek Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: Paul Croxton and Lester Rudd were assigned to the Sullivan Creek Fire near Spotted Bear on the Flathead National Forest when the fire made a sudden, significant run. An officer with the Flathead National Forest was leading their crew to safety when the men disappeared. The fire run necessitated the evacuation of fire camps. In the ensuing confusion, these two men were unaccounted for. Three weeks later, Rudd's body was located on a gravel bar of the South Fork of the Flathead River. It was determined that he did not die of burns. However, his precise cause of death was not determined and was speculated to be either from exposure or ingestion of superheated gases. Paul Croxton, from media reports published as late as December 1929, had still not been located.

incidents.name: Smith Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Joe Aiken, a U.S. Forest Service employee, was transporting drinking water to a fire crew on the Smith Creek Fire on the Pend Oreille National Forest in Idaho when he stopped to give three firefighters a drink. As he did so, a tree fell and hit Aiken, fracturing his skull. Ninety minutes after this tree strike, Aiken passed away.

incidents.name: Bald Mountain Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: U.S. Forest Service employee Archie White was assigned to the Bald Mountain Fire on Selway National Forest in Idaho when he was struck and killed by a green tree. The tree which fell onto White had broken when struck by another tree which had been undermined by fire. White was struck on the head and died instantly. His body was transported by stretcher 15 miles up the Lochsa River to the Powell Ranger Station. White was also a well-known logger in Western Montana.

incidents.name: Cunha Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On November 3, 1929, William Risdon, a rancher in the Watsonville, California area, died suddenly while assisting with fire suppression efforts. Risdon had joined with other local residents and the fire department in attempting to suppress this fire located on private property on Santa Cruz Road. When Risdon collapsed, two other men attempted to revive him with artificial respiration for one hour and 20 minutes. Ultimately, a doctor at the scene pronounced Risdon deceased.

incidents.name: Cheshire Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On March 24, 1930, 67-year-old John Clancy died suddenly while assisting in fire suppression efforts in the Berkshire Mountains of far western Massachusetts. Clancy was one of 30 men who mobilized and were supervised by the local fire warden to help suppress two grass fires, which, together, added to approximately 25 acres. Around noon that day, Clancy suddenly collapsed on the line. Fellow firefighters attempted to revive him, but were unable to do so. It was believed that Clancy succumbed to heart failure from overexertion. Another man, Frank Hinckley, also suffered an apparent heart attack on this incident and was taken to his home to rest. Initially, he seemed to have recovered. However, six weeks later, he passed away from an unspecified illness.

incidents.name: Waterman Canyon Fire Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: On November 21, 1930, fire motorcycle dispatch rider Charles Davis was killed when he was involved in a motor vehicle accident as he rode from his station in Banning to the Waterman Canyon Fire on the San Bernardino National Forest in California. At the time, the fire was burning over an area larger than 1,000 acres. More than 1,000 firefighters were employed to suppress this fire.

incidents.name: Chico Meadows Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Vernon Fritter, a blacksmith in Stirling City, California, died suddenly while rolling hose after suppressing a small fire in Chico Meadows, just north of Butte Meadows. Fritter, 48, had joined a crew of volunteers supervised by California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) Ranger Lowell Meyers to respond to this small fire in the Sierra foothills. The fire was quickly contained with the use of a CDF fire truck. The crew rested and ate dinner at approximately 2100 hours, then began rolling hose--when Fritter collapsed and passed away. His death was attributed alternatively to a heart attack or to heat illness. Fritter's widow filed a claim with the California Industrial Accident Commission and was awarded more than $1,700.

incidents.name: Blacktail Mountain Lookout Hit by Lightning Fatality
incidents.summary: On June 21, 1931, Glen B. Butler, 23 years old, the lookout at the Blacktail Mountain Lookout on the Pend Oreille National Forest (now included in the the Idaho Panhandle National Forests), was struck and killed by lightning while on duty during a lightning storm. A contemporary newspaper article in the Northern Idaho News reported: "...about 4:30 [he] had called the Sandpoint office and talked to them. He called again about 4:45 and said there was a bad storm brewing and for them not to call him again." Butler's body was discovered the next day by Forest Service officials who had gone to the Lookout to investigate why Butler wasn't answering the telephone.

incidents.name: Deer Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality 1931
incidents.summary: Ignited in late July, the Deer Creek Fire burned a large area from Bonners Ferry, Idaho, northeast into the Yaak Valley of Montana on the Pend Oreille and Kootenai national forests. E. D. Murphy, a smokechaser for the U.S. Forest Service, was killed by a falling snag on the Kingsley Creek area of the Deer Creek Fire. Murphy's death certificate indicates that he died at 0400 hours on July 30 from injuries to his head and chest.
incidents.quote: An account from U.S. Forest Service employee Albert Cramer: "I was called to the Deer Creek Fire north of Bonners Ferry on July 26... I was finally released from this fire on August 15. [One night during this assignment] I fed the entire crew [of 300 firefighters] before dark and put all men back out on the fireline again because it seemed that we were going to have to fight to save our camp. About midnight, a tall white pine snag struck one of my men squarely on the head, bursting his head in two pieces... I pulled the entire crew into camp and told them to hit the hay." When this fire was controlled, it became the largest fire that occurred during the 1931 Idaho-Montana fire season, estimated to be greater than 50,000 acres in size.

incidents.name: Canyon Creek Fire Entrapment 1931
incidents.summary: On August 14, 1931, Vernon Creson, a 34-year old World War I veteran, was helping suppres s the Canyon Creek Fire on the Trinity National Forest in California. Creson observed that the fire was making a crown run. He is reported to have made his way on foot to warn another group of firefighters to retreat to safety. However, before he could reach this crew, Creson was entrapped and killed by the fire.

incidents.name: Coffee Mill Fire Entrapment 1931
incidents.summary: Arnold Love, Frank Smith, and James Whalley, three firefighters employed by the California Division of Forestry (later known as the Department of Forestry and Fire Protection, now CAL FIRE), perished while helping suppress the Coffee Mill Fire on the Stanislaus National Forest in the Sierra Nevada Mountains. Though incorrect or misspelled names of the deceased are commonly associated with this incident, these men are among the first firefighters lost in the line of duty on California's wildland fire protection agency. This fire predates the employment of standing fire crews in California. During this era, temporary laborers paid by the hour as emergency firefighters represented the majority of the state's wildland firefighting force.

incidents.name: Snowbird Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: John Moss, a 64-year-old rancher from Carlin Bay on Coeur d'Alene Lake, Idaho, was killed by a falling tree on the Snowbird Creek Fire on the Coeur d'Alene National Forest. Moss was transported by stretcher from the fireline. Approximately one-half later, he died of his injuries--described in his death certificate as a "crushed chest."

incidents.name: Trinity National Forest Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 22, 1931, firefighters led by District Ranger Wesley Hotaling initial attacked an eight-acre fire on the Trinity National Forest, high on a ridge between Soldier Creek and Dutch Creek. After working several hours, at 10:30 p.m., this group of six were relieved by 14 firefighters and sat down to rest and eat dinner. As they sat, a large tree that had been weakened by fire fell into the group. The tree struck three of the resting firefighters, causing minor injuries to two and major injuries to one of their members, 34-year-old Jess Paige. Paige's leg/hip was severely injured and his skull may have been fractured. He was carried two miles by stretcher to a road, then conveyed to a waiting ambulance in Weaverville, and on to the hospital in Redding. Two days later, this World War I veteran passed away at the hospital.

incidents.name: Bell Springs Fire Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: John Homer, a construction worker in Laytonville, California, was killed in a vehicle accident while positioning his car to assist with fire suppression. Homer and a friend were traveling on Bell Springs Road in rural Mendocino County at night when they were stopped along the road by a fire crew and directed to help fight the fire. While Homer attempted to the turn the car around and park on this narrow road, the car slid off the road on a steep hillside. Homer's companion was able to jump clear, but Homer was killed in the accident. Today, it is not known whether Homer and his companion were driving to the fire area to assist or came upon it by accident.

incidents.name: Waldron Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A crew was suppressing the Waldron Creek Fire on the Lewis and Clark National Forest near Choteau, Montana, when five crew members were entrapped and killed. The crew had been led into a 20-acre spot fire located one-quarter mile from the main fire when the fire began to crown and run in the crew's direction. Five of the crew members separated from the rest and headed in the direction of fire's spread. At the time of this entrapment, fireline supervision was away from the immediate area, attending to other tasks. All five men were later found deceased.
incidents.quote: Those lost on the Waldron Creek Fire: Charles Allen, Ted Bierchen, Hjalmer Gunnarson, Herbert Novotny, and Frank Williamson.

incidents.name: Grimes Pass Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Firefighters Herbert Harvey and Nolan Warner were killed when they became entrapped by fire near Grimes Pass on the Boise National Forest, Idaho. The two men were part of group of six firefighters escaping the fire area in a truck when the group stopped to attempt to extinguish a spot fire. The driver attempted to move the truck to a safe location but found it was impossible and abandoned the vehicle, which burned. While they engaged the spot fire, the main fire they had been escaping threatened to entrap the group. The majority of the crew sought refuge in a clearing while Harvey and Warner attempted to outrun the fire. The fire transitioned into the crowns of the trees and caught the two on a midslope road, where they died instantly.

incidents.name: Fire Lookout Hit by Tree Fatality 1931
incidents.fire: Deer Creek Fire (merged with Keno Mountain fire)
incidents.summary: Anton Obermayer, a 22-year-old fire lookout on the Kootenai National Forest, was killed while attempting to escape the Deer Creek Fire in far northwestern Montana on the night of August 27,1931. The lookout may have estimated the fire to be an imminent danger due to high winds that night, or he may have been directed to leave his station by his supervisors. Obermayer was struck by a falling tree while he hiked to safety. When he failed to rendezvous with other firefighters overnight, a search party was sent out the following morning. His body was discovered under that tree that had been felled by the strong winds.

incidents.name: Skalkaho Fire Hit by Rock
incidents.summary: Vernon "Mickey" West, a longtime timberman in Western Montana, was felling a tree with a companion on the Skalkaho Fire in Montana's Bitterroot National Forest when a large rock struck both men. The rock was released from above when a log burned out and rolled toward the men at a high speed. The other crewmember was able to escape with an injury to his foot. West was hit and died on scene.

incidents.name: Yaak Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: John Patrick, a firefighter from Sandpoint, Idaho, died suddenly while engaged suppressing the Yaak Fire in northwest Montana. Patrick, employed by the U.S. Forest Service, was estimated to be between 50 and 60 years of age. The cause of death was apparently a sudden medical emergency.

incidents.name: McDowell Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 5, 1932, 16-year-old Difford Whisnant and his father who lived in Berlin, Oregon, hiked into a fire in the McDowell Creek area, located a few miles east of Berlin. While approaching the fireline to offer assistance to the firefighters, a feller cut down a tree that resulted in the Difford's death. Some sources indicate that the tree being felled may have struck another tree, which was the tree that ultimately struck the boy. He was reportedly killed instantly from a traumatic head wound.

incidents.name: Matilija Fire Entrapments
incidents.summary: Several entrapments were documented on the Matilija Fire, a fast-moving fire on the Santa Barbara National Forest (renamed Los Padres National Forest in 1936). The attached document summarizes four entrapments. The Matilija Fire went on to burn approximately 220,000 acres. Until 2003's Cedar Fire, the Matilija Fire was the largest fire in California's history. It is now among the 20 largest fires in this state's history.
incidents.quote: "The last group of men had hardly scrambled down the hill to a place of safety when the flames swept over the area where the entire 80 men had been working. Had there been a moment’s further delay every man in that sector would have been trapped and burned to death."

incidents.name: Wilson Road Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: John Guiry, 51, was killed by a falling tree while suppressing a forest fire near Wilson River Road in Washington County, Oregon--in what is now the Tillamook State Forest. While mopping up the fire with the rest of the crew, a burning snag fell and struck Guiry, who was then stuck beneath the tree. After he was successfully extracted, the injured firefighter was carried one mile out to the nearest road. However, Guiry passed away before he reached medical care.

incidents.name: The Tillamook Burn
incidents.summary: In August 1933, a large forested area of northwestern Oregon largely constrained to Tillamook County burned. The fire was the first of the expansive wildland fires located in this area that came to collectively be known as "The Tillamook Burn." The same or adjacent areas burned in subsequent large fires in 1939, 1945 and 1951.
incidents.quote: What was different in 1933 that caused this fire to spread over 360 square miles?

incidents.name: Sheep Creek Fire Exposure Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Sheep Creek Fire, burning in August 1933 in the remote and rugged Belt Mountains near Cascade, Montana, employed CCC crews scattered in wilderness temporary fire camps. Three men embarked on an inspection tour to ensure conditions were satisfactory at these spike camps. The 3 men arrived safely at fire Camp 2. Concerned about the exposed position of Camp 3 and the need to check on the wellbeing of other CCC crewmembers, they decided to push on. Enroute, 2 of the 3 men succumbed to the elements.
incidents.quote: Unnamed individuals urged Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) members to not proceed to Camp 3 as a snow storm was intensifying.

incidents.name: Wilson Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Frank Palmer, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollee in Company 1654, was killed by a falling tree on the Wilson River Fire, more generally known as the "Tillamook Burn." Palmer was reportedly patrolling a fireline at night when a green Douglas fir tree without obvious defect fell without warning and struck Palmer in the chest, killing him instantly. Another firefighter who was with Palmer was also injured in this tree strike, receiving what were described as "severe injuries" to his legs.

incidents.name: Griffith Park Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A group of workers organized squads by a Great Depression-era work program were performing manual labor in Griffith Park in Los Angeles, California. When a fire started nearby, numerous workers attacked the fire with handtools. The wind shifted and forced the workers to retreat, reaching dozens of them before they could escape.
incidents.quote: At first, it looked like a small brush fire and there seemed to be almost unlimited manpower available to put it out. Both workers and foremen figured it would be batted out quickly.

incidents.name: Yellow River Bridge Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: Raymond Jonutz, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollee at Camp Perkinstown in Wisconsin, was killed in a vehicle accident on the way to suppress a forest fire on the Chequamegon National Forest. The vehicle carrying Jonutz overturned on the Yellow River Bridge. No further information is readily available.

incidents.name: Banner Grade Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Three firefighters with the State Emergency Relief Administration's (SERA) camp near Julian, California, were entrapped and perished on a fire east of Julian, California, in San Diego County. These three men, Clarence Harris, John Leapley, and Ambrose Williams, were part of a 25-person crew sent to the fire from their camp. The crew became entrapped in a gulch and hiked downhill along a highway to escape, while Harris, Leapley, and Williams either could not or chose not to follow. Instead, they turned uphill and were caught by the flames racing up the slope.

incidents.name: Margarita Fire Fall Fatality
incidents.summary: Edward Cruse, an enrollee with the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) at Camp Fallbrook in California, was killed in a fall while assigned to the water-carrying crew [carrying drinking water] on the Margarita Fire. The exact location of this fire is unclear, but Cruse is reported to have fallen into Temecula Canyon in San Diego County. This information was taken from the document "CCC Members Lost in Forest Firefighting."

incidents.name: Meadow Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Joseph Howard, a 24-year-old firefighter with the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) was struck and killed by a large cedar tree on the Meadow Creek Fire on the Kootenai National Forest in Montana. Howard was killed instantly when the tree fractured his skull. Another CCC firefighter, George Banks, was also injured (back contusions) by the falling tree. The Meadow Creek Fire was controlled at 2,000 acres.

incidents.name: Trout Creek Fire Vehicle Accidents
incidents.summary: On August 6, 1934, two trucks carrying Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) firefighters overturned in separate accidents on a highway in western Montana, injuring 20. The vehicles were transporting these crews back the Ninemile Remount Depot near Missoula from the Trout Creek Fire when both vehicles rolled over. Sixteen firefighters were injured in one vehicle which rolled over near Thomspon Falls. This vehcile was traveling about 25-30 miles per hour when it missed a sharp turn in the road and rolled over. Four more were injured in an accident close to their destination when a tire blowout caused their truck to veer off the road. This vehicle had been traveling about 25 miles an hour at the time of the accident. In both cases the vehicles were open-backed trucks with bench seats along the sides.

incidents.name: Long Point Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember William Mattison, based at the Tahoe-Ukiah CCC Camp near Nevada City, California, was mobilized with a fire crew to fight a fire near Grizzly Creek in the North Columbia area on the Tahoe National Forest. Mattison and two fellow crewmembers were assigned to watch two cat-faced trees burning on a steep slope 100 feet above Grizzly Creek. At approximately 0230 hours on the morning of August 13, one of the trees broke and fell toward the men. While his two comrades took refuge in the roots of a fallen tree, Mattison was struck. His injuries were determined to be a fractured skull, broken ribs, a broken arm and a broken leg. It is believed that he was killed instantly. Mattison is incorrectly cited as having lost his life on a fire in Idaho, possibly the Pete King Fire.
incidents.quote: One of the trees broke and fell toward the men, who--in the dark--could not judge the direction of the tree's fall,

incidents.name: Bear Springs Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: John Everitt was the Forest Supervisor of the Shasta-Trinity National Forest in California. On the afternoon of August 25, 1934, he left the fire camp on the south end of the Bear Springs Fire to scout the situation. Soon afterward, the fire increased activity on the south end and the fire camp was relocated. Everitt's path was retraced through tracking the following day. He apparently became entrapped by the advancing fire and eventually sought shelter by digging a shallow hole with his hands and lying flat in it. His body was discovered in that shallow hole.
incidents.quote: His loss as a forest supervisor will be keenly felt and his quiet, pleasant personality will be missed by his fellow officers.

incidents.name: Washington Hit by Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 27, 1934, Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember Russel (sometimes spelled Russell) Blakely was hit by a rock while fighting a fire on the Okanogan National Forest, somewhere in the vicinity of Winthrop, Washington. Blakely, who received a fractured skull, was attended to by medical staff from 1400 to 1630 hours, when he was pronounced dead.

incidents.name: Alder Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Walter Kolniak, an 18-year-old Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember, was killed on a fire near Alder Creek in the vicinity of St. Maries, Idaho, at 1500 hours on September 2, 1934. Kolniak's death certificate lists the cause of death as "hemorrhage and internal injuries" resulting from him being struck by a falling tree. No additional information is readily available.

incidents.name: Woodward Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: In the early afternoon of September 4, 1934, William Gillespie was struck and killed by a snag while suppressing the Woodward Creek Fire on the Flathead National Forest in Montana.

incidents.name: Clearwater County Fire Hit by Tree Fatality 1935
incidents.summary: Carl A. Carlson, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember stationed at Camp P-269 near Headquarters, Idaho, on Washington Creek was killed by a falling limb or tree on a wildfire in Clearwater County, Idaho.
incidents.quote: On his death certificate, Carlson is listed as an 18-year-old gardener. However, convincing evidence indicates that he may actually have been 16 years old. On August 9, 1935, a fire was reported in forested land on Scofield and Beaver Creek, burning in timber and slash on lands owned by the lumber company, Potlatch Forests, Inc. A total of approximately 1,000 firefighters were mobilized to fight this fire, which was initially driven by high winds and burned close to 1,000 acres. Carlson was struck by a falling tree or limb and suffered numerous traumatic injuries. These were listed on his death certificate as: "extensive compound skull fracture of both right and left side, broken tibia and fibula above the ankle, and femur fracture." The accident is listed as occurring at 0535 hours on August 11. Carlson reportedly died from to his injuries within the next few hours.

incidents.name: Vader Fire Hit By Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: William Maxwell, an 18-year-old from Chicago, Illinois, employed by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) at the camp near Winlock, Washington, was struck and killed by a large snag while working to suppress a fire in nearby Vader. The fire threatened this small community of Vader. The entire firefighting force of the local CCC camp was mobilized to fight it.

incidents.name: Costa Mesa Hay Fire Hit by Vehicle Fatality 1935
incidents.summary: George W. Wallace, Assistant Forest Ranger with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was pinned between the back of a fire engine and a delivery truck as he studied a map en route to a hay fire. The engine crew was ordered to relieve the firefighters on scene at the hay fire, who had been on the fireline all night. On their way to this incident, Wallace asked the driver to stop and turn on the back flood lights so that he could study the map. At 0315 hours in foggy conditions, as Wallace stood on the road at the back of the engine with the map, a delivery truck struck him. Wallace was taken to the hospital but died very soon afterward. Another firefighter in the engine also suffered minor injuries in this accident.

incidents.name: Chatsworth Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A large group of Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) firefighters were mobilized from their Bass River Camp 225 in Tuckerton, New Jersey to fight a fire in the pine barrens. A firing operation on one portion of fireline experienced a wind shift and entrapped a large group of firefighters who attempted an escape in multiple trucks. While a large group escaped the area, another truck crashed in the heavy smoke from the fire run. This truck's occupants were burned over. Five of these firefighters received severe burn injuries and died either at the scene or shortly thereafter. Eight other firefighters injured in this entrapment were hospitalized.
incidents.quote: Those firefighters who perished on the Chatsworth Fire: three CCC crewmembers, Stanley Carr, John LaSalle, and Edward Sullivan; State Forest Ranger Ira Morey; and Whitesville Fire Department firefighter Kingsley White.

incidents.name: Little Rockies Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Several firefighters, nearly all untrained, were entrapped by a fire run in the Little Rockies area south of Malta, Montana. At the time of the entrapment, 400 firefighters were engaged on this fire, including: residents of Malta, miners from the nearby mines, and 20 geology college students led by Dr. Maxwell Knechtel. The volunteers were placed under the direction of a U.S. Forest Service ranger, James Pewitt. Pewitt was the only trained firefighter leader on this entire fire. It is unclear whether the three were in the cave and left, or were overcome trying to reach the safety of the cave. During this crown run incident, several other firefighters received burn injuries from which they recovered. The coroner's inquest included several witness statements criticizing the lack of adequate supervision and the use of so many untrained firefighters to attempt to suppress this fire.
incidents.quote: When a wind shift caused a sudden crown run between 1200 and 1300 hours, a group of firefighters took refuge in a cave. Firefighters John Roles, Cameron Baker, and Sawyer Brockunier were overcome by the fire and perished.

incidents.name: Black Hills Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Archie Murphy, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crew member based in a camp in the Black Hills near the South Dakota-Wyoming border was killed when he was struck by a falling "jack pine" while assigned to a fire in the Black Hills area. Considering this location, "jack pine" most likely refers to lodgepole pine. Murphy died from his injuries at the Fort Meade Army Hospital near Sturgis, South Dakota.

incidents.name: Three Lakes Fire Hit by Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: Thomas Denehy, an employee of Western Pacific Railroad based in Virgilia, California, was killed by a falling rock while suppressing the Three Lakes Fire on the Plumas National Forest. Denehy had been dispatched with other railroad employees to assist in suppressing this fire located in the Three Lakes area, near Bucks Lake. Denehy was struck in the chest by a rock rolling down a steep slope--that knocked him 200 feet downhill. He was carried out by fellow firefighters to the railroad at Camp Rodgers resort, where he died before medical help could arrive.

incidents.name: Marshfield Forest Fire Response Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Joe French, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollee in Eugene, Oregon, was killed in a vehicle accident while en route to a fire on the Siuslaw National Forest near Coos Bay (known as Marshfield until 1945), Oregon. The truck in which French was riding left the roadway and drove into a canyon. This information was taken from the document "CCC Members Lost in Forest Firefighting."

incidents.name: Roosevelt National Forest Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: G. F. Carmichael [full name unavailable] was a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollee killed by an unknown cause on a fire on the Roosevelt National Forest in Colorado. The specific date of his death in 1937 is also unavailable.
incidents.quote: One of the earliest documented firefighter fatalities in Colorado history.

incidents.name: Welcome Lake Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: A total of 400 Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) firefighters, divided into 15-person crews, were assigned to the 1,200-acre Welcome Lake Fire on the Huron National Forest in Michigan. Andrew Lindgren was a U.S. Forest Service fire foreman assigned to supervise all or a part of this group of firefighters. When the fire crowned in a pine plantation, Lindgren pulled his crew back to a safe location. Lindgren was ensuring that all of his crewmembers were out of danger when he was caught by the fire and perished. A Forest Service inquiry into his death indicated that Lindgren was missing for approximately 15 minutes before his body was found. During this same incident, another of the CCC crewmembers, 22-year-old John Latuszick [spelling possibly incorrect], received second degree burns, but survived.

incidents.name: Shasta National Forest Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: Albert Bomer was killed by a falling tree on a forest fire on the Shasta National Forest, sometime in mid-August of 1937. He was a member of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) stationed at Camp Leaf in Siskiyou County south of MacDoel. Very few details of his death are readily available. Considering the fire activity in Northern California in 1937, he was likely killed on a small initial-attack fire. According to media reports, Bomer suffered a skull fracture and other injuries from the accident.

incidents.name: Blackwater Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Lightning ignited the Blackwater Fire on August 18, though it was not detected until August 20. At detection, the fire was two acres in size at the bottom of the drainage. By late August 20, the fire had grown to 200 acres, and was staffed with Civilian Conservation Corps firefighters and overhead. Work continued on August 21, when fire behavior increased dramatically with the passage of a cold front over the area.
incidents.quote: The Blackwater Fire was the first fatality fire to have significant investigation and study of the event done immediately after the tragedy. This analysis of the fire eventually led to the development of the smokejumper program, a management action to address the time-delay problems encountered for crews responding to the fire.

incidents.name: Ruth Lake CCC Truck Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: An 18-year old California Conservation Corps crewmember crew carrier in the Ruth Lake area, returning to fire camp, when a 32" diameter, 100-foot tall green Douglas-fir tree fell from the roadside and struck the vehicle where he was sitting. Despite rescue efforts, he could not be extricated before he succumbed. The CCC crew had been engaged in firefighting efforts on the Six Rivers National Forest. Nine others in the truck were injured in the tree strike.
incidents.quote: It was believed the tree's roots had been compromised by fire, as the tree did not appear to have any obvious defects which was cause it to fall.

incidents.name: Maple Meadows Fire Hit by Limb Fatality
incidents.summary: Charles Kiser, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember based at Camp Raleigh in Beckley, West Virginia, was killed when he was struck by a limb from a burning tree on the Maple Meadows Fire. Kiser was part of an 18-member crew on the fireline. On the night of April 16, 1938, each member was assigned to hold a portion of line. Kiser went into the green to suppress a slopover when a limb fell out of a tree and struck him, fracturing his skull and breaking his neck. Kiser was taken to the hospital where he succumbed to his injuries two days later. A foreman blamed the accident on "overzealousness."

incidents.name: Shawme State Forest Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Buzzards Bay Deputy Fire Chief Clarence Gibbs, along with volunteer firefighters Thomas Adams, Ervin Draber, Henry Jarvis and Gordon King were entrapped while suppressing a fire at Shawme State Forest near Sandwich, Massachusetts. The fire may have been caused by a group of government workers burning brush to clear an area near a military reservation in the area. Alternatively it is reported as an arson fire. Ultimately the fire that caught the men may have been a backfire that turned into a head fire when the wind direction shifted.

incidents.name: Swamp Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: The Swamp Creek Fire was started by lightning early on the morning of July 16, 1938 east of Lake Koocanusa on the Kootenai National Forest in an area burned in the Northern Rockies Fires of 1910. Initial attack by Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crews contained the fire within handlines, but high winds repeatedly caused the fire to escape those lines. On July 18, John B. Jones, a CCC crewmember based at Camp F-52 near Thompson Falls, was killed when he was struck by a falling snag. The snag caused a fatal skull fracture. Jones' body was carried out from this remote location by fellow crewmembers and a pack mule.
incidents.quote: According to the Independent Ledger newspaper of July 20, 1938: "In many places the fallen timber is piled as high as a man's head."

incidents.name: Pepper Hill Fatality Fire
incidents.summary: Firefighters from the Hunts Run Civilian Conservation Corps Camp near Emporium, Pennsylvania, responded on the afternoon of October 19, 1938 to a reported fire on Pepper Hill Mountain. After initial work of line construction and firing, a crew was ordered to the top of the fire to begin line construction there. While making their way there, a previously undetected fire run caught nine members of the crew, killed seven and injuring one.
incidents.quote: The fire, under a shifting wind, swept across in rear of his party, then up the right flank, trapping the entire party.

incidents.name: San Diego Crew Vehicle Rollover Fatalities
incidents.summary: Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmembers Bruce Allen, 17, and Oral LeRoy Bruner, 19, were killed when the U.S. Forest Service vehicle in which they were riding overturned in Harbison Canyon, San Diego County. The driver and two other occupants were thrown clear of the rolling vehicle and escaped major injury. Media reports describe the truck's front wheels as having "locked up" on a sharp turn, and the vehicle rolling over, coming to rest upside down. It is possible that the men were traveling to a 30-acre fire that was burning in the Alpine Heights area on the Cleveland National Forest.

incidents.name: Smith River Falls Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Hugh McCutcheon, a worker at the Works Progress Administration's (WPA) Westlake camp, was killed by a falling tree on the morning of April 10, 1939, just below Smith River Falls, upriver from Reedsport, Oregon. The tree pinned McCutcheon to the ground. He passed away before being taken to the hospital.

incidents.name: Salmon National Forest Lightning Strike Fatality
incidents.summary: Forestry Foreman Clarence Schultz from Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) Camp Cove Creek was killed by lightning while returning from an initial attack fire with two other CCC firefighters. The men had suppressed the fire and were hiking back to their camp on the banks of the Middle Fork Salmon River. All three firefighters were struck by lightning, although two of the men quickly recovered. These two men, identified as Lawrence and Morris, split duties: Lawrence stayed with Schultz while Morris traveled cross-country for five miles to get help. Schultz, who succumbed to his injuries, was noted as being an employee of the Salmon National Forest since 1925.

incidents.name: Black Hills Fire Hit by Lightning Fatality
incidents.summary: Civilian Conservation Camp (CCC) crewmember Ervin Voegle from Camp F-14 near Custer, South Dakota, was killed when he was struck by lightning while patrolling a fire near Pactola, west of Rapid City. When the storms first started, three firefighters including Voegle sought shelter from the rain. Lightning struck Voegle, only feet from the others. Fellow crewmember Austin Rollag administered artificial respiration immediately but was unsuccessful in reviving Voegle. The other crewmember, Alvin Schneider, ran down the fireline for help.

incidents.name: Rock Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: On July 28, 1939, flames overran crewmen from Paradise Camp F-5, Company 1212, a Civilian Conservation Corp Firefighting Crew, as they retreated from a fire in steep rugged terrain on the Toiyabe National Forest and Winnemucca District-Division of Grazing lands. The fire occurred in Northern Nevada near the small community of Orovada.
incidents.quote: The crew divided into two squads. One squad made their approach to the fire from the north and the other squad made their approach from the west. As the squads closed in on the fire, a sudden violent shift of the winds caused an extreme downhill run toward the squad hiking in from the west. Within minutes the flames raced down the slopes and drainages engulfing five firefighters as they attempted to escape to safety.

incidents.name: Willard Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: John Gulock, a 59-year-old logger from Portland, died suddenly at fire camp while waiting in the pay line on the Willard Fire, Columbia National Forest, near White Salmon, Washington. Gulock's cause of death was listed as "Apoplexy." In 1949, the Columbia National Forest was re-designated to the Gifford Pinchot National Forest.

incidents.name: Camp Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Anthony "Tony" Kukowsky, a Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember from Camp Riggins, was killed during suppression actions on a fire located on Idaho State lands near Knox, Idaho. According to media reports, Kukowsky was struck by a falling snag on the night of August 31 on the 700-acre Camp Creek Fire. He suffered a skull fracture and was being transported tot he hospital when we succumbed to his injuries the following day. The site of the accident was 6 or 7 miles from the nearest road.

incidents.name: Silver Plume Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Paris was mobilized with a CCC handcrew from the camp at Tularosa to attack this fire. He was with three fellow crewmembers involved in suppressing spot fires when the fire ran towards them. An alternate account blames a firing operation on their entrapment. While Paris' three companions were able to escape, Paris became cut off and perished. Newspaper accounts note that the Tularosa CCC camp was under the control of the U. S. Grazing Service. The Grazing Service was combined with the General Land Office in 1946 to form the Bureau of Land Management. Other official documents reference this fatality incident as a case of a firefighter sleeping near the line. No other documentation substantiating this is readily available.
incidents.quote: Jay Vaughn Paris, an 18-year-old Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crewmember, was entrapped and killed on a 300-acre Silver Plume Fire on the Lincoln National Forest, New Mexico

incidents.name: Chipmunk Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) enrollee James Hester was killed by a falling snag on the 2,600-acre Chipmunk Creek Fire on the south side of Yellowstone Lake inside Yellowstone National Park. Hester was based at CCC Camp YNP-1 at Mammoth near the Park's northern boundary. After he was struck by the snag, Hester was transported by boat to the lake's north end, where a road follows the lakeshore. From there he was transported by motor vehicle, but died before reaching Mammoth Hospital.

incidents.name: Cub Point Aircraft Accident 1940
incidents.summary: Pilot Robert Maricich, the Missoula Manager of Northwest Airlines, was killed in a plane crash near Cub Point, Idaho, 25 air miles west of Darby, Montana. Maricich was flying a supply mission for the U.S. Forest Service when it is believed his Travel Air S-6000 was caught in a downdraft and forced down. The other occupant of the plane, Dell Clabaugh, tasked with dropping cargo, was injured in the crash. The Cub Mountain Lookout, Harry Nielsen, witnessed the cargo drop, heard the plane crash and immediately called the accident into the Hamilton Office of the Bitterroot National Forest by telephone. Nielsen then left his Lookout to hike to the scene and administer first aid.
incidents.quote: A rescue plane responded to the scene and a rescue jump was performed by smokejumper pioneer Chester "Chet" Derry. Nielsen, Derry, and a mule train with packer Alvin Renshaw assisted to carry the injured air crewman Clabaugh by make-shift stretcher--made from saplings and canvas--for 20 miles to an emergency landing strip. He was then picked up by an aircraft and flown to Missoula, where he was treated at St. Patrick's Hospital.

incidents.name: Bear Creek Fire Hit by Limb Fatality
incidents.summary: William DeAvilla, a fire crew leader on the Klamath National Forest, was fatally injured on the Bear Creek Fire when a large limb from a lightning‑struck tree fell and hit him while he and two firefighters were attempting to fell the burning tree. Despite a shouted warning, DeAvilla was unable to move clear and was struck on the back of the head, prompting one firefighter to stay with him while another hiked several miles to summon help. An ambulance and a crew of loggers organized by the forest headquarters transported him four miles by stretcher to the nearest road, after which he was taken to a hospital in Yreka. He survived long enough to undergo surgery but passed away roughly 24 hours later at 1950 hours the following day.

incidents.name: Lowden Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) Camp Foreman Arthur Bowman of Cascade Locks Camp (F-7) was killed by a falling snag on a small fire located near the camp. Bowman and Wesley Thurner, a U.S. Forest Service employee working on the Mount Hood National Forest, traveled to the small fire near Lowden Road, west of Larch Mountain. At the fire, they intended to fell this lightning-struck, burning snag. In the process of falling the snag, a piece of the tree fell, striking Bowman on the head and killing him instantly. Thurner was uninjured.

incidents.name: Double Springs Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Oza "Ozie" Moody and George Dyer were riding in the back of a vehicle en route to a fire near Double Springs, Arkansas. As they approached the fire area, a tree fell across the car, injuring both men critically. They were taken to Haleyville, where Moody succumbed to his injuries. It is not clear if the tree felling operation was associated with the fire or was an unrelated logging operation.

incidents.name: Yreka Highway Fire Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Joseph Pryatel, a Foreman with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) in Yreka, was killed in a vehicle accident on scene of a fire that was located on the side of the highway. Pryatel and his crew were called to suppress this wildland fire which started from a vehicle fire on the highway. When their equipment, parked on the highway, was struck by a motorist, four firefighters were injured. Pryatel, who received the most significant injuries, was taken to a hospital in Yreka where he passed away the following morning at 0300 hours.
incidents.quote: Their equipment was struck while parked on the highway and four firefighters were injured.

incidents.name: Tar Gap Fire Exposure Fatality
incidents.summary: Frank Riley was a firefighter with Sequoia National Park at its Ash Mountain Headquarters. This Ash Mountain Fire Crew was dispatched to a fire above Mineral King at Tar Gap. Riley became separated from the crew and could not be found. Several days later, his body was discovered. He was believed to have died of exposure. Riley was a World War I veteran who had joined the veterans' branch of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) until it disbanded. He then joined the Sequoia National Park fire program.

incidents.name: Dutchtown Road Fire Entrapment Fatalities 1943
incidents.summary: Four firefighters on a New Jersey state fire engine were entrapped and burned on a forest fire near Hammonton, New Jersey on March 26, 1943. All four of the burned firefighters were taken to the hospital in Atlantic City and passed away during the following days. One engine crew member survived without injury. Those four firefighters lost on the Hammonton Fire: William Hoover, Alfred Ingersoll, and brothers Carl Luderitz, who was 16 years old, and Ralph Luderitz, who 17 years old.

incidents.name: Lonoak Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: When Morton became separated from the rest of the crew he was surrounded by fire in a sudden wind shift in the flashy fuels. He was taken from the scene of the accident to the hospital in King City, where he passed away the following day. During this period, due to severe workforce shortages caused by World War II, very young people were used in the wildland firefighting service. Morton was assigned to the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) station at Bitterwater.
incidents.quote: Ralph Morton, a 14-year-old high school student from Pacific Grove, California, was part of a crew sent to suppress a grass and brush fire in Monterey County where he was entrapped and suffered fatal burn injuries.

incidents.name: Somersville Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: In the early morning of August 22, 1943, Emile Corsi, one of 150 volunteer and professional firefighters mobilized to suppress the Somersville Fire in Contra Costa County, California, died when he was entrapped and burned. The fire was discovered at 1900 hours and burned through rolling hills of tall, dry grass and chaparral brush. Corsi, a ranch employee, worked to suppress the fire with a backpack pump until a wind shift swept the flames over him.
incidents.quote: He could not escape in time and his cotton clothing caught fire.

incidents.name: Hauser Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A sudden change in wind direction caused the fire to race across the low, flat ridge near the mouth of the gulch, jump the gulch and ignite the brush and grass on the oposite side. This closed the avenue of escape down the gulch for many of the men working above. With the brust aflame on both sides of the constructed line, and burning rapidly up the slope, their bast chance of survival was to take shelter among large boulders in the bottom of the gultch. This most of them did, under the instructions of Forest Officers. A few men escaped over the ridge through the fire to the road, but were badly burned in doing so.
incidents.quote: After the fire had passed it was determined that three men had perished and seventy others were burned, some seriously. Four more succumed to critical burn injuries the following day.

incidents.name: Cave Junction Smokejumper Aircraft Accident Fatality 1944
incidents.summary: Frederick "Fred" Frank, a co-owner and pilot for S and M Flying Service, operated a Fairchild 71 aircraft for U.S. Forest Service smokejumpers in Cave Junction, Oregon. On August 2, 1944, Frank took off with a load of four smokejumpers when the aircraft's engine died immediately after takeoff. Frank safely landed the aircraft on the remaining runway and performed inspections and maintenance on the aircraft's engine. Later that day, Frank attempted a test flight, solo, in the aircraft. At an altitude of only 300 feet, the plane lost power once again, stalled, and crashed. Fred Frank perished in the accident.

incidents.name: Scoggins Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Joe Dillich, a firefighter in Western Oregon, was killed by a falling tree on the Scoggins Creek Fire, part of the great Tillamook Burn of 1945. Dillich was working with an engine to check the fire. He felled a hemlock tree, which fell in an unexpected direction and hit Dillich, killing him.

incidents.name: Wilson River Fire Vehicle Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: Two U.S. Army soldiers, Jesse L. Thompson and Lester A. Ware, were killed and four others were hospitalized when their transport truck rolled over on a curve along the Columbia River Highway (Highway 30) near Westport, Oregon. The truck was part of a convoy of 500 soldier-firefighters mobilized to the suppress the Wilson River Fire, which was part of the 1945 Tillamook Burn. The truck was carrying soldiers of the all-African American 2822 Engineer General Service Regiment from Fort Lewis near Tacoma, Washington.

incidents.name: Williams Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Edward Gates, Dozer Operator for the Los Padres National Forest, and Paul Nesgis Assistant State Forest Ranger with the California Department of Forestry (Now CAL FIRE), were entrapped while suppressing a fire on Williams Hill in Monterey County, California. Nesgis was supervising the construction of dozer line by Gates and other dozers. At approximately 1600 hours, these two men were caught in a box canyon on the flank of Williams Hill. Gates abandoned his machine to attempt to escape on foot--but was overtaken by fire in the dense chaparral. After the fire was contained, Nesgis was reported as missing. His absence prompted a statewide search.
incidents.quote: It wasn't until March the next year that Nesgis' body was finally found on the side of Williams Hill, just outside the burned area.

incidents.name: Clear Creek Fire Hit By Tree Fatalities
incidents.summary: A group of four firefighters had stopped to rest in the early morning of September 15 when a tree outside of the fireline, rotten at the base, fell and struck the group. Graham and Lucas were killed instantly. Lucas was described as a logger and former longtime Forest Service employee who had been on every local fire since 1930. On the Clear Creek Fire, Lucas was directing the construction of dozer lines. Graham was 19 years old and working the fire under Lucas' supervision as a dozer operator.
incidents.quote: Lawrence Graham and Charles Lucas, US Forest Service firefighters, were both killed when they were struck by a 30-inch diameter green fir tree on the Clear Creek Fire, Plumas National Forest, near Keddie, California.

incidents.name: Los Berros Fire Engine Rollover Fatality
incidents.summary: Edward Ordner, a firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was killed when the vehicle he was driving--described as a "hose truck"--left the roadway and rolled over. Ordner was assigned to a fire in the Los Berros Canyon area in San Luis Obispo County that was initially reported at 1315 hours on September 16. Ordner's fatal vehicle accident occurred at 2000 hours the next day. Another firefighter on the truck, riding in the open cab, was able to jump away from the vehicle as it went off the road.

incidents.name: Leopold Grass Fire Medical
incidents.summary: Aldo Leopold is recognized as a pioneer in wildlife management, wilderness, and convervation in the United States. Leopold served in the newly established US Forest Service in Arizona and New Mexico. His essay "Good Oak" served as inspiration for the Wildland Fire Histomap and we seek to honor his legacy of service to others and the land. Like the rings of Leopold's "Good Oak", this project stands as a testament to our own history. Much of it forgotten, silent, lost to time. But as with a tree, when the rings are exposed to examination by human eyes…your eyes…we can remember. And unlike a tree standing silent witness, we can remember loudly as we learn and apply the lessons of our past.
incidents.quote: Aldo Leopold experienced a heart attack and died on April 21, 1948 while fighting a neighbor’s grass fire that escaped and threatened the Leopold farm and surrounding properties.

incidents.name: Barrett Dam Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Duane Poore, a 17-year-old member of the Del Rosa Hotshots, was entrapped and perished while the crew was assigned to the Barrett Dam Fire on the Cleveland National Forest in Southern California. Poore was one of 13 Del Rosa Hotshots along with fire overhead and an engine that were sent from the San Bernardino National Forest to fight this fire on their nearby Forest. He was last seen Friday, July 10. A search found him two days later. It appears that Poore had been entrapped and tried to use a large rock as a place of refuge.

incidents.name: Wisconsin DNR Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (DNR) Equipment Operator Walter Norton died in a vehicle accident while responding to a five-acre fire. Walter was driving to the scene hauling equipment when the trailer hitch broke, causing the trailer to crash into the truck. The truck went off the road and rolled over, resulting in Walter's death. The other firefighter in the vehicle survived the crash.
incidents.quote: Vehicle accidents are the most common cause of death for wildland firefighters

incidents.name: Sawyer Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Late on the evening of August 4, 1949, Lloyd Francis "Frank" Moore, 19, was critically injured when he was struck by a falling snag on the Sawyer Creek Fire, Lolo National Forest, northeast of Seeley Lake, Montana. The incident was investigated by Regional Safety Officer Clyde Bake who determined that Moore was struck by a dead lodgepole pine, 65 feet tall and 11 inches in diameter at the base. Moore passed away shortly after this tree strike.
incidents.quote: He was the youngest brother of Powell District Ranger William "Bud" Moore, who later became Director of Fire and Aviation for the Northern Region (Region 1) of the U.S. Forest Service.

incidents.name: Mann Gulch Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Mann Gulch Fire was discovered in a remote canyon of the Helena National Forest. A Forest Service Fire Guard began initial attack of the fire while 15 smokejumpers parachuted into the area. While headed downhill towards the Missouri River, spot fires emerged below them, cutting off their route to the river. Smokejumper Foreman Robert Wagner "Wag" Dodge successfully set a fire with matches to create an area of black to survive the entrapment. The remainder of the firefighters tried to outrun the fire on foot; two firefighters crested the ridge and took refuge in a rock scree on the lee side, surviving. The other 12 smokejumpers and fire guard perished in the fire or soon afterward from serious burns.
incidents.quote: Wildland firefighters on the Helena National Forest fought more than 57 wildfires during the summer of 1949. But only one of these fires, the thirteenth of the season as luck would have it, would become seared into the collective memory of Forest Service firefighters everywhere.

incidents.name: St Joe National Forest Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Elmer Marks, a U.S. Forest Service employee, was struck and killed by a burning cedar tree while fighting a fire on the St. Joe National Forest in northern Idaho.

incidents.name: Bear Creek Fire Hit by Rock
incidents.summary: A 19-year-old firefighter was injured by a rolling rock while assigned to the Bear Creek Fire on the Payette National Forest near the mouth of Bear Creek, 25 air miles east of Riggins, Idaho. Due to the remote and roadless nature of the injury site, an aircraft dropped an inflatable raft to float the injured man down the Salmon River to a location where he could be transported by automobile. He was taken to the hospital in McCall, Idaho, and recovered from his injuries.

incidents.name: Atlas Peak Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Ernest "Ernie" Covington, a foreman for the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), suffered a fatal medical emergency while supervising firefighters on the Atlas Peak Fire, Napa County, California. Crewmembers on scene attempted to revive Covington as they waited for a doctor and ambulance on the side of the road. However, their attempts were unsuccessful.

incidents.name: Walton Spur Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: Two incidents occurred on the Walton Spur Fire on the Stanislaus National Forest, California, that resulted in fatalities. The fire, also called the Jawbone Fire, eventually burned approximately 7,000 acres.
incidents.quote: One fire fighter was killed by a falling snag. One fire fighter was injured by limbs from the falling tree. One fire fighter died from burn injuries after being entrapped in a gully.

incidents.name: Butte Ranger Unit Engine Accident
