incidents.summary: On October 19, 1949, a CDF fire engine experienced rear axle failure and overturned near Bangor, California, killing three firefighters and injuring a fourth.

incidents.name: Stable Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A wildfire fire started at noon on January 17, 1950 on Camp Carson in Colorado. Within 90 minutes, 20 buildings at the north end of the base were ablaze. The worst wildfire in El Paso County’s history claimed nine lives, injured 50 and destroyed 89 buildings worth more than $5 million at the post.
incidents.quote: Fanned by 50-70 mph winds, the fire rapidly burned a 50-square-mile area.

incidents.name: Las Pilitas Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Three were soldiers with the 60th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Battalion from Fort Ord. Part of a force of more than 100 sent to the fire to assist in suppression, they were were identified as John Smith and Laurence Morris. The third soldier may have been Turley McFarland. The other firefighter who lost his life on this entrapment incident was Gerald "Jerry" O'Reilly, employed with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE). Two days later, rains helped to control the fire, which burned approximately 28,000 acres.
incidents.quote: A crew of 20 men were entrapped between the main fire and a firing operation on the Las Pilitas Fire in San Luis Obispo County, California. Four of these men were unable to escape and received fatal injuries.

incidents.name: Lynx Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Edward Archer was killed by a falling tree while suppressing the Lynx Creek Fire on the Bridger National Forest, Wyoming. Archer, a sawmill operator in the area, came to assist with fire operations on this 60-acre fire. While working with a handcrew, a large piece of a tree fell and hit Archer. He was transported to the road by stretcher then driven to the hospital in Afton, where he was pronounced dead on arrival.

incidents.name: Tillamook Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Carlton "Carl" Gerard was found deceased in a roadside ditch along the Old Toll Road in Tillamook County, Oregon, on the first day of fire suppression on a fire in the state's Tillamook Forest area. The location and position of the body indicated that Gerard was entrapped in a fire run and sought refuge in the roadside ditch. In its first burning period, the fire ran at least five miles. Gerard worked in a sawmill for the Trask Lumber Company

incidents.name: Santa Rosa Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Larry Higgins, a firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), was entrapped and fatally burned on the Santa Rosa Fire near Lake Elsinore. Higgins was on one of the first engines to arrive at the fire. He was in the process of advancing a hoselay when a fire whirl or flareup entrapped him. Higgins, 21-years-old, had joined the state fire agency in April 1952 and was stationed at the Elsinore Fire Station.

incidents.name: Shanti Ashrama Fire Engine Entrapment
incidents.summary: Four California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) firefighters were entrapped and suffered burn injuries. A total of 325 firefighters, including two California Youth Authority handcrews, 15 engines, eight dozers, and tankers contained the fire at 7,000 acres that night. Two of the burned firefighters were admitted in critical condition to the hospital in Livermore, while the other two were treated and released.

incidents.name: Santiago Peak Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) firefighter James Heniser was entrapped and fatally burned while working to suppress a fire on Santiago Peak in Orange County, California on August 25, 1952. Heniser and three others were suddenly surrounded by flames in excess of 6 feet, and Heniser was overcome by smoke or hot gases. He collapsed in an area that was inaccessible due to extreme heat. The three other firefighters reportedly escaped and were hospitalized for heat illness.

incidents.name: Deacon Creek Fire Multiple Incidents
incidents.summary: Tom Hutchins collapsed and died of an apparent heart attack on October 29, 1952, while helping suppress a forest fire on Deacon Creek on the Cherokee National Forest, Tennessee. Hutchins was one of many firefighters on this incident that included: U.S. Forest Service employees, National Guard, and students from the University of Tennessee. A group of four firefighters were entrapped for five hours on this Deacon Creek Fire. Two of the men, local loggers, were admitted to Erwin Hospital for treatment of minor burns and exhaustion.

incidents.name: Crane Mountain Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Virgil Eastman, the District Ranger of the Bigfork Ranger District, Flathead National Forest, Montana, was struck by a falling tree while supervising slash burning. Eastman was struck by snag in a timber harvest unit near Crane Mountain. Another U.S. Forest Service employee was reportedly hit by the same tree, but was not seriously injured.

incidents.name: Santa Barbara County Grass Fire Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: District Fire Warden William Marxmiller, who supervised the county fire station in Goleta, was critically injured when his vehicle went down a 120-foot embankment off of Highway 101. He was taken to Santa Barbara Hospital where he passed away the following day.

incidents.name: Tulare Unit Dispatch Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Herbert Segress, a long-time employee of the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), died suddenly on the evening of June 20, 1953 of an apparent heart attack. Segress was a Dispatcher at the Tulare Ranger Unit Dispatch Office in Visalia. At approximately 2030 hours during his shift, he was asked to take a rest break. He went to the attached barracks to rest. A few minutes later, he was found there, deceased. Segress, 57, had previously been an Engine Operator and Crew Foremen in Porterville, California. He was a veteran of World War I.

incidents.name: Los Padres National Forest Food Poisoning Fatality
incidents.summary: Casique and two other firefighters were taken from camp to the hospital in Santa Maria, California, to treat a sudden-onset illness. Casique passed away in the hospital, while his two colleagues recovered. Casique was one of 125 Bracero Program firefighters assigned to fight fire east of Santa Maria, California, on the Los Padres National Forest. In response to this food poisoning incident, the U.S. Forest Service Regional Office ordered all cans of chicken removed from firefighter rations in the Region. A shipment of serum for treating botulism was also sent to the hospital in Santa Maria to treat any additional food poisoning cases.
incidents.quote: Antonio Alavos Casique, a Michoacan, Mexico, resident enrolled in the Bracero Program to work temporarily in the United States, was sickened and passed away from apparent food poisoning from canned food at fire camp.

incidents.name: Talbot Park Fire Engine Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: As they approached an intersection, a passenger vehicle attempted to cross the intersection and collided with the engine. The engine lost control after the accident and traveled about 90 feet before hitting a utility pole, breaking it off at the ground, and stopped in a roadside ditch. Firefighter Ray Meyer was pronounced dead at the scene of the accident, while Fred Mahoney was critically injured and succumbed in the hospital hours later. Another firefighter also suffered serious injuries but survived, while the remaining four firefighters suffered minor injuries. A child in the passenger vehicle was killed, and additional four occupants were injured.
incidents.quote: An engine traveled at a high rate of speed towards a reported vegetation fire.

incidents.name: Twombley Road Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Corydon "Corey" Goodwin of the Springdale Fire Department was entrapped in his fire engine and perished during initial attack of the Twombley Road Fire in Sanford, Maine. High winds created a high rate of spread as the fire burned through the Maine woods. Reports indicate that Goodwin may have had trouble starting the vehicle as the fire advanced on his location and, ultimately, he could not escape before becoming entrapped. Goodwin may be the first firefighter to perish on a wildland fire in the state of Maine.

incidents.name: Spotted Bear Smokejumper Aircraft Accident
incidents.summary: On August 17, 1953, a Ford Trimotor aircraft with eight aboard crashed near the Spotted Bear Airstrip in Northwest Montana, injuring four. The aircraft was loaded with six Smokejumpers dispatched from Missoula to jump fires on the Flathead National Forest. When high winds prevented safe jumping operations, the plane had landed at Spotted Bear Airstrip. On taking off to return to Missoula, the plane lost power in the left engine and went down. The pilot and three of the Smokejumpers were injured. A rescue plane was sent from Missoula to render first aid to them and fly them back to Missoula. None of the four were seriously injured.

incidents.name: Sugar Loaf Fire Heavy Equipment Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Foster Vernon, a longtime heavy equipment operator for the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), was killed when his dozer rolled over. Another state dozer had reportedly experienced some kind of mechanical failure of the dozer's track while constructing fireline on the Sugar Loaf Fire the previous day. In an effort to tow the machine uphill to where it could be repaired, Vernon's dozer rolled over. Consequently, both dozers rolled over multiple times.

incidents.name: Tunnel No. 6 Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The Tunnel No. 6 Fire was ignited by mine workers with an acetylene torch at the Sierra Buttes Mine above Sierra City, California. Frank Burr, Richard Fierro, and Mel Grodzik were members of the Downieville Forestry Honor Camp Fire Crew assigned to suppress the Tunnel No. 6 Fire. They were caught--and perished--in a steep canyon high in the Sierra Buttes when a wind shift caused the fire to escape its lines and overran them. Their crew totaled 32 firefighters. Two other men with these three who perished were able to escape to the top of the ridge and into the safety of an open area.

incidents.name: Craven County Fire Heavy Equipment Fatality
incidents.summary: James Kennedy, an equipment operator for the North Carolina Department of Conservation's Forestry Division, was killed while constructing tractor-plow line on a forest fire near Cove City in Craven County. The tractor was progressing forward when it struck a tree or stump and threw Kennedy forward into the tractor's brush guards. A few minutes later, he died of his injuries. Soon after Kennedy's body was moved, the fire burned over the area, destroying the tractor.

incidents.name: Seneca Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On September 4, 1955, a fire run trapped several firefighting resources on the Seneca Fire, Malheur National Forest, near John Day, Oregon. In heavy smoke, one man, Elwood Jackson, became separated from his seven-person crew and lost his life in the entrapment. Another firefighter was severely burned. Two bulldozers, whose operators escaped on foot, were damaged by fire. The other firefighters in the area escaped to a bare knoll and waited as the fire subsided around them.

incidents.name: Round Butte Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Wesley Weston, a 41-year-old logger from Bly, Oregon, was entrapped and killed while working on the Round Butte Fire. Weston drove into the fire area with a group of other firefighters who lost sight of him in dense smoke. A search found Weston deceased in the burned area, apparently from suffocation during an entrapment.

incidents.name: City Creek Fire Hit By Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: Herbert Botella, a 29-year-old member of the Red Hats Mescalero Apache wildland fire crew, was killed by a boulder that struck him while assigned to a fire on the San Bernardino National Forest, California. Botella and four crewmates had taken a break to eat just after midnight when someone above them on a steep slope gave a "ROCK!" warning shout. The five firefighters below dispersed to escape, but in the darkness could not see the rolling rock's path. The four-foot diameter rock hit Botella on the head.

incidents.name: La Tuna Canyon Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On November 6, 1955 at 1400, Los Angeles Fire Department Auto Fireman James L. Catlow with E39 responded with the company to Underhill and Verdugo Fire Road to suppress the developing La Tuna Canyon Fire. Hoselays were installed, and conditions were favorable to suppress the fire. A terrain-driven wind hit the La Tuna fire and caused it to increase in speed and intensity. Catlow stayed at the pump through multiple pulses of fire that enveloped him . On November 12, he succumbed to the 3rd degree burns he suffered on November 6.
incidents.quote: The La Tuna Fire increased in intensity and the firefighters on the road could not escape. James L. Catlow ran to the engine's pump controls to ensure water supply to the hoses was kept up, as that was the only protection the other firefighters had.

incidents.name: Coconino National Forest Fire Hit by Tree Fatality 1956
incidents.summary: Allen S. Wilson, Jr., a Coconino National Forest firefighter based in Happy Jack, Arizona, was killed when a burning snag broke and hit him while he was suppressing the Turkey Pen Fire southeast of Flagstaff. According to accounts, he was supervising the falling of this snag when it broke and hit another tree--and subsequently struck him. He lost his footing while trying to escape. Wilson had recently come to the Coconino NF. He had previously been a smokejumper at Idaho City.

incidents.name: Martin Creek Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Gary Fellbaum, a 19-year-old firefighter for the U.S. Forest Service, was killed by a falling snag on the Martin Creek Fire. This 30-acre fire on the Cabinet National Forest in Northern Idaho was in the mop-up phase. Fellbaum had observed the snag and was discussing it with the crew foreman. As Fellbaum turned to walk away, the tree broke and fell, hitting him on the head and back. A crew of eight smokejumpers were ordered to assist. They dropped into the fire to construct a helispot to medevac Fellbaum. Once the helispot was constructed, Fellbaum was flown to a hospital in Sandpoint, Idaho, where he was pronounced dead.

incidents.name: East Highlands Fire Entrapment Fatality 1956
incidents.summary: Eight firefighters were burned, one fatally, in several incidents on the East Highlands Fire in the mountains north of San Bernardino, California. After 2200 on November 19, 1956, two contract dozers were constructing line at the head of Orange Street, west of City Creek Road, when a sudden wind shift entrapped the two dozers and their U.S. Forest Service work leader. One operator and the Forest Service employee received first-degree burns. Edwin Bass was severely burned as he exited his dozer to escape on foot. Bass was taken to the St. Bernadine Hospital where he passed away at 0220 the next day. The other two men took refuge behind a dozer to shield them from the flames.

incidents.name: Inaja Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Inaja Fire was started by a child playing with matches. The fire had burned under Stana Ana wind conditions to 25,000 acres. In the evening, a fire crew was assigned to construct indirect handline into the San Diego River canyon, from the rim to the dry riverbed. A piece of dozer line above the canyon was fired out before line construction commenced into the canyon itself. During line construction, a spot fire was observed about 1000 feet below the crew.
incidents.quote: The wind shifted to blow the spot fires upslope at the retreating crew.

incidents.name: Eight Mile Ridge Fire Smokejumper Aircraft Accident Fatalities 1958
incidents.summary: While on a cargo mission to supply tools and equipment to the Eight Mile Ridge Fire on the Okanogan National Forest, Washington, a smokejumper aircraft crashed in the mountainous terrain north of Winthrop. It was surmised that the aircraft flew into a downdraft from thunderstorms over the fire area, after which the pilot attempted evasive action to escape the downdraft and subsequently lost control. Those who perished in the Eight Mile Ridge Fire aircraft accident: Robert Carlman, Bob Cavanaugh, Keith Hendrickson, and Gerald Helmer.

incidents.name: San Bernardino National Forest Hit by Lightning
incidents.summary: San Bernardino National Forest Fire Control Officers Dennis Brayton and Donald Wests were struck by lightning while on patrol near Running Springs, California. The two were enroute to a lightning-caused fire located four miles east of Green Valley Lake. They had just left their pickup truck and were proceeding on foot when lightning struck approximately 25 feet from them. Both men were thrown to the ground. Brayton recovered and attempted artificial respiration on West before radioing for help. West was transported to the hospital in nearby Lake Arrowhead, where he was pronounced dead.

incidents.name: Silverado Fire Aerial Supervision Fixed Wing Fatalities Crash
incidents.summary: William Archibald and Carl Milligan, pilots who flew both aerial supervision and retardant-dropping missions, were killed when their Beechcraft Bonanza crashed in mountainous terrain near a 100-acre fire in Silverado Canyon, Cleveland National Forest in Southern California. As they circled the fire, the plane appeared to fly into the smoke column and crash into a cliff face at 1230 (controlled flight into terrain). Inflight structural failure has also been cited as the cause of this accident. Both pilots were killed instantly.

incidents.name: Steward Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On December 14, 1958, a large fire in the Santa Ana Mountains of Southern California led to the entrapment death of US Forest Service Ranger Joe Edward Adam. Adam was from the Prescott National Forest, working at the time on fires on the Cleveland National Forest. The circumstances surrounding Adam's death are not readily available. The Steward Fire went on to burn over 68,000 acres.

incidents.name: San Luis Obispo Ranger Unit Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Leo Boyd, a foreman for the San Luis Obispo Ranger Unit of California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was critically burned when his engine stalled in dry grass on a wildland fire near Paso Robles. When Boyd jumped from the back of the stalled vehicle, his clothes caught fire as the fire reached the engine.
incidents.quote: Fire-resistant clothing was not yet available to firefighting agencies; cotton clothing was worn by wildland firefighters.

incidents.name: Dry Creek Fire Entrapment Fatality 1959
incidents.summary: On July 12, 1959, a handcrew was engaged in line construction on the Dry Fire on the Sequoia National Forest, California. James Bastady and another firefighter were sent to replenish drinking water for their crew while they constructed handline in hot weather. At 1230 hours, the fire made another run while the two men returned with water and hiked along an adjacent ridge toward the rest of the crew. The fire crossed below these men, who were walking through the green to rejoin the crew. Warnings shouted by the crew were not heard until it was too late for the men to reach the black. They took refuge in a group of large rocks where they were entrapped by the fire for approximately 10 minutes and received burn injuries. Both men were evacuated by helicopter and taken to hospitals. Bastady was eventually admitted to the U.S. Public Health Hospital in San Francisco, where, five days later, he perished from his injuries.
incidents.quote: If we had had a weather report we would have known that the down canyon winds would start that early in the day. - Statement by the Crew Boss

incidents.name: Decker Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Decker Fire started from a vehicle accident that killed a civilian motorist and injured another. An engine crew responding to the fire was caught in a flare-up, with 6 firefighters receiving burns. Shortly after this, a hand crew in an open-backed truck was impacted by a large firewhirl, burning 3 firefighters, one very seriously. Elsewhere, the hotshot crew was constructing fireline downhill, until fire behavior prompted them to come back up to the road and fire out the area instead, with the intention of connecting the firing operation to black from a fire that had occurred weeks earlier.
incidents.quote: All burned firefighters from the three entrapments were brought to hospitals, where in the coming weeks, 6 perished from their injuries

incidents.name: Woodwardia Fire Retardant Drop Fatality
incidents.summary: Leo Pablano, a firefighter with the Zuni Nation from New Mexico, was assigned to fight the Woodwardia Fire, near Duarte, on the Angeles National Forest, California. On October 16, Pablano suffered a major head injury and passed away at the hospital in Pasadena. Contemporary accounts vary as to whether he received his head injury while trying to escape a drop from a retardant aircraft, or whether the drop itself caused fatal injuries.

incidents.name: Cummings Creek Entrapment Fatality 1960
incidents.summary: Raymond Pike, a Washington logger serving with the Walla Walla penitentiary fire crew was critically burned at approximately 1600 on July 23, 1960, while assigned to the Cummings Creek Fire, Umatilla National Forest, Washington. Pike was suppressing a spot fire outside the line in a strong wind when his injuries were received. Pike was unable to escape the sudden flareup of fire behavior. His injuries were described as third-degree burns over his entire body. Forty-five hours after he was entrapped, Pike died of his injuries at Pomeroy Hospital on July 25.

incidents.name: Crooked Creek Fire Burn Injury Fatality
incidents.summary: ames Spencer Jr. was flown to the hospital in Pomeroy, Washington for treatment of extensive third-degree burns. Spencer, assigned to the Crooked Creek Fire on the Umatilla National Forest, was burned at approximately 1100 on July 24. He passed away that night at 2215. The circumstances under which he received the burns are not available.

incidents.name: Woods Ridge Fire Hit by Tree Limb Fatality
incidents.summary: Rodger McLean, a 26-year-old firefighter with the Stanislaus National Forest, was killed by a falling limb on the Woods Ridge Fire, northeast of Groveland, California, near Cherry Lake. Thunderstorms ignited numerous storms in the surrounding area. While McLean was suppressing the small fire, lightning again struck a tree in the fire area, causing a limb to fall and hit his head.

incidents.name: Tonto National Forest Aviation Accidents
incidents.summary: On June 15, TBM Avenger Tanker Pilot Charles Cochrane was killed when his aircraft crashed into a ridge at approximately 1900 hours in the fire area. Cochrane was flying the converted WWII torpedo bomber from the "Borate City" tanker base for Sonora Flying Service. On June 21, two aerial supervision aircraft, a Cessna 180 and a Beechcraft T-34, collided in midair over a fire on the Tonto National Forest. Pilot Art Goodnow and Forest Service Fire Control Aid Constantine Kodz were killed when their Cessna 180 crashed after this midair collision occurred. The T-34 was able to return to Payson and landed safely.
incidents.quote: Two aviation accidents occurred over fires on the Tonto National Forest, Arizona in a one-week span starting June 15, 1961, resulting in three fatalities.

incidents.name: Ball Mountain Helicopter Crash Fatalities
incidents.summary: Pilot Robert Gilbreath, Deputy District Ranger Samuel Ready, and Fire Control Officer Harold Barnes were killed when the helicopter they were riding in crashed near Ball Mountain on the Sequoia National Forest. The three men had taken off from Kennedy Meadows on a fire detection flight over the Inyo and Sequoia national forests. The Bell 47 helicopter crashed in the High Sierra by Ball Mountain, killing all three occupants. The crash location was not found until four days later, on July 5.

incidents.name: Cochran Gulch Fire Smokejumper Accident Fatality 1961
incidents.summary: Dale Swedeen, Missoula Smokejumper, broke his back when he oscillated into a rock on his first fire jump on the Cochran Gulch Fire, Helena National Forest, Montana, July 8, 1961. The accident rendered him a paraplegic, and he died 31 years later of complications from that accident, at the age of 53.

incidents.name: Sleeping Child Fire Medical Emergency Fatalities
incidents.summary: John Roberts died of an apparent heart attack before reaching the fireline on August 8, 1961. Max Moffett, a 19-year-old firefighter, was found dead in his sleeping bag on August 11, at the Moose Meadows Fire Camp. LaVerne Clifford, Crew Leader, died of an unspecified illness on August 13 while traveling home on a U.S. Forest Service-chartered aircraft.
incidents.quote: Three fatalities were reported on the 26,000-acre Sleeping Child Fire on the Bitterroot National Forest in southwestern Montana. Limited information is readily available on any of these three firefighters who succumbed to medical emergencies.

incidents.name: Silver Creek Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Albert Klingshirn and Louis Watkins were entrapped by fire and passed away during a "blow up" of the Silver Creek Fire, Nez Perce National Forest, near Grangeville, Idaho. The fire made a wind-driven run and increased from 200 to 600 acres, trapping the men on the night of August 30. A third firefighter escaped but received third-degree burns.

incidents.name: Central Pacific Mine Fire Airtanker Accident 1961
incidents.summary: Waldo Hackman, a pilot for P&B Aviation Service, perished when his TBM Avenger single-engine air tanker crashed during retardant operations on the Central Pacific Mine Fire near Forbestown, California. After dropping 180 gallons of retardant ("borate") on the 1,400-acre fire on Robinson Mill Road, the Avenger crashed while attempting to climb over a ridgeline.

incidents.name: Los Posadas Fire Station Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Harry Eitzen, Jr., a 19-year-old college student at the University of California, Berkeley, and a firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was critically burned in a station accident at the Los Posadas Fire Station near Angwin. Eitzen kicked an unburnt rag into the burning pile of rags. The rag ignited instantly and stuck to Eitzen's boot. Reacting in surprise, he accidentally bumped into a container of gasoline that was nearby. An immediate flashfire resulted and Eitzen was engulfed in flames. Firefighter Carl Vogt immediately called for help and attempted to aid Eitzen, himself receiving burns to his hands. Other firefighters used their engine's pump to spray a fog pattern of water and suppress the fire. Eitzen was burned over more than 50 percent of his body. He was taken to the hospital in an ambulance where, at 0630 the following morning, he succumbed to his injuries.
incidents.quote: On the afternoon of September 23, 1961, firefighters were disposing of oil-soaked rags by burning them in a pile outside.

incidents.name: Sierra Madre Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Mike Rushworth, an 18-year-old member of the Dalton Hotshots, was entrapped by a sudden flareup during initial attack of a brush fire near Sierra Madre in Los Angeles County, California. Rushworth was burned over half of his body in varying degrees of severity and remained in the hospital until December 8, 1961, when he passed away.

incidents.name: Timberlodge Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On August 2, 1962, a fire ignited near Midpines, California. An initial attack response involved several fire engines and heavy equipment who arrived at a road junction to begin fire suppression. As line construction began, a spot fire on the east side of a road was observed, followed by a wind shift and a significant head-fire run. Other accounts point to a low-flying B-17 airtanker creating air vortices that may have fanned this flareup. A Sierra National Forest engine crew from the Forest's Jerseydale Fire Station, first in line in attacking the fire, was entrapped by the fire. Four of the firefighters perished; two crewmembers survived with burn injuries.
incidents.quote: Those firefighters lost on the Timberlodge Fire: Thomas Foley, Mario "Martin" Giorgi, John Vaun Rasch, and Raymond St. Pierre.

incidents.name: Mendocino National Forest Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Coleman, a U.S. Forest Service seasonal employee, was engaged in cutting down a burning tree when he was struck by the snag (whether it was the tree he was cutting is not known). The tree strike severely injured both legs. Coleman remained in place while his fellow firefighters treated him for an hour as they attempted to draw the attention of another group of firefighters with a radio. When the injury was reported via radio, a Los Padres National Forest helicopter assigned to the Mendocino National Forest brought a doctor to the area and dropped a chainsaw to the firefighters on the ground. A small helispot was cut and the doctor was flown in, though the spot was not big enough to completely land. Coleman was packaged and flown out to Corning Memorial Hospital, where it landed at 1650. Time since the injury first occurred was more than six hours. Coleman was rushed to surgery, where--after numerous successful resuscitations--he passed away at 0435, Saturday, July 29.
incidents.quote: John Coleman, a 20-year-old college student from Chico, California, was fatally injured by a falling snag while assigned to a lightning fire on the Mendocino National Forest located 20 miles northwest of Paskenta.

incidents.name: Wiggletail Fire Air Tanker Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: Robert Savaria, pilot and owner of a P-61 Black Widow air tanker registered N30020, was killed instantly while maneuvering to drop retardant on the Wiggletail Fire, Tule Indian Reservation, California. Savaria was piloting one of five tankers dropping retardant on this 600-acre grass and brush fire. His twin engine plane was loaded with 1,600 gallons of retardant. Witnesses on the ground reported that his plane hit a ridgetop above Gibbon Creek and subsequently crashed to the bottom of the canyon.

incidents.name: Tuolumne County Heavy Equipment Operator Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: A grass fire in Tuolumne County near Groveland, California entrapped heavy equipment operator James Carlisle with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE). Carlisle, based in Groveland, responded to the fire and was constructing line with other dozers when the fire ran toward his location. Carlisle abandoned his machine to escape on foot. He had run approximately 200 yards when he was overtaken by the running grassfire. Another dozer operator came to Carlisle's aid, constructing a line around his location, while other firefighters provided first aid. The helicopter at Bald Mountain Helibase on the Stanislaus National Forest flew to the fire with a doctor to treat the severely-burned Carlisle enroute to the hospital in Sonora. After 10 days in the hospital with burns over most of his body, Carlisle succumbed to his injuries on July 2, 1964.
incidents.quote: The fire burned almost 2,000 acres, driven by erratic high winds, before it was controlled in 8 hours.

incidents.name: Washington Helicopter Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: Pilot Allen K. Platt was killed when his Bell 47 helicopter, supporting several fires in the area of Chelan, Washington, crashed as a result of a suspected downdraft. Very little additional information is readily available.

incidents.name: Tulare Unit Dispatch Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Edward McKinney, 44, a fire dispatcher at the Tulare Ranger Unit office in Visalia for the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), suffered a heart attack on duty. McKinney passed away at the hospital. He was a 12-year veteran of CDF.

incidents.name: Sleepy Hollow Fire Engine Collision with Train Fatality
incidents.summary: Richard Krejci, a firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was killed when the engine he was riding enroute to a house fire with vegetation threat in the Sleepy Hollow area near Chino, struck a passing freight train. The engine, an open-backed, two-axle truck, was responding with red lights and siren on Etiwanda Avenue when it skidded and struck the train. The rear of the engine broadsided a freight car, throwing Krejci from the back of the vehicle, killing him. The other occupants of the engine were injured.

incidents.name: Fairview Hollow Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: The ranger and four crewmembers had completed about 200 yards of hand line when they heard a loud roar from below. The ranger assumed the noise was from the fire making a run at them from below. The ranger who was firing the handline behind the squad, yelled for the firefighters to run to safety. The ranger ran south, across the head of the adjacent hollow. Three crewmembers ran down into the hollow, where the fire overran them, all three died. The fourth crewmember ran back uphill into the backfired area, suffering only minor burns.
incidents.quote: The fire danger was rated as "moderately low".

incidents.name: Copernicus Peak Lookout Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Wanda Woods, the fire lookout at Copernicus Peak on the Santa Clara Ranger Unit of the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE), passed away of an apparent heart attack in her lookout station while on duty on the night of October 6, 1965. At 1900, Woods had called to the CDF Smith Creek Fire Station, seven miles away, indicating that she was experiencing chest pains and would radio if they got worse. Later that evening, radio calls to Woods from the Ranger at Smith Creek went unanswered. Therefore, a telescope engineer from the nearby Lick Observatory was asked to check on her. She was found unresponsive on her bed in the lookout. While Eva Schicke is recognized as the first female firefighter in CDF/CAL FIRE service to lose her life in the line of duty on the 2004 Tuolumne Fire, Wanda Woods is the first recorded female employee of the California state fire service to pass away on duty, according to the California Fire Foundation's Memorial database.

incidents.name: Alaska Smokejumper Practice Jump Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Davis was in his second season with the Alaska Smokejumpers, engaging in practice training with other returning smokejumpers. During that practice jump, jumpers were exiting the Douglas DC-3 in three-person groups or "sticks" and attempting to land in a 20-acre clearing on the University of Alaska Experimental Farm. The three jumpers in Davis' stick all landed in trees, with Davis far away from the others. The two others in Davis' stick freed their parachutes and the rest of the planeload of smokejumpers landed around the jump spot. Still Davis was not seen or heard from. His fellow smokejumpers assumed he was in a tree and freeing himself and his parachute. Eventually alarm was raised at Davis' continued absence, and he was located hanging in a tree. Davis was cut down and attempts at resuscitation were made but were unsuccessful. It was determined that during his letdown procedures from the tree, a line of his parachute was looped under his helmet, and he strangled to death.
incidents.quote: Arden Davis, Jr., a smokejumper based in Fairbanks, Alaska, was killed by strangulation in a practice jump near College, Alaska.

incidents.name: Loop Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: In a canyon near the boundary of the Angeles National Forest, a flareup on the Loop Fire overran the El Cariso Hot Shot Crew.
incidents.quote: The direction of fire spread changed, and it swept up a chimney canyon, entrapping and burning over the crew.

incidents.name: Camp Pendleton Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Five U.S. Marines were entrapped and perished in a 4,000-acre fire at Camp Pendleton nearOceanside, California the day after the fatal Loop Fire in Los Angeles County. The Marineswere on a ridge overlooking Piedra de Lumbre Canyon when the fire outflanked them andtrapped them. Four of the Marines either were discovered already dead or perished shortlyafterward, while another, Henry Terrazas, was taken to the military hospital with burns over85-90 percent of his body. Terrazas died in the hospital the following day. Those lost on this fire at Camp Pendleton: Lewis Connor, Leslie Hendrix, Cecil Henshew,Henry Terrazas, and Rodger Zarbok.

incidents.name: Siskiyou Smokejumper Project Work Drowning Fatality
incidents.summary: Three smokejumpers from the base at Cave Junction, Oregon, jumped into a remote site on the Siskiyou National Forest to construct a helispot. Their packout hike required a crossing of the Illinois River to the River Trail. A smokejumper swam across the river with a rope tied around his waist that was meant to be used to tow a raft with gear across the river. The selected crossing area was calm, but became more rapid just downstream. As he approached the far side of the river, he drifted downstream into faster water and was quickly pulled further downstream.
incidents.quote: The other two smokejumpers attempted to keep him from being swept away by pulling on the rope, but eventually determined that letting go of the rope was Smith's only chance of getting out of the water.

incidents.name: Slaughter Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Rolfe Hoyer, employee of the Apache National Forest in southeastern Arizona, was entrapped and killed on the Slaughter Fire. Details of the Hoyer's death may be somewhat unreliable. He was reported to have been the recreation and lands officer on the Apache NF, and was acting as Fire Boss (IC) when the fire grew in intensity when it reached pre-commercial thinning slash. Hoyer then tried to outrun the fire, and reportedly could not hear warnings shouted to him by firefighters on a nearby road.

incidents.name: Sundance Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Sundance fire, burning in timber, advanced 16 miles in 9 hours and created spot fires 10 to 12 miles northeast of the fire origin . Rodarte and Collins were considered to be safe in their pre-planned safety zone.
incidents.quote: Rodarte and Collins were found under the bulldozer. It is not known if they sought shelter there or were pinned there.

incidents.name: Bailiff Fire Fall Fatality
incidents.summary: The Bailiff fire had begun in a house near Cabazon in Riverside Co. Santa Anas were blowing and 24,000 acres burned in 36 hours. The Baliff Fire flared up at night on a steep slope. Fellow firefighters last saw Rios poised on a big rock near Cabazon shortly before a sudden wind whistled down the eastern slope of Mt San Jacinto sent them scurrying from an advancing wall of flame. An autopsy showed Rios had suffered a fractured skull and was burned to death. He added that preliminary reports indicated Rios may have fallen while trying to escape a flare-up.

incidents.name: Liebre Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On June 21, 1968, Fire Captain Phil Goodell, 47 years old, of the Los Angeles County Fire Department was assigned to the Liebre Fire burning in the Castaic area of Los Angeles County, California. When flames overran Engine 382 on a power-line access road, the crew took shelter beneath the apparatus. Captain Goodell stood between them and the advancing fire, courageously operating a hose line in an effort to shield them. He was ultimately overtaken by the flames and suffered fatal burn injuries. Captain Goodell gave his life to protect his crew, who sustained burns but survived. Goodell succumbed to his injuries at the USC Medical Center on June 24.
incidents.quote: Captain Goodell gave his life to protect his crew, who sustained burns but survived.

incidents.name: Ainscough Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: John Irving Worley, a heavy equipment operator for Santa Barbara County stationed at Buellton was entrapped and severely injured while operating a bulldozer on the Ainscough Fire near Los Alamos, August 17, 1968. It was reported that Worley was one of 45 men entrapped, with two others receiving burn injuries. Worley jumped from his dozer during the entrapment, and broke both legs, possibly when the uncontrolled bulldozer ran them over. He was severely burned and spent 10 days in the burn unit of Los Angeles County General Hospital until he succumbed to his injuries on August 27. During his stay at LA General a constant vigil was kept by members of LA County Fire Department. The Ainscough Fire burned a total of about 700 acres on the west side of Highway 101 north of Los Alamos.

incidents.name: Canyon Inn Fire Entrapment 1968
incidents.summary: The Canyon Inn Fire (also called Canyon Fire) started on August 23, 1968 under Santa Ana wind conditions in the mountains adjacent to Azusa, California. The fire burned rapidly, including onto the Angeles National Forest. The following day, the juvenile firefighters of Los Angeles County Crew 4-4 were deploying a hoselay when they were overrun by fire and perished. These eight crewmembers of Crew 4-4 lost on the Canyon Fire: Gregory Banks, Duane Battle, Larry Carlin, Arthur Mendible, Robert Rivera, William Rodriguez, George Thomas, and Earl Walzer.

incidents.name: Tehama County Fire Engine Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Gerald Davis, a 17-year-old student seasonal firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (now CAL FIRE) was killed when the engine on which he was riding rolled over into a creek when a culvert collapsed. The engine crew had been fighting fires all week in the Sierra Nevada foothills following a lightning bust that ignited 600 fires. While returning from checking fires in eastern Tehama County, the 8-ton, 1963 Chevy fire engine rolled upside down into a dry creek bed when the culvert on Carpenter Ridge Road on which they were traveling collapsed under them. Davis was seat-belted into the vehicle, but was crushed underneath it. An 18-year-old firefighter was also injured, while the 17-year-old driver and the foremen were uninjured in the accident.

incidents.name: Melendy Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: At approximately 1315 hours on August 1, 1970, while engaged in suppressing the Melendy Fire in San Benito County as a member of the Hollister Forest Fire Station crew, Forest Firefighter Arthur D. McMillan, aged 17, suffered serious burns. He was flown by a U. S. Forest Service helicopter to the Hazel Hawkins Hospital at Hollister, California, where McMillan was diagnosed with second-degree burns on his hands, arms, shoulders, face and legs. He was transferred to hospital in Monterey where he was treated and expected to recover without disability.
incidents.quote: Realizing that the grassy patch would burn immediately, he selected an area where the flames seemed relatively low and attempted to jump through the flames into the burned area where, he felt, he would be safe.

incidents.name: Laguna Fire Analysis
incidents.summary: The Laguna occurred on September 26, 1970 on the Descanso District of the Cleveland National Forest. The report encompasses the events prior to the fire, suppression action on the fire, costs, major control and organizational problems. It is hoped that this Fire Analysis will improve future fire control management and to train personnel in practical management of the overall fire control job--with specific emphasis on planning and the performance required to prevent fires from becoming large.
incidents.quote: This is a detailed analysis of the Laguna Fire which was caused by powerlines downed by an oak tree that had fallen during extreme Santa Ana winds. The powerline caused several fires to start simultaneously along an east facing slope.

incidents.name: Sand Hill Fire Dozer Transport Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: Cecil Griggs, Monroe Wilkes and Otis Wilkes were killed when they were crushed in a dozer transport following a vehicle accident responding to a wildfire in the Sand Hill area of Chesterfield County, South Carolina. The three men, identified as South Carolina Forestry Commission forest rangers, were transporting the dozer on a lowboy trailer on a forest road when the vehicle slid into the ditch. In the accident, the chains holding the dozer to the trailer broke and the machine toppled into the cab, killing the men.

incidents.name: Mack 2 Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On September 19, 1971, Vista Grande Tanker Crew Foreman, Robert Miller was fatality burned while trying to escape a flare-up. Vista Grande Tanker Crewman Ronald Courts sustained minor smoke inhalation.
incidents.quote: Miller almost made it to safety. His surviving colleague reached the highway 3-5 seconds eariler.

incidents.name: Secret Mountain Fire Aircraft Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: Pilot Harold D. Slay of Wright Flyte Service and Coconino National Forest, Flagstaff District Ranger Rollo Julander were killed in an aircraft accident while observing the Secret Mountain Fire (also recorded as the Slide Fire) near Sedona, Arizona. At 1410 the aircraft struck trees and crashed, resulted in fatal injuries to both occupants. The NTSB final report summary indicates there was no engine malfunction, but does not give a cause for the accident.

incidents.name: Romero Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: During an extended shift on October 7, a team of dozers constructed indirect line in preparation for firing operations. During the transition to night shift, downslope winds fanned the flame front into a firestorm that overtook six firefighters.
incidents.quote: The lead cat stopped and weathered the fire storm. The second cat tried to dig in and was not successful. The ground was too hard and the firebreak too narrow. All on the second cat died. All on the lead cat survived, but were badly burned.

incidents.name: Bear Fire Helicopter Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: On August 26, 1972, a Bell 205 A-1 carrying a load of firefighers to the Hines Peak helispot on the Bear Fire crashed, killing a total of six people. Though exact details of the accident aren't readily available, it is reported that the helicopter with two pilots and nine firefighters suffered a compressor stall in its single engine resulting in a loss of power and subsequently crashed into a steep canyon wall at approximately 1441 hrs. Those lost in the Bear Fire helicopter crash were: George Z. Aguilar, Jr., Jesus Irigoyen Corral, Ramon Guizar, Filomeno Romero, and James Ronald “Donaldson” Runningdeer. All were firefighters mobilized from the Sacramento River Valley in Yuba County, possibly through the Mendocino National Forest. The pilot, also lost in the accident, was Earl L. Lady with Evergreen Helicopters based in Oregon.

incidents.name: Bell Valley Fire Burn Injury Fatality
incidents.summary: On Saturday, August 11, 1973 at approximately 1635 hours, while engaged in fire control activity on the Bell Valley Fire, California Department of Forestry Firefighter Steve Hark Arrollado received third degree burns over approximately 40 percent of his body and second degree burns over 20 percent of his body. Thirteen days later, as a result of these burn injuries, Firefighter Arrollado died.
incidents.quote: With the public address system on the truck Linton ordered Arrollado "Get out of there, come to the truck."

incidents.name: Tuolumne Unit Helicopter Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: The mission of the helicopter was to patrol powerlines, and upon completion of this task, the aircraft was returning to Columbia airport. On board, a CDF fire prevention officer spotted a brush fire, one of several fires ignited in the region on that day. He requested to be dropped off at the site of the fire. In either attempting to land or in taking off again, the helicopter struck electrical wires and crashed. The CDF prevention officer and another CDF employee were injured in the accident. Helicopter pilot Dick Rodgers and firefighter Lynn R. Douglas were killed.

incidents.name: Lost Hills Fire Medical Fatality
incidents.summary: Thomas Rugan Cotter, a battalion chief with Kern County Fire Department in California, suffered a fatal heart attack while on scene of a range fire in the Lost Hills area of Kern County. Further information regarding the fire and the death of Cotter is not readily available.

incidents.name: Decker Fire Hit by Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: Wellesley "Wes" Hartman was killed by a rock while suppressing the Decker Fire near Lake Sherwood in Ventura County, California. Hartman was a firefighter was Los Angeles County Fire and took part in the initial attack of the brush fire that ultimately burned 145 acres. Hartman was killed when he was struck on the head by a rock dislodged from a bulldozer working in steep terrain about him and other firefighters.

incidents.name: Nevada Bell 206 Crash
incidents.summary: At approximately 1005 hours on July 5, 1976, on the King Fire on Bureau of Land Management lands south of Carson City, Nevada, a Bell 206 helicopter was shuttling four firefighters into a mountain top helispot. This was the seventh flight of the day flown by this pilot into the same location. Approximately one-half mile north of the landing site, the aircraft went into a very tight spiraling turn to the pilot's left, spun two or three times, and crashed into the ground. The pilot, James Davidson with Arizona Helicopters, and two of the passengers, John Ivins and Ken Carvin, both Nevada Division of Forestry firefighters, were killed. The two surviving passengers received serious injuries.
incidents.quote: The remaining passenger could remember nothing except the scream of a girl and a feeling of falling.

incidents.name: Battlement Creek Fatality Fire
incidents.summary: The Battlement Creek Fire was estimated to have started July 11, 1976 on BLM lands in Western Colorado. Hotshots arrived on the fire on July 16 and began a firing operation that continued the following day. The Mormon Lake Hotshot crew was assigned to line improvement and firing on the ridgeline while another crew fired on a different part of the fire in the draw below them. The line construction squad of the Mormon Lake crew relocated down the ridgeline to the safety zone as the flame front from the other firing operation neared the top of the ridge, but the firing squad of 4 crewmembers was cut off from the safety zone. The firing squad turned and attempted to follow the ridgeline back uphill, where they became entrapped. Three perished while the fourth suffered severe burn injuries. The Mormon Lake crew was wearing fire-resistant shirts, non-fire-resistant work pants, aluminum cap-style hard hats, and canvas cruiser vests that they wet down and draped over their heads.
incidents.quote: The Battlement Creek Fire resulted in some substantial changes in federal wildland fire management. This incident was the catalyst for the mandatory use of fire shelters and fire resistant clothing. It also demonstrated the need for closer interagency coordination between federal, state, and local wildland fire agencies.

incidents.name: La Mesa Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: The La Mesa Fire had started west of the park on June 16, crossed through the park, and continued onto the lands of Los Alamos National Laboratory. According to the National Park Service, Aldaz collapsed after running to the NPS engine during an evacuation triggered by a sudden increase in fire behavior during a firing operation on Highway 4. Aldaz was taken by a coworker to the park entrance to meet an ambulance, but perished there.
incidents.quote: Bandelier National Monument trail maintenance employee Juan "Johnny" Aldaz perished from a heart attack on the La Mesa Fire in the Ponderosa Campground area.

incidents.name: Cart Creek Fire
incidents.summary: On July 16, 1977, three US Forest Service firefighters were entrapped and killed when a sudden wind shift drove an intense headfire over three handcrew squads. The fire overran and killed three U.S. Forest Service personnel: Gene Campbell, age 57, Forestry Technician; David Noel, age 36, Youth Conservation Corps Camp Director; and Forestry Aid Dwight Hodgkinson, age 23.
incidents.quote: At about 1455 the fire suddenly intensified, changed direction, and drove forward in an intense headfire toward three squads building firelines. The fatalities occurred in two separate accidents within a few seconds after the change in fire intensity.

incidents.name: Bass River Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: A fire started around 1500 hours; this was in an area that had a history of large, fast moving wildfires. Nine units responded and disengaged at 1545 hrs. A brush truck with four people aboard responded to the incident after being called at 1600 hrs. It is not clear why, but this unit mistakenly proceeded into the fire area. At 1800 hrs, a reconnaissance helicopter spotted the charred truck on a narrow, dirt road.
incidents.quote: It is not clear why, but this unit mistakenly proceeded into the fire area.

incidents.name: Honda Canyon Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: This fire provided for the first and only Department of Defense hotshot crew being established in 1981. While this fire was not the specific reason for the adoption of national standards regarding training, physical fitness, Red Card qualifications, nomex use and fire shelter use; it is one in a string of multi-fatality fires that occurred across the country in the late 1970s that drove home the need for such standards.
incidents.quote: As high-pressure and low-pressure systems collided, the fire’s course shifted rapidly, taking a more northerly direction along Vandenberg’s coastline and threatening the high value Air Force assets in its path.

incidents.name: Weitchpec Dump Fire Engine Accident
incidents.summary: A Forest Service fire engine from the Six Rivers National Forest crashed while en route to multiple fires in the area of the Weitchpec Dump. The engine responded from Orleans to a call for assistance from CDF (now CAL FIRE) and was driving towards the fire location when it crossed the center line on a corner and clipped the rear of an unloaded log trailer in the opposing lane. The engine then left the roadway and rolled 250 feet down a slope to the Klamath River where it stopped before entering the river. Three engine crewmembers were killed in the accident: Richard Montano, David Perrine, and Gayle Tsutsumi. The other two engine crewmembers were seriously injured but survived.

incidents.name: Camp 11 Physical Training Medical Emergency Fatalities
incidents.summary: Both trainees collapsed on the training course at Camp 11 near Acton and were flown to a hospital where core temperatures exceeded 108 degrees.
incidents.quote: On August 8, 1978, LA County Fire trainees Joseph Hughes and Timothy Rodriguez died of heat stroke during physical training in 106-degree heat.

incidents.name: Airco 53 Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: On August 18, 1978, Airco 53, a Cessna O-2 Skymaster aerial coordination aircraft for the California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) crashed while assigned to a fire in the area of the Carrizo Plains. Information regarding the circumstances of this accident are not readily availabe. Killed in the accident were pilot Joe Holstine, CDF fire captain Paul Belveal, and firefighter Scott Sanford.

incidents.name: Mendocino Unit Fire Air Tanker Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: The aircraft, registered N448DF, was contracted to the California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) when it impacted trees and crashed, resulting in a post-crash fire. According to media reports, the aircraft was in a right turn when the right wing struck the ground. The aircraft, out of control, then struck an unoccupied car. Pilot James Lippitt was killed in the accident. Debris from the accident also struck and injured two firefighters in the vicinity. The fire was contained at 8 acres by five CDF engines, two helicopters, two hand crews, and an additional air tanker. The cause of the accident was not determined. though witnesses indicated that the plane seemed to "falter" while on its retardant run and the pilot seemingly tried to steer the aircraft away from the fire area, over a road, and into an open space. The aircraft instead hit Branscombe Road.
incidents.quote: A Grumman S-2A Tracker air tanker crashed while on a low pass for a retardant drop near Laytonville, California at 1746 on August 20, 1978.

incidents.name: Shasta Unit Heat Illness Fatality
incidents.summary: A 21-year-old California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) Timothy J. Holsinger succumbed to heat stroke while assigned to a prescribed fire. Air temperature on the day of the burn was about 100 degrees Fahrenheit. Holsinger had been assigned to the Humboldt Ranger Unit.

incidents.name: Sanborn Fire Heat Illness Fatality
incidents.summary: Morrison's engine was one of four that responded to the brush fire around 1500. Some reports indicate Morrison had shown signs at various times during the fire response of suffering from exhaustion, illness, or heat-related illness. He was last noticed replacing a broken hose at 1745. His absence was noted around 2200 when the crews took their first rest. A search that evening was unsuccessful, and Morrison's body was not found until 1000 the next day.
incidents.quote: Samuel P. Morrison, a brand new firefighter with the California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) was found deceased on his first wildland fire.

incidents.name: Charles Creek Fire Airtanker Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: Gayle Eaton, a Redding-based pilot on contract to the California Department of Forestry (CDF, now CAL FIRE) was killed when his S-2 air tanker crashed during the approach to a drop on the Charles Creek Fire on the Plumas National Forest. The fire burned 244 acres on the south side of Charles Creek, 7 miles north of Frenchman Lake. Any NTSB report that may have been performed is not available, and the cause of the accident is not clear.

incidents.name: Two Creek Drainage Air Tanker Accident
incidents.summary: On their second series of retardant drops near Superior, MT, an airtanker made a high pass over a fire and then an approach for a second pass. The fire was located near the top of a mountainous ridge on an even slope that provided an easy target for a retardant drop. Once the pass had been made, no retardant had been dropped. Immediately after the airtanker passed over the drop target, it made a steep left turn and impacted a densely timbered hillside.
incidents.quote: Toxicology reports indicated the presence of alcohol in one of the pilot's blood.

incidents.name: Ship Island Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On July 26, Pattee and a line scout were both located at the helispot when a spot fire became established below them and made a run to their location. The men piled crew gear in the center of the helispot and then deployed their fire shelters. The line scout found he had to move his fire shelter several times to move away from the heat of the burning gear. Kyle Pattee, without gloves to help hold the hot fire shelter material, was unable to escape the intense heat of the gear fire and lost his life.
incidents.quote: As the fire burned quickly around the helispot, it ignited the personal gear, creating an intense fire within 12 to 15 feet of the firefighters.

incidents.name: Deadman Flat Fire Engine Entrapment
incidents.fire: Rosevear Gulch (aka Deadman Flat no 1298) Fire
incidents.summary: On July 31, 1979, on a fire burning in grass and sage on the Bureau of Land Management's Boise District in Idaho, two ground tankers were working in tandem, taking flanking action on the fire's southeast sector. Around 1830, the wind shifted 90 degrees causing the fire to run directly at the lead tanker. In response, the lead tanker's driver proceeded to backup and had traveled approximately 128 feet when the engine died and the fire completely engulfed the truck. The driver had some difficulty releasing his seat belt and was burned when flames came through the window. He exited the right side of the tanker and ran 50-60 feet to safety where the crew was waiting. The crew administered first aid and requested the fire helicopter for evacuation. Within 8-10 minutes after the accident, the patient was enroute to St. Alphonsus Hospital in Boise . Не received second and third degree burns on his face, hands, and elbow. He remained hospitalized for five days. The truck was a total loss.

incidents.name: Spanish Ranch Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The initial attack strategy was to direct attack with engines on either flanks, drop retardant line at the head of the fire, and build an indirect dozer line on a ridge in front of the head of the fire. An engine crew was assigned to the indirect dozer line to be in place in case a firing operation was needed. Fire found alignment in a topographic chimney and made a run towards the dozer, whose operator pushed an area of bare soil and deployed fire curtains in the dozer. The finger of fire was then pushed sidehill by strong winds, entrapping the engine crew on the indirect dozer line.
incidents.quote: A sudden crosswind downdraft acts upon a finger of fire and drives the flames across the entire slope of dry vegetation forcing a dozer operator to deploy fire curtains and overcame a CDF engine crew killing 3 that day and a forth died from burns almost 7 months later.

incidents.name: Creek Road Fire Entrapment 1979
incidents.summary: On September 20, 1979, California Department of Forestry contract dozer operator Carl F. Hofmeister was widening a firebreak on the Creek Road Fire when he was overrun by fire. After the fire had passed by him, he began pouring water over his head and body from a jug and began calling for help. A Ventura County Fire Department Fire Captain/Crew Superintendent started to his location with a burn kit. Upon arrival, they observed the Mr. Hofmeister was beginning to suffer from shock. They began immediate first-aid treatment on Mr. Hofmeister's face, hands, and upper body. A Ventura County Fire Department helicopter was dispatched to the accident scene to transport the burn victim to Ventura County General Hospital. After initial treatment there and an assessment of the his burn injuries, he was taken to the Sherman Oaks Burn Center by helicopter for further treatment.
incidents.quote: As he was working on the fire, he noticed a change in wind direction and observed fire about three or four hundred feet below him and moving rapidly towards his location. He stated, “The fire made a great big 'bang' like a cannon. Also, a whirlwind developed thirty to forty feet high carrying soot, leaves, and fire… it was on me so fast I did not have time to get under the dozer."

incidents.name: Mack Lake
incidents.summary: On May 5, 1980, the Crane Lake prescribed fire was conducted in jack pine forests on the Huron National Forest in Michigan. Less than two hours after ignitions began, the fire spotted outside of the ignition unit and became the Mack Lake Fire. The fire ran 4 miles east before a cold front passage caused the southeast flank to become a wide head fire front. Working of the left (north) flank of the fire, a Forest Service tractor-plow operated by James Swiderski was entrapped by fire in a dense jack pine stand. After first turning the tractor to the north away from the advancing fire, Swiderski then left the tractor and attempted escape on foot. His position was overrun by fire and he perished.

incidents.name: Masters Fire Supply Drop Aircraft Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: Pilot Farrell Gale and firefighters Todd Harrison, Daniel Hase and Joe Bass with the Bureau of Land Management, died on July 11, 1980, when their Cessna U206 Super Skywagon aircraft crashed. The mission had been to drop supplies to firefighters on a 2-acre fire. The NTSB summary report indicated that the cargo was not rigged with its parachute properly and the parachute became snagged on the aircraft tail upon exit causing the plane to crash into an isolated peak of the Schell Creek Range.

incidents.name: Santa Teresa Hills Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: On Monday, August 11, 1980, Fire Captain Franklyn C. Knapp-Smith died in a vehicle accident while fighting a fire in Santa Teresa Hills in the City of San Jose. Firefighter trainee David Hirschman suffered a broken arm, (3) broken ribs, and back injuries. The firefighters were attempting to recover their Engine on a steep slope with a Dozer winch. The winch line seperated from the Dozer, causing the Engine to roll down the hill crashing into a concrete canal.
incidents.quote: Several firefighters asked him if he wanted to put chock blocks down.

incidents.name: Dog Bar Fire Dozer Entrapment
incidents.summary: On October 7, 1980, at approximately 1445 hours, Heavy Equipment Operator Robert Walton received first and second degree burns to his arms and face when his bulldozer was overrun by fire while constructing fireline on the Dog Bar Fire in the California Department of Forestry's Nevada-Yuba-Placer Ranger Unit. Walton was transported to the Sacramento Burn Center. His right forearm and both elbows were burned by radiant heat through his flame-resistant shirt which was stretched tight while reaching for the fire curtains and shielding his face at the same time. Also, radiant heat burned the back of his ears while getting off the machine to escape the fire on foot. He left the dozer running and in reverse hoping that it would walk out of the fire before burning. It travelled approximately 15-20 feet at which time it lodged between two trees and stopped. Total backup distance from dozer line to the point the dozer lodged against trees was 100 feet.

incidents.name: Ransom Road Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: Four fires were ignited on the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge near the NASA facility at Cape Canaveral, Florida. At approximately 1605 a tractor-plow became stuck on a stump and was abandoned. On foot, the firefighters continued to attempt escape, and deployed a single shelter in a small opening. They were found critically burned.
incidents.quote: He had forgotten his fire shelter when he left the tractor. He could not sit on the seat with his shelter strapped on.

incidents.name: Dawson Fire Dozer Entrapment
incidents.summary: On June 17, 1981, while engaged in suppression actions on the Dawson Fire, California Department of Forestry (CDF) Fire Captains Michael Williams and Dale Brusewitz were approached by two civilians who offered the use of their bulldozer to help suppress the fire. Captain Brusewitz subsequently gave both men explicit instructions to work on a narrow dirt road. The men proceeded into a small drainage on the dirt road to carry out this assignment. When they reached a point just beyond the lowest point on the road, the wind stopped blowing and became calm. The canyon filled with smoke, hiding the dozer from CDF personnel on the ridgetop and from an engine crew that had just entered the canyon. After a very short time, the fire spotted across the road and the slope above the dozer's location. The slope burned in a matter of a seconds. Both of the civilian dozer team members received extensive second- and third-degree burns to their faces, arms, chests, and backs.

incidents.name: Elizabeth Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Gilbert Lopez, Engine Foreman, Angeles National Forest, was killed on July 15, while taking suppression action on a fire.
incidents.quote: An Angeles National Forest engine crew was assigned to the Elizabeth Fire. The engine foreman and three crew members were working on a spot fire when fire downslope and upwind was reported by the fifth crewmember who had remained on the ridgetop at the engine. Warned of the developing upwind fire, the foreman and crew returned to the engine. The foreman directed the crew to leave the area. The foreman and crew became separated during the evacuation, with the crew going west, toward a volunteer fire department unit who shouted warnings, and the foreman and engine going east. The foreman safely escaped into the burned area, but returned apparently in search of a crew member. The foreman, Gilbert Lopez, was then overtaken by the fire and killed.

incidents.name: Canoe Landing Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Wisconsin DNR equipment operator Donald Eisberner, 48, died in the line of duty on April 24, 1982 on the 274-acre Canoe Landing Fire in Eau Claire County. The Canoe Landing Fire was caused by an unattended campfire. Fire spread to dry grass and into a young pine plantation. Don was one of the first firefighters to arrive at the scene and began plowing on the fireline. With a sudden wind shift, the fire turned and trapped Don and his tractor plow unit.

incidents.name: BLM Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: On August 23, 1983, the operator and one passenger were driving south of Durkee, Oregon in their Bureau of Land Management Chevrolet engine when the vehicle's right rear duals came off and the rear of the truck fell to the pavement. The side pack and the break drum was damaged in this incident. The passenger received a gash to the head which required three stitches.
incidents.quote: The lugs began to break off, one or two at a time, until finally there was only one or two holding. The last one finally broke off, at which point both wheels worked off the hub, letting the rear drop.

incidents.name: Baldy Fire Burnover
incidents.summary: On July 13, 1984, the California Department of Forestry (CDF) and Lakeshore Fire Protection District responded to a structure fire in the incorporated City of Clearlake, California. Shortly thereafter, the fire spotted into CDF lands. During this control effort, two Lakeshore Fire Protection District firefighters were burned. Firefighter Craig Scovel received superficial burns to the arms and face. Firefighter Michael Mattioda received third degree burns to 70-90% of his body. The next day, Firefighter Mattioda succumbed to his injuries at the Chico Community Hospital.
incidents.quote: Shortly afterwards, Chief Parker came out on the County Net radio requesting the helicopter for a medivac of a burned firefighter.

incidents.name: St Marks Pond Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: At 1530 hours on March 31, 1985, Ranger Tommy Thomas began plowing on the approximately 400-acre St. Marks Pond Fire. Moving south, he found the head fire had been suppressed by a barrier of clear cut pine that had recently been control burned. Thomas then decided to attempt to hold the left flank of the fire along a grassy road bed. He then noticed the wind shifting and the fire crossing the road ahead and behind him. The fire moved rapidly north onto him, forcing him to leave the tractor and protect himself in a small pond with his fire shelter.
incidents.quote: "It should be noted here that refresher training on the use of fire shelter took place just 2 days prior to the incident. If anything can be learned from this incident, it is the importance of an ongoing fire behavior and safety training program"

incidents.name: Lodge Fire
incidents.summary: The Lodge Fire on the Warm Springs Reservation in Oregon began in mid-afternoon on June 23, 1985. Six individuals were injured while trying to suppress the fire and one person died.

incidents.name: Lake Mountain Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On July 4, indicators of another major fire behavior day were observed, and at 1400 fire intensity increased. At 1700, crews moved to pre-identified safe areas. At 1730, four crews and two fallers deployed fire shelters in two locations. The shelter deployment lasted 90 minutes to 2 hours. No injuries were reported.
incidents.quote: 82 fire shelters were deployed on the Lake Mountain Fire

incidents.name: Butte Fire Entrapment 1985
incidents.summary: A massive 3,500-acre crown fire run entrapped 73 firefighters, forcing them to deploy fire shelters in dozer safety zones on the Salmon National Forest.
incidents.quote: "During the deployment everyone was really scared. You didn't know what to expect...Everybody knew it was pretty serious. It was definitely a life and death matter." Mike Parsons, EMT Carson Hotshot Crew

incidents.name: Colorado BLM Helicopter Crash Fatalities 1986
incidents.summary: On August 5, 1986, an SA-315B Lama helicopter carrying one pilot and three BLM helitack crewmembers crashed in Western Colorado, killing all aboard. The helicopter was dispatched out of Montrose to check a reported fire in the area between Delta and Hotchkiss. Witnesses stated that the helicopter clipped powerlines, causing separation of the main rotor blades. The helicopter then fell to the ground near the Gunnison River, killing all four occupants: Pilot Jim Daugherty, and BLM helitack crewmembers Philip Hamilton, Harald Siewers, and Lee Steingoetter. Richard Tyler, lost on the 1994 South Canyon Fire in Colorado, was also a member of this crew but was not aboard the aircraft during the accident flight.

incidents.name: Anderson Creek Fire Vehicle Rollover
incidents.summary: Four firefighters were killed and 17 others were injured when an Idaho National Guard truck overturned on the way to the Anderson Creek Fire Camp from the Anderson Creek Fire, Boise National Forest. The 5-ton dump truck rolled down an 80-foot embankment along Danskin Creek Road, 35 miles northwest of Boise, about 5:30 a.m. Aboard were two guardsmen drivers, a crew of firefighters from the Jemez Pueblo, New Mexico, and a BLM crew liaison officer. Killed in the accident were Jemez Pueblo firefighters: Anthony Pecos, Andrew Waquie, Benjamin Waquie, and Allen Baca.
incidents.quote: The truck rolled about 80 feet down a 70 percent slope from the road. A number of the 19 crew members were thrown from the vehicle.

incidents.name: Maple Road
incidents.summary: On May 22, 1987, at approximately 1227 hours, a Firefighter I with the Hesperia Station, San Bernardino Ranger Unit, received 2nd and 3rd degree burns while engaged in initial attack fire control operations on the Maple Road Fire near the town of Hesperia in San Bernardino County. The firefighter was treated at the scene, transported via San Bernardino Sheriff's Helicopter to San Bernardino County Hospital where she was treated and released. The following day, the firefighter experienced an increased discomfort and was was transported via helicopter to the Sherman Oaks Burn Unit.

incidents.name: Battle Mountain Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: The Pine Ridge Job Corps firefighting crew spent July 21, 1987 constructing fireline in a steep, dry, V‑shaped canyon on the Battle Mountain Fire near Hot Springs, South Dakota, where afternoon temperatures rose above forecast and fire behavior intensified. As heat rapidly built in the canyon, supervisors directed the 14‑person crew to move toward a rocky secondary safety zone on the west slope. While climbing, the fire made a high‑intensity uphill run, cutting off escape and forcing the crew to deploy fire shelters within rock crevices, where the combination of natural rock protection and shelters allowed everyone to survive without injuries. After the fire passed, all personnel were accounted for, escorted out, medically evaluated, and found healthy; most returned to duty the next day.
incidents.quote: There was not sufficient flat area for the entire crew to deploy their shelters in the normal manner. Instead, most of the crew deployed into crevices in the rocks, pulling the shelters over them.

incidents.name: Crank Fire 1987
incidents.summary: At around 1700, thundercells moved over the fire causing the fire to increase in intensity into a crown fire that burned over the 3 engines and hand crew, who sought shelter in an opening in the forest and deployed fire shelters. The entrapped firefighters were forced to moved from this initial deployment site and redeploy on a road about 40 minutes after the initial crown fire initiation. The group of 25 firefighters left their fire shelters and walked out of the fire area at 1810. In all, 17 of the 25 firefighters were taken to area hospitals with various injuries. Burn injuries were characterized as "a few first and second degree burns." Two firefighters were transferred to a burn center.
incidents.quote: On August 30, 1987, 25 firefighters from USFS engines, CDF Engine 2276, and Intermountain Inmate Crew 1 deployed shelters during a burnover on Lassen-Modoc Unit.

incidents.name: Klamath National Forest National Guard Vehicle Fatality
incidents.summary: National Guardsman Donald Gormley was part of a mobilization to Northern California fires when he was killed in a vehicle accident. Gormley was driving a military vehicle in the mountainous terrain west of Etna, California, when his vehicle left the roadway and rolled down the embankment at about 2050 hours. He was killed int he accident.

incidents.name: Whalen Fire Air Tanker Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: The crew reported trouble maintaining proper speed and dropped their retardant on the fire. At about the time the pilot dropped the retardant, a structural failure occurred and the right wing separated from the airframe along with the tip of the left wing and the tail booms. The fuselage with both engines and most of the left wing attached encountered terrain impact and burned as a unit.

incidents.name: Lauder Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The Lauder Fire ignited early on September 29, 1987 near Willits, California. Initial attack resources included engines, heavy equipment, and two helicopters from the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (now CAL FIRE). One helitack crew deployed on the right flank, while the second helitack crew deployed to the top of the fire on the ridge. The helitack crew on the flank began to cut a trail through the dense brush to hike up to the top of the ridge to assist. Fire behaviour increase dramatically and the helitack took refuge in the black and deployed fire shelters. The ground was very hot from smoldering fuels. The entrapped firefighters all received burn injuries, while one firefighter, Denis Cullins, perished at the scene.
incidents.quote: As they hiked up the hill, fire behavior increased dramatically and entrapped the 5-person helitack crew.

incidents.name: Sanderson
incidents.summary: After a major wind shift, 2 tractor operators attempted to load up their tractors and move to a different location. Their escape forward was blocked by fire. After having trouble loading the tractor in the rear, both operators had to run for safety.
incidents.quote: Both transport units were completely destroyed.

incidents.name: Wampee Bay
incidents.summary: Two rangers with a tractor plow unit deployed fire shelters when a wildfire that was a result of an escaped site prep burn being conducted by a private timber company creeped into a rugged swampy area.
incidents.quote: At approximately the same time the tractor became stuck, the fire began to build.

incidents.name: Stockyard
