incidents.summary: While creating a double plow line along an old road and within a plantation, conditions changed Flames started to build behind Tractor 2 and the operator fled through the plantation. The tractor was completely burned out and the operator received 2nd and 3rd degree burns.
incidents.quote: The findings state that there was a miscalculation on how close to the edge of the fire they should develop the line.

incidents.name: Altamont Fire Injuries
incidents.summary: On July 11, 1988, at approximately 1454 hours Morgan Hill ECC received a report of a grass fire at Midway South of Highway 580. Confirming reports from Mt. Oso Lookout indicated multiple fires. The Emergency Command Center proceeded with a medium level dispatch. Engines 1680 and 1661 were among the initial attack units dispatched. Upon arrival the Incident Commander confirmed multiple fires under severe wind conditions. Engine 1661 was assigned to the western most fire north of Highway 580. Upon evaluating the situation, proceeded to a knoll above the fire in an unburned area, where the burn incident occurred. Engine 1680 was assigned structure fire protection off Old Altamont Road. During this assignment, FAE Douthit observed a metal building in the path of the fire. In his efforts to suppress the spread of the fire, he spotted the engine in an unburned area above the fire where the burn incident occurred.
incidents.quote: The July 11, 1988 grass fires near Highway 580 prompted a medium-level emergency response in which Engines 1661 and 1680 encountered multiple rapidly spreading fires under severe winds, ultimately leading both crews into unburned areas where burn incidents occurred.

incidents.name: Clover Fire Deployment 1988
incidents.summary: On July 14, 1988 at about 1730, Dan Shelly, John Dunfee, and Christin Covan were involved in a fire shelter deployment incident in Yellowstone National Park. The incident occurred while they were attempting to protect the Calfee Creek Cabin from the Clover Fire. They became overrun and had to deploy their shelters. They had only two shelters between the three of them and had to double—up. No one was injured in the incident.
incidents.quote: The deployment site was located in a large meadow just north of the Calfee Creek Cabin... The fire was actively burning, crowning, and torching.

incidents.name: Madison Gulch
incidents.summary: During the late afternoon of July 26, 1988, the Madison gulch Fire started on the south facing slope along the Petty Creek Road. The next day, the intensity increased to the point that all line building activity had to be abandoned. Spotting started to occur east of the fire. The crew started running backwards in the direction that they had come from but one crew member Lester Begay fell, became disoriented and ran the opposite direction. The crew boss chased him and they were both separated from the rest of the crew. They were eventually helped find a path to safety by a Helicopter pilot directing them via radio. During this time, one fire shelter was deployed and Begay was placed inside by Durgeloh for a period of 1 to 3 minutes.
incidents.quote: The critical nature of this deployment cannot be over stressed. It was truly a matter of luck that the situation did not result in serious injuries or more likely two fatalities.

incidents.name: Crow Agency Engine Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Cheryl Old Horn Deputee, a firefighter with the Bureau of Indian Affairs based in Crow Agency, Montana, was killed in an engine accident while fighting a brush fire. Deputee was operating a pump on the back of her fire engine when the brakes failed and the vehicle rolled into a ravine and turned over, pinning her underneath. She was reported to have died instantly in the accident. Deputee was a member of an 18-person initial attack crew.

incidents.name: Sequoia National Forest Leadplane Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: After leading an airtanker on its second retardant drop, a leadplane executed a steep pull-up left climbing turn when a mishap occurred. The pilot, Charles Watkins, was killed instantly during the mishap sequence and the aircraft was destroyed.
incidents.quote: The aircraft “impacted the ground in a near vertical, nose-down position.”

incidents.name: Lost Fire Repeater Mission Helicopter Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 19, 1988, an Aerospatiale SA315B (Lama) supporting the Lost Fire transported a Helitack Crewmember, two Communications Technicians, and cargo to the repeater site in the Cloud Peak Wilderness, Bighorn National Forest. The helicopter began to spin violently and the pilot was unable to control the rotation and they began to descend toward the rocks below. The helicopter descended 400 feet rapidly and rotated four to six times before the tail rotor guard struck the rocks. It continued to rotate another 90 degrees before impacting on an easterly heading at a nearly level and upright orientation with considerable forward velocity. The dynamic forces generated by the weight of the passenger in the left front seat, Merrin Rodgers, on impact caused his seat belt to fail. He was subsequently thrown from the helicopter feet first and was propelled into the rotating main rotor blades and was fatally injured. The other occupants of the helicopter survived but sustained injuries.
incidents.quote: While flying reconnaissance for a proper landing site at 10,000 feet MSL and 100 feet above the terrain, the helicopter began to spin violently to the left.

incidents.name: Eagle Bar
incidents.summary: At about 2210 hours on August 25, 1988, there was a shelter deployment of the Umatilla Regular Forest Service Type II Crew and two overhead personnel. The deployment took place below and about one—quarter mile northwest of Kinney Point on the Eagle Bar Fire, Payette National Forest in Region 4. There were no serious physical Injuries although one individual of the Umatilla Crew sustained a small burn on the calf of his leg.

incidents.name: Silvertip Ranch Storm Creek Fire
incidents.summary: Fire shelters were deployed by 48 personnel on the Storm Creek Fire. The circumstances of the deployment are reviewed.

incidents.name: Dinkelman Fire Helicopter Crash Fatality 1988
incidents.summary: A Bell 204B with external longline and bucket was supporting firefighting operations by the state of Washington on the Dinkelman Fire southeast of Entiat when it crashed, killing both pilots. The helicopter was owned by a Canadian aviation company and piloted by two pilots, Lincoln McGowan and Jean Verville. The final investigation report gives the cause of the crash as a fracturing of the main rotor shaft, resulting in an inflight breakup. Factors included gusty, high winds, and the low experience level of the pilot flying the aircraft.

incidents.name: Canyon Creek Fire Entrapment 1988
incidents.summary: A total of 107 people of Division A of the Elk Creek Zone deployed their shelters in a safety zone on the ridge between Moudess and Jakie creeks as the fire burned over the area. There were no fatalities or injuries requiring hospital treatment.
incidents.quote: Sometime around 1630 the main fire front blew through the saddle below the safety zone and all around its perimeter igniting gear stowed at the outer edges away from personnel locations.

incidents.name: Red Bench Patrick David Fatality
incidents.summary: A crewmember was fatally injured when he was struck by a falling tree on the Red Branch Fire, Flathead National Forest. A large live Western Larch, approximately 3 feet, 6 inches DBH 136 feet long, fell directly onto the group.
incidents.quote: Crewmembers were standing just off the roadway waiting to be relieved from the night shift.

incidents.name: Clover Mist Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Edward Hutton was killed by a dead falling snag on October 11, 1988 during mop up operations on the Clover Mist Fire, Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming.
incidents.quote: They retreated to where they thought was a safe area downhill from the drop site among some trees and awaited the drop.

incidents.name: Shelley Fire Deployment
incidents.summary: At approximately 1230 MDT, June 24, 1989, the Shelley Fire crossed control lines and made a major run parallel to Division D, resulting in the deployment of 41 fire shelters.
incidents.quote: The personnel involved in the deployment were not immediately removed from the fireline or debriefed.

incidents.name: Eagle Fire Three Entrapment Incidents 1989
incidents.summary: On July 7, 1989 at approximately 1427 hours, a vegetation fire was reported 5 miles south of Janesville in the Lassen/Modoc Ranger Unit. The following day, the fire behavior conditions were moderate, as the day progressed, however, fire activity increased and the behavior again became extreme. Three incidents occurred on July 8 where fire shelters were deployed. Four CDF firefighters were burned during hose lay operations on a spot fire, while a dozer and engine crew deployed shelters in a safety zone.

incidents.name: Black Tiger Fire WUI
incidents.summary: A human-caused wildland fire starting on July 9, 1989 in a scenic part of the Rocky Mountains near Boulder, Colorado, swept through residential areas nestled among the trees. Within the first five to six hours after ignition, 44 homes and other structures were destroyed and many others were damaged. The fire was not completely extinguished until four days later, after burning almost 2,100 acres. Loss estimates of homes and natural resources amounted to $10 million, and the cost to control the fire was another $1 million. More than 500 fire fighters from local, state and federal fire agencies worked to eventually contain the fire and protect the numerous other homes built in the rustic surroundings. Some of the fire fighters’ own homes were threatened or destroyed by the fire. Only a few minor fire fighter injuries were reported and one resident was hospitalized from burns.
incidents.quote: "I was choked with smoke, and once I had to wait for a wind to blow the smoke away because I couldn't see the road. I cried like a baby when I got to the end of the road."

incidents.name: Liberty Fire Firefighter Death
incidents.summary: Ron Nelson reported to the Medical Unit tent at the Liberty Fire between 0700 and 0730 on 9/17/89. The medical unit leader and an EMT, examined Nelson and took his blood pressure. Nelson was instructed to go to his sleeping area to rest. At about 1530 hours, it was discovered he passed away in his sleep.
incidents.quote: The review team found a number of indications that Mr. Nelson was either hiding his condition or denying it.

incidents.name: Dude Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The crew worked through the morning improving indirect firelines. At around 1415 hours, the fire made a significant run, entrapping the crew in the canyon. Eleven crewmembers were cut off and deployed fire shelters.
incidents.quote: Six crewmembers perished during the entrapment, and five other firefighters suffered burn injuries.

incidents.name: California Fire Entrapment 1990
incidents.summary: At 1440 hrs on June 27, 1990, fire overran a CDF (now CAL FIRE) crew that was attempting to backfire a handline. The fire was burning on moderate to steep slopes, in light vegetation during shifting winds and extreme temperatures (110 degrees F, 9% relative humidity). Two fire crew firefighters received burn injuries to which they succumbed in the following days, and the rest of the crew (15 firefighters) received varying degrees of injury. The fire occurred in the Domenigoni Mountains, on the Riverside Ranger Unit near Hemet, California. The firefighters lost on the California Fire were Victor Ferrara and Aaron Perry
incidents.quote: Two fire crew firefighters succumbed to their injuries. The entire crew suffered burns and/or smoke inhalation injuries.

incidents.name: Recer Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: At approximately 1335 on August 13,1990, a snagfell on a CDF firefighter working on a hoselay attempting to contain a spotfire.
incidents.quote: There was insufficient time to fell the snag and felling it would also have been hazardous.

incidents.name: Snowshoe Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Julius Starr, assistant fire management officer of the North Umpqua District, Umpqua National Forest collapsed in the fire camp of the Snowshoe Fire on the Malheur National Forest, Oregon. Starr was provided emergency medical care at fire camp, and was unconscious but breathing when he was transported to the hospital in John Day. Starr was later flown to Bend, where he passed away in the hospital.

incidents.name: Wasatch Mountain Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Sheriff's Deputy Blake Wright and Public Works employee Ralph Broadhead were entrapped and killed on the Wasatch Mountain Fire on the night of August 26. The two men were cutting fireline in the initial attack phase of the fire when they were cut off by the rapidly expanding fire. Their bodies were discovered at 0330 the following day.

incidents.name: Silver Fire Helicopter Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: The pilot was killed when his aircraft lost power and crashed in steep burned-over forest on the Silver Fire, Colville Indian Reservation, Washington. The pilot was performing bucket drops on the fire, and had had the water bucket's cinch strap (which controls the volume of water allowed into the bucket) replaced earlier in the day. During a drop at around 1746 hrs, the pilot remarked over the radio that he was "heavy." Witnesses observed a puff of smoke come from the helicopter, which then lost altitude and crashed into terrain
incidents.quote: The cinch strap was bought at a hardware or sporting goods store, it was not provided by the manufacturer.

incidents.name: Wynoochee Fire Air Tanker Crash Fatalities
incidents.summary: A small private plane crashed near Wynoochee Lake killing both occupants and starting a fire. In the initial attack response to the fire after discovery the following day, a leadplane and air tanker were dispatched to help suppress the fire. Immediately after the drop, the aircraft impacted log landing area and subsequently broke apart.
incidents.quote: The accident was attributed to the aircraft entering a "low and slow" flight configuration following the retardant drop, and the pilots not jettisoning the remainder of the load nor applying full additional jet power.

incidents.name: Ziploc Fire Lead Plane Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: On the last run before returning for fuel, attempting to direct a retardant drop into an arroyo, the lead plane pilot indicated the drop area by rocking the Baron's wings, then initiated a sharp left rising turn. The turn continued until the plane impacted trees and the ground in an inverted orientation. The plane burned after impacting the ground. The pilot, Henry Kim, was killed in the accident.

incidents.name: Routt National Forest Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Kevin Doyle Keel, a US Forest Service firefighter from Tennessee, was hit by a tree and suffered fatal injuries on a small initial attack fire on the Routt National Forest, Colorado. Routt and a squad boss were sent to initial attack a 1/4 acre fire on September 18. The two firefighters contained the fire at around 2300 hrs that night, and took a break. Shortly after, a tree fell and struck Keel in the chest. The squad boss was unable to contact anyone via radio, and left to get help. By the time the squad boss returned after contacting hunters and sending them to for help, Keel had succumbed to his injuries early in the morning of September 19.
incidents.quote: It was noted that the fire occurred in an area of forest impacted by pine beetles, leaving standing dead trees.

incidents.name: Collins Fire Burn Injury 1992
incidents.summary: On April 14, 1992, on the Collins Fire, a Firefighter I from the California Department of Forestry (CDF) Engine Company 3563 received burn injuries to his right leg during mop-up operations. While advancing a hose line toward a hot spot, the firefighter stepped and fell into an abandoned beaver lodge located within the burned area. He was treated immediately by CDF Emergency Medical Technicians on scene and was transported by San Bernardino County Sheriff's Aviation aircraft to the Sherman Oaks Burn Center. The firefighter received second and third degree burns over six to eight percent of his body.

incidents.name: Round Lake Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: A Winema National Forest employee deployed his fire shelter while assisting the Oregon Department of Forestry with the Initial Attack of the Round Lake Incident
incidents.quote: Dan worked the rest of his shift on the fire and was released the next morning.

incidents.name: Benton County Fire District Engine Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Paul Bjorklund was riding on the back of a brush truck manning a water nozzle when the driver lost control, the truck rolled, and Bjorklund was killed.

incidents.name: Cascade Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Julie Ann Young, an employee on a Boise National Forest fire crew, was killed by a falling snag on a fire near Cascade Reservoir in Idaho. Young was reportedly installing a hoselay to the fire when a dead tree fell and struck her around 1600 hours. Fellow firefighters quickly responded, beginning CPR and requesting air medevac. When paramedics arrived via helicopter, they determined that Young had perished.

incidents.name: Lamartine VFD Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Dean Pucker suffered a heart attack while on the scene of a wildland fire.

incidents.name: El Dorado National Forest Air Tanker Accident Fatalities 1992
incidents.summary: This Douglas DC-7B airtanker had been operating from Stockton Air Tanker Base, California and had made several drops of retardant on the southeast edge of a fire on the El Dorado National Forest. The planned drop was to be made from north to south about one mile west of the upper dam at Union Valley Reservoir. On approach to the retardant run, the DC-7B pilot indicated he was experiencing engine trouble and exited the traffic pattern to the right. The trailing SP2H and the air attack watched the DC-7B continue towards gently rising terrain. The pilot declined to jettison the retardant load as he worked through the engine issue. The aircraft then turned to the right and pitched up, jettisoning the retardant before impacting trees. The DC-7B then impacted the ground in steep terrain and the aircraft was destroyed. This accident sequence occurred at around 1225 hrs. Both pilots, Leonard Martin and Charles "Chuck" Sheridan, were killed.

incidents.name: DeSoto Fire District Railroad Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Anthony V. Calhoun was responding to a brush fire in Pumper 841 when he crossed the railroad tracks and was struck by an oncoming train. The impact totally destroyed the truck and killed Firefighter Calhoun.

incidents.name: Whisky Fire Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: As the crew traveled along the indirect line, a green tree fell, causing the accident. The injured firefighter was stabilized at the scene and then transported by litter to the vehicles, arriving there approximately 0530 hours. He was then transported by ambulance to Siskiyou General Hospital in Yreka. After being treated at the hospital, he was released at approximately 0900 hours on October 28, 1992.
incidents.quote: They heard the tree making noises seconds prior to the accident.

incidents.name: Crowley Fire Department Engine Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Brush truck overturned while being moved to an alternate location on the fireground. The accident killed Firefighter Jeffrey Glenn Osmun.

incidents.name: Buchanan Rx Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: At 3:40 p.m. on Thursday, April 22, a rapid, unexpected, short-duration increase and shift in wind caused the fire below the road to crown and move across the road. Sixteen people were involved in the fire shelter deployments and entrapments that resulted. Forestry Aid Frankie Toledo, member of the Jemez Pueblo, was above the road and did not escape the flame front, as he ran uphill towards a ridgeline.

incidents.name: Glen Allen Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: Approximately 35 minutes into their work, during a short break, the fire was evaluated, options and safety considerations were weighted, and the decision was made to continue a downhill cut along an underslung line. Within the next 5 minutes, 2 would lose their lives, 2 would be seriously burned and 5 others would narrowly escape.
incidents.quote: The fire behavior was in a manner consistent with expected burning conditions based upon terrain, weather and fuels.

incidents.name: Marre Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Within 15 minutes of Division C/D's arrival at the Safety Zone, the entrapment began with an under-story run with some trees torching at the northwest corner. Within 3- 4 minutes of the first run, a crown fire hit the west half of the Safety Zone sending a sheet of embers approximately 100 feet overhead. The embers landed south of the Safety Zone and immediately ignited the windrowed brush and trees pushed to the edge by the dozers that created the Safety Zone. At that moment, Division C/D lost sight of the firing crew, including the TFL, and noticed that the visibility going out of the east end of the Safety Zone was virtually nil due to the smoke from the backfire. At that point, the Division Supervisor made the decision that the only safe thing to do was to stay in the Safety Zone. He directed the engine crews to abandon their hoselay operations, to get into their engines and stay there unless their engines caught fire.
incidents.quote: This is a review of the entrapment incident on the Marre Fire that occurred on the morning of Saturday, October 2, 1993, when the fire jumped containment lines on the west flank, trapping several pieces of firefighting equipment and personnel in the process.

incidents.name: Tuskegee NF Prescribed Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On February 26, 1994, District Ranger Bedford Cash of the U.S. Forest Service, was conducting prescribed burning in the Tuskegee National Forest when he suffered a fatal heart attack.

incidents.name: Easter Sunday
incidents.summary: The Easter Sunday Fire was reported in Eau Claire County near August, Wisconsin at 1400 on April 3, 1994. Initial attack began on the left flank and head of the fire, which was burning in grass with oak on ridges within the fire area. An engine attack engine began disabled before reaching the fireline, and firefighters proceeded on foot with backpack pumps. A wind gust fanned the flames from 1-2 feet in length to 20-25 feet. Firefighter Robert Waskiewicz fell as he retreated from the advancing flaming front with the other firefighters and some local residents who were assisting in suppression. Waskiewicz was wearing turnout gear (coat, helmet and boots), but received 3rd degree burns over 50% of his body as the fire burned over him. He lived for 15 days following the entrapment, but ultimately succumbed to injuries resulting from his inhalation of super-heated gases.

incidents.name: Sunset Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: A wildfire started on Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge and was named the Sunset Fire. Eventually, a Type I Incident Command Team was ordered to manage the growing fire. The Type I Team returned the fire to the Refuge's responsibility the afternoon of April 4, 1994. The Refuge Fire Management Officer became the new Incident Commander (IC). Suppression activities continued, and, on April 13, 1994, a burnout operation was initiated to secure a portion of the perimeter. During this burnout operation, the fire escaped and was initial attacked. The fire shelter deployment occurred during this initial attack.
incidents.quote: The vehicle stalled after crossing a gully.

incidents.name: Mackenzie Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The Mackenzie fire located 40 miles SW of Kingman AZ was approximately 150 ac at 1300 on 6-1-94. The fire rapidly increased in size with rates of spread exceeding 50 chains/hr in the Desert Brush Fuel Model 4. Temperatures were near 100 degrees with RH in the single digits. The deployment of shelters occurred at approximately 1400 hrs in a granite boulder field at the base of a very steep slope in a dense brush filled shallow drainage. The boulder field was made up of 8 to 15 foot diameter round granite rocks that had numerous horizontal and vertical crevices from 1 to 10 feet wide. It was within the crevices that three members of a hotshot crew deployed their fire shelters on the ground and on the boulders themselves. Curtis Heaton sustained 2nd degree burn to shoulder.

incidents.name: Coffee Pot Fire Entrapment 1994
incidents.summary: The Coffee Pot Fire was first reported at 10:24 a.m. on Sunday, June 5, 1994, to the Albuquerque Zone Fire Dispatch Center. At 6:00 a.m. on June 9, an IMT was assigned to manage the Ryan Complex on the Cibola National Forest which included the Coffee Pot Fire. On June 14, 1994, five members of the Globe Interagency Hotshot Crew were working on the east side of Apache Kid Peak near the switch-backs on Forest Trail 46. Between 8:15 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. the fire made a strong run up the east side of the Peak. The five decided it was necessary to deploy their fire shelters to protect themselves from the fire.

incidents.name: Agua Fria Grassland Prescribed Burn Near Miss
incidents.summary: On Thursday, June 23, the Phoenix District BLM, Tonto and Prescott National Forest conducted a 3000 acre desert grassland prescribed burn. Of the 3000 acres, 2500 were BLM and 500 acres Tonto National Forest. Fuel types being burned were 90 percent tobosa grass with 10 percent snakeweed, mesquite, catclaw and cactus. Total resources assigned to the burn were 29 people, 5 fire engines and 1 helicopter. At approximately 1600 hours, a close call occurred on Division A of the prescribed burn. Two firefighters (1 BLM, 1 Tonto NF) who were burners were removed by helicopter because the fire threatened their safety.
incidents.quote: The fire thenhooked around the ridge to the East and cut off #1 and #2's primary escape route back to the road.

incidents.name: South Canyon Fire Entrapments
incidents.summary: On the afternoon of July 6, 1994 near Glenwood Springs, Colorado the South Canyon fire spotted across the drainage and beneath firefighters, moving onto steep slopes and into dense, highly flammable Gambel oak. Within seconds, a wall of flame raced up the hill toward the firefighters on the west flank fireline. Failing to outrun the flames, 12 firefighters perished. Two helitack crew members on top of the ridge also died when they tried to outrun the fire to the northwest. The remaining 35 firefighters survived by escaping out the east drainage or by seeking a safety area and deploying their fire shelters.
incidents.quote: While fire behavior during the afternoon of July 6, 1994, can be characterized as extreme, it was normal and could be expected given the environmental conditions. Neither leadership roles nor a cohesive organizational structure stabilized before the blowup.

incidents.name: Tyee Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On July 27, Paul Hodges died after suffering a heart attack while driving a tanker truck on a wildland fire. Hodges was a contract employee for the USFS and a volunteer with the Chelan County Fire Protection District #9.

incidents.name: Butler Creek Fire Air Tanker Accident Fatalities 1994
incidents.summary: A P2V-7 airtanker crashed into steep terrain during an unguided retardant drop on the Lolo National Forest, resulting in two pilot fatalities.
incidents.quote: The airtanker malfunctioned and dropped half its load prematurely, then crashed into terrain 350 feet below a ridge while maneuvering for a second drop.

incidents.name: Livermore Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The Livermore Fire on the Blackfeet Indian Reservation, Montana, had exhibited erratic, explosive fire behavior for several days, causing crews to disengage and retreat to safety zones on multiple occasions.
incidents.quote: On August 5, 1994, the fire entrapped a group of 20 hand crew members and two engine crew members. The group could not communicate with the aircraft circling above them, and did not have a full picture of their situation. They removed the fire shelters from their cases and partially deployed them, but ultimately determined a full deployment was not necessary as the fire behavior subsided.

incidents.name: Union Township Fire Department Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On September 3, Captain Earl Detty, Jr. of the Union Township (OH) Fire Department responded to a report of a fire in the woods. Arriving, on the scene, Captain Detty, Jr. discovered a legal campfire. He suffered a heart attack and died while walking back to his fire engine.

incidents.name: Supply Cache Truck Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Robert L. Johnson, a driver at the National Interagency Fire Center base camp, was killed when his truck was struck by another vehicle while enroute with supplies to a wildfire.

incidents.name: Blackwell Fire Helicopter Crash Fatality
incidents.summary: In September 1994, a U.S. Army CH‑47D Chinook helicopter supporting firefighting operations on the Payette National Forest crashed while attempting to land at the Davis Ranch helispot. After placing its external bucket on the ground, the helicopter became unstable, pitched over, and overturned, ending up upside down. During the mishap, a rotor blade struck the fuselage and fatally injured flight engineer John King. Of the five people aboard, one was killed, one seriously injured, and three sustained minor injuries.
incidents.quote: The aircraft was completely destroyed.

incidents.name: Cedar Mountain Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Between 1730 and 1735, the second crew noticed the fire building in intensity below the road. The fire initiated a run out of the creek, across the road, up the ridge, and spotted below the road on the other side of the ridge. This separated Mary Jo Brown from the other firefighters. Three firefighters including Mary Jo Brown decided to deploy their fire shelters in the road. One of the other firefighters moved, redeployed, and then using her shelter as a shield ran off the mountain. Mary Jo Brown moved, redeployed, and perished in her shelter.
incidents.quote: "Go back the way we came - go back down the road!"

incidents.name: East Providence Volunteer Fire Department Medical Emergency Fatality 1995
incidents.summary: On January 26, Chief Lathan Grant Smith, Jr., of the East Providence Volunteer Fire Department died after suffering a heart attack while fighting a brush fire. Chief Grant was a founder of the East Providence VFD and a career firefighter with the Talladega Fire Department.

incidents.name: Claude Volunteer Fire Department Apparatus Hit by Train Fatalities
incidents.summary: On January 31, Firefighters Marcus King and Jared Lee Wright of the Claude Volunteer Fire Department were killed when their fire apparatus was struck by a train while they were fighting a brush fire on a railroad right-of-way. Both Firefighters suffered severe traumatic injuries and died several days later. Firefighter King was 15 years old at the time of his death. Firefighter Wright was 18 years old.

incidents.name: Willard Fire Department Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: Firefighter Ernestine Garcia died when she was thrown from a fire engine in a rollover accident while responding to a brush fire. The vehicle apparently hit a soft shoulder on the side of the road, crossed the road and rolled over. The driver, a 17-year-old junior firefighter, was hospitalized for multiple injuries. He was permitted to drive to fires but prohibited from operating on the ground until turning 18.

incidents.name: South China VFD Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On March 29, Deputy Chief Norman Prime of the South China Fire Department died of a heart attack while fighting a brush fire.

incidents.name: Arkansas SEAT Aircraft Accident
incidents.summary: On April 9, 1995, a WSK PZL M-18A Dromader Single Engine Air Tanker crashed near Pine Bluff, Arkansas after its engine failed to respond during a low‑altitude maneuver over a fire, leaving the pilot unable to regain power or dump the aircraft’s load; the airplane subsequently stalled, entered a spin, rolled twice, and struck the ground at a steep angle, where it was destroyed by fire, and the pilot sustained serious injuries but survived.
incidents.quote: The plane made two complete rolls before striking the ground at about a 45 degree to 60 degree angle.

incidents.name: Butterfield Ranch Fire Midair Collision
incidents.summary: On June 21, 1995, a USFS Lead Plane (Beech 58) and C-54G Airtanker collided in midair near Ramona Airport after returning from the Butterfield Ranch Fire. Both aircraft broke apart and crashed 1 mile east of the airport, killing all three flight crew members aboard both planes.
incidents.quote: A DOUGLAS C-54G & BEECH 58P WERE ON A FIRE SUPPRESSION MISSION... TANKER 19 WAS ON THE INITIAL APPROACH... WHEN THE TWO PLANES COLLIDED.

incidents.name: Wayne Fire Department Hit by Vehicle Fatality
incidents.summary: On April 19th, Firefighter Mathew Hatcher died of abdominal injuries after being pinned between two fire trucks at a grass fire. He was at the rear of one truck starting the pump when a second truck pinned him.

incidents.name: Clark Peak Fire Multiple Incidents
incidents.summary: Multiple incidents on the Clark Peak Fire on the Coronado National Forest, Arizona, in April and May 1996, comprising refusal of a handline construction assignment due to LCES concerns, and a mishap during aerial ignitions.
incidents.quote: "I applaud the decision not to take the assignment and again state that "IT'S OK TO SAY NO" and that there will not (shouldn't be) any future threats or ramifications to the people involved." James T. Johnston, Type 1 Safety Officer

incidents.name: Dome Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On April 26, 1996, 48 firefighters deployed their fire shelters on the Dome Fire, Santa Fe National Forest. One of the firefighters suffered second-degree burns on the back of both of his hands, another reported he also suffered burns during his deployment. None of the other 46 firefighters reported any injuries. A model 20 engine from the Jemez Ranger District was destroyed by the fire.

incidents.name: Globe Hotshots PT Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Michelle Smith disappeared during a training run and was found dead twenty-six hours later. According to the autopsy report, she died of heat exhaustion and dehydration. There was no sign of struggle or foul play.

incidents.name: Autumn Hills Fire Burnover of Cameraman
incidents.summary: The Autumn Hills Fire began on Sunday afternoon, June 23, 1996, in a wildland-urban interface subdivisıon located within the Sierra Forest Fire Protection District of the Nevada Division of Forestry in Douglas County. The Sierra Front IMT assumed command of the fire at 2135 hours. The Rocky Mountain Incıdent Management Team arrıved over the course of the afternoon of June 24, 1996. An independent journalist located in the area traveled to the scene of the fire during the initial attack period on June 23 to film fire behavior and firefighting activity. While he filmed, the fire experienced sudden flare-up, described as a blow-up, necessitating an escape from the fire area. The journalist jumped into the pickup bed of a firefighter, intending to film as they left the area. As they made their way through the extreme fire behavior along the road, the journalist received partial thickness burn injuries to the face.
incidents.quote: Had Mr. Conway run from the fire, he likely would have died.

incidents.name: Dillon County Fire Department Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: On June 24th, Firefighter Ronald Lupo was responding to a field fire at approximately 7:10 pm. While enroute, his vehicle was struck on the right front side by an oncoming van. He was rushed to the hospital and died later that night from internal injuries.

incidents.name: Sierra
incidents.summary: The accident occurred at 1635 on June 24, 1996 on Division X of the Sierra Fire, Sequoia National Forest while Crew 4 was constructing direct handline. The crew was being supported by water bucket drops from Helicopter 523. During one of the bucket trail drops, local winds, terrain winds and rotorwash combined to briefly flare up the light, flashy grass fuels and push the fire downhill onto and around 8 members of Crew 4. The 8 crew members escaped downhill, but two firefighters sustained burns. All members of the crew had proper Personal Protective Equipment. The sequence of events did not allow for deployment of fire shelters.
incidents.quote: There is a concern from the team that no more rules, orders, pins, stickers, cards or decals result from this incident.

incidents.name: Dano Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: On August 19, 1996 a lighting-caused fire was reported on the rim of the Clarks Fork Canyon below Bald Ridge on the Clarks Fork Ranger District. The fire was approximately two acres. The fire was 75% contained by 1100 hours. By about 1300 hours strong winds combined with hot temperatures and low humidity caused the fire to jump the line. By mid afternoon, the fire had grown to approximately 200 acres and was still spreading as the winds continued. Five of the eight firefighters were removed by helicopter. The fire burned over the helispot before the remaining three could be evacuated, causing an entrapment. Shortly after 1500 they deployed their fire shelters in a crevice on a cliff. The firefighters were not injured and all were safely evacuated. Two air tankers dropped fire retardant to assist in protection of the firefighters.

incidents.name: BLM Nevada Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 25th, Firefighter John Gray was repairing a water tender between fires when he died of a heart attack. After he collapsed, a fellow crew member began CPR and called an ambulance.

incidents.name: Agua Canyon Fire Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: At approximately 9:30 p.m. on August 26, 1996, National Park Service Ranger Michael A. Beaulieu was responding to the report of a wildfire near the Agua Canyon viewpoint in Bryce Canyon National Park. At milepost 11.8 on Route 10, he failed to negotiate a curve on a rain-slick road. The vehicle left the road, sheered a large tree, and continued rolling down an embankment. Although both airbags deployed and Ranger Beaulieu was wearing a seatbelt, he suffered a massive head injury and died instantly. The crash was discovered approximately 45 minutes later by campers, who summoned authorities.

incidents.name: Summit
incidents.summary: On 8/24 and 8/25 the Summit Fire, one of the four fires comprising the Bull Complex, made major runs on the southern flank and crossed over onto the Malheur. With the acknowledgement of the IMT, fire staff personnel on the Malheur organized and dispatched approximately 8 crews, 5 engines, and 9 miscellaneous overhead to take suppression action on the Summit Fire. At approximately 1800 hours on 8/26, 53 firefighters traveling in 5 vehicles, became entrapped when their escape route was compromised. The engine paint was completely heat scorched. The engine was the only vehicle to sustain damage. There were no physical injuries.
incidents.quote: Some individuals deployed fire shelters and held them up against bus windows as a precautionary measure.

incidents.name: Marple Branch II
incidents.summary: In addition, six hand-crews were forced to abandon their line construction assignment, and make an emergency exit to the Crew Carrier Vehicles (CCV). The upper most five crews were able reach their CCV in a timely manner. The sixth crew that was committed to the lowest point in the operations was impacted by heat and smoke on their exit and incurred flame impingement to their vehicle upon their exit. An unauthorized burn-out operation had taken place in Division E. The main fire spread was influenced by the burn-out operation. After the review, it is unclear if the burn-out operation caused Division G's "Close Call."
incidents.quote: At the Marple Incident on Wednesday, August 28, 1996 at approximately 1430 hours, a situation occurred in Branch II, Division G. The Division G supervisor received second degree burns on his left ear and his vehicle was damaged on the left side.

incidents.name: Dutch Flat Fire Entrapment 1996
incidents.summary: A Type 2 IMT is assigned to the Upper Humboldt Complex of lightning fires in northern Nevada. On day three of the assignment, on August 31, 1996, the Incident Commander, two Ops Chiefs, an Ops trainee, and a DIVS met near one of the main values at risk (a mine) to formulate a plan. They implement an impromptu firing operation. During the firing operation a fire whirl forms, causing an entrapment with burn injuries.

incidents.name: Shepard Mountain
incidents.summary: The Shepard Mountain Fire blew-up when a high-velocity, unpredicted wind event moved the fire approximately 8 miles in less than 11 hours. The fire spread rapidly down-canyon, growing from approximately 800 acres to 8,000 acres in that time. Fire behavior was extreme, exceeding any ability to control the fire.
incidents.quote: 13 firefighters deployed fire shelters in three different locations.

incidents.name: Lizzie Springs Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: On October 3, 1996, weather conditions allowed the north and east perimeter of the Lizzie Springs Prescribed Fire unit to be burned first providing a control line so that the remainder of the unit could be completed. The critical Lizzie Creek drainage was then burned to take advantage of the higher fuel moisture. Burning continued and the unit was completed in October 4 and all people involved felt good about their accomplishments. On the eighth day (Oct. 12) after the burn, the fire escaped early in the evening when dry conditions and high winds prevailed. On Oct. 13 a Type 2 Incident Management Team was ordered by the District FCO (Burn Boss trainee) to take over the fire that ultimately burned about 350 areas in heavy subalpine timber.
incidents.quote: On the eighth day after the burn, the fire escaped early in the evening when dry conditions and high winds prevailed.

incidents.name: Calabasas Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: A sudden fire run up an 80% brush-covered slope overran structure protection positions, causing 2nd and 3rd degree burns to multiple firefighters.
incidents.quote: The six members of Glendale Engine 24 and Los Angeles City Engine 10 were injured at approximately 1244 hours on October 22, 1996

incidents.name: San Carlos Indian Reservation Reconnaissance Aircraft Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: A Beech 95-B55, N8KB, collided with terrain during a routine fire reconnaissance of the San Carlos Indian Reservation (SCIR), San Carlos, Arizona. The aircraft was being operated by Safford Aviation, under an exclusive use contract to the Bureau of Indian Affairs as a public-use aircraft. The aircraft was destroyed during the impact sequence and subsequent post crash fire. The certificated commercial pilot and his observer received fatal injuries.
incidents.quote: The mission was a routine fire patrol.

incidents.name: San Benito County OV-10 Aircraft Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: David Robert Kyle, pilot, departed from Meadows Field, Bakersfield, California, on a local training flight. Witnesses at the station reported seeing the aircraft fly by their location at approximately 200 feet above the ground and enter a right roll to a near inverted attitude. It then was observed to reverse the direction of roll in what appeared to be an attempt by the pilot to level the wings. The aircraft was then observed to impact the ground in a 90-degree right bank with approximately a 30-degree nose down pitch attitude.
incidents.quote: Kyle, an experienced helicopter and fixed wing pilot, had logged just 21 hours on this aircraft type; this was cited as a factor in the accident.

incidents.name: Flat Fire Civilian Entrapment/Fatality
incidents.summary: A member of the public unaffiliated with the wildland fire response to the Flat Fire on the BLM Richfield District in Utah was entrapped and passed away while trying to more a friend's trailer to safety.
incidents.quote: Extreme fire behavior conditions prevented any opportunity to successfully attempt a rescue.

incidents.name: Logan Fire Entrapments
incidents.summary: 8/6: There was an unexpected windshift from NE to SW winds which resulted in a shelter deployment involving an engine resulting in minor injuries 8/7: There was a shelter deployment involving 3 dozers and a pickup truck. Fortunately a helicopter was able to transport 4 people away from the site.
incidents.quote: Two entrapments occurred on the Logan Fire. The first involved two hotshot crews and seven engines performing a burnout operation in Div A on August 6, 1997 at approximately 1400. The second involved three dozers and a strike team leader constructing line in Div X on August 7, 1997.

incidents.name: Anderson Ranch Fire Vehicle Burn Damage
incidents.summary: The Anderson Creek Fire started on August 8 at approximately 1445. The location is northeast of section 23, northwest of section 24, T. 1 N., R. 9 E. at the confluence of Lester Creek and the South Fork of the Boise River, Anderson Ranch Reservoir. It was reported by Trinity lookout and an employee doing a Goshawk survey. A fire burning on the east side of Lester Creek at the confluence of the South Fork Boise River outflanked the line construction efforts and also spotted to the north side of the drainage adjacent to the control operations. The combination of these two events caused a rapid uphill run with 10 to 15-foot flame lengths. The crew retreated into their safety zone, the burn, with one person experiencing heat and smoke problems. Vehicle 4965 was damaged by the passing flame front.
incidents.quote: Forest Service vehicle 4965, a 4x4 3/4‑ton pick‑up, sustained damage to the emergency brake, front tires, windshield wipers, paint/chrome, and the plastic grill components.

incidents.name: BLM Prescribed Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Assistant Fire Management Officer Ottonello died due to an asthma attack at a prescribed burn. Respiratory arrest led to heart failure. Crews initiated CPR, but to no avail.

incidents.name: Colorado City Water Tender Rollover Fatality 1998
incidents.summary: Firefighter McKinney was driving a converted tanker from one brush fire to another when he lost control of the tanker as it crossed a narrow bridge. The tanker rolled three times after the right rear wheels of the vehicle caught on a concrete guardrail. A firefighter who was a passenger in the tanker was injured in the collision. Firefighter McKinney was ejected.

incidents.name: Leggett Fire Air Tanker Crash Fatalities
incidents.summary: On June 27, 1998, at 2024 mountain daylight time, a Lockheed SP-2H (U.S. Navy P2V-7), N14835, owned and operated by Neptune Aviation Service, Inc., of Missoula, Montana, and contracted to the U.S. Forest Service, was destroyed when it collided with trees about 5 miles west of Reserve, New Mexico, on the Leggett Fire. According to both the U.S. Forest Service and Neptune Aviation Service, Inc., the crew of N14835 (call sign "Tanker 8") had been engaged in fire fighting operations all day. The first officer, an initial attack trainee pilot, was in the left seat. The pilot in command was in the right seat.
incidents.quote: Carrying 2,450 gallons of retardant, the airplane had made a dry pass on the fire zone about 2020, then circled around to make a second pass and release its load. According to witnesses, the airplane struck trees while in a nose low, right wing low attitude. Upon ground impact, the airplane exploded and burned. Pilots Jerry David Donahue and Charles Franklin Key were killed in the accident.

incidents.name: Banner Queen Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: The Banner Queen Prescribed Fire, an approximately 650-acre project in mature chaparral, was planned on BLM-owned land within CDF's Direct Protection Area in the El Centro Resource Area. The burn was first ignited on July 1, 1998, at approximately 1235 hours. This first ignition was a test burn ignited on a ridge top on the Southeastern portion of the burn block. Shortly after ignition, two spot fires occurred. A 10 person crew, with the assistance of helicopter bucket drops were able to contain the first spot. One of the helicopters (H-538, a type II with fixed tank) experienced a malfunction with the tank door and had to shut down for repairs after making only one droр. The second spot grew to about 2 acres, despite efforts to suppress it. This spot fire spread into steep terrain that was inaccessible and unsafe for ground crews. When the spot fire reached four acres in size, the prescribed burn was declared an escape.
incidents.quote: Malfunction of the helicopter's belly tank was a critical factor in the escape.

incidents.name: Crane Swamp Fire Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: A strike team leader with two dozers was struck by a tree while directing line construction in heavy brush on the Crane Swamp Fire in Florida. One of the dozer operators saw the STL's boots sticking out of the brush and stopped to initiate medical care and evacuation.

incidents.name: Alabama Forestry Commission Medical Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Goodwin was stricken with a heart attack at the scene of a wildland fire. The fire was caused by children playing with bottle rockets. Firefighter Goodwin had been operating on the scene for about four hours. He had been plowing a fire line.

incidents.name: Southern Oaks VFD Hit by Vehicle Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Hamilton was on the back step of a pumper as it was relocated at the scene of a brush fire. The pumper was backing up, Firefighter Hamilton was on the back step to secure hose that had been reloaded. As the pumper backed up, Firefighter Hamilton attempted to warn the driver about a utility pole that was behind the apparatus. He apparently lost his grip and was crushed between the pumper and the pole. His right leg was amputated below the knee. Despite the efforts of local EMS providers, Firefighter Hamilton died of hypovolemic shock (loss of blood).

incidents.name: Los Angeles County Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Carrasco was killed in a vehicle collision while working as a member of an inmate handcrew. The brush/engine vehicle in which he was riding rolled over. Eleven others were injured.

incidents.name: Lincoln National Forest Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: The engine in which he was riding was stuck by a pickup truck that crossed the center line and impacted the engine along the left underside and rear dual wheels. The engine flipped and landed upside down. Firefighter Hernandez was wearing a seat belt but was partially ejected from the vehicle. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
incidents.quote: Juan Manuel Hernandez, Jr., USDA Forest Service firefighter with the Lincoln National Forest, was killed in a vehicle collision while working near Willows, California.

incidents.name: West Mountain 2 Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: At approximately 0400 hours on September 19, 1998, a shelter deployment of a Salt Lake County Crew Representative took place approximately one half mile west of the Payson Dump on the West Mountain 2 fire, Uinta National Forest in Region 4. West Mountain is located approximately 60 miles south of Salt Lake City on the southeast end of Utah Lake.
incidents.quote: The deployment was executed more as a precautionary measure than for life threatening reasons. No injuries were sustained.

incidents.name: Edna Fire Air Tanker Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: Airtanker Pilot Nagel was killed in the crash of a Grumman TS-2A airtanker when he misjudged his maneuvering altitude and impacted the terrain. He had made two drops on the Mount Edna fire near Banning, California and was preparing to make a third. Other factors that contributed to the crash were the mountainous terrain, tailwind conditions, and turbulence in the area. Airtanker Pilot Nagel was an employee of San Joaquin Helicopters, a contractor to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

incidents.name: Taylor Fire Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Captain Wall (age 44) died at the Taylor fire in Riverside, California. He was protecting exposed dwellings when he told other firefighters that he did not feel well and collapsed. Captain Wall died of a heart attack.

incidents.name: San Benito-Monterey Unit Heavy Equipment Rollover Fatality
incidents.summary: Roger DeWayne Bookout‚ 34‚ a heavy fire equipment operator for the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (now CAL FIRE)‚ died on November 18‚ 1998‚ in an unwitnessed heavy equipment rollover while performing fire break maintenance work.

incidents.name: Waters Gulch Prescribed Fire Incident
incidents.summary: A prescribed fire unit on Northern California's Shasta-Trinity National Forest was ignited by aerial ignition with helitorch on January 11, 1999. While ignitions were in progress, a weather observer inside the unit was nearly entrapped and burned. The observer escaped the unit without injury and ignitions were suspended.
incidents.quote: When the pilot spotted Anna on the ground, he immediately shut off the helitorch, contacted the Ignition Boss, and left the area.

incidents.name: Casa Grande Fire Entrapment 1999
incidents.summary: Fire behavior became extremely active as the spot fire increased in size and several strong upslope and across slope runs were experienced. At approximately 1430 on May 4, 1999, the fire made a run that entrapped four fire fighters by cutting off their escape route. Two of the fire fighters deployed their fire shelters. No injuries were experienced by the four entrapped fire fighters, and after the fire passed through the area, forces were regrouped and suppression operations resumed.

incidents.name: Donnelly Flats Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On July 11, 1999. on the Donnelly Fire on U.S. Army Fort Greely lands in Alaska, seven smokejumpers were separated into two groups. One group was looking for spot fires in an unburned area and the other worked on improving the fireline. As the fire activity increased, the decision was made to pull off the line. Visibility was poor due to vegetation. As the smokejumpers began to run down the line, they saw a whirlwind come out of the black, picking up embers and re-igniting burned and unburned material. This whirlwind cut between the two groups and forced them to take refuge in the "black" safety zone. One smokejumper was overtaken by the whirlwind and received first and second degree burns. He received medical attention; no permanent damage occurred.
incidents.quote: The black spruce had been burned very well with only the trunks standing allowing the smokejumpers to make quick, good progress. Wattenbarger looked back again and realized that the fire whirl was still on the same course as the jumpers and they began to make direction changes but the whirl still seemed to follow them. As it gained ground, the fire whirl began to "suck" air from in front of the smokejumpers and the wind increased picking up ash and debris and cutting visibility to only a few feet. As Wattenbarger followed, he got hung up on a small spruce tree; he dropped his beater, and tried to continue. Before he could get around the tree, he lost sight of his companions and the wind increased to the point where he thought he was going to get picked up so he grabbed for the nearest tree. Before reaching the trunk it ignited and began glowing orange, as did everything he could see around him including the ground.

incidents.name: Lowden Ranch Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: On July 2, 1999, a prescribed fire ignited by personnel from the Redding Field Office of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) escaped control and was declared a wildland fire. The Lowden Ranch Fire grew to approximately 2,000 acres and destroyed 23 residences before it was contained under management of a California Department of Forestry (CDF) incident management team. BLM’s director of the National Office of Fire and Aviation assembled an interagency team to determine the factors that caused the prescribed burn to escape. This is the review team’s final report.

incidents.name: Wagon Box Fire Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: Five crew members received burn injuries at three different times and locations. The crew superintendent removed the crew from the fireline after the final burn injuries were sustained to allow crew members to receive medical treatment.
incidents.quote: Resources were being requested continuously for the fire as it continued to grow in size.

incidents.name: Sadler Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Six firefighters were entrapped by wildland fire as they conducted a backfiring operation on the Sadler Complex in Elko, Nevada.
incidents.quote: The briefing started without an announcement, and some of the crews and overhead missed part or all of it.

incidents.name: Wilson Gulch Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: A prescribed fire escaped on the BLM's Upper Snake River District, Shoshone Resource Area, in 1999
incidents.quote: More collaboration is needed between the Resource Area and Fire Management in weighing the alternatives for the timing of the burns in this fuel type.

incidents.name: Jones Fire Hit/Run Over Fatality
incidents.summary: Hit or Run Over by Vehicle
incidents.quote: Jones Fire Hit/Run Over Fatality

incidents.name: Delmont Volunteer Fire Department Fatality
incidents.summary: n March 6, 2000, a 62-year-old volunteer firefighter was overrun by a wind-driven grass fire while pulling uncharged hose in a pasture near Delmont, SD. The victim was transported to a regional hospital where he died 9 days later of complications from burns.
incidents.quote: As fire moved up the ravine toward the suppression crew, the nozzleman ran toward the fence line to escape the fire and heat. He collapsed at the edge of the fence line, due to the burn injuries he had received.

incidents.name: Smokejumper Refresher Qualification Jump Fatality
incidents.summary: On April 29,2000, David J. Liston, a temporary forestry technition (smokejumper) with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), AFS, at Ft. Wainright, Alaska, was fatally injured in a pre-season refresher qualification jump.
incidents.quote: The evidence shows that Liston's drogue parachute deployed but the main parachute did not.

incidents.name: Engine 73 Damage
incidents.summary: During initial attack operations on the Clover Fire, located on the Long Valley portion of the Blue Ridge/Long Valley Ranger District of the Coconino National Forest, Engine 73 (E-73) became cut-off from their escape route and was forced to abandon their vehicle. The crew escaped to another engine (E-71). E-73 was destroyed by fire. Two E-73 crewmembers sustained minor injuries to the hand and face.

incidents.name: Cerro Grande Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: In Spring 2000, staff at Bandelier National Monument in New Mexico prepared and approved a Prescribed Fire Plan for the Upper Frijoles 1 and 5 Burn Units. This burn plan covered a project area of approximately 1000 acres located in the northwest portion of Bandelier National Monument and adjacent to the Santa Fe National Forest in north-central New Mexico. On May 4th, Phase I of the prescribed fire was ignited and eventually escaped the planned boundaries, becoming known as the Cerro Grande Fire. It ultimately spread into the town of Los Alamos, New Mexico, destroying 235 structures and also spread onto lands administered or owned by the Santa Fe National Forest, the Los Alamos National Laboratory, and the San Idelfonso and Santa Clara Pueblos.
incidents.quote: "As both the Los Alamos and other recent fires demonstrate, much of the risk to communities--as well as to federal forests--can be reduced by fuel reduction efforts on adjacent lands." - Statement of Barry T. Hill, Associate Director - Energy, Resources, and Science Issues, Resources, Community, and Economic Development Division (during Testimony Before the Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health, Committee on Resources, House of Representatives)

incidents.name: Spade Fire Firing Operation Lawsuit
incidents.summary: On September 9, 2006, Judge Molloy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Montana, ruled on a tort action against the U.S. Government brought by Allstate Insurance and a group of private landowners who had lost property in a wildland fire suppression operation during the Spade Fire in the Bitterroot Valley of Western Montana during August 2000. Judge Molloy ruled in favor of the government.
incidents.quote: "Plaintiffs' complaint alleges that Government firefighters destroyed Plaintiffs' property by negligently lighting backfires on August 6, 2000, during firefighting operations in Montana's Bitterroot Valley. Defendant claims immunity from suit under the discretionary function exception to the Federal Tort Claims Act. After review of the pleadings, briefs and submissions, in my view, the Defendant is correct . . ."

incidents.name: Concow Fire Engine Entrapment 2000
incidents.summary: On Tuesday, September 19, 2000, at approximately 1515 hrs, a CDF engine crew was involved in a burn over situation that developed into a fire shelter deployment. During the course of structure protection, a decision was made to increase the safety provided by the escape road by firing the vegetation along both sides of the roadway for approximately 100 yards. After completing their firing operation, the crew realized the route back to their engine was cutoff by fire. They deployed their fire shelters for protection for the heat until the fire crossed the roadway. One firefighter received a minor burn to his left forearm, the other firefighter suffered from heat exhaustion.

incidents.name: Concow Fire Hit by Tree 2000
incidents.summary: On Tuesday, September 19, 2000, a CDF engine company engaging in initial attack fire suppression activities was involved in an accident with a falling oak snag. During initial attack the fire captain on the engine recognized that several snags along the road just ahead of the engine posed a significant risk. The fire captain elected to walk, swamping in front of the engine. A firefighter was assigned to drive the engine. The fire captain had noticed a snag that had fallen across the road and had the firefighter driving the engine stop at what appeared to be a safe location. While the engine was stopped, a snag just above the road and the engine snapped, falling on a second firefighter and the engine. The firefighter sustained minor injuries from the tree, and the engine sustained moderate damage.

incidents.name: Concow Fire Public Evacuation Burn Injury 2000
incidents.summary: At 0225 hrs on September 20, 2000, a CDF on the Concow Fire responded to a residence int he path of the fire. The engine captain entered the structure and found nobody awake at the time. Meanwhile a firefighter from the engine stretched two hoselines to protect the house. The captain located a sleeping resident and awoke her, then began to assist her in leaving the home. The fire impacted a detached garage and involvement of the residence was imminent. The firefighter broke down the hoselay for immediate retreat. The captain could not convince the resident to leave the home, as she feared for the safety of her pets. The captain followed the resident back into the home and began closing interior doors to slow fire spread as the home became involved. The resident could not escape through the small bedroom window, the captain used this as means of escape from the home. The fire captain received burns to 11% of his body. The engine escaped the area, the resident perished in the structure.

incidents.name: Smith Fire Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: Two nearly simultaneous incidents occurred on two separate divisions of a 10-15 acre wildland fire in Calaveras County, California. The results of these two incidents were first and second degree burns to three California Department of Forestry firefighters and a twisted knee and ankle to another California Department of Forestry firefighter.
incidents.quote: The initial attack, although a sounds decision, was downhill.

incidents.name: Larkspur Fire Protection District Work Capacity Test Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighters were called to the scene, and they provided emergency medical care. Captain Shaffer was transported to a local hospital. He was pronounced dead 10 minutes after his arrival at the emergency room.
incidents.quote: Captain Jay Shaffer was half way toward completion of a 3-mile pack test to become certified to fight wildfires when he collapsed of an apparent heart attack.

incidents.name: Beaver Rim Engine Burn Over
incidents.summary: On July 4, 2001, Brush Engine 941 and Water Tanker 931 responded to a fire on Sheep Mountain, with the Brush Engine crew hiking about 30 minutes to reach the fire burning in grass, sagebrush, and scattered trees. As a thunderstorm shifted fire spread around 1750 hours, the firefighters retreated south along the ridge and asked for their engine to be moved. By around 1800 hours, Water Tanker 931 reported that Brush Engine 941 was already in view and had most likely been burned over.
incidents.quote: They could see Brush Engine 941's location and that it was most likely already burned over.

incidents.name: Cottonwood Creek Fire Airtanker Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: On July 10, 2001, about 1114 Pacific daylight time, a Rockwell International S-2R-1200 (Thrush), N4947X, was destroyed by impact forces and a post-crash fire after colliding with terrain approximately 20 miles southwest of Cottonwood, Idaho. The pilot, Douglas Gilbert, was the sole occupant of the aircraft and was fatally injured. The flight originated from Craigmont, Idaho, approximately 35 minutes prior to the accident. The airplane, loaded with approximately 450 gallons of fire retardant, departed Craigmont, Idaho, at 1040. The pilot reported to fire crews on the ground that he was going to fly down the east flank of the fire, through the smoke, and drop the retardant.
incidents.quote: A witness on the ground stated the airplane approached from the southwest, near the top of the canyon. He reported that initially he didn't see the airplane, but could only hear it flying down the east flank of the fire. Shortly thereafter, he reported seeing "…a big ball of fire several hundred feet below me, and thought he [the pilot] must have hit something.

incidents.name: Thirtymile Fire Fatalities
incidents.summary: On July 10, 2001, four Forest Service fire suppression personnel were killed after they became entrapped and their fire shelter deployment site was burned over by the Thirtymile Fire, in the Chewuch River Canyon, about 30 miles north of Winthrop, Washington. 14 members of the Northwest Regulars #6 Type 2 crew were suppressing spot fires along the road when the flame front cut off their escape route down canyon. They retreated up the canyon to find a safe spot with extensive rock scree above the road, where they met two civilians fleeing down the canyon.
incidents.quote: At 5:24 p.m., the behavior of the fire changed dramatically. In spite of the lack of forest vegetation and brush in the immediate vicinity of the crew, the immensity of the fire overwhelmed the area and the crew. The abruptness of this change appears to have caught the crew by surprise. They were not in a heightened state of readiness. Shelter deployment was no longer optional but essential if any were to survive.

incidents.name: Virginia Lake Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: A line scout and a contract dozer operator were entrapped on the Virginia Lake Fire on the Colville Indian Reservation. They retreated into a meadow, used the dozer to clear a deployment area and deployed their fire shelters. Both individuals were in their shelters for a period of 30 minutes. As soon as the fire front passed, the individuals were picked up by helicopter and transported off the fire.
incidents.quote: They each had mild smoke inhalation and one had a small burn on his hand that needed no additional treatment.

incidents.name: Labor Fire Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: The crew spent the night laying hose and cold trailing hot spots outside of the main fire area. The next morning, Firefighter Rendek was cutting down dangerous trees (falling snags) with a chainsaw. Firefighter Rendek said that he only needed a few more minutes to work and then he was going to rest. As he walked downhill to his work area, a pine tree with a diameter of 11 inches fell and struck Firefighter Rendek on the head and shoulders. When other firefighters reached Firefighter Rendek, he was not breathing and a pulse could not be found. CPR was initiated and then stopped when Firefighter Rendek began to breathe on his own. Firefighter Rendek’s condition deteriorated and CPR was reinitiated. Firefighter Rendek was removed from the remote area where he was injured via a pickup truck and an All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV). CPR was in-progress until Firefighter Rendek was placed on a medical helicopter approximately one hour and 45 minutes later. Firefighter Rendek died in flight.
incidents.quote: At approximately 1:00 a.m., Firefighter David Rendek and other wildland firefighters were organized as a crew and sent to size up a lightning-caused wildland fire near Sula, Montana on the Bitterroot National Forest. When they arrived, they found that it was too dangerous to fight the fire in the dark due to steep terrain and a large amount of dead wood. The decision was made to wait until morning to fight the fire.

incidents.name: Alkali Rim Prescribed Fire Review
incidents.summary: On September 20, 2001, on the Alkali Rim Prescribed Fire, an increase in fire behavior--fueled by a wind switch and relative humidity--led to five firefighters using their escape routes and safety zones. No employees were injured and no fire shelters were deployed. After this escape event, the igniters’ crew leader immediately assembled the crew members and had an initial crew de­briefing. At approximately 1500 hours, all personnel on the prescribed fire gathered for a meeting to discuss the activity. By 1530 hours, they were back to burning and burned until approximately 1630.
incidents.quote: At 1400 the fire increased in intensity with the wind switch and lowering relative humidities and began a short crown fire run. The group of igniters made the decision to use their escape routes to safety zones.

incidents.name: 70 Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: While working spot fires on the 70 Fire below Highway 70 in the North Fork Feather River canyon northeast of Oroville, California, two engines became entrapped by a sudden upslope fire run. Seven firefighters deployed fire shelters in the black, while two others escaped up the hoselay to a midslope road where the engines were parked. Once the flaming front had passed, all firefighters returned to their engines, when another fire run forced them to return to their fire shelters on the road. In this second deployment, nine firefighters used fire shelters to survive the entrapment. One firefighter received a minor burn to the back of the neck.
incidents.quote: After the wave of flames subsided, they went back into their engine only to have another wave of flames and heat force them out of their engine and they redeployed.

incidents.name: Daddy Ridge Fatality
incidents.summary: On November 10, 2001 at 6:31 p.m., Hairold Strode, a seasonal Division of Forestry employee, was killed when a wildfire overran his crew near the top of a narrow hollow on the Daddy’s Ridge Fire.
incidents.quote: The interaction of light flashy fuels, steep and rocky terrain, and an undetected ignition below the crew.

incidents.name: Cameron Volunteer Fire Department Water Tender Accident
incidents.summary: The driver survived with injuries after being airlifted, but White died of internal trauma after being trapped in the crushed cab.
incidents.quote: On November 19, 2001, a 2,000-gallon water tender suffered brake failure and rolled down a 50-foot embankment in West Virginia, killing firefighter Clifford White Jr.

incidents.name: Back Forty Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: On March 24, 2002, a wildland fire was reported on private land in northeastern Tennessee. Two federal firefighters (one U.S. Forest Service employee and one U.S. Department of Interior, Fish and Wildlife Service employee, were assigned to initial attack the Back Forty Fire. The two firefighters were dispatched to the scene and began flagging a dozer line. Shortly after arrival at the incident, at approximately 1330 hours, the employees were entrapped and deployed their fire shelters. The fire burned over them. There were no injuries.
incidents.quote: Nelson and Garland then burned a spot, raked it out, and cleared an area for their shelter deployment.

incidents.name: Engine 3561 Entrapment
incidents.summary: Engine 3561 responded from Owens Valley Camp, arrived on scene at approximately 1320 hrs and initiated suppression action by attempting to get to the head of the fire. While driving through the green to access the head of the fire, Engine 3561 suffered a rapid air loss to the brake system and became immobile. The fire advanced beyond Engine 3561 on the west and south side of the engine. A sudden change in wind direction and speed caused the fire to advance directly towards the engine at a rapid rate. Despite efforts by the crew from Engine 3561 and units of the Bishop Fire Department, the fire consumed Engine 3561 at approximately 1404 hrs. The Fire Captain and both Firefighters suffer smoke inhalation in the attempt to save Engine 3561. The Fire Captain and Firefighters were transported to a local hospital for treatment and placed off duty by the treating physician for three days due to smoke inhalation.

incidents.name: Anderson/Danskin Escaped Prescribed Fires
incidents.summary: Two prescribed burns escaped during a strong cold front passage, resulting in a 400-acre wind-driven crown fire managed as a single wildfire operation.
incidents.quote: Prescribed fire typifies the concept of 'managing the unexpected.' Weather is oftentimes not perfectly predicted, and human judgment must be used.

incidents.name: Sanford Escaped Prescribed Fire Review
incidents.summary: On April 22, 2002, the planned 1,500-­acre Sanford Prescribed Fire is ignited on the Dixie National Forest’s Powell Ranger District. On May 13, eleven miles southeast of the Sanford Prescribed Fire project, the planned 2,000­-acre Adams Head Prescribed Fire is ignited. By June, these two prescribed fires escape their containment boundaries and become the 78,000­-acre Sanford Wildland Fire.
incidents.quote: What had started out as a prescribed fire to help prevent future catastrophic fires had turned into a catastrophic fire with the destruction of important fisheries and undesirable smoke impacts.

incidents.name: Cannon Fire Aircraft Fatalities
incidents.summary: Fatigue cracking in the center wing box caused both wings to fold upward and separate during leveling maneuvers.
incidents.quote: On June 17, 2002, a C-130A airtanker experienced inflight structural wing failure during a retardant drop on the Cannon Fire near Walker, CA, killing all three flight crew members.

incidents.name: Parachute MVA Fatalities
incidents.summary: On June 21, 2002, at 1720, a 15-passenger van carrying 11 firefighters from La Grande, Oregon to the Hayman Fire in Colorado was involved in a one-vehicle accident one and a half miles east of Parachute, Colorado on Interstate 70.

incidents.name: Price Canyon Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On June 30, 2002, The Price Canyon fire was ignited by a railroad train on BLM lands north of Price, Utah. The initial attack response included a mix of resources including 8 smokejumpers. Shortly after arriving on the fire, a group of five smokejumpers carried out a firing operation to create a safety zone for themselves and their gear and to secure that flank of the fire. Fire behavior of the main fire increased until the fire experienced a column collapse, sending fire running towards the jumpers. They became entrapped, with three outrunning the fire on foot and two deploying fire shelters for over 30 minutes. The smokejumpers were uninjured.
incidents.quote: All five jumpers immediately began running.

incidents.name: Marble
incidents.summary: Exposed to the high winds, the fire burned rapidly across the upper slopes of Marble Mountain and caused firefighters at the North Marble Fire to deploy fire shelters in a rockslide at about 2130 hours. These firefighters remained in their fire shelters for about 1-½ hours, enduring high heat, smoke, and embers entering their fire shelters from underneath. Firefighters at the East Marble Fire were preparing to enter the black at about 2130 hours when information over the radio on fire status convinced them to walk out. They discarded their line gear and, with fire shelters in hand, walked down and out of the canyon. None of the firefighters suffered burns or other physical injuries. All six firefighters attended a Critical Incident Debriefing.
incidents.quote: Lightning started two fires on Marble Mountain the afternoon of July 14, 2002. Two initial attack modules of three firefighters each were formed to suppress both fires. Both fires were in a remote location with steep slopes, dense vegetation, and no roads. Both initial attack modules were inserted by 2000 hours. By 2100 hours, winds began to increase at a steady pace.

incidents.name: Big Elk Fire Air Tanker Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: On July 18, 2002, at 1840 mountain daylight time, a Consolidated-Vultee P4Y-2, N7620C, under contract to the U. S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service and piloted by a commercial pilot, was destroyed when it impacted into mountainous terrain 6 miles southwest of Estes Park, Colorado. A post-crash explosion and fire ensued. Prior to the impact, the airplane's left wing separated and aircraft control was lost while maneuvering to deliver fire retardant on the Big Elk wildfire, burning in an area northwest of Lyons, Colorado.
incidents.quote: The witnesses then said the left wing "folded upward" and severed at the "left wing-fuselage point." They all described "slurry" coming out and "fire erupting" from the area where the wing separated. The witnesses said the airplane rapidly descended and impacted into the hillside.

incidents.name: Tool Box Complex Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: A contract 20-person “Ferguson 53 Crew," deployed their fire shelters while in an area that had been constructed as a safety zone by a bulldozer. The deployment lasted approximately 15 minutes. Later that evening, crewmembers were treated by medical personnel in fire camp for burns and smoke inhalation. Eleven crewmembers were then transported to St. Charles Hospital in Bend, Oregon. Two crewmembers had received minor burns and nine crewmembers were impacted by smoke inhalation. They were all treated and released.
