incidents.quote: "I ordered the deployment to calm the fears and give protection against the heat."

incidents.name: Stanza Engine Rollover Fatality
incidents.summary: Lassen National Forest Engine 11 (Type III) with a five-person crew was moving slowly along a single lane Forest Service road on the Klamath National Forest approximately 20 miles south of Happy Camp, California. The driver side tires left the outside edge of the road and the Engine rolled off the road and down a steep slope approximately 1000 feet down. The driver, the engine captain, and one fireman from the rear passenger compartment were ejected and fatally injured.
incidents.quote: All occupants were wearing seatbelts. Three crewmembers were ejected from the vehicle and fatally injured as it rolled down the hill.

incidents.name: Tiller Complex
incidents.summary: The employee took a break to swim in the South Umpqua River that is immediately adjacent to the Helibase. The employee was swinging from a rope swing tied to a tree along the riverbank when she lost her grip and fell to the ground. She rolled and slid into the water. Coworkers assisted her, the on-site medic stabilized her, and she was medevacked to the Rogue Valley Medical Center in Medford, Oregon. The employee incurred a severed spinal cord and crushed vertebrae.
incidents.quote: The helicopters were down due to an inversion.

incidents.name: Curve Fire Engine Entrapment
incidents.summary: On September 1, 2002, at approximately 1400 hours, three engines (2 Angeles National Forest and 1 San Bernardino National Forest) assigned to the Curve Fire had traveled on a one-way single-lane dead-end road. They were assigned structure protection and evaluating the situation to see if they could protect several cabins. As the three IA engines positioned near the cabins, they noticed a wall of flames traveling upriver toward them. As propane tanks began venting, the engines moved farther up the dead-end road to locate a safety zone. The engines were trapped, but positioned themselves in the safest place possible. All individuals stayed in their engines and although shelters we not deployed, two were used inside the cab of one engine to shield the heat. At least one engine crew used their SCBA because of excessive smoke in the cab. There were no injuries. The San Bernardino engine received heat damage to: paint, melted lights, and radio antenna. At least 6 cabins were destroyed.

incidents.name: Leona
incidents.summary: On September 3, 2002, at approximately 1415 hours, two Los Angeles County Fire Department Engine crews responded as part of a first-alarm assignment to a wildland fire located at 37881 Bouquet Canyon Road in the Angeles National Forest. The fire was impinging on a structure that one of the engines had been assigned to protect. Due to the radiant heat, the engine crew decided to enter the engine. One of the occupants suggested that they use their shelters to deflect the radiant heat from entering the engine cab. They used two shelters to wrap the engine's rear windows of the engine. The crew members remained in the engine's cab for 3-5 minutes as the flame front passed. The Captain checked all of the crews for health and injury and found everyone OK. The damage to one engine consisted of blistered varnish on the ladder and some melted plastic on the control panel on the engine's left side.
incidents.quote: Due to the radiant heat, the engine crew decided to enter the engine. One of the occupants suggested that they use their shelters to deflect the radiant heat from entering the engine cab.

incidents.name: Metolius Research Natural Area Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.fire: Metolius Research Natural Area prescribed fire
incidents.summary: Two Metolius Research Natural Area (RNA) units--both 28-acres in size--were burned on October 9, 2002. At 0900 the next day, a six­-person group arrived at a spot fire on Unit 12 to patrol and mop-up hot spots as needed to contain the burn within its containment lines. At approximately 1500 hours, a large volume of smoke was observed on Unit 62. The handcrew's leader investigated and found the fire had escaped the containment lines and was burning rapidly uphill to the east. They initiated suppression activities, including the use of aerially-delivered retardant. On the morning of October 11, when the fire continued to burn actively and required more retardant, the incident was declared an escape.
incidents.quote: At approximately 1500 hours, a large volume of smoke was observed on Unit 62.

incidents.name: Deary Motor Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: On October 22, 2002, at 1230 hours, an Idaho Department of Lands Type 4 750-gallon engine rolled on State Highway 3, approximately five miles south of Deary, Idaho. The injured driver was transferred to Harbor View Hospital in Seattle where he was reported in stable condition with 2nd and 3rd degree burns over 30 percent of his body. There were no other passengers, injuries, or vehicles involved.

incidents.name: Shuttle Recovery Helicopter Crash
incidents.summary: A Bell 407 helicopter involved in the search for Space Shuttle Columbia debris crashed in the Angelina National Forest. Five crew members were aboard the helicopter. There were two fatalities and three injuries.
incidents.quote: While establishing a 125-foot out of ground effect hover during a search and recovery mission of Columbia Space Shuttle debris, the helicopter lost power without warning, descended rapidly into a forest with 80-foot tall trees, and impacted the ground.

incidents.name: Sink's Canyon Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: Personnel on Unit PF2 of the Sink’s Canyon prescribed fire in Wyoming experienced a wind shift that caused the fire to burn into the established MMA (Maximum Management Area) and subsequently out of the MMA. The fire also flared up from a spot fire on April 13 and burned four more acres outside of the MMA and into the MMA for Unit 3.
incidents.quote: Finding: It was never declared an escaped prescribed fire. Due to the lack of a clear-cut definition in the burn plan, there was never a definite decision point. Recommendation: Develop a clear definition of an escape based on values at risk, resistance to control or other parameters for each prescribed fire.

incidents.name: A Bar Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On the afternoon of May 11, 2003, while conducting initial action on the A-Bar Fire on the Sierra Vista Ranger District, Coronado National Forest, the fire spotted across a two-track road and cut off a Type 6 Engine and crew. Recognizing the situation, the crew foreman and two crewmembers burned out a 40’ by 80’ safe zone. The crew then deployed shelters and the fire burned around the safe zone. There were no injuries and the engine received very minor damage.

incidents.name: Sawtooth Rx Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On May 14, 2003, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Fort Apache Agency fire fighter Rick Lupe sustained burn injuries while working on a prescribed burn operation. At approximately 1430 a lookout reported an increase in fire behavior activity on the southeast portion of the burn. Mr. Laupe advised the lookout that he would recon the area of concern. A short time later, the area being investigated by Mr. Lupe experienced extreme fire behavior, burning 30 acres. Mr. Lupe attempted to deploy his fire shelter but strong winds ripped the shelter from his hands. Mr. Lupe was evacuated to the Arizona Burn center but died from his burns several days later.
incidents.quote: “I tried deploying my shelter, but the fire took it away from me, I walked through it, it happened so fat, so fast, it came from behind me."

incidents.name: Blanco Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: This is the final report on the Blanco Prescribed Fire escape that occurred in the Bureau of Land Management's Albuquerque Field Office lands on June 4, 2003. The test fire and primary ignition rapidly developed into a crown fire, with spotting occurring over the black lines and outside of the planned ignition area and the Maximum Manageable Area. Spotting distances were estimated at up to ½ to ¾ of a mile. The onsite holding forces were unable to contain the multiple spots outside of the planned perimeter, which resulted in the declaration of an escaped prescribed fire. The escape was declared contained at 1900 hours on June 8, 2003.
incidents.quote: The onsite holding forces were unable to contain the multiple spots outside of the planned perimeter.

incidents.name: Cherry Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: The Cherry Prescribed Fire on the Verde Ranger District, Prescott National Forest, was ignited on June 16, 2003, escaped the burn unit the next day, and was declared a wildland fire.
incidents.quote: At approximately 1630 hours, an unpredicted wind shift from the southwest to the southeast caused the fire to spot over the pre-established control line on the southwest flank of the unit. This spot fire was quickly contained at 150 acres by resources on-site, helicopter and water bucket, and airtankers, maintaining the fire within prescription and eliminating the threat to private lands

incidents.name: Tucannon Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: On June 29, the fire escaped the project area, resulting in approximately 12 acres of spot fires within a 50-acre perimeter.
incidents.quote: The Pomeroy Ranger District has a long history of using prescribed fire. The District program is considered one of the more progressive in the Region in their prescriptive use of fire on landscapes and utilization of contracts to expand the program beyond current organizational levels

incidents.name: Inyo Tree Fatality Incident
incidents.summary: A 4-person trail crew was engaged in post McNalley Fire erosion control and trail rehabilitation. On July 19, 2003, between 0400 and 0430, a 40” diameter, approximately 136 foot tall, dead Jeffrey Pine tree fell and struck the victim while sleeping in her tent. The tree did not show signs of any fire damage, but apparently had root rot.

incidents.name: Cramer Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: On the morning of Tuesday, July 22, two helicopter rappellers from the Indianola helirappell crew, Jeff Allen and Shane Heath, rappelled onto a ridgeline above the fire to cut a helispot. By midafternoon the handcrews that had been flown into the fire were pulled off the fireline due to increased fire intensity at the lower helispot. Shortly thereafter, the rappellers called for a helicopter to pick them up, saying that it was becoming very smoky. A helicopter was launched to retrieve the two rappellers but was unable to land due to extremely poor visibility. The bodies of Jeff Allen and Shane Heath were found, neither firefighter was in a fire shelter.
incidents.quote: "We've got fire down below us and the smoke is coming right at us. So just make them [the helicopter] hurry up."

incidents.name: McGinnis Flats Fatality
incidents.summary: Late afternoon on July 25th, one helicopter pilot was killed when the ship he was flying crashed while working on the northern section of the McGinnis flats fire near Keller, WA.

incidents.name: Cramer Fire Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: On July 29, 2003, at approximately 1630 hours on the Cramer Fire on the North Fork Ranger District/Salmon-Challis National Forest, a member of a Type 1 Interagency Hotshot Crew was injured in a chainsaw-related accident while performing the duties of a swamper working to improve a helispot. The swamper (injured person) sustained injury to the back of the leg when struck by the chainsaw bar tip. The faller and crew foreman immediately assisted the swamper to the helispot. The crew EMT administered first aid. The patient was evacuated via helicopter to a local hospital for treatment. The injury consisted of a seven-centimeter laceration to the right posterior thigh--just above the back of the knee, with involvement of tendon and muscle. Treatment included tendon and laceration repair. The patient was discharged from the hospital the next day and released to home from the Cramer Fire.

incidents.name: Rough Draw
incidents.summary: A formal review was conducted to address raised concerns about the qualifications of a type II Maryland fire crew and about the actions of the incident management team (IMT) they were serving under on the Rough Draw Fire after a retreat to a safety zone.
incidents.quote: "I am concerned about the effect of allegations made and want to set the record straight."

incidents.name: Lightning Complex Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: On August 28, 2003, at approximately 1915 hours, five individuals from StrikeBack #2, a Pacific Northwest contract 20-person crew, were injured when their crew cab pickup rolled. The crew had been released from the Lightning Spike Camp to travel to the Lightning Complex Incident Command Post located in Joseph, Oregon to be demobed the following morning. The crew had traveled approximately 10 miles from the Lightning Spike Camp when--for an unknown reason--the vehicle left the Dug Bar (County Road 735) and rolled approximately 300-feet down a steep slope. Although two of the crew were ejected from the vehicle, all occupants were thought to have been wearing seat belts. Two crewmembers were transported by helicopter to Sacred Heart Hospital in Spokane, Washington. Three crewmembers were transported by ambulance to Wallowa Memorial Hospital in Enterprise, Oregon.
incidents.quote: Five individuals were injured when their Ford F-350 crew cab pickup rolled

incidents.name: Devil Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The involved personnel were assigned as holding forces during a firing operation along a ridge in steep terrain. The firing operation started at approximately 2235 hours. The firing operation could not get the fire to carry, and was terminated at approximately 0050 hours. About 10 minutes later, the main fire activity increased dramatically, causing fire on the opposite side of the ridgeline. The fire spread quickly upslope toward the personnel. The dozers and crew, realizing that they could not make it to a designated safety zone, began to clear an area. When it became apparent that the fire would reach them before they could complete a safety zone, 53 firefighters deployed their fire shelters, and remained inside for approximately 10 to 15 minutes. The 2 dozer operators took refuge on their dozer (enclosed cabs). After the area was safe to travel, they walked down to a safety zone, before being transported to the incident base.
incidents.quote: On August 29, 2003 at 0115 hours, three CDF inmate crews, two dozers, and two overhead were entrapped on the Devil Fire, Santa Clara Complex.

incidents.name: Cascade II Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: On September 23, 2003, the Cascade II Prescribed Fire was ignited on the Uinta National Forest. This 1,000-acre prescribed fire escaped from its planned boundaries and became a 7,828-acre wildfire that was contained seven days later.
incidents.quote: “. . . For many Utahns, the (Cascade II) fire wasn’t a positive event. People with respiratory ailments suffered as a thick blanket of smoke enveloped metropolitan areas in Salt Lake and Utah counties. School recesses and soccer games were canceled in some communities. The Utah Department of Environmental Quality advised senior citizens, children and anyone with heart disease or breathing problems to stay indoors and avoid the smoke. Again, prescribed burns are one of many tools the Forest Service uses to clear mountain brush. Under ideal conditions, the fires are contained to the specified area. But given persistent drought conditions and hotter-than-normal temperatures in recent days, many people have questioned why the Forest Service elected to conduct this prescribed burn at this time. . .” October 1, 2003 Editorial - Salt Lake City Tribune

incidents.name: Berg Unit #3 Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: The Berg Unit #3 Prescribed Fire on the Nez Perce National Forest, Idaho, was ignited via helicopter aerial ignition in September 2003. On October 2, 2003, the prescribed fire escaped the unit boundary and required suppression by multiple resources, including air tankers.

incidents.name: Cedar Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On October 29, 2003 four people were overrun by fire while defending a residential structure located on Orchard Lane in the community of Wynola, in rural San Diego County. One crewmember died at the scene and the three others were provided treatment and then airlifted to a Burn Center.
incidents.quote: The fire made a wind-driven run through heavy brush directly toward their position, covering a distance of approximately one-half mile in just less than two minutes.

incidents.name: St Sebastian Prescribed Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On February 24, 2004, at St. Sebastian River Preserve State Park in Florida, a prescribed fire was planned for burn units SSR 82 (136 acres) and SSR 85 (147 acres). During a burnover, three firefighters were injured. They were administered first aid on scene, including applying water to cool their burns. They were transported in a truck to the nearest paved road where the ambulance was located.
incidents.quote: The gust of wind that caused the fire to escape was short lived and the fire behavior subsided after a brief but intense run.

incidents.name: Forts Lake / Franklin Creek VFD Fatality
incidents.summary: Driving, Fatality, Vehicle Incident or Accident
incidents.quote: Forts Lake / Franklin Creek VFD Fatality

incidents.name: Firefighter Fall Injuries
incidents.summary: During suppression actions on a wildland fire in Kentucky, firefighter John McManus lost his footing on the top of a cliff and fell down a 30-foot embankment, landing on his back. He was able to radio for help. McManus, who broke his back and arm in the fall, went through exploratory surgery on his back at Central Baptist Hospital in Lexington, Kentucky.
incidents.quote: He was just backsetting the fire when he lost his footing on the top of a cliff.

incidents.name: Unity Frost Prairie VFD Fatality
incidents.summary: Assistant Chief Fred Tutt collapsed at his home and died after returning from a grass fire where he had complained of not feeling well.

incidents.name: Midewin Hotshot Fatality
incidents.summary: One firefighter was killed and another severely injured in an accident that occurred while the Midewin Interagency Hotshot Crew was en route to their home base after being released from a fire assignment in Florida. The Midewin Hotshots, based in Wilmington, Illinois had been assigned to the East Fork Fire on the Apalachicola National Forest.
incidents.quote: The three crewmember's destination was to a restaurant on the opposite side of the interstate to check for fellow crewmembers.

incidents.name: Long Jim III Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: On May 5, 2004, the Long Jim III Prescribed Fire was ignited on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon National Park. The prescribed fire escaped the burn unit that same day and was declared a wildland fire. After the prescribed fire was declared a wildland fire, the Burn Boss assumed the role of the Incident Commander and the Burn Boss Trainee assumed the role of Operations Chief.

incidents.name: Work Capacity Test Fatality
incidents.summary: Other firefighters taking the test and on standby for the test proviced immediate medical assistance. He was transported to the hospital but still succumbed to the cardiac-related illness.
incidents.quote: About two-thirds of the way thorugh the arduous work capacity test, Protection Unit Supervisor Lawrence "Larry" Hoffman collapsed.

incidents.name: Work Capacity Test Fatality
incidents.summary: Assistant Chief Richard Grudzinski and other members of his fire department were completing the low-intensity version of the annual work capacity pack test. Firefighters went back to the firehouse. While at the fire station, Chief Grudzinski was seen checking his pulse frequently. At the time, the frequent checks did not cause any concern. Approximately 1 hour and 45 minutes after completing the test, Assistant Chief Grudzinski collapsed due to a heart attack. Firefighters who heard the dispatch rushed to Assistant Chief Grudzinski's home to assist EMS responders. Despite all efforts to revive him, Assistant Chief Grudzinski died.
incidents.quote: After the completion of the test in 14 minutes and 1 second, Assistant Chief Grudzinski commented that the test had "kind of kicked his butt."

incidents.name: Dammeron Complex SEAT Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: On June 17, 2004, a Single Engine Airtanker (SEAT) crashed on the Dammeron Complex in southern Utah, killing the pilot, Wayne Turner, 58, of Big Sandy, Montana. The aircraft had just completed a retardant drop while flying less than 100 feet above down-sloping terrain. Immediately after the drop, the aircraft pitched down and descended steeply into wooded terrain. The pilot did not report any problems prior to the accident.

incidents.name: Bitteroot Hotshot Crew MVA
incidents.summary: On June 30, 2004, the Bitterroot Hotshots were on their way to their last shift on a fire on the Cibola National Forest when their crew buggy was involved in a head-on collision with a recreation vehicle (RV), killing the RV’s driver and injuring crewmembers. The driver of the RV reportedly lost control of the vehicle after a tire blowout. Two ambulances and a lifeguard helicopter responded to the wreck. Six of the Bitterroot Hotshots were injured and transported to hospitals in Socorro and Albuquerque. Four of the hotshots were treated and released in nearby Socorro. The other two crewmembers were transported to Albuquerque where one was in critical condition and the other crewmember was in "guarded" condition. The driver of the RV was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash.
incidents.quote: The driver of the RV died at the scene.

incidents.name: Mataguay Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: On July 13, 2004, a firefighter on the Palomar Hand Crew from the Cleveland National Forest received a first-degree burn to the right side of his face and a small second-degree burn to his right elbow while assigned to the Mataguay Fire, located in Northeastern San Diego County on the California Department of Forestry's Monte Vista Ranger Unit.
incidents.quote: When the firefighter realized that he was taking too much heat he prudently backed away.

incidents.name: Waterfall Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Initial attack forces from multiple jurisdictions were holding fireline along the eastern flank of the Waterfall Fire with engines, hand crews, and a dozer, supported by aerial resources. As the fire progressed to the south, light and variable winds eased and the down canyon/down slope winds increased. This wind change increased fire behavior significantly and generated profuse spotting. Approximately 10 vehicles were unable to egress out of the area before being over run by the fire. Several vehicles were left in place due to the congestion and their operators evacuated the area on foot. Some personnel, due to the congestion, were forced to stay within the safety of their vehicles as the fire burned through the area.
incidents.quote: A technical rescue was required, resulting in diversion of suppression resources.

incidents.name: Citrus Fire
incidents.summary: On July 22, 2004, helicopter rotor wash and a 180-degree wind shift generated a sudden fire whirl that overran USFS Engine 39 on the Citrus Fire. The Engineer suffered 1st-degree burns to his face, neck, and hands before entering the cab; fire damaged airlines and locked engine brakes.

incidents.name: Straylor Helicopter Accident
incidents.summary: A Call-When-Needed Type 3 Helicopter crashed while conducting a reconnaissance and mapping mission on the Straylor Fire in the California Department of Forestry's (CDF) Lassen-Modoc Unit, injuring the pilot and two CDF employees who were onboard.
incidents.quote: The helicopter was unable to achieve sufficient lift to avoid a pine tree and struck it with a main rotor blade approximately 40 feet above the ground. This resulted in a complete separation of the hub and main rotor blade assembly from the aircraft.

incidents.name: Wenatchee Helicopter
incidents.summary: A Bell 205A1 helicopter was destroyed when it impacted heavily wooded, mountainous terrain approximately 20 miles northwest of Leavenworth, Washington. The helicopter was dispatched with a tandem sling load to deliver firefighting supplies as requested by the smoke jumpers first to Incident 698 and then to take the remainder of the supplies to Incident 697. Prior to the impact, the helicopter's tail rotor struck a tree and aircraft control was lost while hovering out of ground effect with an external load. The pilot, Mike Ward, the sole occupant, was fatally injured.
incidents.quote: The purpose of the external load flight was to deliver equipment to a crew of smoke jumpers fighting a fire in heavily wooded, mountainous terrain.

incidents.name: Tuolumne Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: On September 12, 2004 at approximately 1345 hours seven members of California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection Columbia Helitack (Copter 404) crew had to take emergency action when a sudden wind shift and fire flareup overran their position. The helitack crew was constructing handline during the initial phases of a fire. The crewmembers saw the wind shift occurring and immediately utilized their escape routes to the identified safety zones. However, due to steepness of slope and rapid change in fire behavior, they did not all reach safety. Three firefighters suffered minor injuries and Firefighter Eva Schicke was entrapped and killed.
incidents.quote: The fire reacted to the directional wind shift and the backing fire became a spreading fire that turned up-slope with the wind. Firefighters at scene estimated the elapsed time from the wind shift to the burnover was less than 30 seconds with the total wind event lasting less than 2 minutes.

incidents.name: Grant West Prescribed Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Daniel Holmes died on October 2, 2004 when the top of a burning snag fell, striking him on the head resulting in fatal injuries. The accident occurred on the Grant West Prescribed Burn, located in the Grant Grove area of Kings Canyon National Park. Daniel was a member of the Arrowhead Interagency Hotshot Crew, based at Sequoia & Kings Canyon National Parks.
incidents.quote: The falling top of a white fir tree in Kings Canyon National Park squelched a bright light of positive energy and boundless life.

incidents.name: Sabine NF Helicopter Crash
incidents.summary: Three people died in a helicopter crash while conducting a prescribed burning operation in the Sabine National Forest 11 miles southeast of Center, Texas. There were no survivors.
incidents.quote: According to USFS personnel, the voice making the distress call appeared to be that of the ignition specialist, not the pilot. The call was, “Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, we are going down.”

incidents.name: Alley Springs Glade Prescribed Fire After Action Review
incidents.summary: On April 4, 2005, the Ozark National Scenic Riverways Fire Management Staff conducted a 265-­acre prescribed fire at Alley Spring, located six miles west of the town of Eminence. During this project, the fire escaped firelines and burned approximately 130 acres of mostly Missouri Department of Conservation lands. Three firefighters were treated for heat exhaustion and dehydration. An ATV was also destroyed by fire.
incidents.quote: Personnel could not hold the line.

incidents.name: Mailbox Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: At approximately 1200 hours on May 13, 2004, U. S. Forest Service and Florida Division of Forestry firefighters responded to a wildland fire on the Osceola Ranger District near Lake City, Florida. A U. S. Forest Service firefighter died while working on the fireline. The deceased firefighter was assigned as a Safety Officer on the incident.
incidents.quote: Mr. Henderson apparently collapsed approximately 33 feet inside the fireline on an old fireline in an area of unburned fuels.

incidents.name: Slaughter Gulch
incidents.summary: A lightning caused fire burned an engine when crews were not able to return in time to move or protect the vehicle.
incidents.quote: Mountain Big Sagebrush combined with Cheat Grass can exhibit quick runs with very intense heat.

incidents.name: Black Ridge Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: On September 15, 2005, the Black Ridge Prescribed Fire was initiated as a single-­day project 363 acres in size on federal lands managed by the Burns District of the Bureau of Land Management. At approximately 1300 hours, a dust devil carried embers across a disc line approximately 25 feet wide, starting several spot fires. By 1315 hours, the slopover reached the top of the ridge with several crew personnel attempting to keep the fire from establishing on the ridgetop. The fire kept moving to the east and upslope faster than the crew personnel could keep up. By 1600 hours, the fire was contained. Although this prescribed fire escaped and burned private lands, it was never declared a wildfire.
incidents.quote: A dust devil traveled across the north line, carrying embers across a disc line approximately 25 feet wide, starting several spot fires.

incidents.name: Carlton VFD Water Tender Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Rice was driving tractor-trailer water tender as his department was providing mutual aid to the Hamilton, Texas Fire Department in fighting a large grass fire located west of Hamilton on Highway 36. At about 1430 hours, Rice lost control of the truck while rounding a turn on Farm-to-Market Road 219, causing it to overturn. Rice was not wearing a seat belt and was ejected from the truck when it flipped. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

incidents.name: The Victims and Survivors of the Texas and Oklahoma Wildfires
incidents.summary: Prolonged drought, strong winds, and extreme fire danger conspire to trigger the explosive grass fires that rage across Texas and Oklahoma in late 2005 and early 2006. These historic fires kill 25 people—including 4 firefighters; evacuate thousands of residents; destroy hundreds of homes, structures, and outbuildings; and burn millions of acres. An estimated 5,000 head of cattle also perish and more than 2,000 miles of fencing burns.
incidents.quote: For three and a-half months—from Dec. 1, 2005 to March 17, 2006—12,072 wildfires ignite in Texas.

incidents.name: Chisholm Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On February 18, 2006, at approximately 3:35 p.m., a Georgia Forestry Commission ranger operating a tractor-plow fire suppression dozer became entrapped while on initial attack of a the Chisholm Fire in Clinch County, Georgia. The ranger had to deploy his fire shelter inside the tractor and suffered 2nd-3rd degree burns to the arms and face.
incidents.quote: The operator emerged from the shelter and called the chief ranger on the tractor radio to report the situation, and that he felt burned and blistered . The supervisor called a local ambulance, went to the aid of the operator and escorted him back to the highway. He was able to walk out on his own.

incidents.name: Mendocino Unit Physical Training Medical Emergency Fatality
incidents.summary: Captain Henry completed his mandatory hour-long physical fitness activity. Captain Henry’s workout that day consisted of lap swimming approximately 1 mile. After completing the workout, Captain Henry reported to the Parlin Fork Conservation Camp at 0800hrs. At 0830hrs, he assumed control of an inmate fire crew. At approximately 1030hrs, Captain Henry led his crew on a conditioning hike. After returning to the office his heart did not feel right and he fell. Others began CPR and a medical helicopter was summoned. When helicopter paramedics arrived, a defibrillator was attached and a shock was delivered. ALS-level treatment was continued during Captain Henry’s flight to the hospital. Despite these efforts, Captain Henry was not revived.
incidents.quote: At the completion of the hike, Captain Henry returned to his office and told others in the office that his heart did not feel right. Captain Henry stood up and fell to the ground, striking his head on the desk as he fell.

incidents.name: Camden Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: Three firefighters were waiting along a bladed woods road for a dozer line to be anchored in preparation for holding and back burning on the Camden Fire. When the fire began advancing toward the firefighters they proceeded to one of two planned safety zones. One of the firefighters encountered an area of radiant heat from the fire. He was wearing full PPE including goggles and shroud, which he used. He received second degree burns in an area around his nostrils.
incidents.quote: "Firefighter A" suffered second degree burns around his nose due to 'a blast of heat' from the flaming front.

incidents.name: Tennessee RX Fatality
incidents.summary: During dozer line construction in preparation for a pine understory prescribed burn, Forest Technician Mark Stanley, instructed a dozer to push down a dead snag.Upon engaging with the blade of the dozer the dead red oak, approximately 10” dbh, and 50 feet tall, suddenly broke loose at ground level. Stanley was struck by the falling tree near its tip. T
incidents.quote: When the snag began to fall he again looked up and saw Stanley walking toward him with his head down and his MT 1000 radio microphone in his hand.

incidents.name: Sarge Creek VFD Fatality
incidents.summary: Fire Chief Robinson was operating a fire department vehicle in a pasture while assisting with a controlled burn. Shortly after refilling the tanker, Robinson was run over by the vehicle for reasons still under investigation. He succumbed to his sustained injuries.

incidents.name: Dunes State Park Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: The planned Trail 3 Prescribed Fire encompassed 26 acres in the northwest corner of Dunes State Park. Fuels consisted of dune grass, hardwood leaf litter and wetland grasses. Weather at the time of ignition was within prescription with winds South at 3­4, temperature in the mid 60s, sky cover 0­10% and Rh 34%. The National Weather Service did not expect the lake breeze to set up. A spot fire quickly grew and began to spot ahead of itself. The rate of spread was very quick and other spot fires were observed 25 feet ahead of the fire. At this time, it was determined that suppressing the fire was beyond the capabilities of the resources assigned to the prescribed fire.
incidents.quote: "Trust your gut not your bravado – The fire should have been shut down after the spot fires and fire whirls were observed. When you see fire behavior that indicates the possibility of heightened intensity with only a relatively small amount of fire on the ground, you had better consider what your resources can handle and what type of fuels are outside of the burn block." - statement of RXB2 involved

incidents.name: Wilson Wildland Fire Use Vehicle Fire
incidents.summary: The Zion National Park Fire Use Module was assigned to the Wilson Wildland Fire Use incident on the Gila National Forest in New Mexico. The Fire Use Module’s 2002 Ford F-450 Super Duty crew truck with an S&S Fire Rescue Support package caught fire and burned. There was no active wildland fire in the immediate area of the truck when the vehicle fire occurred.
incidents.quote: The crew truck was a total loss.

incidents.name: NM State Driving Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Aguilar died from injuries received when the apparatus he was operating drifted onto the shoulder of the road, and with a steering wheel overcorrection caused the vehicle to roll. It was reported that Aguilar was not wearing a seat belt and was ejected from the truck.

incidents.name: Ball's Canyon Fire Near Miss
incidents.summary: During the June 27, 2006 Balls Canyon Fire, Engine #1 became threatened while working on a dozer line in dense ponderosa pine, prompting failed radio attempts and a rapid rescue by a CDF heavy equipment operator and the Engine #2 captain, who transported Engine #1’s crew to safety at a hilltop. At the same time, STCR #1 led their crew into a previously burned area to avoid the advancing crown fire and linked up with an Interagency Hotshot Crew that guided them to a safer, less smoky location. All hilltop resources were then directed to a nearby meadow, and with multiple helicopter and airtanker drops, Engine #1 was saved from damage. By 1600, all Division A forces had retreated to the meadow, with STCR #1’s crew arriving several hours later.
incidents.quote: STCR #2 ordered the engine captain to drop their hoses, and immediately back out of their location and get up to the hilltop safety island.

incidents.name: Scorpio Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Two firefighters from the BLM Salt Lake Helitack Crew were entrapped while conducting burnout operations on the Scorpio Fire in the Hog Up Mountains. The incident occurred when downdraft winds from a thunder storm caused the Scorpio Fire to become erratic and extreme, cutting them off from their escape routes and safety zone. One member of the crew felt it necessary to deploy his shelter for protection. The other crew member sought refuge from the smoke and embers in a wash.
incidents.quote: There was a lack of communication between personnel on the fire

incidents.name: Big Draw Fire Engine Run Over Injury
incidents.summary: On July 2, 2006 at approximately 1900 hours, a firefighter participating in suppression activities on the Big Draw Fire in Idaho. The firefighter was working with a hose at the left front of his Type 4 engine, when he apparently tripped and fell to the ground. His legs were run over by the left front tire of the engine--breaking his right femur and fracturing his left foot. His condition was stabilized on scene and he was transported to Magic Valley Hospital in Twin Falls, Idaho, via a U.S. Forest Service helicopter that was assigned to the fire.
incidents.quote: His legs were run over by the left front tire of the engine breaking his right femur and fracturing his left foot.

incidents.name: Sawtooth Complex Entrapments
incidents.summary: Three entrapments occurred to resources dispatched for structure protection in which four firefighters received minor injuries, and two fire engines and a command vehicle received minor fire damage.
incidents.quote: Continue to re­evaluate fire weather and current burning conditions.

incidents.name: Little Venus Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: While the module followed a trail into a backcountry area, the module noted a major change in fire behavior, pushing the fire towards their location in an intense run. Radio communication in the remote area was very difficult. The module reversed course and hiked back towards their vehicles at the trailhead when the fire forced them to deploy fire shelters next to a streamcourse. One crewmember separated from the rest and deployed her shelter in a different location. All module crewmembers survived the entrapment without injury.
incidents.quote: On July 18, 2006, 10 members of a fire use module (wildland fire module) became entrapped and deployed fire shelters while hiking into their camp location on the Little Venus Fire, Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming.

incidents.name: Tallahassee Entrapment
incidents.summary: On July 27, 2006, a Forest Ranger in the Tallahassee District was involved in a burn­over incident. The Ranger was plowing on the right flank of the fire in an enclosed cab JD650 when she was overtaken by smoke. Unable to see, the Ranger's tractor became hung up on some trees and was burned over while the Ranger was in the tractor's cab. With assistance from other personnel on the scene, she exited the tractor.
incidents.quote: After exiting the tractor and moving toward the safety zone, the ranger fell forward. She landed on her hands and suffered second degree burns on one hand and minor burns on the other hand and face.

incidents.name: Titus Fire Helicopter Crash Fatalities
incidents.summary: Two pilots died when suddenly their helicopter crashed into the Klamath River after a long day battling wildfires at the Titus Fire portion of the Happy Camp Complex. The pilots were on a contract for the U. S. Forest Service (USFS), and employed by the Heavy Lift Helicopters Inc. of Apple Valley. The cause of the crash is still to be determined.
incidents.quote: Titus Fire Helicopter Crash Fatalities

incidents.name: Krassel Helicopter Accident
incidents.summary: On August 13, 2006, at approximately 1730, helicopter N355EV, an AS350 B3 (H125) under contract to the Forest Service, crashed on the Payette National Forest 18 miles west of Yellowpine, Idaho. The pilot and three Forest Service employees on board were fatally injured. Those lost in the accident were: Michael Lewis, Lillian Patten, Quin Stone, and Monica Zajanc.

incidents.name: Elko BLM Engine 1949 Rollover
incidents.summary: On August 14, 2006 at approximately 1915 hours, while traveling between two initial attack fires approximately 30 miles northwest of Wells, Nevada, a Bureau of Land Management heavy fire engine left the graveled roadway and rolled over. All five firefighters in the engine were transported to Northern Nevada Regional Hospital in Elko, Nevada. Four were treated for minor injuries and released. The fifth firefighter received treatment for a broken arm.

incidents.name: Devils Den Fatality
incidents.summary: On August 17th, 2006 on the Fillmore Ranger District, Fishlake National Forest, just east of Oak City, Utah, a local firefighter lost his life as a result of a burn over incident.
incidents.quote: After working his way down the canyon, Koyle asked for helitack support and directed water bucket drops on hot spots. Koyle received reports of additional fire activity above and below his location.

incidents.name: Mountain Fire Air Attack Fatalities
incidents.summary: A pilot and firefighter died when their OV­10 aircraft crashed as they worked a wildland fire in remote TulareCounty. The cause of the incident is still under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board.
incidents.quote: Both occupants on board Air Attack 410 were fatally injured.

incidents.name: LEO Vehicle Rollover
incidents.summary: On September 20, 2006 at 1300 hours, a Law Enforcement Officer (LEO) from the Mark Twain National Forest was returning from a two-week fire assignment on the South Fork Complex out of McCall, Idaho. While traveling eastbound on Interstate ­70 five miles east of Brewster, Kansas, the LEO lost control of the vehicle, rolling over in the center median. The LEO was transported to a local hospital, treated and released. The vehicle was destroyed.

incidents.name: Day Fire Helicopter Crash
incidents.summary: On October 1, 2006, on the Day Fire on the Los Padres National Forest, an exclusive use Sikorsky S­64 helicopter had just emptied the portable retardant tank of retardant (approximately 200 gallons) and was going to add some water from another portable tank located approximately 25 yards away. Attempting to put the snorkel into the portable water tank, the snorkel contacted the tank's exterior side and was momentarily hung up on the tank's flange. The aircraft began to spin, hit the ground and rolled over. Both pilots egressed the aircraft, received minor abrasions, and were evaluated on­ scene by paramedics. They were transported to a local hospital and were released that same day.

incidents.name: Day Fire Water Tender Rollover
incidents.summary: At approximately 1550 hours on October 4, 2006 on the Day Fire on the Los Padres National Forest, a contracted water tender drove off the side of the road--rolling over approximately five times until it came to a stop 165 feet below the road. The water tender sustained major damage. The operator was ejected from the cab on the second or third revolution. The operator received minor injuries, including cuts and bruises. He was transported via the Ventura County Air Squad to the Ventura County Medical Center. He was treated and released.

incidents.name: Esperanza Fire Entrapment Fatalities
incidents.summary: The Esperanza Fire was reported on October 26, 2006 at 1:11 a.m. within the jurisdiction of the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE). At approximately 7:15 a.m., five wildland firefighters from Forest Service Fire Engine 57 were overrun by the fire. All five firefighters were fatally burned by a sudden, intense fire run up a steep drainage below their location.
incidents.quote: From the onset, the Esperanza fire behavior was very common to that of other fires that have burnt there in the past.

incidents.name: Millerton Fire Department Fatality
incidents.summary: Hector “Sandy” McClune died on a small brush fire. He had an apparent heart attack while working at the scene of an outdoor fire.

incidents.name: Steed Creek Road Accident Fatalities
incidents.summary: The impact caused an explosion resulting in both vehicles being destroyed. Each vehicle was occupied by the drivers only and both drivers died at the scene.
incidents.quote: A vehicle and a tractor trailer truck collided on a two lane state highway on the Francis Marion NF.

incidents.name: Catawba Volunteer Fire Department Vehicle Accident Fatality 2021
incidents.summary: On April 15, 2007, Firefighter Derek Poole was returning to the fire station in his privately owned vehicle, from the scene of an arson fire set in the woods, when he missed a stop sign at the road’s intersection and crashed into another vehicle. Firefighter Poole was ejected from the car. He passed away on Monday, August 9, 2021, from the injuries he sustained in the accident. Firefighter Poole was also a member of the West Iredell Fire Department.

incidents.name: Cessna 185 Crash
incidents.summary: On May 1, 2007, a Cessna A185F on skis experienced main gear attachment bolt failure during a glacier landing roll near Haines, Alaska. The investigation determined that rather than fuel exhaustion due to lack of fuel quantity, the engine actually failed due to fuel starvation as a result of the improper installation of the fuel selector lever during the 100-hour inspection.
incidents.quote: When the pilot selected "both" tanks the fuel valve assembly actually shut off fuel flow from the wind tanks. The pilot made an emergency landing on a small pond, but due to the size of the pond after touchdown the aircraft left the pond, hit an embankment became briefly airborne and flipped over. The main landing gear attachment bolts to the right ski sheared during the landing roll in deep snow, resulting in a nose down, and structural damage.

incidents.name: Stag Road Fire
incidents.summary: A tractor plow operator was burned when the Stag Road Fire briefly flared up and entered the open tractor cab. At the time of the incident, the tractor plows were 15 – 20 feet off of the fire’s edge, within the indraft. Flame lengths were reported as waist high. Winds were erratic, as the area was feeling the effects of a sea breeze.
incidents.quote: The intensity of this flare-up forced the tractor plow operator to jump off of the tractor.

incidents.name: Bolli Fire Water Tender Rollover
incidents.summary: The Type II water tender was traveling at an estimated 5 – 10 miles per hour on a slight uphill grade on a straight section with good site distance when the driver’s side tires left the hardened road surface, collapsing the road edge and causing the vehicle to roll and slide down the embankment approximately 200 feet.
incidents.quote: The driver was ejected during the rollover and suffered lacerations to the head and a broken thumb. The water tank was separated from the chassis and the truck cab was sheered off.

incidents.name: Woodland Wildland Fire Use Smokejumper Canopy Collision
incidents.summary: Smokejumpers were dispatched by the Gila National Forest to the Gila Wilderness Area to support management of the Woodland Fire. Two smokejumpers were injured during the jump.
incidents.quote: Their parachute canopies collided above the ground

incidents.name: Angora Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: No significant injuries were sustained, neither individual was hospitalized, and all firefighters in the vicinity were safely evacuated from the fire.
incidents.quote: Two Forest Service employees assigned to the Angora Fire on the Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit were entrapped by fire and deployed fire shelters.

incidents.name: Madison Arm Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Engine B’s supervisor directed the others in the entrapment situation to turn around and go to an open area with light fuels. This site was the only break in the timber in the area. Upon arrival at the site, they were instructed to immediately implement a burnout operation. The crews involved in the entrapment describe changing wind directions and a storm cell to the north that was driving the wind changes. Eight Forest Service employees (two engine supervisors and their crews) and the contractor were entrapped.
incidents.quote: It’s a “new world” and we should anticipate fire behavior in places and at times that are out of character with what we have experienced in the past. An “expect the unexpected” mindset for fire behavior, along with the growing complexity of our work (values at risk, abundant urban interface, etc.) should set the context for all involved with planning and implementation of strategy and tactics, when giving and accepting assignments, and assessing whether adequate LCES safety precautions are in place.

incidents.name: The Jungle Prescribed Fire Review
incidents.summary: The Jungle Prescribed Fire Review Team’s overarching framework was not to find out—in hindsight—what the burning crew did "wrong," but to look at the "system" that was in place during the Jungle Prescribed Fire, and how people individually and collectively made sense of the dynamic fire.
incidents.quote: "When something goes wrong, we want to look at the entire system, the whole environment—and not automatically say that the employee did something wrong."

incidents.name: West Basin Burnover
incidents.summary: A Type 2 handcrew was assigned to the western flank of the West Basin Fire southeast of Jackpot, Nevada. While constructing hotline, the crew boss was scouting ahead of the crew. The crew boss went out of sight of the squad bosses and crew for a short time. The crew boss radioed the squad bosses that the smoke was impacting his view of the fire and location of the crew. While working his way back to the crew, the crew boss suffered burns to his face, arm and leg. Radio communication indicated that the crew boss had been burned over and was injured. He was flown by a helicopter assigned to the incident to Magic Valley Regional Medical Center and later transported to the University of Utah Burn Center for treatment. He was released to his home unit the next day.

incidents.name: Seven Oak Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Conditions quickly changed and the burning intensified on the Seven Oaks Fire. The winds increased and began changing directions. Realizing they were losing control, the firefighters dropped their nozzles and retreated toward the engine and the pond identified as their safety zone. Captain 4452 was separated from his crew and retreated to his engine and sought refuge in the cab. The engineer and seven firefighters entered the small pond and deployed fire shelters for extra protection as buildings and trees burned around them.
incidents.quote: This entrapment resulted in burn and respiratory injuries to all nine employees, the total loss to one Model 5 fire engine, and major fire damage to one Model 1 fire engine.

incidents.name: Alabaugh Canyon Fire Entrapement and Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: The firefighters were conducting burn out operations around a residence in the wildland urban interface. The two firefighters sustained a range of superficial and significant burns due to a sudden, intense crown fire near their position as they were deploying the fire shelter.
incidents.quote: Two Black Hills National Forest firefighters were entrapped by the fire and deployed a single fire shelter.

incidents.name: Schultz Fire Water Tender Rollover
incidents.summary: A water tender operator moved the water tender to the right side of the road to allow several vehicles to pass. After the vehicles passed, the water tender approached a curve in the road and remained on the road's right side. As the right wheels traveled onto the road's shoulder it gave way. As the right front tire began to slide down a ten-foot embankment, the operator was able to get the tire back on the road. The rear tires, which support the load, caused the shoulder to give way even more. The momentum of the water in the tank shifting caused the water tender to slide down the embankment and roll to the right. The water tender came to rest on its cab. The operator and passenger were wearing seatbelts and hardhats and were not injured.
incidents.quote: Carrying 3,000 gallons of water on the Shultz Fire, the 10-foot embankment gave way, causing the vehicle to overturn onto its roof; seatbelts prevented injuries.

incidents.name: Zaca Fire
incidents.summary: A heavy duty truck with a fixed tank contracted to clean portable restrooms drove off the Figueroa Mountain Road. The driver was flown by Santa Barbara County Fire Helicopter 309 to Cottage Hospital in Santa Barbara. The driver received a fracture to the leg.
incidents.quote: The vehicle traveled approximately 200 feet over-the-side.

incidents.name: Wood Creek Fire ATV rollover accident
incidents.summary: As a member of the Fuels Crew tasked to perform burnout operations behind a dozer fire line, the employee was operating an ATV with a group of six ATV’s. While traversing a slope on an ATV designated trail, the employee’s ATV rolled to the left down a steep slope. The employee received injury to his left side pelvic region. The employee was stabilized by his crew members and transported by Life Flight helicopter to a local hospital.

incidents.name: Elk Fire Drowning Fatalities
incidents.summary: Deputies, volunteers, a swift water rescue team, a California Highway Patrol helicopter, Klamath National Forest firefighters and Elk Complex incident personnel responded to the Klamath River at Clear Creek, approximately 7 miles south of Happy Camp, CA. The body of one victim was recovered from water approximately 10 to 15 feet deep. Both victims were employees of a kitchen organization assigned to the Elk Complex and were swimming in the Klamath River during off-duty hours.
incidents.quote: The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Department received a call for assistance from a swimmer reporting a possible drowning of two of his companions.

incidents.name: Norcross Helicopter Crash (Elk Fire)
incidents.summary: The pilot was killed when his Bell 205 Helicopter crashed near the Elk Fire. He was providing logistical support to crews when the accident occurred.
incidents.quote: On July 23, 2007, at approximately 1020; a Bell Model 205A-1 owned by Idaho Helicopters, Inc. of Boise, ID, on a call-when-needed contract to the federal government, crashed on the Klamath National Forest 12 miles South/Southeast of Happy Camp, California. T

incidents.name: Trapper Ridge WFU
incidents.summary: On the morning of July 24, 2007, two members of the Silver State Interagency Hotshot Crew (IHC) were struck by a hazard tree(s) that fell while they working as a crew constructing fireline on the Trapper Ridge Wildland Fire Use (WFU) incident.

incidents.name: Loon Fire Helicopter Crash
incidents.summary: Their distress call was picked up by an Air Attack plane on a guard channel and was relayed to the Copeland Helibase. A Bell 212 Helicopter with four emergency medical technicians was dispatched to transport the pilot and mechanic to McCall, Idaho for medical treatment. The mechanic was treated and released. The pilot remained in the hospital.
incidents.quote: While flying a water bucket mission supporting the Loon Fire, a Bell 214ST Helicopter crashed on approach to a dip site. The pilot and a mechanic were on board and exited upon impact.

incidents.name: Ahorn Fire Fire Shelter Deployment FLA
incidents.summary: On July 28, at 1537 a Division Supervisor, assigned to Division Zulu deployed a fireshelter. The fire fighter had been positioned as a lookout on an unmanned division on thesouthern flank of the fire to observe several spot fires that had been burning for several days.
incidents.quote: It is OK to deploy a fire shelter, and experience has shown it is better to deploy ina good spot sooner rather than later.

incidents.name: Poe Cabin Fire
incidents.summary: The three remaining crewmembers had to run a few hundred feet down the road through the heat to get to the lower meadow. All three sustained radiant heat burns to their necks and arms - the last one received 2nd and borderline 3rd degree burns to the face and arm, and fell and injured a knee during the escape.
incidents.quote: The next series of events all happened in less than two minutes. The winds started to shift and there was a curl of smoke over the line and an ember wash into the green side of the line. They were cut off from the top meadow by this pulse of fire; and the call was made to pull out down to the lower meadow as fire started to cross the road.

incidents.name: Cascade Complex Entrapment
incidents.summary: Meanwhile, after climbing out of their wrecked garbage truck, the driver and passenger discussed their predicament. As they walked, the terrain blocked their view of the fire to the south and west. Once they rounded a corner, about a third of a mile below the wrecked truck, the fire came into view. They turned around, spotting a concrete culvert catch basin against a steep cutbank with very little vegetation where they could take cover.
incidents.quote: They had survived a crash and a burnover and were still alive. They took stock of their injuries—the driver’s bloody face, some cuts and scrapes, a few burn holes on their jacket, and a minor burn on the passenger’s arm.

incidents.name: Little Goose Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: As the firefighters were driving, the fire had made a rapid run from below and blocked their primary escape route. They chose to back down the road to where they could turn around and at that point the fire made another run blocking their secondary escape route. Now with no escape routes available, the firefighters decided to remain in the cab of the truck and maneuver the truck back and forth between pockets of burning fuel.
incidents.quote: “In the time it took us to jump in the truck and start west towards the safety zone, the fire started to crest the ridge in the canopy.”

incidents.name: Cascade Complex Motor Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: As the truck careened off the road, it rolled on its side and slid across the dirt and brush before coming to rest in a small clump of trees. The driver sustained a bleeding head injury, lost consciousness and fell onto the passenger. After a few minutes, though, the driver regained consciousness and the two occupants were able to climb out a window of the overturned truck.
incidents.quote: He made it through a couple of hairpin turns by hard braking, but the brakes became soft at the next turn. He decided to drive the truck off the road to stop it by running up the slope.

incidents.name: Cascade Complex Smoke Exposure
incidents.summary: Over the next few days, medical unit visits made a significant jump from the level prior to the fire burning around the camp. Records indicate significant numbers of referrals to the medical clinic in Cascade on the days following August 14. Most of the visits to the clinic were for respiratory ailments, including bronchitis and pneumonia. One individual was hospitalized for three days with bacterial pneumonia.
incidents.quote: They discussed smoke conditions and mitigations with the IMT. The Cascade Complex IC responded that the location still provided the best support for line operations.

incidents.name: Cascade Complex Burn-By
incidents.summary: The IMT expected the main North Fork fire to burn to the northeast, but instead the smoke column tilted to the east resulting in a heavy ember shower and intense fire activity on several fronts around camp. Many of those interviewed felt that the fire burning around the camp was much more severe than they had anticipated.
incidents.quote: Increased fire activity in the vicinity of ICP triggered the Cascade Complex IC’s decision to implement the ICP Stay-in-Place plan at 3:45 p.m.

incidents.name: Rombo Fire Saw Accident
incidents.summary: The sawyer, crewmembers, crew Superintendent, Safety Officer, and Incident Commander are questioning if firefighters should have been in this area, considering the difficult tree conditions. They were engaged here to mop up the fire close (100 feet) from the control line. However, a Division Supervisor points out that this area is representative of many, if not most of the fire, and many other fires. Many sawyers may not consider this situation particularly dangerous, and may also take it on.
incidents.quote: A snag, to the right of the target area, was somehow dislodged, and fell back, hitting the sawyer in the ribs on the back right quadrant of his torso.

incidents.name: Woodview Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: They saw the blow up at about the same time. The fire crossed the line behind the tractor. One person fell, dropped his torch, then got up and started running down the line. They caught up to the tractor and were able to get inside. Three in the cab was a tight fit., but all three went down the line to safety. They would not have survived without the environmental cab.
incidents.quote: Thought they could hold the fire to a small acreage.

incidents.name: Pine Fire Dozer Entrapment
incidents.summary: Heat began to build up in the cab and the Operator attempted to deploy the reflective fire curtains. Heat and fumes in the cab made breathing difficult. The Operator then exited the dozer, through the rightside door, and sought refuge in a “sandy area” near by. The Operator sustained 2nd and 3rd degree burns to both hands and fingers, the left elbow, the nose, left side of the face, and the left ear.
incidents.quote: After working for a short time the Operator noticed flames on the left side of the dozer. The Operator placed the dozer in reverse to back out of the area but the engine stalled.

incidents.name: Engine 3144 Rollover
incidents.summary: On September 19, 2007, at 1545 hours, two BLM fire employees from the Bakersfield Field Office were responding to a wildland fire in their BLM Light Engine 3144. While coming out of a right turn in the road, the back dual tires came upon a soft portion of road bed, causing the vehicle to swerve to the left. Taking evasive action, the driver first pulled right and then to the left again. The rear wheels then dropped into the uphill side sandy ditch, forcing the vehicle to swerve off the road and over the right side of the embankment. The vehicle rolled twice side-over-side before coming to rest right-side-up approximately 62 feet below the embankment. The engine's two occupants received minor injuries.

incidents.name: Butler II Fire Crew Carrier Rollover
incidents.summary: On October 1, 2007, a Crew Carrier with eight Forest employees from the Heaps Peak Helitack were involved in a single-vehicle rollover. The crew was in route to a mop-up assignment on the Butler II Fire near Big Bear Lake on the Mountaintop Ranger District of the San Bernardino National Forest. The vehicle rolled several times down a 100 percent slope, coming to rest 235 feet below the highway--stopped by heavy timber. All employees were wearing seatbelts. Seven escaped with little or no injuries; one sustained moderate injuries to his shoulder. Two employees were kept in the hospital overnight for observation. The crew compartment, although it sustained damage, was structurally sound and protected the crew from more serious injuries.
incidents.quote: The driver, attempted to regain control, but over corrected, struck another guard rail and went airborne off the side of the hill about 90 feet before hitting the hillside. The vehicle landed on its driver side first, crushing the driver cab, where upon the crew compartment separated from the cab and chassis. The two units then rolled several times down a 100 percent slope coming to rest 235 feet below the highway, being stopped only by heavy timber.

incidents.name: Colorado Fire Dozer Rollover Fatality
incidents.summary: CAL FIRE Heavy Fire Equipment Operator (HFEO) was assisting to extract D4645 that had become immobile due to topography and loose soil conditions. While constructing a bench below D4645, HFEO's dozer slipped off the side of the hill, rolled, and came to rest 154 feet down the drainage.
incidents.quote: "I’m not going back there, I have no reason to go back down that cliff again, that wasn’t comfortable.”

incidents.name: Santiago Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Twelve Orange County Fire Authority firefighters were advancing a progressive hose lay on a hillside near a road cut along Santiago Canyon Road in eastern Orange County. Upon reaching the top of the 200-foot hill, their hose line apparently ruptured, causing them to run out of water. As fire encroached upon their position, the firefighters deployed their fire shelters.
incidents.quote: All twelve firefighters escaped injury.

incidents.name: Volusia County Fire Training Incident
incidents.summary: The Volusia County Fire Department's special operations team for wildland fire operations was conducting its monthly drill, with 14 career team members in attendance at the fire department's training site. The drill consisted of a refresher course for qualified operators culminating with the felling of three dead trees on the property.
incidents.quote: The tree moved 135 degrees away from its intended fall.

incidents.name: Charles Taylor Road Fire
incidents.summary: On March 25, 2008, a North Carolina Division of Forest Resources tractor plow operator was entrapped and burned during initial attack in Bertie County. Unexpected wind shifts pushed a 20-foot flame front over the tractor plow in young loblolly pine plantings, inflicting burn injuries to the operator. Basic first aid was applied to the Tractor Plow crewman’s right ear due to redness. The next day, the Tractor Plow crewman was directed to seek medical attention at Bertie Memorial Hospital due to a visible blister appearing on his right ear and right temple. The Tractor Plow crewman returned to work that day after being diagnosed with 2nd degree burns to his right ear and temple.
incidents.quote: A Tractor Plow crewman radioed the Forest Fire Equipment Operator (FFEO) about a spotover and advised that he needed to “get out of here because there was fire all around me”.

incidents.name: Frye / Whitmire Escaped RX
incidents.summary: Discusses the RX Burn Plan, Qualifications, Communications, Weather & Predictive Services, Resource Allocation, Leadership & Decision and aslo Documentation & Preparing fro a Review. Making
incidents.quote: The Escaped Prescribed FIre Review document explains the "lessons learned".

incidents.name: Cleveland NF Dozer Fatality
incidents.summary: The dozer operator was pronounced dead on the scene by the Coroner.
incidents.quote: The dozer operator was performing work in steep terrain when his D-6 dozer rolled over and he appears to have been ejected.

incidents.name: Chino Valley Water Tender 66 Rollover
incidents.summary: On April 17, 2008, firefighting personnel from the Chino Valley Independent Fire Protection District were actively engaged in suppressing a working grass fire in a Wildland Urban Interface area within the incorporated City of Chino Hills, located in southwestern San Bernardino County, California. Two firefighters received minor injuries when they were involved in an off-road single-vehicle rollover accident in Chino Valley Independent Fire Protection District's Water Tender 66 during suppression of this grass fire.
incidents.quote: During the attempt to traverse the side slope portion of the hillside, the driver felt the rear of the vehicle begin to slide. He turned the wheels upslope and accelerated, at this point the driver’s side tires began to “dig-in” the soft dirt, the vehicle overturned. The vehicle rolled onto the driver’s side and continued over, it came to rest on the passenger side on a steep portion of the hillside. The driver and passenger exited the vehicle through the driver’s side window.

incidents.name: Chitty Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: Declared a wildfire on April 22, the Eagle Wildfire was contained without further incident on April 28th.
incidents.quote: A spot fire across Eagle Creek the afternoon of April 20, quickly spread beyond the capabilities of assigned resources and fire managers chose to fall back to a previously identified contingency line (a two lane forest highway).

incidents.name: Indians Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: One crew member with serious burns was flown to a burn center and two others were transported by ambulance to a local hospital. The most seriously injured crewmember remained in the burn center for more than a week. The two other crewmembers were treated and released.
incidents.quote: Three of the crew successfully removed the shelters and wrapped them around their backs while continuing efforts to exit the area. The fourth crew member had difficulty deploying his shelter and continued running until he reached the engine. The entrapment occurred when the rotating plume had developed.

incidents.name: Elkhorn 2 Declared Wildfire Review
incidents.summary: Two days after ignitions, on June 14, the prescribed burn was declared a wildfire.
incidents.quote: The planned 10,490 acre prescribed fire eventually burned 2475 acres within the original project area and 3724 acres outside the project area.

incidents.name: Valley Incident Vehicle Rollover Accident
incidents.summary: Oak Glen 3 was returning to Oak Glen Conservation Camp from a vegetation fire, the Valley Incident in the area of Wilson Valley Road and Highway 371. On Wilson Valley Road the Engine Crew Transport struck the embankment on the side of the road and rolled onto its right side. Three California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation firefighters sustained moderate to serious injuries. Twelve others received minor injures. The Fire Captain also received minor injuries. The Engine Crew Transport was a total loss.
incidents.quote: Utilize extreme caution when driving on unfamiliar roads, especially in rural and rugged terrain.

incidents.name: South 1 Fire
incidents.summary: Engine 242 was moping-up on the South 1 Fire when a snag struck the Engine Boss. The firefighter received injuries to their left eye/face and left shoulder. The medical unit was notified and the medical plan was implemented. Nansemond-Suffolk Volunteer Ambulance County was called to transport the injured crew member. After retrieving the patient, at 1427 hours, the ambulance personnel requested an air ambulance. The helicopter landed at ICP at 1448 hours and flew the patient to the Sentara Norfolk General Trauma Center.
incidents.quote: Spotter yelled “snag”!

incidents.name: Walla Valley Fire Helicopter Collision
incidents.summary: Michael McDonald was killed in a private medical helicopter collision. Five other occupants of the two air ambulances were also killed and one occupant is listed in critical condition. Two responding ground personnel also received minor burns when the wreckage sustained a secondary explosion.
incidents.quote: While being treated at the local clinic for a spider bite he experienced an adverse reaction to the medication and was being transported by a private air ambulance to Flagstaff Medical Center.

incidents.name: Ashmead Firefighter Fall
incidents.summary: FF1 was Care Flighted to St. Mary’s hospital in Grand Junction; he was treated for several minor injuries and was released later the same day.
incidents.quote: While down climbing, FF1either lost his grip or stumbled and lost his balance, he fell approximately twenty feet, landing on his back on a pile of rocks at the base of the cliff.

incidents.name: Butte Lightning Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The firefighter suffered 2nd-degree burns to both legs and was evacuated via Stokes basket to a helicopter for transport to UC Davis Burn Center.
incidents.quote: As I turned to step out of the black and into the dozer line my right leg went straight through the dirt into a pocket of extremely hot coals.

incidents.name: Dutch Creek Tree Felling Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighters carried the injured firefighter, by litter, to a location where he was hoisted into a USCG Helicopter. They arrived at the Redding Municipal Airport, where in consultation with a Mercy Hospital Emergency Room Physician, pronounced his death at 1710. The Coroner later determined the cause of death to be blood loss due to blunt force trauma to firefighter’s left leg.
incidents.quote: At approximately 1350, a firefighter called ICP for medical assistance for severely injured firefighter. Emergency medical personnel responded and treated the injured firefighter for severe bleeding.

incidents.name: Camel Hump Falling Incident
incidents.summary: The injured rappeller was flown directly to Central Washington Hospital in Wenatchee for treatment and was noted that the medivac operation performed on this incident was nearly flawless.
incidents.quote: On July 25, 2008 a rappeller sustained a fractured vertebra when he was struck by a snag that had been cut during a falling operation

incidents.name: Panther Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Although DIVS 1 had fully deployed his new generation fire shelter, the intense heat of the fire and its residence time exceeded the capability of the fire shelter. The deceased firefighter was recovered the next day.
incidents.quote: While conducting a reconnaissance of the fire line, the Panther Fire made a major run and rapidly overtook the ridgeline where DIVS 1&2 were located. They attempted to escape but found their escape routes cut off. At that time DIVS 1 elected to deploy his fire shelter.

incidents.name: Panther Fire Medevac Hoist
incidents.summary: Although the injured party was ultimately extracted from the injury site successfully, the operation seriously compromised the safety of all parties involved. The final consequences from this one Medivac expanded the size of the fire, caused destruction of firefighter equipment and compromised the safety of fire fighters on the ground.
incidents.quote: In 2008 on the Panther Incident, (Klamath N.F.) a fire fighter was injured on the line in a remote area. The I.C. requested a Medivac based on the seriousness of the injury.

incidents.name: Lime Complex Tree Incident
incidents.summary: Two guardsmen jumped to safety, one sustaining cuts on his leg and the other one receiving cuts to forearm and leg.
incidents.quote: When the tree landed, the MCAD noticed several National Guard personnel had moved further up the line to observe the snag falling and when the snag began rolling down the line several Guardsmen had to jump out away from the snag to prevent being struck.

incidents.name: Oak Mesa Fire Fuel Geyser
incidents.summary: He eventually was diagnosed as having 1st and 2nd degree burns on his face, neck, upper right extremity, and elbow and wrist as well as a head laceration requiring 3 sutures.
incidents.quote: A member of a Hotshot crew, participating in wildfire suppression duties on the Oak Mesa Fire, was burned and received a head laceration while performing sawyer duties after a fuel geyser.

incidents.name: Carlton E-921 Water Tender Rollover
incidents.summary: On August 2, 2008, Carlton (Private) Water Tender, E-921, was involved in a single-vehicle accident during fire suppression repair activities on the Shasta Lightning Series, north of French Gulch, California. The accident resulted in minor injuries to the driver, who was transported to a Redding area hospital, held for observation and released. Water Tender E-921 received major damage.
incidents.quote: The soil on the right side of the road collapsed and the water tender began a slow roll over the embankment.

incidents.name: Iron 44 Helicopter Crash Fatalities
incidents.summary: Attempted overweight takeoff resulting in impact with trees and terrain

incidents.name: Maverick Fire
incidents.summary: On August 6 th gas line personnel were at the “pig launcher” on the southeast perimeter of the fire to repair a leaking gasket. The 300 psi of gas isolated in the pig launcher and associated piping was vented to allow for the repair. Several firefighters assigned to the Maverick Fire reported hearing the gas venting(s) followed by a “strong rotten” egg odor. Soon after, some crewmembers from theUpper Colorado River Interagency Type 2 Crew experienced symptoms consistent with H2S exposure while conducting mop­up activities downwind of Oil & Gas personnel working at the pig launcher. These symptoms included nausea, headaches and some dry heaving. Those affected withdrew to higher ground and began to recover.
incidents.quote: Maverick Fire Hydrogen Sulfide Gas Exposure Incident

incidents.name: Potamus Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The fire was a result of ongoing widespread lightning activity, and was reported at 25 acres in light, flashy fuels on August 7, 2008. One Type l Interagency Hotshot Crew (IHC), three Type 6 engines, and two overhead were engaged at the fire by mid-afternoon. The fire was active with occasional torching initially but became a backing, flanking fire. While fire fighters were engaged, the fire experienced a significant wind event associated with a passing thunder cell, causing a rapid acceleration in rate of spread and intensification of the fire activity. Fire fighters and one engine-retreated; another engine was burned over, resulting in a total loss.
incidents.quote: The weather was unstable, with numerous convective cells reported that afternoon.

incidents.name: Headache
incidents.summary: Ignited on June 18, 2008 the NF5 Prescribed fire was monitored for 54 days while meeting objectives before being declared the Headache Wildfire on August 8, 2008. The wildfire determination was based on exceeding environmental parameters and the lack or resources to staff the fire.
incidents.quote: Another causal agent contributing to the wildfire declaration was the perception by the district that resources would not be available to work on the NF5 burn. Between August 9th and August 11th the district had a lightning bust causing 13 fires. Four of these new starts were being managed as WFU events and the remaining nine were under suppression. District personnel were stretched thin even with assistance from off-forest resources. Contingency resources were not immediately available for the NF5 burn/Headache wildfire.

incidents.name: Big Bradley Fall Incident
incidents.summary: On August 21, 2008, North Carolina Division of Forest Resources and North Carolina Wildlife Resource Commission personnel were performing a holding action on the Bradley Falls Fire. While scouting the fire, Assistant District Forester Curtis Jessen, of the North Carolina Division of Forest Resources, suffered critical injuries after falling at least 50 feet from Big Bradley Falls.
