incidents.name: Mystery Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The fire was located in timbered terrain with overgrown vegetation. After successfully controlling the fire, the Engine crew began mop-up operations. On day two of mop-up, the injured firefighter was spraying various hot spots along the fire perimeter with a mixture of foam and water. While spraying a particularly steep area, the firefighter slipped on the wet ground and began to fall backwards. As he fell, he extended his right arm to catch himself and felt a searing pain in his right arm; he had inadvertently placed his bare hand in an ash pit.
incidents.quote: The Mystery Fire was reported on August 9, 2015 at 2041 hours Pacific Standard Time. The fire was one of 130 fires spotted that day after lightening passed through the area earlier that day/night.

incidents.name: Big Hill Smokejumper Accident
incidents.summary: The injured smokejumper indicated in his post-accident interview the jump was “very routine” and even reminded himself “don’t be complacent” before exiting the door. He flew a left hand pattern to set up his approach to the jump spot. At this time, he was in “deep brakes” which is a steep descent angle because he didn’t want to overshoot the jump spot into the trees. When he was about 20 to 30 feet off the ground, he realized he was in too deep of a descent and didn’t have enough elevation to correct his trajectory. He landed just short of the jump spot into a steep embankment.
incidents.quote: Big Hill Smokejumper Accident

incidents.name: High Meadow Rollover
incidents.summary: On Thursday, August 13, 2015, a vehicle returning from a backhaul mission with fire damaged fence material, was involved in a rollover accident. The driver was the only occupant in the vehicle at the time of the accident. The driver received minor injuries, was treated on scene and transported to a hospital in St. George where he was seen and released.
incidents.quote: High Meadow Fire, Extensive Damage to Cab and Body of a 2012 Ford F-350 Stake Bed Truck.

incidents.name: Bayberry Fire Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: On August 13, 2015, at 1443 hours, a CAL FIRE Model 34 fire engine (E1), staffed with one fire apparatus engineer and two firefighter I’s, was dispatched to a vegetation fire on Bayberry Lane off of Marysville Road in the Browns Valley area. At approximately 1459 hours, E1 was traveling northbound on Marysville Road, near the intersection of Bayberry Lane and was involved in a solo vehicle accident. The CAL FIRE fire apparatus engineer and two firefighter I’s suffered minor injuries.
incidents.quote: FAE1 swerved to the left to avoid a collision and went off of the west side shoulder of Marysville Road at approximately 45-50 mph.

incidents.name: Cornet Fireline Explosion
incidents.summary: First, fire crews are notified that a storage shed in the fire's path contains blasting caps and dynamite. All hazardous materials are removed from this shed, but fire crews are not aware that another nearby building also contained dynaminte.
incidents.quote: When a fire moves through an area reported to have explosives, how long should we wait before we go back in?

incidents.name: Vehicle Radio Problems
incidents.summary: While heading out to check on a repeater site location, this incident’s two Communications Technicians were stopped by the Division Q Supervisor and the Engine Strike Team Leader, who shared their concern about being unable to transmit or receive on their radio from inside their vehicle, a 2015 Ford F-150 truck.
incidents.quote: Communication Technicians verified that communications were hampered when trying to use the radio from inside the vehicle.

incidents.name: Windy Ridge Fire Skidgine Rollover
incidents.summary: In past reviews it is often stated that we should: “Know your equipment limitations and limitations as an operator.” This sentiment was expressed on this incident. How do we figure out limitations?
incidents.quote: "I was 99% done."

incidents.name: Helicopter Equipment Backhaul
incidents.summary: While backhauling many miles of hose, port-a-tanks and other equipment from the 790 Fire, chokers were introduced for efficient backhaul of hose. However, because some of the helicopter longline remote hook (HELR) qualified folks were still out on the fireline—a thorough briefing was not provided to all that would be involved in this operation.
incidents.quote: Helicopter Transport of External Cargo; Backhauling Equipment from the Fireline.

incidents.name: Twisp River Fire Burnover Fatalities and Injury
incidents.summary: On August 19, 2015, USDA Forest Service firefighters Richard Wheeler, Andrew Zajac, and Tom Zbyszewski perished while engaged in initial attack on the Twisp River Fire. A fourth member of the crew was critically injured with severe burns after their type 6 engine left the road in dense smoke.
incidents.quote: “We were just driving through the fire and you can’t see your hand in front of your face.”

incidents.name: Twisp River Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: After experiencing a wind shift the Twisp River Fire forced a heavy euipment boss, trainee, and dozer operator to seek refuge in a garage. As fire conditions worsened their refuge caught fire and to get away from the intense heat, they ran to Woods Canyon Road just above the wye where they deployed their fire shelters. The dozer operator’s beard was singed, and he burned his arm. The heavy equipment boss burned his hand because he had taken his glove off earlier to operate his radio, and all three had burned their ears and faces.
incidents.quote: “It went from daylight to midnight at the flick of a switch.”

incidents.name: Rattlesnake UTV Rollover
incidents.summary: Six firefighters on two UTVs (two drivers, each with two passengers), are returning from a scouting mission on the southwest corner of the Rattlesnake Fire. They are exiting the area—now traveling downslope—on the same jeep trail that they’d entered on. As the second UTV starts its descent, the passenger-side wheels slide into the wash-outditch area. The UTV comes to a stop. It is leaning severely over onto the machine’s passenger side. It is “hung-up” on its frame’s undercarriage.
incidents.quote: “I wasn’t concerned about the terrain. I’ve operated my own Ranger [Polaris Ranger UTV] in similar terrain and road conditions.” UTV Operator whose machine slid into ditch.

incidents.name: Kettle Complex Bucket Powerline Strike
incidents.summary: On the Renner Fire on the Kettle Complex in Northeast Washington, a Type I Helicopter with a 150-foot longline is completing bucket work when—on its first approach for a dip operation at a new dip site (that had not previously been used)—its bucket strikes a residential power line. The pilot expertly maneuvers the aircraft backwards to unfold the bucket from the power line and safely returns to the helibase to debrief and take a tactical pause.
incidents.quote: “The normal visual cues were not there, no poles seen, no houses seen. And, due to the winds, there was no reflection on the water. I was showing another pilot the powerline and it took them several minutes to locate the line even though it was right below them.” Helicopter Pilot

incidents.name: Coffee Kit Flashover RLS
incidents.summary: On the Grizzly Complex this August, a spike camp crew worker who was a Job Corps student awoke at 0330 for their work shift. As the student went through their motions of starting the coffee kit, they noticed that this particular coffee kit was not functioning the same as others that they had used in other fire camps. The student then made an adjustment with a wrench and noticed propane flowing immediately. Upon realizing the propane bottle valve was on all the way, the student quickly shut down the propane from the propane bottle valve.
incidents.quote: This particular coffee kit was one they had not yet used and had not started it up the night before to test it out.

incidents.name: Coffee Kit Flashover Rapid Lesson Sharing
incidents.summary: On the Grizzly Complex, a spike camp crew worker, who was a Job Corps student, awoke at 0330 hours for their work shift. They proceeded to their first assigned task of the day, making coffee using a coffee kit that makes approximately 20 gallons of coffee. The student had difficulty getting the propane gas used to heat the coffee kit to flow. They turned each of the knobs on the three adjustment points of the coffee kit—with no success. The student then made an adjustment with a wrench and noticed propane flowing immediately. Upon realizing the propane bottle valve was on all the way, the student quickly shut down the propane from the propane bottle valve. After a few seconds, now that propane was flowing, the student grabbed the lighter to light the propane burner. They slightly opened the valve located at the propane bottle and clicked the lighter once—with no flame developing. They clicked the lighter again. A huge plume of fire flared-up into the Job Corps student’s face and body.

incidents.name: Grizzly Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: About a mile down the road, we feel the front of the engine slide a little. We figure we are on the shoulder. However, unfortunately, there is no shoulder. Because it is night operations we can’t see the terrain below us. But, earlier, we’d seen some horribly steep cliffs. During the roll, my mind and thoughts are going so fast.
incidents.quote: We end up closing the gap so we won’t become lost and hold-up an operation that might need us. One of my crewmembers describes this as a “sense of urgency” . . . I don’t want to get separated and lead four or five engines down the wrong road. It goes from: “Maybe I can pull up” to “No, we’re tipping” to “We’re rolling”.

incidents.name: Cougar Creek Blackhawk Bucket Operations
incidents.summary: The Bambi bucket has its own flight profile—it wants to spin. However, due to their lack of visibility from the aircraft, the crew may not be able to visually see just how spun-up the longline and bucket is becoming. The longline almost certainly needs to be 80% unspun before the bucket enters the water. Therefore, the speed of the descending bucket into the dip site can directly affect the condition or position of the guy lines and longline as it is being pulled out.
incidents.quote: “Time Out” Taken at Helibase – Conference Held. After the “timeout” and the conference was held, twisted guy lines and bucket hang-ups have not been reported on this incident.

incidents.name: Stump Hole Leg Burn
incidents.summary: About lunch time, a firefighter sees a smoke and starts walking to it to determine what will be needed to put it out. Without warning, the “solid ground” on which the firefighter is walking suddenly gives way. The firefighter falls into an unseen ash pit.
incidents.quote: Without warning, the “solid ground” on which the firefighter is walking suddenly gives way.

incidents.name: First Creek Watertender Rollover
incidents.summary: Two feet of “soft shoulder” had been introduced on the downhill side of the road by the Dozer. Several large rocks had rolled out of the fire and landed on the road—narrowing it even more. This obstruction required the driver to steer toward the false shoulder to avoid these large rocks.
incidents.quote: This is his first fire assignment and his second day on the line. The rollover happened 12 hours into his shift.

incidents.name: Chelan Complex Moving Vehicle Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: At approximately 0900 while traveling south on USFS Road 3107 from the Black Canyon Road to Drop Point 75 on the Chelan Complex, an incident rental pickup truck (2015 Ford F150) was impacted by a falling green spruce tree (estimated 14-inch DBH) that fell from a six-foot cut bank above the road. The tree landed directly on the vehicle’s hood. Fortunately, the vehicle’s operator was not injured.
incidents.quote: The driver reported that he saw the tree falling but was unable to react quick enough to avoid the impact.

incidents.name: Snake on Helicopter
incidents.summary: So we land and shut down. The snake now slides into a hole in the cowling under my seat. While we are looking for it, he pokes his head out a few times—and retreats back inside the cowling. We pull the helicopter apart trying to find the darned snake—but we never do locate it. We make the decision to put the aircraft back in service—even though the snake could be anywhere. Eight days later, while the relief pilot is in flight, the snake crawls out again. The pilot lands and the fuel truck driver grabs it. It is confirmed to be a bull snake. It is released unharmed.
incidents.quote: About five minutes after taking off, I look down and there’s a snake looking up at me.

incidents.name: National Guard Medics
incidents.summary: On the Carpenter Road Fire in Northeast Washington, Army National Guard Medics helped fill a critical need for trained EMTs and Paramedics. National Guard Medics are trained for the battlefield. They bring knowledge, experience, and equipment that fits well into the wildland fire environment. This was tested in a case of anaphylactic shock after a bee sting. The injured firefighter was transported from his work location to the drop point where a Guard Medic Team was staged. They assumed patient care, helped coordinate with an air ambulance, and then handed off the patient to an air ambulance.
incidents.quote: “Integrate the National Guard Medics into your plan after a job shadow session. This will give them an opportunity to better understand the operation prior to their first shift by themselves.”

incidents.name: Engagement Dilemma
incidents.summary: The deliberate, patient approach displayed by the Incident Management Team during this event contributed to an operational tempo that allowed and encouraged personnel to “go slow to go fast.”
incidents.quote: Miles of uncontained fire edge + values-at-risk + wind event = Engagement Dilemma.

incidents.name: Miners Peak Medical Evacuation
incidents.summary: Tom’s EMT experience helped him to quickly assess that Steve was severely injured.He assisted Steve to the bed in the cab and then woke John. At 0505 a medical emergency was declared to Incident Command Post (ICP) Communications. The two men initiated the Firefighter Incident Form assessment and evaluated Steve’s injuries to include a broken back and head injury with laceration. A medical evacuation was requested.
incidents.quote: Tom woke at approximately 0430 to the sound of moaning and located Steve on the stairs of the lookout.

incidents.name: Sawyer Feet Burns
incidents.summary: A sawyer noticed that he could still feel the heat coming from the ground adjacent to the tree he was planning to cut. He mixed cool dirt with the coals for approximately 15 minutes until the work area was sufficiently cool. For the next couple minutes, the sawyer stood in this same area—that they had just cooled down and prepared—while he successfully dropped the tree. Walking away from the stump, the sawyer began to experience intense pain and heat in both feet. He sat down and took both boots off. Initially this felt better, but the pain returned and blisters began developing on both sides of both feet.
incidents.quote: The sawyer’s leather firefighting boots show no signs of heat-related damage.

incidents.name: Black Widow Spiders
incidents.summary: When the Incident Management Team on the Kettle Complex in northeast Washington moved base camp, they encountered an unexpected hazard. The new site was prepared using a dozer to level the ground. Bark chips were brought in to calm the dust and prevent mud holes if it rained. They soon discovered that this new location was already occupied—by a resident population of black widow spiders. These spiders were living underground in old rodent burrows. When the ground was disturbed, they came up to the surface.
incidents.quote: They soon discovered that this new base camp location was already occupied: by Black Widow Spiders.

incidents.name: 9-line Lessons
incidents.summary: The 2015 fire season in the Pacific Northwest (Oregon and Washington) saw thousands of firefighters deployed and more than one million acres burned. There have been many accidents requiring medical transports and medevacs. In addition, a number of lessons associated with reporting medical emergencies have emerged.
incidents.quote: “Most people freeze the first time they run through the 9-line, so we want their first time to be practice.”

incidents.name: Rapid Extraction Module Support
incidents.summary: The main objective and purpose for these pre-staged rescue teams is to provide firefighters emergency extraction and reduce the time needed for individuals to receive medical attention who are unable to egress under their own power in difficult terrain. Having the ability to be flexible within the fire environment and being available 24-hours a day in dynamic situations makes the REM an invaluable resource.
incidents.quote: “Wildland firefighting is an inherently dangerous profession. While safety is the primary concern during all operations, unintended incidents do occur which result in injury or illness to firefighters. It is the intent of the Rapid Extraction Module Support (REMS) to provide firefighters who are unable to egress under their own power, a safe and secure transport off the fireline while simultaneously receiving the appropriate medical attention.” From the January 2015 Rapid Extraction Module Support ICS Position Manual

incidents.name: Rough Fire Pinned by Burning Log
incidents.summary: As the sun continues to rise, a large dead-and-down buckskin pine with high rollout potential, begins burning actively. The crew clears the area downhill of the tree and a Saw Team begins bucking the three-foot diameter downed tree to remove unburned fuel and secure it. After finishing up the line both below and above the tree, a crewmember goes back down to tie-in a piece of the line. As the crewmember moves below the bucked tree, the log rolls toward him—eventually taking him down and trapping him underneath. The log comes to rest against a green tree, pinning the crewmember under the burning log. The Saw Team and additional crewmembers hear the screaming and rush to their pinned crewmember’s aid. With as many as eight Hotshots all pushing and pulling, they are able to move the log enough to free firefighter. The Superintendent wasted no time declaring a medical emergency and calling in a lat/long to Division.
incidents.quote: Inspite of all this, it took an hour for Advanced Life Support and a Rapid Extraction Module to arrive on scene. From the time of injury until the patient arrived at the hospital took almost three hours.

incidents.name: Perdida Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The Perdida Fire was started by lightning on June 23 at approximately 1900. It was managed for multiple objectives utilizing the full range of fire management practices to help achieve ecosystem sustainability, including its interrelated ecological, economic, and social components. On the day of the accident, firefighters were igniting fuels to reduce fuel loadings and encourage sprouting in oak brush. A firefighter received severe burns to both legs, back, and left arm while utilizing a drip torch. Basic medical care was provided on site and the firefighter was transported to Albuquerque Airport by an air ambulance before being taken to the University of New Mexico Burn Center by ground ambulance.
incidents.quote: As they made the second pass, Igniter #2 ignited his left pant cuff and boot. He noticed the flames and attempted to pat them out. At the same time he saw his leg on fire, he threw the drip torch in his left hand away from him. Being surrounded by brush, he attempted to get to a clear area.

incidents.name: Refueling Drip Torch Burn Injury
incidents.summary: Two of the three firefighters are sprayed with the fuel. When the torch mix hits the ground, it contacts some hot parts of the line and ignites.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Tries to Pat Flames Out—But Can’t

incidents.name: Rolling Rock Near Miss
incidents.summary: The Incident Commander Type 5 Trainee was located approximately 15 feet downslope from the rock—directly in its trajectory. He dove to the south and was able to miss the fall of the rock by a few feet. Another firefighter was able to grab the ICT5 Trainee’s clothing—preventing him from rolling down the steep slope face. The rock rolled approximately 200 vertical feet until it struck the gully at the bottom of the ridge. No one was hurt.
incidents.quote: As the rock started to roll down the steep slope, crew members—per their training—instantly yelled "Rock!"

incidents.name: Mop up Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: The Chelan Fire in Washington. A member of a 20-person crew who was assigned to mop-up “fell through the ground” and suffered 2nd degree burns just below the top of their boot. “Fell through the ground”? Yes, with the severe drought, all available fuel sources seem to be fully consuming. This includes some of the vast root systems of trees as well as the large woody piles that are often covered over by logging roads.As the firefighter was walking on what was described as “solid ground” they stepped on a weak spot where a tree root had once been. This void was now filled with hot ash.
incidents.quote: If it's never happened to you, ask yourself: "Is it because I am good - or because I've been lucky?"

incidents.name: Clearwater Fire Dozer Power Pole Strike
incidents.summary: A D-5H High-Track Grapple Dozer and a CAT 320 Excavator are rehabbing dozer line along a residential power line. Because the sun is in his eyes, the Dozer Operator does not see how close he is to a power pole. As he turns his Dozer to the left, the grapple on the back of the machine collides with the power pole, breaking it off. The power lines strike the top of the Dozer and arc. The Dozer Operator remains in the cab. After quickly analyzing the situation, he decides to drive out from under the hazard to reduce the chances of causing a fire or of human injury. The nearby Excavator Operator—who doesn’t see the power pole strike suddenly notices that the power lines are moving/swinging. He immediately drives his machine away from the power line right-of-way and parks.
incidents.quote: The quick recognition and successful actions by the personnel involved in this power pole strike Incident Within-an-Incident prevented a more serious outcome—including serious personal injury—from occurring.

incidents.name: 3 Incidents Tactical Pause
incidents.summary: During a one-week timespan, a Hand Crew experienced three significant injury/medical events:  Rolling Rock Injury: The first occurred while the crew was breaking for lunch and a rock rolled loose above them—striking a crewmember in the arm.  Exposure Event: The second event consisted of an “exposure” incident to several crew members who complained of headaches while mopping-up near an oil field and naturally occurring carbon monoxide vents.  Firefighter Falls: The third event was a crewmember falling and sliding approximately 100 feet—requiring a medevac for his injuries.
incidents.quote: “We explained to the crew how this was a pause for their welfare and safety. The crew had no issues of sitting down and partaking in this. Their first thoughts were that the crew was being singled out. But after our discussion, they became comfortable with this process.” RLS Facilitator

incidents.name: Valley Fire Structure Protection
incidents.summary: When the supervisors returned to the south end of Stonegate Road, conditions had in fact changed and the fire that was benign came back to life as the wind shifted and intensified. The brush field to the east of the neighborhood was actively burning with embers landing throughout the neighborhood. The crew and engine company now had many priorities. Homeowner’s garden hoses were deployed house by house as the fire burned in a northwesterly direction through the brush field threatening house after house. Ladders found in yards were thrown and crewmembers sprayed down roofs as others fell more trees in the backyards. As this was a very different tactic and strategy for a hand crew, many crewmembers were put in new rolls in a very dynamic situation. At one point, one of the crewmembers asked the Foreman what to do. His reply was, “make a difference”.
incidents.quote: Embers were swirling in every direction and you could feel the trucks being pulled towards the fire due to the inward air currents being pulled by the fire. The black smoke column was blocking out the sunlight and it was beginning to get very dark.

incidents.name: Valley Fire Shelter Deployment
incidents.summary: Helitack A observed increased spot fires in the pine needles and leaf litter along the southwest side of the goat pen. They started to extinguish the spot fires but there were too many. At approximately 1402 hours, the brush covered slope to their east completely torched into a wall of flame. The wall of flame sent a significant wave of radiant heat through the goat pen and onto the firefighters. They could feel their faces burning from the radiant heat and all four firefighters ran to the fence, climbed over, and ran towards the steel garage. At the steel garage Helitack A started to deploy their fire shelters.
incidents.quote: The wall of flame sent a significant wave of radiant heat through the goat pen and onto the firefighters.

incidents.name: Lumpkin Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On September 14, 2015, one of the private bulldozer operators (Operator E-1) and two CAL FIRE Dozer Bosses (DOZB1 and DOZB2) returned to the site where the dozers were left the night before, to build a plan for the removal of the bulldozers. The main fire was burning one ridge to the west. During the meeting, a slope reversal occurred and the main fire became established in the drainage directly below Operator E-1, DOZB1 and DOZB2. The fire intensity increased significantly. Operator E-1, DOZB1, and DOZB2 attempted to retreat uphill along the dozer line. During the retreat the group was cut off and could not make it to the road ahead of the advancing fire. All three individuals turned and ran downhill where they were assisted to safety by communications with Helicopter 205 (C205) and a Field Observer (FOBS1), who was honking his vehicle horn to give them a direction of escape. The two private bulldozers were burned and were rendered inoperable. No injuries occurred.
incidents.quote: In the afternoon on September 13, 2015, two private bulldozers became stuck on Division Delta (DIV D) while operating on the Lumpkin Incident.

incidents.name: Drip Torch Leg Burn 3
incidents.summary: I was on a firing operation on a prescribed fire, bringing fire behind me with a drip torch.After going through a very thick patch of brush (more than 10-feet tall) I felt my right leg getting hot.I looked down to realize that my Nomex pants were on fire from drip torch fuel.
incidents.quote: I got down on the ground and started to roll and throw dirt onto my leg—which finally put the fire out.

incidents.name: Falling Area Control
incidents.summary: The Falling Boss immediately called the falling team on tac and told them a truck was coming down the road and to stop cutting. BUT it was too late the more experienced faller, with over 50 years of experience, was just finishing his back cut on a 20 inch, 80 foot tall tree and the tree was “in flight”. The Rehab Division was coming around a left hand corner when the tree come crashing down, parallel to the road missing him and his truck by less than 30 feet.
incidents.quote: Does a “Road Guard” always have to be a person?

incidents.name: Crooked Creek Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: At approximately 1645 hours on Sept. 29, 2015, while performing direct line construction on the Crooked Creek Fire, a Swamper’s hand was struck by a running chainsaw. The injury resulted in two lacerated fingertips and minor abrasions on the Swamper’s left hand.
incidents.quote: “I felt the impact, but felt no pain.I then looked down at my handand said: ‘Oh F%#*!’” Swamper 1

incidents.name: Bone Point Prescribed Fire/RX Wildfire Conversion Review
incidents.summary: The review found that the wildfire declaration element within the burn plan was worded with a stricter interpretation than the Interagency Prescribed Fire Planning and Implementation Procedures Guide.
incidents.quote: To achieve objectives the burn was scheduled to be “in season” when conditions were warm and dry.

incidents.name: Flat Ridge Escaped Prescribed Fire FLA
incidents.summary: The fire crossed onto private property and was threatening private structures. The private structures consisted of a small cabin, 2 camp trailers with separate roof structures, and miscellaneous small outbuildings. The on-scene type 6 engines were requested to provide structure protection. The two engines completed a wetline around structure and withdrew due to fire approaching structures. After the fire passed the structures the type 6 engines returned and continued mop-up around the structures.
incidents.quote: Prescribed fire attempts in previous years have been unsuccessful due to heavy grazing and lack of grasses to sustain fire spread throughout the sagebrush and aspen stands.

incidents.name: Arapaho Declared Wildfire Review
incidents.summary: On October 16, 2015, a prescribed burn implemented by the U.S. Fish and Wildland Service (FWS) on the Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) escaped control lines and was declared a wildfire
incidents.quote: Arapaho Declared Wildfire Review Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge

incidents.name: Log Rolled Over Firefighter
incidents.summary: The log primarily impacted David’s chest and glanced off the left side of his upper cheek and head. Upon assessment by coworkers and an EMT, David indicated that he was having sharp pains while breathing; however, his main complaint was pain in his chest.
incidents.quote: “The log didn’t look bad. I didn’t think it would roll. One quick cut and we’re done.” The main log broke free, rolled and chased David down the hill. Within 10 to 15 feet the log overtook David, rolling over him.

incidents.name: Tug Strike on Helicopter
incidents.summary: The helicopter is typically parked with the skids hanging over the front edge of the dolly so that the tug can stay connected for storage in the hangar, thereby reducing the number of times that an approach has to be made to reconnect the rig. Normally, with the helicopter centered on the dolly, the nose of the helicopter would be behind the edge of the dolly. Damage was caused by the towing apparatus hitting the front of the aircraft.
incidents.quote: The shifter “safety catch” is held together by yellow electrical tape. Defective parts should be replaced as soon as possible or the vehicle should be placed “out of service” until repairs are completed.

incidents.name: Rock Creek Prescribed Fire Burn Injury
incidents.fire: Rock Creek Prescribed Fire East Side Block
incidents.summary: One of the FFT2’s caught his left foot between two rocks, twisting his left ankle and causing the firefighter to fall backward. The firefighter was holding the drip torch during this fall.
incidents.quote: Thirteen days after the burn injury, the injured firefighter received an initial skin graft and will continue to be evaluated as the injury heals.

incidents.name: North Divide ATV Incident
incidents.summary: While performing hazardous fuels pile checks, an ATV operator was abruptly thrown from his ATV resulting in a broken collar bone and minor damage to the ATV.
incidents.quote: “We need a more vigorous ATV training for our operators that offers and focuses on a breadth of field training exercises."

incidents.name: Zimmer Ridge Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: Mystic District personnel ignited 62 machine piles in the Elmo Timber Sale on February 2nd. These piles were patrolled and checked every day leading up to the escape on February 10.
incidents.quote: Zimmer Ridge Escaped Prescribed Fire

incidents.name: Firefighter Hit by Vehicle
incidents.summary: The northern portions of Oklahoma saw several fires break out Thursday. Washington County fire crews battled a large fire in the Wann area. And in Nowata County, fires broke out along Highways 169 and 60. One firefighter is recovering after troopers say a man hit him while driving through the smoke. It was a scary situation in Nowata on Highway 60 between Nowata and Vinita when the firefighter, working the scene with the Centralia Fire Department, was trying to pull some hose and was struck by a driver going through the fire scene. The firefighter was airlifted to an area hospital in Tulsa with a broken leg. The good news is the fire is contained; and Shawn Christian, the chief of the Centralia Fire Department, said the firefighter is expected to be OK.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Hit by Vehicle

incidents.name: Mulholland Fire Hit by Rock Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Jones was working as part of a hand crew in a steep ravine on a fire in Agoura Hills-Malibu, California, when a large rock fell about 100 feet from the hillside above and struck her in the head.
incidents.quote: Mulholland Fire Hit by Rock Fatality

incidents.name: Oklahoma Firefighter Run Over
incidents.summary: Lt. Lyle Crandall with the Ponca City Fire Department was seriously injured Friday afternoon [February 26] while responding to a reported grass fire. Lt. Crandall and one other firefighter were on a special detail when the call came in. They had to respond back to the fire station to pick up a brush pumper. During this transfer, Lt. Crandall was accidentally run over by the front tires of the fire engine. Lt. Crandall received immediate treatment from the other Ponca City firefighters and was taken by ambulance to the hospital where they were met by a medical helicopter. Lt. Crandall was flown immediately to OU Medical Center in OKC. He sustained traumatic injury to his left foot and leg as well as his right leg.
incidents.quote: Lt. Lyle Crandall with the Ponca City Fire Department was seriously injured Friday afternoon.

incidents.name: Firefighter Hit by Vehicle 2
incidents.summary: Kris Rowe was in the man well -- a steel platform with railings on the bed of the brush truck--where the firefighter stands to protect himself. Rowe was spraying the fire that was nearing the road when 18-year-old Jonathan Curb drove through the smoke and accidentally hit him.
incidents.quote: A Lone Grove firefighter was hit by a vehicle Monday on Meridian Road while working to help extinguish a grass fire.

incidents.name: Remote Area Falling Accident
incidents.summary: While attempting to fall this hazard tree, a coast live oak snag, the tree strikes the faller—resulting in a broken clavicle, broken scapula, five broken ribs, a bruised lung, a puncture through the lower lip, and minor abrasions.
incidents.quote: “When we know we have areas of poor communications and we plan to work in those areas, we really need to examine how we will communicate with EMS if we have a bad outcome.”

incidents.name: Engine Bed Mounting Bracket Failure
incidents.summary: The steel straps used to mount the bed to the frame on this Type 6 Engine with a Model 52 pump package were not substantial enough to withstand the load of the pump package. The 1/4" steel plate used was insufficient to handle the stress.
incidents.quote: The bed had been mounted to the frame with six pieces of steel strap—all of which were compromised.

incidents.name: Dozer Transport Bed Mount Failure
incidents.summary: During daily equipment inspections, heavy equipment operators noticed broken welded brackets and missing bolts used to attach equipment beds to truck frames. These mounting brackets and bolts secure the equipment beds to the truck transports that are used to haul firefighter equipment such as bulldozers.
incidents.quote: This failure could result in severe equipment damage and possible injury to our employees who are operating this equipment.

incidents.name: Initial Attack Water Tender Rollover
incidents.summary: Two men were injured after a Waukomis fire truck ran off the road Thursday afternoon near Bison while responding to a fire call. Waukomis Fire Department personnel were responding to a controlled burn that got out of control northeast of Bison when the tanker overturned. The 2,000-gallon water tanker was traveling south on Leona Mitchell toward Osborne Road when it went off the right side of the road and rolled, coming to rest on its side.
incidents.quote: Initial Attack Water Tender Rollover

incidents.name: State Game Land 311 Prescribed Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: At approximately 13:35 the burn crew noted and communicated a shift in fire spread direction, unexpectedly pushing down a steep (40-45%) slope. The fire crossed fire lines into several areas of wooded leaf litter causing crews to employ suppression tactics. The crew member was injured when the leaf litter fuels he was working in flared up, caused by a strong downslope wind gust. Flame lengths quickly increased from <1 foot to 3-5 feet within seconds. The firefighter was engaged in direct attack from unburned fuels at the time of the flare up. He was burned as he passed through the “knee high” flame front in route to his safety zone (the black). He was transported via medical helicopter to a burn unit in Pittsburgh, PA.
incidents.quote: On March 23, 2016, a Pennsylvania Game Commission Game Lands Maintenance Supervisor was injured while serving as an FFT2 on a prescribed fire.

incidents.name: Alabama Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: On March 30, 2016, Firefighter Tucker responded from home with his son, Austin, a 16-year-old Junior Member of Lynn Fire & Rescue, to a grass and woods fire on Winston County Road 37. Once units cleared the fire scene, Firefighter Tucker was driving with his son back home when, for a cause still to be determined, their privately owned pickup truck veered off of the highway and struck an empty logging trailer parked nearby. Firefighter Tucker succumbed to his injuries sustained in the early morning hours of April 2, 2016.
incidents.quote: Two firefighters were driving back home when, for a cause still to be determined, their privately owned pickup truck veered off of the highway and struck an empty logging trailer parked nearby.

incidents.name: Vehicle Backing Accident
incidents.summary: Truck 1 turned around at this limited space area and was staged facing out. This left very little room for additional vehicles. When the driver of Truck 2 pulled toward the private gate and attempted to back into a small parking area space, the left rear portion of Truck 2 struck left front quarter panel of Truck 1.
incidents.quote: When backing up alone, do a complete 360-walk around. Backing without a spotter should only occur after the driver has gained as much situational awareness as possible.

incidents.name: Aircraft Damage During Ground Handling
incidents.summary: On March 31st 2016, at approximately 1445, a Beechcraft King Air Be9L aircraft was being backed into a hangar via ground handling tug and came into contact with another aircraft which was stationary in the hangar. Both aircraft sustained damage.
incidents.quote: The National Business Aviation Association (NBAA) estimates damaged caused by “Ground Handling” to be around $100 million a year in direct cost.

incidents.name: Prescribed Fire/Rx Felling Accident
incidents.summary: During mop-up operations on a prescribed fire slop-over a sawyer was struck by a portion of a felled snag.
incidents.quote: The blow was forceful enough to knock the sawyer down, leaving contusions on the right forearm, right bicep, and right chest area.

incidents.name: Aircraft Landing Incident
incidents.summary: On landing the left engine went to take-off power, un-commanded, and aircraft started to depart the runway. During subsequent actions to control the aircraft, brakes were applied and on ground contact the right main tire failed.
incidents.quote: Unexpected response makes for interesting ride!

incidents.name: Engine Air Brake Failure
incidents.summary: During Initial Attack, one of the county's Type 4 Engines—built on an M-923/925 military surplus chassis experienced a mechanical failure. The engine became immobile as fire approached. The operator escaped unharmed to a safety zone. Fire eventually moved through and the engine sustained minimal damage.
incidents.quote: Any wildland engine with air brakes that is used in a direct attack should be inspected for exposed brake lines that could be in danger of melting and locking the brakes in an unsafe location.

incidents.name: Rocky Mount Fire Review
incidents.summary: Through cooperative efforts between Rockingham County Fire and Rescue, the Virginia Department of Forestry, and the National Park Service, there was no damage or loss of structures or critical infrastructure. Burnout operations occurred off of the Park boundary in the Beldor Hollow area and fire “slop-overs” occurred near the Rocky Bar, Simmons Gap, and Sunshine Valley communities. These areas were contained as quickly as possible.
incidents.quote: “Even if we’d had people on that day, by the time they get near the fire it’s already pushing 50 acres. What are five people going to do on a 50-acre fire with no road access? It wouldn’t have made a difference in our decision-making or on the ultimate outcome. Yeah, we may have been able to evacuate hikers sooner, but fighting the actual fire, no way.”

incidents.name: R6 Physical Training Incident
incidents.summary: The 2 EMTs immediately recognized Anna was is need of medical attention and raced down the hill to her. She collapsed into them as they grabbed her under the arms, assisting her to the shade of a tree at the side of the road.
incidents.quote: “Anna’s heat stroke might well have been fatal on a remote fireline far from medical care.”

incidents.name: Prescribed Burn Unit 9 & 11 Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: A private minivan rear-ended a government vehicle operated by the Burn Boss during a prescribed burn. Smoke from a wind shift had impeded visibility on Highway 5.
incidents.quote: Seconds after the radio traffic to close the road was transmitted the Burn Boss called on the radio “I have been hit, dial 911.”

incidents.name: Vermont Heart Attack Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Lapierre succumbed to his injury after suffering a heart attack while operating at the scene of a brush fire on April 27th, 2016.

incidents.name: Smokejumper - Lost Handle Malfunction
incidents.summary: After sitting in the aircraft, prior to jump, the drogue 3-ing, drogue release handle, and the cutaway (main release) handle all moved from the desired position.
incidents.quote: The jumper stated that two attempts were made to pull the cutaway (main release) handle.

incidents.name: Black Hills NF Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: Sometime following his departure the injured crew-member drove himself at least 41 miles to a medical facility where he admitted himself for treatment. He did so without notifying his supervisor or any fellow crew-members
incidents.quote: “I couldn’t tell there was anything wrong.”

incidents.name: Day One Physical Training (PT) Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: As early as 1200 hours, Jay started experiencing leg cramps. EMTs noticed Jay’s pale, hot, dry skin and stopped him to evaluate. Based on their evaluation, Jay was removed from the training and taken to a hospital.
incidents.quote: From the perspective of the crew in this instance, the activities that day were not excessive.

incidents.name: Pack Test Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: During the pack test a firefighter on a Type 2 hand crew was sent to the hospital with symptoms of Rhabdo.

incidents.name: Physical Training (PT) Rhabdomyolysis Incident
incidents.summary: During the first week of physical training a firefighter on a Type 1 hand crew was sent to the hospital with symptoms of Rhabdo. The firefighter was admitted to the hospital, and was released the next day.

incidents.name: Montrose Fire Civilian Extraction
incidents.summary: Resources assigned to the Montrose Fire discovered a civilian in the fire area who needed medical assistance. They began a 9 Line assessment of the patient.
incidents.quote: All parties involved in this IWI exhibited professionalism and mutual trust for the expertise of their associated disciplines.

incidents.name: Black Springs Bucking Accident
incidents.summary: While making the final cut, the suspended 20-inch diameter log explosively snaps in a dropping, swinging blow into the Sawyer.
incidents.quote: Are we asking our Sawyers to act beyond their training and position descriptions to cut large numbers of insect-killed trees on a continuing basis?

incidents.name: Coyote Fire Medical Extraction
incidents.summary: On May 17, 2016 a member of a Wildland Fire Module stepped backwards into an agave plant on the Coyote Fire in the Guadalupe Mountains National Park.
incidents.quote: Four days after filing his claim, there were still issues with seeking treatment—even at home—until the doctor declared an emergency “due to possible loss of the leg” and convinced the administration to allow the surgery.

incidents.name: Foss Lake Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: There were noticeable increases in wind speeds and subsequent fire behavior. Fire crews were having a difficult time catching the spot fire and could not successfully start the pump. They were asked if they needed heavy aircraft.
incidents.quote: “We were trying to stay ahead of when green-up would occur or we would lose the chance for the summer."

incidents.name: Prescribed Fire (Rx) Fuel Cap Near Miss
incidents.summary: The engine operator spotted a piece of ignited bark with embers falling toward the cooperator. The engine operator called out—but wasn’t heard. At the same time, the engine operator noticed a “large flare up” and the saw stopped.
incidents.quote: As the cooperator lifted up on the chaps, fuel on his boot and under the chap’s left leg reignited.

incidents.name: Bloodborne Pathogen Food Incident
incidents.summary: Many resources were spiked-out at two remote spike camps. Food was prepared at the restaurants and delivered to the spike camps and ranger station, which was serving as the Incident Command Post. An individual was eating his evening meal at a spike camp when he bit down on a “used” bandage that had been in the meal’s mashed potatoes.
incidents.quote: He was eating his evening meal when he bit down on a “used” bandage that had been in the meal’s mashed potatoes.

incidents.name: UTV Spring Pole Near Miss
incidents.summary: A spring pole had entered the top, forward, and right portion of my UTV’s roll cage. The spring pole deflected against the rear window (behind the passenger’s head), bending the metal head rest and continued to arc down along the seat to the left, eventually ending up pressing across my lap (driver’s side)—with the tip protruding about three inches outside the door frame.
incidents.quote: “I glanced over at my passenger, fully prepared to see a decapitation and blood spurting everywhere.” UTV driver, certified ASI ATV instructor

incidents.name: Mule Ridge Fire Chainsaw Fuel Geyser
incidents.summary: A firefighter sustained a burn injury to his right forearm after he was sprayed by fuel that was ejected from his saw after he opened the fuel filler cap to release pressure.
incidents.quote: If your chainsaw dies, you might catch on fire.

incidents.name: NezPerce - Clearwater National Forests Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: Mike noticed the swelling had increased in his biceps enough that it was difficult to straighten his arms. His urine color had become dark (cola colored).
incidents.quote: “Mike was not on our radar, he was never struggling with PT”

incidents.name: Pony Fire Crew Carrier Near Miss
incidents.summary: The Crew Carrier skids sideways over to the opposite side of the road where it does a 180-degree turn and crashes into the bank backwards—stopping on the side of the road it started on, now facing the wrong direction.
incidents.quote: The road curves and an object (water bottle) rolls from under your driver’s seat toward the control pedals. You try to kick the bottle out of the way.

incidents.name: Turkey Fire Camp Overrun By Fire
incidents.summary: The IC was correct. The green meadows did not burn. But the fire managed to find a narrow strip of needle cast, maybe six inches wide from an oddly angled tree, that led across the green meadow grass into the camp area.
incidents.quote: But, as the group rode into camp, everyone’s jaw dropped. Everything in their camp had burned.

incidents.name: Saddle Mountain Medical Extraction
incidents.summary: Two low-angle rope rescue systems were set up to facilitate a smooth 1/3rd of a mile extraction down the mountain. From the moment the team began the descent to the time the patient was placed into the ambulance was <1 hour.
incidents.quote: In summary, one of the many successes of this medical extraction was how these two hotshot crews focused on the mission and respected input from others regardless of the color of their hard hats.

incidents.name: Akawana Fire Camp Fire
incidents.summary: At approximately 0400, a food unit worker and camp night watchman simultaneously investigated smoke coming from the fire camp’s west side in the nightshift sleeping area. They discovered a wind-driven fire burning with two-foot flame lengths.
incidents.quote: Folks scramble to wake people up and help put out a fire that erupts in the Akawana Fire’s fire camp sleeping area at 0400 hours.

incidents.name: Juniper Fire UTV Rollover
incidents.summary: The UTV immediately slid to the right and went into the ditch, flipped over, and rolled down the ditch line. The UTV ended up on its top with fuel leaking.
incidents.quote: Prior to this incident, I was on the fence about wearing a firefighter hardhat verses 3/4 shell motorcycle helmet when operating/riding in UTVs and ATVs. Not anymore. From now on, it’s the 3/4 helmet every time!

incidents.name: Homestead Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: On the afternoon of June 16, 2016 a county engine was assisting the BLM on the 25 acre Homestead wildfire. Members of the county engine crew were assigned to use a chainsaw to support direct fireline construction. At approximately 1630 hours the county chainsaw operator. sustained minor burns to the face during chainsaw refueling. The injured firefighter was evaluated by an on-scene EMT and was transported by ground from the fire area to a regional hospital where he was evaluated and released.
incidents.quote: This incident meets the criteria of a “Wildland Fire Accident” as defined by the Interagency Standards for Fire and Fire Aviation Operations (the Red Book)

incidents.name: Aspen/Pine Canyon Fires Fall While Hiking
incidents.summary: While propelling downhill and trying to stop, he noticed a piece of rebar sticking out of a pile of rocks. In attempting to miss this rebar, the Safety Officer fell—losing his hardhat—and hitting his head on rocks.
incidents.quote: Working in pairs allowed quick recognition of the problem and quick medical response.

incidents.name: Fire Shelter Damage and Delamination
incidents.summary: At first glance, the shelter appeared to be in good condition. However once the plastic packaging was removed from the shelter and was unfolded, several areas showed exposed inner-lining as well as signs of delamination.
incidents.quote: After removing the shelter from the fire gear, there appeared to be several small holes in the shelter packaging and dirt was noticeable within the packaging.

incidents.name: Deer Creek Fire Engine Damage
incidents.summary: After the tire fire suppression, the crew thoroughly surveyed the Type 4 for damages and discovered the leaking brake air line.
incidents.quote: At first, they didn’t notice anything obvious—until they started-up the Type 4’s engine.

incidents.name: Beaver Creek Fire Incident Documentation
incidents.summary: In August, the Incident Business Advisor (IBA) assigned to the Beaver Creek Fire recommended that the agencies order an Archivist to scan and catalog all the documents related to the fire. At first, the agencies were hesitant to agree to this request due to a concern that a complete set of these documents could not be provided. But eventually the agencies did agree and the Archivist (a DOCL) started this work. The documents are now scanned and named following the established document system. The original set of documents will be stored by the incident agency.
incidents.quote: At first, the agencies were hesitant to agree to this request due to a concern that a complete set of these documents could not be provided.

incidents.name: Dog Head Fire Medical Preparedness
incidents.summary: The Rapid Extraction Module (REM) is a new resource in thisarea provided by the Santa Fe Fire Department. “The intent of the SFFD Rapid Extraction Module (REM) is to provide Incident Management Teams with a highly specialized resource capable of responding anywhere on an incident to provide technical rescue and lifesaving medical interventions”. Dr. Linda Stogner is the medical director of several local clinics and is a former wildland firefighter. Dr. Stogner was available to treat injured firefighters and advise the Medical Unit Leader on patient transport decisions. In one instance, the doctor was able to quickly stich-up a cut on the arm of one individual, resulting in timely treatment and return to work, as well as a cost savings. Dr. Stogner also treated multiple heat-related injuries.
incidents.quote: “We had a little trouble getting the contract approved for the doctor, but I pushed because it just felt like the right thing to do.” Incident Commander

incidents.name: Short Fire Medical Emergency
incidents.summary: When the crew assisted the Crewmember out of the truck, he was not able to stand on his own. They laid him down on the ground. The Crew Boss then started looking for the Operations Section Chief (Ops) but was not able to locate him. He also called Division “Charlie” on the radio and informed him of a Crewmember having heat-related problems. BC4 had already called the County 911 Center and ordered the closest Life Flight to respond and the closest ambulance (two-hour response) to respond. The order for Life Flight 3 and the ground ambulance was placed with the county 911 Center at 2054 hours.
incidents.quote: The Crewmember became unresponsive and had a seizure that lasted approximately 30 seconds.

incidents.name: Fish Fire Rhabdo Incident
incidents.summary: On or about June 21, 2016, a member of a USFS Type 1 hand crew was sent to the hospital with symptoms of Rhabdo.

incidents.name: Ponderosa Prescribed Fire UTV and ATV Burn Damage
incidents.summary: One of the Wildland Fire Module members was asked to go back to the parking site to acquire an ATV/UTV to scout out other activity. Upon arrival of the site he found that all 4 vehicles had burned up.
incidents.quote: The report indicates that the cause could not be determined as to how the vehicles burned.

incidents.name: Erskine Fire Burn Over Dozer Transports
incidents.summary: On June 24, 2016, two CAL FIRE dozers were assigned to Division Echo of the Erskine Fire in Kern County. At approximately 1445 hours, while parked on a paved road, one dozer transport was totally destroyed while the other sustained moderate fire damage. The operators of the dozers were constructing fire line approximately two miles away when the incident occurred. There were no injuries associated with the incident.
incidents.quote: Kelso Road Burn Over - Dozer Transport(s)

incidents.name: Sequoia and Kings Canyon NP Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: Reports of Rhabdomyolysis have been on the rise for the past five years. Most summer months do not pass without yet another heat related illness or Rhabdo FLA and their associated lessons becoming available.
incidents.quote: If he had ignored his symptoms, there is a good chance he could have ended up in the hospital for a much longer stay and risked permanent damage to his kidneys or liver.

incidents.name: Cedar Fire Shelter Deployments
incidents.summary: Six members of the Navajo Interagency Hotshot Crew deployed fire shelters when a sudden change in fire activity occurred. They moved into a previously burned area and deployed their fire shelters. All of the firefighters were able to walk out of the fire area and were transported to hospital and released that evening.
incidents.quote: As a result of the predictive weather and values at risk, the Type 1 IMT had made a deliberate decision not to actively engage any personnel on the six-mile uncontained southwest flank.

incidents.name: Montana Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: As they approached this curve, the firefighter/driver noticed the recreation specialist tap the brakes of the flatbed, so E2028 further slowed to a “walking pace.” That’s when the first of two Subaru wagons came toward them at a relatively high rate of speed. The firefighter/driver was concerned that the first oncoming Subaru was traveling at such a speed that it would not be able to stop before colliding with the engine. To avoid the possibility of a head-on collision, the firefighter/driver reacted quickly by veering slightly to the right to give the first vehicle room to pass. As E2028 continued to creep forward, its front right tire sank into the soft berm of the freshly graded road.Seconds later, E2028 made a ¾ roll downslope, landing with the undercarriage against a mature spruce tree, approximately 30 feet below the road.
incidents.quote: The firefighter/driver was concerned that the first oncoming Subaru was traveling at such a speed that it would not be able to stop before colliding with the engine.

incidents.name: Chamberlain Tree Felling Accident
incidents.summary: During tree falling operations a sawyer was struck in the helmet by a falling branch. The impact knocked the sawyer to the ground. The sawyer was hospitalized and released with a fracture of the C-6 vertebra.
incidents.quote: The decision by the Duty Officer, working in conjunction with Forest leadership, to insist on a higher level of care for the patient was critical for the eventual accurate assessment of patient’s condition.

incidents.name: Trailhead Fire Dozer Rollover
incidents.summary: Dozer becomes stuck on a steep slope during line construction. Repeatedly instructed to wait for help, the dozer continued trying to climb the slope, resulting in a roll-over.
incidents.quote: Walking down the slope, they could see the dozer struggling to make it up the slope—some large trees were preventing the dozer’s blade from going past.

incidents.name: Crew Carrier Tire Failure
incidents.summary: Traveling westbound on Interstate 10 in the right-hand lane at approximately 65 mph, just outside of Tucson, AZ, the driver heard a loud “Bang!” followed by the vehicle immediately pulling extremely hard to the right side of the highway. Due to the loss of operational control, the driver was not able to keep the crew carrier from striking the guardrail. After the crew carrier’s right front quarter panel struck the guardrail two or three times, the vehicle remained in constant contact with the guardrail until it came to a complete stop—approximately 40 feet from the last strike.
incidents.quote: “I had no way of stopping the vehicle from hitting the guardrail.” Crew Carrier Driver

incidents.name: Cracked Windshield on Fire Engine
incidents.summary: I was driving southbound on the 101 Freeway enroute back to the Forest from a cover assignment when a rock hit the front windshield of my Fire Engine. I believe it came from a tractor trailer which was right in front of my Engine. The damage did not obstruct my vision. I proceeded to drive.
incidents.quote: The lesson here is to always be prepared for any hazardous situation that may threaten the safety of your crew or apparatus.

incidents.name: Airtanker Wing Tip Strike
incidents.summary: During retardant loading operations at an Air Tanker Base, a DC-10 Very Large Air Tanker (VLAT) struck the side of a hangar while on the ingress to a retardant loading pit.

incidents.name: Denio Engine Rollover Fatalities
incidents.summary: At approximately 1700 hours, a Winnemucca District BLM engine with a crew of three was involved in a single-vehicle accident while on patrol south of Denio, Nevada. Air and ground ambulances were immediately dispatched. Two firefighters succumbed to their injuries, and onefirefighter was flown to Reno, Nevada via air ambulance. Preliminary indications are that the right rear tire of the engine failed, causing the engine to roll
incidents.quote: A BLM engine with a crew of three was involved in a rollover accident while on patrol south of Denio, Nevada. Two of the crew were killed and one was injured.

incidents.name: McLeod Lands on the Interstate
incidents.summary: A Montana State wildland engine was returning from Miles City to Plains on Interstate 90 when a McLeod tool was air-lifted from the back of the engine and landed on the Interstate. A pickup truck following the engine ran over the tool, destroying this vehicle’s left front tire. The leader of the engine stopped and the crew helped the pickup driver change the tire, then followed him into the closest town and purchased a new tire for him.
incidents.quote: It seems it took Interstate speed and a strong head wind to dislodge this tool and lift it high enough to clear the top of the water tank and sail off the rear of the engine.

incidents.name: Pacheco Fire Engine Burn Over
incidents.summary: On July 12, 2016, a CAL FIRE Type 3 Model 34 engine (E1) attempted to start a mobile attack toward the head of a vegetation fire. Firefighters deployed two lines, but before they could anchor and start the mobile attack, the main fire and several spot fires converged on the fire engine. One firefighter took refuge in the engine, and one firefighter ran into the green. The engine sustained damage from the fire. Neither firefighter was injured.
incidents.quote: On July 12, 2016, at approximately 1314 hours, CAL FIRE and local government resources were dispatched to a vegetation fire in the vicinity of Langford Pacheco Road and Milton Road in Calaveras County.

incidents.name: Tok River Fire Equipment Burn Damage
incidents.summary: The crew disconnected the bucket and began loading gear back on the helicopter. When the crew began packing the bucket, the Pilot told them to leave it and get on the helicopter. The decision was made to leave the rest of the gear and get in the Helicopter. After taking off, the helicopter made several revolutions around the area hoping to be able to land again and retrieve their gear. The fire continued burning in the direction of the Landing Zone, growing from approximately 16 acres at 1730 to an estimated 100 acre sat 1810. The helicopter bucket, a chainsaw, a pump, and a flight helmet were all eventually consumed by the approaching fire.
incidents.quote: The pilot was concerned that if the column dropped too close on the ground, he wouldn’t have enough visibility to off.

incidents.name: Oregon SUV Rollover
incidents.summary: While returning to quarters in a government-owned Dodge Durango, two first-year wildland firefighters encounter a gravel washboard road surface on a sharp corner. The vehicle loses traction and spins 180 degrees, leaving the road backwards, completing a slow rollover, and coming to rest on its side in a sunken marsh.
incidents.quote: “Training matters. This actually happened to me. Stuff can go bad quickly.” - Vehicle Driver

incidents.name: Colorado Vehicle Collision
incidents.summary: A pre-positioned interagency Type 2 IA crew was traveling on I-25 after receiving a resource order. A vehicle accident ahead caused a large accident which involved two crew trucks, sending five crew members to the hospital.
incidents.quote: At 1501, as Squad 2 breathed a sigh of relief for successfully avoiding hitting the vehicles in front of them, the squad was hit from behind by a “jack-knifed” semi-truck.

incidents.name: Physical Training Hike Heat Stroke
incidents.summary: While on a training hike, a crew discovers a fire has started below them. Two crew members separated from the main group hurry to a safer location, and one of them suffers a major heat stroke.
incidents.quote: Tom told John: “We’re in a bad spot, don’t panic. Watch your footing, but we need to move faster because we’re walking too slowly.”

incidents.name: Physical Training Hike Heat Stroke
incidents.summary: During their descent, open flames from a fire that had just started below them began to grow.In a hurry to get out of harm’s way, John turned his ankle and needed to hold onto Tom’s line gear to continue progressing. Once in a safe spot, John collapsed, became unresponsive, and lost consciousness. A Cal Fire helicopter assigned to the fire diverted, picked up John, had him assessed by a Paramedic, and flew him directly to a medical center.
incidents.quote: “We have to train like we work. Actually we train harder than we work. We train hard to work hard.” Captain Sam “This was one of the most severe cases of heat stroke that we have ever seen.” Physician at the Hospital

incidents.name: Cliff Creek Wildfire Review
incidents.summary: Implementation and the resulting fire effects monitoring data shows that the burn met fuels and resource objectives for the local unit. The burn maintained the previous fuel treatments and built a substantial buffer for the values in Granite Creek which will pay dividends for years to come. Additionally, the burn created a nice mosaic that did not negatively impact the viewshed or any other resources. While this strategy turned out to be a success in this case, it might not always work out this way depending on all those environmental and social-political factors that we may or may not have any control over but need to be considered when identifying the appropriate strategy.
incidents.quote: “Overall, my observations are that the fuel reduction project played a significant role in the Jack Pine subdivision ultimately being a defendable space.” Jackson Hole Fire/EMS Captain

incidents.name: New Hampshire Firefighter Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Waterbury was transported to Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center where he was pronounced dead from nature of fatal injury still to be determined.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Waterbury suffered a medical emergency while fighting a brush fire in Lyme, New Hampshire.

incidents.name: Kent Fire Snake Bite
incidents.summary: The Kent Fire’s progression was halted at approximately 1800 hours on this first day. At approximately 1050 hours the next day, Whiskey Division reported a medical emergency that consisted of a rattlesnake bite to the shin of a crewmember on a Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation (DNRC) Engine.
incidents.quote: The crewmember never saw or heard the snake that bit him. Initially, he was unsure if he had even been bitten.

incidents.name: Little Den Fire Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: At approximately 0715 hours, a Battle Mountain District employee was involved in a single-vehicle accident while returning to Battle Mountain, Nevada. A ground ambulance was immediately dispatched with the employee transported to hospital.
incidents.quote: Little Den Fire Vehicle Accident

incidents.name: Soberanes Fire Dozer Rollover Fatality
incidents.summary: On July 26, 2016, at approximately 2310 hours, a Call-When-Needed (CWN) dozer was operating on Division T of the Soberanes Incident in Monterey County, CA. The dozer had to maneuver around an engine which was pumping a hose lay. The dozer proceeded slowly over an embankment. During this maneuver the dozer rolled onto its left side and roof. Fire line personnel immediately responded in an attempt to assist and treat the operator who unfortunately succumbed to his injuries at the scene.
incidents.quote: During the rollover the operator was ejected from the cab and became pinned underneath the left sweep of the dozer.

incidents.name: Single Engine Air Tanker Wire Strike
incidents.summary: While conducting fire suppression operations, a Single Engine Air Tanker (SEAT) struck a powerline while on final approach for a drop. The pilot was unaware of the strike at the time it occurred. Following the successful drop, the pilot looked out at his left wing and realized that numerous (21) vortex generators (see photo on right) were missing. He informed the Air Attack Group Supervisor (ATGS) and it was recommended that he go to Lewiston, Idaho. However, the Pilot decided that he would return to base at McCall, Idaho.
incidents.quote: SEAT Strikes Powerline

incidents.name: Spunky Fire Hit By Water Drop
incidents.summary: On July 29, 2016 at approximately 2000 hours, ten hotshot crew members were hit by a water drop from a helicopter equipped with a fixed tank during an initial attack on the Angeles National Forest
incidents.quote: The flight crew received no radio transmissions providing feedback that a load of water was dropped onto a ground crew.

incidents.name: Trailer Disconnect
incidents.summary: After closer inspection, we noticed that the small piece of metal that is normally pulled up under the ball when the trailer is connected onto the ball was too low and not in the correct position to hold the trailer onto the ball.
incidents.quote: All Towing Attachments Seemed Adequate and Proper– So How Did This Happen?

incidents.name: Tokewanna Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: On the afternoon of July 29, 2016, a fire crew member from the Great Basin Smokejumpers was injured while scouting fireline on the Tokewanna Fire. Burn injuries were sustained to the hands, thighs, ears, nose and cheeks. The firefighter was transported by air ambulance to the Salt Lake Burn Center and admitted. The injured firefighter continues to work with the Salt Lake City Burn Center medical team to determine priorities for treatment while staying at a nearby lodging facility.
incidents.quote: At approximately 1545 hours on July 29, 2016, an accident occurred on the Tokewanna wildfire, a multi-jurisdictional wildfire southwest of Rock Springs, Wyoming.

incidents.name: Pioneer Fire Fuel Geyser Burn Injury
incidents.summary: On Friday, July 29, at approximately 1400, a sawyer received 2nd degree burns to his lower arm when fuel from his chainsaw sprayed onto his arm and his saw and then combusted.
incidents.quote: He told the Saw Boss: “I haven’t looked at it yet. How bad is it?”

incidents.name: Butte 2 Fire Pump and Roll Engine Incident
incidents.summary: As the Engine was moved to the next ignition location, both crew members were seated in the cab. The hard line was wrapped around the driver’s side mirror and was being held by the driver to maintain tension on the line. While navigating a left-hand turn—with the hose’s nozzle end wrapped around the mirror—slack in the line allowed the hose to be caught under the outside dual tire on the driver’s side. This caused enough force to detach the mirror from the vehicle. There were no injuries and no other damage to the vehicle except for the broken mirror.
incidents.quote: While navigating a left-hand turn—with the hose’s nozzle end wrapped around the mirror—slack in the line allowed the hose to be caught under the outside dual tire on the driver’s side. This caused enough force to detach the mirror from the vehicle. There were no injuries and no other damage to the vehicle except for the broken mirror.

incidents.name: Pioneer Fire Radio Cloning Corruption
incidents.summary: If you get “Group 99” displayed on your radio screen, the radio is corrupt.
incidents.quote: “Is this a super radio? I have never seen a radio with 99 groups. How is this even possible?”

incidents.name: Twin Trees Fire Broken Ankle
incidents.summary: There was not visible swelling or bruising and he couldn’t feel a break. Jumper7 said his ankle just felt “weird, kind of loose.” The JIC wrapped the ankle to immobilize it and kept Jumper7 at the jump spot. The JIC remained engaged with Jumper7 and continued to assess how he was feeling and his pain level. Soon, the pain level Jumper7 was feeling elevated to a pain level 7. With this increased pain level, the JIC made the decision to get Jumper7 off the hill for evaluation and treatment.
incidents.quote: “I was concerned on how he landed. I needed to confirm the extent of his injury.” Jumper in Charge

incidents.name: Cracker Box Fire ATV Loading Accident
incidents.summary: He landed behind the trailer in a “seated” position. As the ATV fell backward, it caught the operator on the back of the helmet and, from the seated position, folded him forward at the waist, with the ATV coming to rest on top of him.
incidents.quote: The crewmember had a “Chance Fracture” of the 11th thoracic vertebra and would require surgery.

incidents.name: Power Line Fire Bulldozer Damage
incidents.summary: When Dozer #1 was about ten feet from the bottom of the drainage the operator felt the dozer “nose down.” Having little to no visibility through the dust and smoke, but feeling the motion of the dozer, the operator engaged the brake. As the dozer continued to slide downslope, the operator pushed the blade down to help him stop—but the dozer was already committed to what would later be found as a nearly vertical cutout from erosion in the bottom of the drainage.
incidents.quote: Dozer #1 stopped and talked with Dozer #2, asking his opinion about going down the slope. Dozer #1 and Dozer #2 shined their lights into the drainage to assess the intended line. Both operators felt it was a little steep; however, they could see the bottom of the drainage and the fire edge on the opposite side.

incidents.name: Strawberry Fire Tree Strike Fatality
incidents.summary: Justin Randal Beebe was a man of great character and humbleness. He lost his life on August 13, 2016, while cutting a hazard tree during suppression efforts on the Strawberry Fire, Great Basin National Park, Nevada.
incidents.quote: “It didn’t look like it was going the way you thought it’d go.”

incidents.name: Blue Cut Fire Structural Defense of Fire Station
incidents.summary: The temperature was 99 degrees and the relative humidity was 3%. The winds were blowing up Cajon Canyon from the south at 17 miles per hour. As it moved from the north to the east, the fire spotted across Highway 138. The Mormon Rocks Station was located directly in the fire’s path.
incidents.quote: “When I looked at the driveway (egress) out toward Highway 138 it was a No Go. It was blocked by a huge fire whirl that was coming north across the stubble field toward the station.”

incidents.name: Arizona Highway 95 Tire Blowout
incidents.summary: Chase Truck U-3665 was returning from a severity assignment near Nephi, Utah. Approximately 50 miles from theirhome unit, the operator experienced a violent shaking of the truck chassis followed by a catastrophic failure of the driver’s side rear tire. Outside air temperature when this tire failure occurred was 115 degrees Fahrenheit. This failure caused the truck to "fishtail" across the center line into the northbound lane of Highway 95. The operator was able to bring the truck back to the southbound lane and come to a stop without further incident. The spare was mounted onto the truck and the remaining three tires were visually inspected and pressures were checked. The trip then continued on without further incident.
incidents.quote: The spare was mounted onto the truck and the remaining three tires were visually inspected and pressures were checked. The trip then continued on without further incident.

incidents.name: Blue Cut Fire IA Structure Protection
incidents.summary: During the attempt to locate remaining residents and inform them to evacuate to a safer location, two County Fire Type 3 Engines were overrun by the fast-moving fire at a residence—where two civilians had remained on the property.
incidents.quote: Firefighters had asked the residents to leave multiple times but they refused.

incidents.name: Withers Fire Engine Burn Damage
incidents.summary: At approximately 2330 hrs a Forest Service engine crew was conducting a burnout operation in light, flashy fuels. An unexpected wind shift occurred which caused the fire to outflank the engine. While trying to exit the area the engine suffered heat damage based on poor visibility and a slow egress from the area. No injuries occurred.
incidents.quote: Scorch damage to Forest Service Type 6 engine.

incidents.name: Blue Cut Fire Helicopter Low Drop
incidents.summary: Personnel assigned to a CAL FIRE Engine Strike Team suffered minor to severe injuries from a Type 1 Helicopter water drop while engaged in wildland firefighting operations.
incidents.quote: When directing helicopter drops, the ground contact must have a clear and unobstructed view of the target area to ensure ground personnel are clear of the drop area.

incidents.name: Soberanes Fire Tree Felling Injury
incidents.summary: When the Sawyer made the back cut (boring in), the tree shuddered. A six-foot long branch/limb broke off and started falling to the ground.
incidents.quote: “When I got to him and lifted him up, there was blood everywhere. I was scared.”

incidents.name: Chimney Fire Pulaski Injury
incidents.summary: On August 19, 2016, a CAL FIRE California Conservation Crew (CCC) hand crew was assigned to Division A on the Chimney Fire in San Luis Obispo County, California. While constructing hand line, a CCC firefighter was swinging at brush when the pulaski hand tool struck a limb, resulting in a temporary loss of control, and struck a CCC Supervisor (C1) on the left elbow. The resulting impact caused a laceration to the elbow approximately two (2) inches in length and fractured a bone. An Incident Within an Incident (IWI) was immediately implemented per the Incident Command System 206 Medical Plan (ICS 206). The C1 was treated at scene by paramedics and flown to a nearby hospital for further treatment and evaluation.
incidents.quote: Pulaski Injury to Crewmember

incidents.name: Lebec Fire Hit by Rock
incidents.summary: On August 19, 2016, at approximately 1530 hours, CAL FIRE Helicopter 305, with the helitack crew, was assigned to the Lebec Fire in Kern County, California. While completing hand line in a steep narrow drainage, the helitack Fire Captain (FC) was struck on the helmet by a rock approximately twelve (12) inches in diameter. The rockwas loosened by another helicopter assigned to the fire which made a water drop above the FC. The speed and force of the rock caused the helmet’s suspension system to lacerate the head of the FC. The FC was treated and transported by paramedics to a local hospital by ground ambulance for further evaluation and treatment of the injury.
incidents.quote: Rolling Rock Caused by Water Drop

incidents.name: Cherry Road Fire Retardant Drops
incidents.summary: Once assured that they could safely proceed, TF1 began slowly moving down the steep, rocky road toward the heel of the fire. Right away, one engine blew a tire. The TFLD advised that engine to return to the top and find a safe place to change the tire. Before the Task Force was halfway down, the passenger side rear tire on the TFLD’s rental vehicle sustained a three-inch gash in the sidewall. From the TFLD’s limited vantage point along the two track, it appeared that the fire activity was picking up.
