The TFLD reported to the IC that the safest course of action was to leave the disabled vehicle, get in with one of the engines, and return to the top of the ridge with the rest of the Task Force.
incidents.quote: Both Engine and TFLD Vehicles Have Tire Issues, TFLD Abandons Vehicle; SEAT Drops Retardant to Help Protect It.

incidents.name: Cedar Fire Night Aviation
incidents.summary: Without the water dropping capability at night, there would have been structures lost at Wofford Heights and personnel safety compromised by the increased exposure to extreme fire behavior.
incidents.quote: “We were digging line next to the fire. I looked up and there were 25-foot flames. H-531 came in, cooled it down,and we continued digging line.”

incidents.name: Sand Ledges Fire Dozer Burn Over
incidents.summary: At approximately 1300 on the 21st while constructing fire line, the bulldozer suffered damage when a wind shift occurred, causing the wildfire to change direction. The bulldozer lost power during the event, and was damaged from the passing flame front. The bulldozer operator was not hurt during the incident, but the left side of the bulldozer was charred, air intake melted, and a window was broken. The Bulldozer is still operational.
incidents.quote: On August 21st 2016, at approximately 1420, a Bureau of Land Management (BLM) dozer was overtaken by the flame front of the Sand Ledges Fire.

incidents.name: Plumas NF Firefighter Fatality
incidents.summary: Engine Operator Ian Howard was assigned to Engine 16 from the Beckwourth Ranger District of the Plumas National Forest and prepositioned for firefighting at the Paskenta Work Center on the Mendocino National Forest.
incidents.quote: Engine Operator Ian Howard was found in the morning deceased from a nature and cause of fatal injury are still to be reported.

incidents.name: Cedar Fire Use of Water Scoopers
incidents.summary: Scoopers are a good supplement to our needs and reduce our need for Air Tankers.
incidents.quote: "I couldn’t believe how fast the Scoopers dropped water and came back.”

incidents.name: Broadway Fire Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: After a moment of cutting some of the desired holding wood, the tip of the saw bar contacted the placed wedge and kicked back toward the sawyer. The sawyer’s left leg was contacted with the bar and chain one half-inch above the top of his leather boots and one half-inch below his chaps.
incidents.quote: He immediately stopped the saw, set it on the ground, lifted his pants, and saw three cuts made to the inside shin area of his left leg.

incidents.name: Soberanes Fire ATV Incident
incidents.summary: All of a sudden the rear wheels of the ATV shifted to the left just as it came to a complete stop. The operator stepped off and moved quickly away. Almost immediately, the ATV began to roll on its side.
incidents.quote: Don’t hesitate to step away and let equipment sustain damage—better it than you!

incidents.name: Beartown FD Crew Carrier Fatalities
incidents.summary: Firefighters Alan Swartz and James Shelifoe, Jr. were killed when the fire apparatus (crew vehicle) they were riding in on Interstate 35W near Blaine, Minnesota, crashed into the median barrier and rolled a number of times. Several other firefighters riding in the truck were seriously injured and transported to the hospital. The firefighters, members of the Beartown Fire Department’s Type 2 wildland handcrew, were on their way to work the Box Canyon Fire in Utah when the crash occurred. The fatal incident remains under investigation by authorities
incidents.quote: Two firefighters were killed and several injured when the fire apparatus (crew vehicle) they were riding in crashed into the median barrier and rolled a number of times.

incidents.name: Soberanes Fire Watertender Close Call
incidents.summary: A watertender was full of water on a stretch of road he had already been up and down several times. As he approached a slight curve in the road he had no special concern—and then he felt the right rear duals give way.
incidents.quote: “This was a minor situation with the potential to become disastrous.”

incidents.name: Gap Fire Tree Strike
incidents.summary: A sawyer was impacted across his line gear backpack by a Shasta red fir pole. As the tree was felled, it became hung-up. When it was subsequently pushed, it rebounded—ultimately making contact with the retreating sawyer’s line gear pack on his back.
incidents.quote: We must be able to temper the overwhelming urge to rush in to put a hung tree onto the ground. The tree’s change in position/condition may have radically elevated the complexity far beyond our qualifications.

incidents.name: Canyon Fire Shelter Deployment and Entrapment 2016
incidents.summary: On September 19, 2016, extreme fire behavior and a 60-foot fire whirl forced resources on Division Z into a safety zone on Vandenberg Air Force Base. Multiple engines and personnel sheltered in vehicles and one firefighter deployed a shelter; two firefighters were hospitalized for smoke inhalation.
incidents.quote: When asked “How scared were you on a scale of 1 to 10?” multiple crew members replied “9” and “10.” Their escape was approximately 600 to 700 yards.

incidents.name: Canyon Fire Water Tender Fatality
incidents.summary: Ventura County Fire Engineer Ryan Osler died from injuries sustained in a fire apparatus crash while it was negotiating a traffic circle enroute to the Canyon Fire on Vandenburg Air Force Base. According to media reports, the water tender truck was loaded with 2,000 gallons of water and struck a curb in the roundabout then overturned. Two Firefighters were in the vehicle when it crashed. The passenger (Engineer Osler) was killed, while the driver suffered minor injuries. The fatal incident remains under investigation by authorities.
incidents.quote: Two Fire Engineers were injured, one fatally, when a water tender with 2000 gallons of water struck a curb in aroundabout then overturned.

incidents.name: Soberanes Fire Dozer Rollover
incidents.summary: While working on suppression repair the dozer became “a little too parallel” to the slope and the dozer overturned. The operator walked away from the incident, but was transported to a local hospital as a precaution.
incidents.quote: While working on suppression repair the dozer became “a little too parallel” to the slope and the dozer overturned.

incidents.name: East Maury Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: At 14:00 on the second day of the prescribed fire during a patrol, a column of smoke was spotted near the north handline (adjacent to private property). Upon further investigation, it was determined that the burn had escaped control lines with a spot fire approximately 0.5-1.0 acre in size, burning actively.
incidents.quote: The Burn Boss was informed that resources from Oregon Department of Forestry were not able to be used for prescribed burns due to lack of a payment mechanism

incidents.name: Minam 4 Escaped Prescribed Fire Review
incidents.summary: This prescribed burn plan elements regarding holding and contingency were followed and the unit was patrolled by air and on foot, the day of and the day after the initial ignition, by the Burn Boss and other assigned personnel. The initial spot fire that caused the Minam Fire was located via a helicopter recon at approximately 1900 hours on September 30, 2016. It was too dark and remote to make an attempt to physically locate the spot fire and take any suppression action. The following morning the Burn Boss and two other personnel walked into the area where the reported spot fire was located. The Minam Fire was declared on Saturday in on October 1, 2016 at 1030. The decision was made to have the incident managed as a Type 3 incident and resources were ordered and a briefing was conducted the following morning. Resources were in place and taking suppression action on the fire by midmorning on October 2, 2016.
incidents.quote: Seasonal Severity, Weather, and On-Site Conditions Leading Up to the Wildfire Declaration.

incidents.name: Pingree Hill Prescribed (Rx) Fire Fuel Geyser Burn FLA
incidents.summary: As he opens the cap the fuel sprays out in two distinct bursts spraying liquid and vaporized fuel on his stomach area and right arm. He quickly realizes this is a very dangerous situation.
incidents.quote: “The one thing I hope comes out of this is that people will give it one last second thought…before you pop the cap”

incidents.name: Fire Captain Hit by Tree
incidents.summary: On Tuesday, October 11, 2016 CAL FIRE La Cima 3 (LCM 3) was assigned to a grade project for the Helix Water District in San Diego County. The project consisted of clearing brush and falling trees around an old diversion dam near Ramona, CA. At approximately 1:40 PM, while the Fire Crew Captain was supervising a crew member sawutilizing a chain saw to fall a tree, the Fire Captain was struck by branches from the falling tree. The Fire Captain was transported to the hospital for injuries to his lower arm and hand.
incidents.quote: MVU Fire Captain Injury

incidents.name: Mingus Mountain UTV Rollover
incidents.summary: As the UTV descended down the earthen bank, the right front steering drive wheels grabbed the ground really hard. “The steering wheel was ripped from my hand, turning the UTV sharply into the bank,” the operator explained.
incidents.quote: Accidents can happen in the blink of an eye. Even if “you’ve been there—done that” and are an experienced operator.

incidents.name: Little Valley Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.fire: Little Valley Prescribed Fire / Little Valley Fire
incidents.summary: The Little Valley Prescribed Fire was conducted by the Nevada Division of Forestry (NDF) between Oct. 4-7, 2016. Mop-up began immediately upon completion of each unit and continued through Oct. 13. In the early hours of Oct. 14, at approximately 0138 hours, a wildland fire—subsequently named the “Little Valley Fire”— was detected along the ridge between Little Valley and Washoe Valley. Influenced by exceptionally high winds, the wildland fire pushed down canyon into a subdivision along Franktown Road. While rapid response and evacuation of residents saved human lives, tragically, the fire destroyed 23 homes and 17 outbuildings before it was contained.
incidents.quote: “The Nevada Division of Forestry fuel treatments and prescribed fire policy is established to treat fuels and mitigate threats to the public, and to protect, enhance, restore and/or maintain critical plant communities.” Nevada Division of Forestry Administrative Manual, Fire Treatments and Prescribed Fire, 06040.0

incidents.name: Cajete Prescribed Fire Project
incidents.summary: The first engine arrived on scene at 1615 hours. The second engine arrived at 1700 hours. When the first engine arrived on scene, the shed was completely engulfed in flames. The firefighters recognized that they did not have the proper equipment or qualifications to engage in the structure fire. Protection efforts were implemented on the adjacent building and the shed was allowed to burn. While an official fire cause could not be determined, it appears that a smoldering root may have burned under the handline and ignited the woodpile adjacent to the shed.
incidents.quote: It was later discovered that a five-gallon propane cylinder had been stored in the shed and exploded during the structure fire.

incidents.name: Kentucky Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Collett was airlifted to Pikeville Medical Center for treatment but succumbed to his injuries the evening of November 17th.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Collett suffered head and arm injuries on October 29th while working a wildland fire incident when a tree limb fell and struck him and the fire apparatus he was on.

incidents.name: Maple Springs Fire Leaf Blower Fuel Geyser
incidents.summary: Feeling like productivity would be greater if they filled the leaf blower while it remained on the operator’s back, FF #2 opened the dolmar and then proceeded to open the leaf blower fuel tank. This caused a geyser of fuel to erupt from the leaf blower.
incidents.quote: FF #3, located downhill of this refueling operation, looked up to see: “a fireball and FF#2 on fire.”

incidents.name: Oklahoma Dual Wheels Engine Incident
incidents.summary: Kaibab National Forest Engine 631 was traveling to the Party Rock Fire in North Carolina when the Operator felt a change in driving characteristics in the engine handling—and a wheel from the passenger-side rear duals passed them.
incidents.quote: While driving their Engine down Interstate 40, the Operator suddenly feels a change in driving characteristics as one of their passenger-side rear duals suddenly passes them!

incidents.name: Arkansas Vehicle Fire
incidents.summary: The employee decides to perform a three point turn. While attempting this turn-around maneuver, the vehicle’s front tires drop into a ditch that is approximately one-foot deep and two-feet across. The ground clearance on this particular vehicle is 7.8 inches and the tread on the tires are not very aggressive. The Jeep’s bottom A-arm becomes lodged in the ground and the vehicle becomes high-centered on the exhaust pipe. Realizing that the vehicle is not coming out of the ditch, the employee decides to call for help. The employee can’t hit a repeater on the vehicle radio so tries to do so on their handheld. By walking eastward, the employee eventually makes contact with the District Office. While asking for help on the radio, the employee turns around toward the vehicle and sees flames under the front end. The employee quickly relays to the office that the vehicle is on fire.
incidents.quote: While asking for help on the radio, the employee turns around toward the vehicle and sees flames under the front end.

incidents.name: Airtanker Wing Tip Strike RLS
incidents.summary: A corporate Gulfstream Jet taxied between another private business jet and Tanker 4, resulting in the underside of the Gulfstream jet’s left wing tip winglet striking the entire width of the underside port wing tip of Tanker 41.
incidents.quote: You can never let your guard down. You can never relax in aviation.

incidents.name: Chimney Tops 2 Fire Review
incidents.summary: The review team concluded that a lack of wildland fire preparedness during a period of drought conditions favorable to wildfires overwhelmed National Park Service response to the CT2 fire. Though the review team concluded that the firefighting decisions made by the personnel involved were commensurate within their knowledge and experience in fighting wildland fires in the region, this report recommends enhanced preparedness and fire planning based on fire-conditions assessments, and adherence to the National Park Service wildland fire program and policies. These recommendations will likely enhance the capability of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park to respond to a wildfire event with similar or greater fire weather conditions in the future.
incidents.quote: The unprecedented Chimney Tops 2 Fire event exposed several wildland fire situational preparedness and planning weaknesses at the Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Despite these weaknesses, the review team found no evidence of wanton disregard or negligence by anyone at the park.

incidents.name: Redmond Smokejumper Fatality
incidents.summary: It’s not clear that any single person had the responsibility and authority to communicate a clear leadership message and intent—to synthesize the information and articulate a choice and a rationale. So nobody did.
incidents.quote: “In any moment of decision, the best thing you can do is the right thing, the next best thing is the wrong thing, and the worst thing you can do is nothing.”

incidents.name: Maple Springs Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: During the early morning hours of November 30th while assigned to the Maple Springs Fire in North Carolina, Darryl Elden Vielle, a member of Blackfeet Tribal Agency Camp Crew 3 was found deceased in his motel room. Cardio pulmonary resuscitation was administered by local emergency personnel and initially they had determined the individual may have passed several hours earlier prior to the discovery.

incidents.name: Two RX Fire UTV Incidents
incidents.summary: Two UTV Incidents occurred within one week in South Carolina. These incidents highlight the inherent dangers we face on a day-to-day basis that we often consider “routine.”
incidents.quote: The back wheel went slightly off the bladed berm....

incidents.name: Mississippi Brush Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: According to news reports, when another firefighter on a hoseline asked the Chief to reposition the apparatus, there was no response. Fire Chief Mathews was immediately removed from the truck, given CPR, and then transported to Jefferson Davis Community Hospital where he was pronounced deceased. According to a statement from the Coroner, the nature of fatal injury was a massive heart attack.
incidents.quote: Fire Chief Matthews was found unconscious in the driver’s seat of the fire apparatus he was operating on the scene of a brush fire working to protect a nearby church.

incidents.name: Dozer Transport Tire Blowout FLA
incidents.summary: A dozer transport occupied only by the driver, was involved in a single vehicle accident that resulted in destruction of the transport. Tread from the front left tire was thrown and the tire blew out. This caused the truck to veer leftward. Quick reaction by the operator lessened the effect of the blown tire and gave time for the transport to decelerate before impact with mature pine trees off the left shoulder of the road. No significant personal injury was sustained.
incidents.quote: “As I was slowing and edging to the left, I saw a “soft spot” in the vegetation, a strip where no trees grew, only the dense shrubs. I tried to aim for that, but was unsuccessful.”

incidents.name: Inmate Firefighter Project Work Injury
incidents.summary: A CAL FIRE Oak Glen Fire Crew was assigned to a tree limbing work project in Oak Glen, CA. After performing an elevated limb cut, a violent reaction occurred that affected the rope and the climbing system causing injury to an Inmate Firefighter.
incidents.quote: There is no department policy on tree climbing operations; crew followed industry standards for the operation

incidents.name: JA Ranch Prescribed Fire Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: Crews working on the JA Ranch in Donley County had everything under control until a juniper tree was torched and sent embers outside the controlled area. The second fire was nearly contained when an extremely rare phenomenon called a fire-whirl caused it to get out of control.
incidents.quote: The fire whirl burned two firefighters on their hands and face.

incidents.name: Prescribed Fire Tree Cutting Injury
incidents.summary: The Sawyer cuts for a second, then stops. Finding it difficult to see where the edge of the face cut is, the Sawyer takes a moment to brush off debris from the bark. (The Sawyer does this to prevent the possible cutting of the holding wood.) The Swamper says to keep going. The tree stood up for a second on its stump. Then I noticed it beginning to angle back toward us and our escape route. I took another step or two back, and just as I turned to exit farther via my planned escape route, I noticed the tree seemed to be coming directly toward me and this escape route.
incidents.quote: “I was knocked face down, with my head facing left. I saw the bar of the saw six inches from my face. I could tell it was running, and was worried the chain brake had somehow been disengaged.”

incidents.name: Green Mountain PT Hike Search and Rescue
incidents.summary: A module consisting of seven people performed an arduous physical training (PT) hike in an area that was familiar to some, but not all of the crew members. There was not a marked trail or route up the mountain for the intended hike. One crewmember ended up exceeding the pace of the rest of the crew, becoming separated from all crew members and without communication. While ascending to what was perceived to be the summit, the crewmember noticed he had reached a different location. The crewmember began a descent down the mountain, ending up in an unfamiliar drainage. Through excellent teamwork by the crewmembers, supportive leadership, and line officers, a coordinated search and rescue effort was initiated, resulting in the crewmember’s safe return.
incidents.quote: Not all who wander are lost, but some people might think you are and respond accordingly.

incidents.name: 119 Road Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The 119 Road Fire ignited around 2100 hours on March 23, 2017, and rapidly burned 100 acres of grass, brush, and timber, showing unusually aggressive behavior for nighttime conditions. During the initial attack, three volunteer firefighters operating a Type 6 engine on the west flank were entrapped when a sudden wind shift intensified the fire and heavy smoke reduced visibility, preventing the Engine Boss from identifying an escape route. As heat and smoke increased, the engine and pump stalled, and the flaming front overran the vehicle, injuring two firefighters—one with minor burns and another with bruised ribs—and destroying the engine. After the flames passed, the firefighters inside the cab escaped and tried to suppress the engine fire, while the firefighter outside survived in part because they had pre‑wetted the surrounding area before being overrun.
incidents.quote: The fire spread was very rapid with a short residual time at the engine’s location, but the engine still caught fire.

incidents.name: Wewoka Prescribed Fire Escape
incidents.summary: The Wewoka Agency, Bureau of Indian Affairs, implemented the Self Prescribed Fire on March 15, 2017. This prescribed fire’s area encompassed 515 acres inside the “Self Property” on Seminole Tribal Fee land. It is estimated that this broadcast burn was the first application of fire on this ground in 12 years. On March 24, the prescribed fire escaped on its northwest corner. The possible cause of this escape may have been embers from the prescribed fire unit.
incidents.quote: The Self Prescribed Fire Escape review process has been a valuable learning process for the Region and Agency. The Fuels Management Program will implement the recommended actions to better our knowledge and skills in prescribed fire.

incidents.name: Arizona Engine Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: The employee ran a 1.5 mile run with a time just under 15 minutes. Complained of being tired and feeling a little sick. Drank fluids and felt better but then so then began vomiting. Supervisor determined he needed medical care, at which point adjoining county agency initiated an IV, and ambulance was ordered. Determined to have rhabdomyolysis. Released 5 days later when CK levels in kidney came back to an acceptable level. The supervisor told the ambulance driver that the employee needed to be tested for Rhabdo, as well as telling the patient in talking with the receiving Doctor at the hospital. The firefighter was released after spending five days in the hospital.
incidents.quote: This patient was a seasonal firefighter returning to work on his first day back.

incidents.name: New Mexico IHC Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: This medical incident happened on day 3 of the firefighter showing up to work for the season. The firefighter performed the following physical activities: Pack Test day one, Strength Training day two, Moderate Run day three. On 4/06/17 the firefighter experienced muscle cramping, swelling, dark urine (Coca-Cola or Tea colored), weakness, muscle stiffness and decreased range-of-motion of the joints. The patient was transported to the hospital, and diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. The firefighter was released after spending eight days in the hospital.
incidents.quote: The patient was transported to the hospital, and diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis.

incidents.name: Doubleside Fire Tractor Entrapment
incidents.summary: The Okeechobee District responded to a wildfire in a high fire danger area known as “the prairie” in Okeechobee County. During initial attack operations a type 2 tractor plow unit was overrun by fire causing the AC filter to catch fire, resulting in a total loss of the equipment. The fire plow itself sustained only minor damage resulting from this incident. The firefighter was not injured.
incidents.quote: I told everyone to clear the channel but everyone kept talking.

incidents.name: Bienville Prescribed Fire UTV Incidents
incidents.summary: On the National Forests in Mississippi, Bienville Ranger District prescribed burn, two different Utility Task Vehicles (UTVs), at two different times, became temporarily immobilized on an active railroad track.
incidents.quote: Prescribed fire operations in the southeast are often complicated by Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) issues. This prescribed fire was conducted around an active railroad line. Railroad lines have a unique set of risks and hazards associated with them. This particular railroad line is active with fast moving trains at speeds greater than 50 mph.

incidents.name: Washington Smokejumper Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: When the rookies are recruited, they are told to start working out. The first day of rookie training was normal he was staying hydrated. Some candidates were cramping, which is pretty normal. On the second day he appeared overheated and when asked a question, he could not answer a simple question. They thought it was heat exhaustion but he had drank lots of water. They took him into an air conditioned room, all vitals were normal except temp was about 100. Because he could not answer what he had for breakfast and did not know if he had urinated that day, they took him to the ambulance, but still thought he was overheated or dehydrated. They give an IV and went to the hospital. T
incidents.quote: The firefighter appeared to be in good physical condition, muscular and fit. He was previously in Special Forces, so strenuous work outs were not uncommon to him.

incidents.name: Marion County Helicopter Accident
incidents.summary: A Bell 206B helicopter pilot was completing bucket drops on a brush fire in Marion county. He landed at a nearby landing zone, refueled, and completed 3 or 4 additional drops when the accident occurred. After lowering the bucket into the water and filling it, he pulled the bucket from the water and immediately felt "a severely out of [balance] condition to the right." He assumed that the bucket cables were entangled in the right landing skid, so he released the water from the bucket. The condition persisted, so he rocked the helicopter to attempt to free the cable; however, this was not successful. He then released the cable with the cargo release button. He heard the "clunk" sound that was typical with releasing the bucket, then he heard another "clunk." The helicopter then began to spin violently and crashed into the water.
incidents.quote: The pilot freed himself from the cockpit, inflated his personal flotation device, and swam to shore.

incidents.name: IHC PT Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: At the beginning of May, during the first week of critical training with the Logan Interagency Hotshot Crew, Ricky (not the employee’s actual name) was diagnosed with Rhabdomyolysis. He was subsequently hospitalized for eight days.
incidents.quote: “My own personal irrational reasoning and denial almost convinced me to wait to go to the ER the next morning. My take-away from this experience is that sometimes you get hurt and the tough thing to do is admit that.”

incidents.name: West Mims Fire Tractor Plow Burnover
incidents.summary: A tractor plow became stuck on a stump just as a wind shift caused a flanking fire to become a head fire. The tractor plow operator was able to walk to safety, but the tractor plow unit was overrun by fire.
incidents.quote: Radio communications were confusing. It was not clear to the overhead if the tractor plow operator was still with the machine.

incidents.name: California Type 1 Crew Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: During line up on the second day of crew training, a 25 year old male firefighter complained of cramps during a PT hike. Symptoms were muscle cramping, nausea and vomiting. EMT’s provided IV fluids and transported to hospital. This event occurred the first day of crew training and the patient was seen at the ER the second day. The patient was transported to the hospital, and diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. The firefighter was released after spending three days in the hospital.
incidents.quote: A Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK) test was administered, with a result of 17,000

incidents.name: Crane Island Fire Tractor Plow Entrapment
incidents.summary: A Florida Forest Service (FFS) type 2 tractor plow unit became stuck and was overtaken by fire during suppression operations on the Crane Island Fire.
incidents.quote: In preparation for the passing of the fire front, T-89 Ranger activated his tractor protection system for the belly pan. He ensured all his PPE was donned, exited the cab, and began to wet down the left side of the tractor; the right side was too hot at that moment. Seminole 614, a local type 3 helicopter, made an initial bucket drop on T-89 before the front arrived. The smoky conditions forced the operator back inside the cab of T-89. The fire front passed over T-89.

incidents.name: Kern County FD Fatality
incidents.summary: On May 18, 2017, Fire Engineer Brian Massey started a 48-hour shift by participating in a wildland firefighting class which included strenuous simulation training, causing him to vigorously exert himself. At 0800hrs on May 20, 2017, Massey completed his shift which, in addition to the wildland firefighting training, included several emergency response calls. Later that day, while at home, Massey suffered a significant medical event.
incidents.quote: Fire Engineer Brian Massey suffered a fatal medical event after participating in a wildland firefighting class which included strenuous simulation training, causing him to vigorously exert himself.

incidents.name: Pinal Fire Drone Intrusion
incidents.summary: On May 20 at approximately 1805, an Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS)—or drone—was spotted 60 yards from the Pinal Fire Helibase at approximately 50 feet above ground level. The UAS was flying in the designated flight path of this incident’s helicopters where they were making their descents to land at the Pinal Fire Helibase, located within the city limits of Globe, Arizona. Helitack personnel were able to track the UAS while it was in flight, they observed the aircraft descend and land at a nearby residence in the vicinity of the Pinal Fire Incident Command Post. . The LEO had enough information to go make contact with the UAS operator and was able to confiscate the UAS and cite the individual.
incidents.quote: The UAS intrusion within the TFR posed a serious safety concern for incident pilots and fire personnel involved in helicopter aviation missions on the Pinal Fire.

incidents.name: Moose Creek Prescribed Fire UTV Fire
incidents.summary: While using a 2013 Polaris 6x6 UTV on a prescribed fire, an accumulation of fine fuels located in an enclosed compartment under the UTV’s floorboard and above the skid plate ignited. This fire melted a four-inch hole in the skid plate and floorboard and caused extensive damage to wiring and the gear selector cable.
incidents.quote: Typically, UTVs function without damage driving through low-intensity flames.

incidents.name: South Dakota Engine Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: While taking the "Arduous" Work Capacity Test, a firefighter collapsed. EMTs on scene began treating him immediately and transported him to a local hospital. Upon initial diagnosis, he had very high enzyme levels, leading them to believe he may have rhabdo. He spent several days in the local hospital before being transferred to the hospital in Rapid City for further tests and treatment, where again he was treated for rhabdo. Once released from the hospital in Rapid City he was put on light duty. Several weeks later, he suffered some effects from the rhabdo and collapsed again after standing from a seated position at lunch

incidents.name: Utah IHC Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: The firefighter was assigned to project work, running a chainsaw on a 12 hour shift. 15 tanks were run by the individual. At end of shift individual was cramping intermittently all over upper and lower body and urine was dark yellow. Hydration and stretching done that night. Next day little relief prompted doctor visit. Patient’s symptoms were localized muscle soreness, muscle cramping, weakness, stiffness and decreased range-of-motion of joints, decreased coordination, fatigue, headache/fever plus nausea/vomiting.

incidents.name: Ishi Incident Hit by Tree Fatality
incidents.summary: Inmate Firefighter Matthew Beck was leading a crew clearing brush to contain a fire when a 120-foot tree uprooted and fell on him. Beck suffered major head neck, and back injuries. The remote location of the incident posed challenges for medical responders and before life-flight crews could get to him, Beck passed away.
incidents.quote: Inmate Firefighter was clearing brush to contain a fire when a 120-foot tree uprooted and fell on him.

incidents.name: Oregon Smokejumper Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: Three days prior to the incident the employee states that he worked out his arms extremely hard during PT and was somewhat fatigued and sore prior to driving to the Ranger District to work. On May 24th he drove to the District where he worked climbing large trees, removing hazard limbs, topping trees and falling trees through May 26th. On Friday May 26th he noticed that his forearms and biceps were swollen, but continued to work. After driving back to the base from the field work on May 26th he unloaded his gear and was getting ready to go home for the weekend. He stopped to use the restroom and noticed that his urine was extremely dark colored. He decided to seek medical treatment and drove himself straight to the hospital where they diagnosed him with Rhabdomyolysis.
incidents.quote: I was sore from the work out but personally and physically I felt fine, didn’t think much about it

incidents.name: Memphis VFD Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Ketchum died at the scene from injuries sustained and the passenger, John Chancellor, was treated and flown to the University Hospital in Columbia, Missouri, with serious injuries. According to initial reports, seat belts were not in use at the time of the crash.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Jesse Ketchum was responding to an outdoor (field) fire call when the fire apparatus he was operating crashed while negotiating a curve and overturned several times, ejecting Ketchum and a passenger in the vehicle.

incidents.name: Chase Truck Hits Power Pole
incidents.summary: As the chase truck was coming into the left hand curve the vehicle continued in a straight direction and struck the guard rail. As the vehicle traveled along the guard rail the support post broke and the railing twisted and the right side front bumper began riding on top of the rail. The fourth post did not break and the truck went up and over the rail into heavy black berry brush and continued approximately 120 feet and hit a power pole.
incidents.quote: “Suddenly, and for reasons I do not know, we were suddenly headed for the guard rail.”

incidents.name: Boundary Fire Broken Leg
incidents.summary: As Crewmember 2 climbed the ladder and approached the roof’s edge (at about the 7-foot-high rung), the ladder began to slide away from the structure rapidly. When the ladder slipped, Crewmember 2’s left foot became caught in the rung of the ladder. The impact to the deck, combined with his body weight landing on the ladder, caused his lower left leg to break.
incidents.quote: Crewmembers working in the area heard Crewmember 2 yelling for help.

incidents.name: Temple Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: This was the first time this particular saw acted up all day, dying mid-cut through a branch of a small juniper tree as flames crawled up from the base. After trying to restart it a few times, the Sawyer walked into the green and popped off the cap. The fuel tank was still half-full, so he closed the cap, believing that it was fully sealed. Unbeknownst to the Sawyer, fuel leaked out of the saw’s tank and onto his chaps as he walked back to the juniper. The fire that consumed his legs and feet blew up after he approached the tree again to finish the cut. He would later learn that two other resources on the fire also experienced issues that day with fuel caps that wouldn’t seal properly on chainsaws of similar make and model. In both cases, the fuel caps were replaced without incident.
incidents.quote: Fire singed the Sawyer’s beard as he fumbled with the buckles on his chaps. Heat leapt up at his face, rising from the fire that engulfed the ground at his feet…his chaps…his pants. “Drop and roll!” the Swamper yelled.

incidents.name: Bowie Fire Radio Cloning Issues
incidents.summary: Several KNG radios were cloned successfully where no errors were detected. However, the tones did not transfer. Further research found that this issue was noted in a “Relm Wireless Bulletin” (BKSB-1043) issued on July 29 last summer.
incidents.quote: It is important that all firefighters who carry KNG radios have their radio serviced by their agency’s radio center before the fire season to be sure all upgrades have been installed.

incidents.name: Dead Dog Fire Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: The collision involved a Government Owned Vehicle (GOV) and a Privately Owned Vehicle (POV) operated by a member of the public not associated with fire suppression. The two vehicles collided at low speeds. Both received damage to the front driver’s side corner panel.
incidents.quote: Radio traffic indicated the road was closed and due to the fire behavior conditions. GOV Truck-1 did not expect there to be traffic traveling southbound on this road.

incidents.name: Highline Fire Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: On the morning of Tuesday, June 13, a hotshot experienced a case of rhabdomyolysis while hiking into the Highline Fire. This was the hotshot crew’s first roll of the season and the second shift of the roll. It had taken two days of driving and one day of staging to get assigned to this fire.
incidents.quote: The Crew EMT began a thorough examination of Bill. He was sweating profusely, his skin was tenting (a slow return of the skin to its normal position after being pinched—which can be a sign of dehydration) for 8-10 seconds and was hot to the touch, although Bill was shaking uncontrollably and feeling cold.

incidents.name: Frye Fire Strep Throat Outbreak
incidents.summary: A Spike Camp began getting a rapid influx of firefighters complaining of an unknown illness. This Spike Camp was located two plus hours away from the Incident Command Post (ICP). No one had complained of illness down at the ICP. Therefore, this illness appeared to be isolated at the Spike Camp. A “Doc in a Box” strategy was discussed and determined to be the best course of treatment for all personnel at Spike Camp.
incidents.quote: The aggressiveness of this particular outbreak—and with nearly 300 firefighters potentially exposed—was considered a risk to the local communities.

incidents.name: Golden Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: A crewmember was performing in the role of sawyer and was sawing line on the west flank of the fire. After sawing for approximately 30 minutes he shut the saw (Stihl MS-460) off to get clarification on cutting a tree. The sawyer then attempted to start his saw several times without success then turned the saw on its side and opened the fuel cap. A geysering effect occurred spraying fuel into the sawyer’s face and up his right arm. Fuel began to run down the bar of the saw, into the black which then ignited causing the fire to run up the saw and onto the sawyer.
incidents.quote: Personnel need to be trained to recognize the symptoms of vapor lock

incidents.name: Nara Visa Fire Department Fatality
incidents.summary: On Wednesday, June 21, 2017, while attempting to fill tankers on a wildland firefight involving several local fire departments, Firefighter John C. Cammack fell from the back of a firefighting apparatus as it was escaping from wind driven flames that had switched direction and burned over their location. A second firefighter,KylePerez, was also hanging onto the truck as it drove through the flames and was injured.
incidents.quote: Firefighter John C. Cammack fell from the back of a firefighting apparatus as it was escaping from wind driven flames that had switched direction and burned over their location.

incidents.name: Brake Failure on Type Four Engine
incidents.summary: The driver attempted to stop the vehicle using the service brake, but the brake bottomed out to the floor. Even though there were no alarms or low pressure warning lights, the driver immediately recognized something was wrong with the primary brake system and was able to use the emergency brake to bring the vehicle to a slow stop. Due to this quick action, no injuries or damage to the engine occurred. Upon inspection, the Engine Crew was able to identify a loose air hose that was not connected to any metal coupling. Examination of the fitting found that the compression ring was loose and had not been pressed onto the air hose. The coupling fitting was retightened and a brake check was performed. No further issues were found and the crew was able to get the engine to a certified mechanic.
incidents.quote: Potential brake loss on 2016 International 7400 SFA 4x4 Type Four Engines with a Boise Mobile Equipment (BME) apparatus/pump package

incidents.name: Oregon Type 2 IA Crew Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: During fireline mop up operations, the patient started to feel dizzy, had a loss of balance, and was shaking uncontrollably. The patient’s symptoms included overall weakness, decreased coordination, and fatigue. The patient was provided with IV fluids and transported to the hospital. The patient was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. The firefighter was released after spending two days in the hospital.

incidents.name: Nevada Type 2 Crew Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: This medical incident happened on day 12 while the patient was on a fire assignment in Utah. The patient was digging line uphill in a non-shaded area. Patient started noticing soreness and fatigue to one of his upper extremities before informing nearby EMTs. This occurrence happened after eating lunch. Patient was feeling dizzy, fatigued, with upper extremity pain. Patient had minimal lunch intake prior to incident. The EMT’s provided 2 liter Bolus NS IV fluids. Electrolyte tablets with water. The patient was then transported to and seen at the Incident Medical Unit.

incidents.name: Cable Fire Dozer Swamper Close Call
incidents.summary: On Saturday, June 24, 2017, at approximately 2:35 PM, while making access to the Cable Incident in San Bernardino County, California, a CAL FIRE Caterpillar D6NXLDozer (D1) was unable to progress due to very steep and loose terrain. While facing downhill, D1 requested a United States Forest Service (USFS) Dozer (D2) for a winching operation. While coordinating the winching operation, the Swamper (DS2) from D2 climbed on the D1 driver-side tracks to establish communications, due to inoperability of the assigned tactical frequency. While DS2 was conferring with D1, an unexpected movement of D1’s tracks occurred, forcing DS2 to jump off and away from D1 to avoid serious injury.
incidents.quote: A significant finding during the review showed the parking brake, throttle control, and hydraulic lock-out switch are in very close proximity to the steering control.

incidents.name: Medical Emergency During Travel Status
incidents.summary: While driving in travel status, a crew member began having a seizure. The driver pulled over and a phone call was immediately made to 911 requesting an ambulance to respond to their location. The crew recognized that they were in relatively close proximity to a town that had a hospital. At this same time, the firefighter stopped seizing, was conscious and was breathing. The crew elected to self-transport the firefighter to the hospital. The patient was admitted to the hospital and spent one night following the initial ER visit, and then two additional nights later in the week. The patient was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis.
incidents.quote: The patient had been performing PT moderately throughout the week, but felt no serious soreness. The patient had three seizures in one hour on Sunday, June 25,

incidents.name: Crescent Fire Hot Water Burn Injury
incidents.summary: An Assistant Fire Engine Operator received burns from extremely hot water when a 1½-inch hose failed near the pump panel on a Type 3 fire engine. The AFEO was injured while pumping a hose lay in extremely steep terrain.
incidents.quote: “I had been hit by IED in Afghanistan. I’d rather go through that than be burned again.”

incidents.name: Lakeside Fire Chainsaw Incident Fatality
incidents.summary: Fire crews were clearing brush and working with air crews to successfully defend a threatened mobile home park when the injury occurred. Despite all efforts by medical personnel, Inmate Firefighter Anaya passed away on July 11, 2017
incidents.quote: Firefighter Frank Anaya was treated on scene and taken to the hospital in critical condition on July 5, 2017, after suffering a chainsaw injury to the leg while working a fire near Lakeside, California.

incidents.name: Brianhead Fire Aerial Ignition
incidents.summary: An aerial ignition operation on July 7 was perceived differently by those involved. The perspective from the air was of an operation that successfully executed the plan and achieved the desired effects. The perspective on the ground was much different – ground resources felt confused and put at risk
incidents.quote: Yeah, it was my first time in the front seat.

incidents.name: Utah Engine Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: The patient was mopping up in 102 degree heat and experienced extreme cramping throughout the entire body. The cramping went from light to extreme very quick. The patient also experienced swelling, weakness, stiffness and decreased range-of-motion of joints, decreased coordination, fatigue, increased heart rate, increased respiratory rate, and agitation. The local EMT’s provided IV fluids and light snacks. The patient was then transported to a hospital. The patient was admitted and spent 24 hours in the hospital. The patient was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis and a heat related injury.

incidents.name: Six Rivers Physical Training Fatality
incidents.summary: Fire Engine Operator William "Bill" Jaros, a crewmember on Engine 312 of the Six Rivers National Forest’s Gasquet Ranger District/Smith River National Recreation Area, was on a conditioning hike with several crewmembers when he became ill and collapsed. Immediate life-saving efforts were initiated by his fellow crewmembers; however, they were unable to revive him. The cause of death is under investigation through the Del NorteCounty Coroner’s office.
incidents.quote: Fire Engine Operator was on a conditioning hike with several crewmembers when he became ill, collapsed, and was unable to be revived.

incidents.name: Whittier Fire Shelter in Place
incidents.summary: With fast moving fire on both sides of the Circle V Ranch Camp and a primitive Forest Service Road as the only access, a decision was made to send in the Forest Patrol to assess the situation. The Forest Patrol makes the decision to shelter in place with 60 children and 22 counselors and teachers.
incidents.quote: “The IC made the decision to risk a lot to save a lot (82 people, including 60 children).”

incidents.name: YCC Medical Pack Out
incidents.summary: On July 13, a knee injury left a Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) crewmember unable to hike out of the field. A Wildland Fire Module and a County Search and Rescue assisted in carrying out the crewmember.
incidents.quote: The bull charged again, scattering the crew.

incidents.name: Cheyenne River Fire Fuel Geyser
incidents.summary: While operating a Stihl 461 on a 95F day on a wildfire bucking-up a burning cottonwood tree, the saw quit running. Checked the fuel tank, more than half full. Tried choking saw, no go. Remembered likely vapor lock. Moved away from fire and popped open the fuel cap. Fuel geyser blew-up into face. Thankfully, was wearing sunglasses, helmet, Nomex to prevent some damage. Rinsed gas off face with about one gallon water. Dried out Nomex and stayed out of fire remainder of time.
incidents.quote: Rapidly opening the cap while saw was still hot is what got me! Could have turned out way worse!

incidents.name: Return Travel Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: On July 16, 2017, while driving to his duty station in the early morning hours after returning from a nearby initial attack wildfire, a Forest Service employee fell asleep at the wheel and was involved in a motor vehicle accident. The driver was uninjured but significant damage occurred to government and public property.
incidents.quote: “An airbag is a horrible alarm clock! I don’t recommend it.”

incidents.name: Burdette Fire Case Study
incidents.summary: On July 16, 2017, a lightning strike ignited a wildfire within the Burdette Inventoried Roadless Area (IRA) on the Ninemile Ranger District of the Lolo National Forest in western Montana. Because of the complexities and nuances involved in managing and ultimately suppressing the wildfire, the Rocky Mountain Research Station (RMRS) Innovation and Organizational Learning (IOL) Research, Development, and Application (RD&A) chose this fire—the Burdette Fire—as a case study.
incidents.quote: The RMAT tradeoff analysis estimated 655 “person days” of firefighter exposure for the direct suppression approach and 4,116 for the indirect strategy.

incidents.name: Whittier Fire Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: While Swamper 1 was pulling brush, he felt something touch the palm of his right hand and realized it was the guide bar and chain. He immediately pulled back and held his hand. “I didn’t want to look and hoped it was just a nick,” he would explain later. The Sawyer could not see his Swamper’s hand because it was obscured by the thick brush. Meanwhile, Squad Leader 1 declared a medical emergency over the radio to Captain 1 who relayed the information to the Yankee Division Supervisor. It was determined that a helicopter hoist would be the most appropriate method to get Swamper 1 off the hill.
incidents.quote: “When you step back and objectively look at what we do on the side of the hill with a chainsaw, it is incredible that this type of thing doesn’t happen more often.” Saw Program Coordinator

incidents.name: Florence Fire Tree Strike Fatality
incidents.summary: While part of a 20-person crew staging an initial attack on a forest fire in the Seeley Lake Ranger District of the Lolo National Forest in Montana, Firefighter Trenton Johnson was struck by a falling tree. He was flown to a Missoula hospital for treatment, but passed away from the injuries he sustained when struck.
incidents.quote: A Firefighter was struck by a falling tree and passed away from the injuries he sustained when struck.

incidents.name: Onion Creek House Unit Escaped Prescribed Fire
incidents.summary: On Wednesday, July 19th, 2017 the Wildland Conservation Division of Austin Water conducted a prescribed burn on the Onion Creek management unit, located near Buda, Hays County, Texas, owned and maintained by Austin Water. During the initial stages of the operation, a spot fire ignited outside the burn unit and expanded rapidly onto an adjacent privately owned ranch. Resources on scene were not able to control the fire. A wildfire conversion was declared and additional resources from within the region were requested as emergency responders.
incidents.quote: The spot that produced the escaped fire occurred while the Type 6 engine was refilling with water.

incidents.name: Martin Fire Multi Vehicle Collision
incidents.summary: A hill and a cloud of dust restricted visibilty for approaching crews from seeing the gated access point where the POV was partially obstructing the road resulting in a multi-vehicle collision.
incidents.quote: Vehicle 3 then crests the hill and enters a large cloud of gravel dust that significantly reduces driver visibility

incidents.name: 101 1 Fire Heat Related Illness
incidents.summary: Three firefighters began to experience heat related illness on an initial attack fire in Texas.
incidents.quote: “It’s not all about the water; we have to supplement it”

incidents.name: Flat Top Mountain Fire Rhabdo Case
incidents.summary: A firefighter working on this fire from a local Volunteer Fire Department suffered apparent heat exhaustion. The weather at the fire had temps over 100 degrees with relative humidity in the 40-50 percent range. When the ambulance arrived to transport the firefighter to the hospital, the Oklahoma Forestry Service’s Type 3 Incident Commander recalled a Rhabdomyolysis “Rhabdo” briefing his agency held while he was deployed in Arizona this June. Before the ambulance left, he told the Paramedics to have the doctors check the firefighter for Rhabdo.
incidents.quote: The firefighter’s Chief called the Type 3 Incident Commander to thank him for having the presence of mind to request the Rhadbo test. He said that the Emergency Room doctors informed him that this potentially saved the firefighter’s life.

incidents.name: IMT Demob Vehicle Accident
incidents.summary: A Northern Rockies Type II Incident Management Team member sustained non-life threatening injuries in a single vehicle accident while driving home following successful completion of a 14 day fire assignment. At approximately 1430 on the 28th, while driving down a long straight stretch, the driver dozed off, lost control of the vehicle, crossed the opposing traffic lane, and went into the ditch. When the vehicle went into the ditch the driver woke up. The vehicle continued off the road, over a large embankment where it went airborne, landed hard on its wheels, remained upright, and came to a stop.
incidents.quote: The effects of cumulative fatigue are often delayed and not obvious.

incidents.name: Stuart Fire Smokejumper Injury
incidents.summary: At 1545 the fire was sized up and the decision was made to staff the incident with all 7 smokejumpers on board. The first two jumpers left the plane an encountered variable wind conditions throughout their entire flight. The first jumper landed in the spot with no issue, however he immediately reported shifting and gusting winds at tree top level. As the second jumper approached the jump spot, the tail end of his parachute caught the top of a dead tree, causing the jumper to pendulum forward and impact the ground on his right side.
incidents.quote: Any and all fire programs should strive to provide employees with the ability to knowledgeably and confidently respond in the case their coworkers are hurt.

incidents.name: Pole Creek Fire Burn Damage to Engine
incidents.summary: During the burn out, the winds initially were blowing over the road. Visibility was poor for approximately one-half hour. By nightfall, the winds were blowing in and the fire activity died down. The burn out was tied-in and completed at approximately 2200 with no holding concerns or spotting. E601 went off shift at 2330. The morning after the operational period, during the daily PM check, E601’s crew members noticed scorched decals and a melted driver’s side mirror on the engine. It was determined that this damage likely occurred during the burn out operation when the visibility had been poor for that one-half hour time period.
incidents.quote: The west road was a relatively flat, somewhat maintained two track. The fuels were very thick sagebrush patches, especially where the prep was not complete.

incidents.name: Pole Creek Fire Heat Related Illness
incidents.summary: Medic/EMTs revived the patient by quickly placing him in an air-conditioned crew buggy on the dozer line, placed ice packs to groin/arm pits, removed fire shirt, kept him in shade. Elko Dispatch informed the IWI IC that the Flight for Life helicopter was not available, but the local Bureau of Land Management Initial Attack helicopter wasavailable. 40 minutes later, the patient was flown off of Division G to ICP by the BLM helicopter, where the patient was transferred to the Flight for Life helicopter and air transported to the hospital in Elko.
incidents.quote: I was notified by the Inmate Crew that I had a "man down."

incidents.name: Devils Lake Fire Hit by Tree
incidents.summary: A sawyer was felling an 8-10 inch DBH snag, which was approximately 30 feet tall. The Sawyer yelled “Back Cut!”. Moments later, the snag started to fall toward its lay. At that same time, a crewmember—not part of the Saw Team—was walking through the cutting area, bumping up the road. This crewmember was struck by the snag as it was falling. It was observed that the crewmember took a glancing blow to the head, knocking his hard hat off, then struck his shoulder knocking him to the ground.
incidents.quote: The Crew Boss’ intention was never to fall snags after dark.

incidents.name: Lolo Peak Fire Tree Strike Fatality
incidents.summary: Witham was given CPR and other emergency medical aid by fellow firefighters and was then airlifted to a hospital in Missoula, Montana. Despite all efforts,Witham passed away as a result of his injuries.Firefighter Witham was a member of the Vista Grande Hotshot crew based in Idyllwild, California.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Brent Witham was struck and killed by a falling tree while working on the Lolo Peak fire in Western Montana.

incidents.name: Sandy Fire Hit by Tree
incidents.summary: The injury took place at 1900 hours. Patient assessment and the 9 Line Medical Incident Report form determined that this was a “Routine-Green” severity of emergency (not a life threatening injury or illness). However, because of the terrain, the hot temperatures, and extraordinary effort that would be needed to transport by hiking, the decision to use air support was made.
incidents.quote: On August 3 a contract firefighter was injured when struck by a limb from a snag while working on the Sandy Fire on the Shasta Trinity-National Forest.

incidents.name: Devils Lake Fire HRI Extraction
incidents.summary: On August 4 at 1930 hours a medical emergency is declared in Division Delta on the Devils Lake Fire, located eight miles southeast of Bly, Oregon. At first, this medical event seems like a routine medical on the fireline for a heat-related illness. However, it quickly becomes complicated by decisions made on the ground and a lack of authority for the Incident Management Team to order an air ambulance. The Patient receives medical treatment, but the timeline and turn of events could have resulted in a negative outcome had it been a more serious injury or trauma incident.
incidents.quote: 911 Dispatch did not recognize the IMT as a “legitimate entity” able to order a medivac ship

incidents.name: Minerva Fire Hit by Tree
incidents.summary: On August 4, 2017, at approximately 0922 hours, an Interagency Hotshot Crew sawyer was struck by the top half of a snag that was being felled. The crew was prepping dozer line ahead of a planned backfire when the incident occurred. The injured firefighter was transported by the incident medevac helicopter to the incident helibase then transferred to a life flight helicopter and flown to Renown Hospital in Reno.
incidents.quote: The often-repeated mantra “If you see something, say something” seems overused at times, but the Sawyer Trainer felt that this event reinforced this message.

incidents.name: Swan River State Forest Lightning Strike
incidents.summary: At 2130 hours, the local unit was informed of a lightning strike and tree on fire at the camp/retreat where severity resources were staged for emerging incidents. There was a Type 2 Initial Attack Crew and two Engine Crews staying at the camp, which also contained a mobile shower trailer for the crews to use. Three individuals were in or near the shower trailer when the strike occurred.
incidents.quote: Take the opportunity to practice mock medical emergencies of varying complexities. I know our unit has talked about doing training exercises involving a medical emergency each year, but we had not yet gotten to it this season.

incidents.name: Engine Parked in Black Fire Damage
incidents.summary: A Type 6 Engine was sitting in cold black. When parked, there were no open flames or any hot spots under the vehicle. Suddenly, another engine noticed flames coming from underneath the Engine's cab. The Engine Boss and the Crewmember jumped out of the vehicle and started spraying with hardline hose. No firefighters were injured, but the engine became inoperable.
incidents.quote: This engine that caught fire underneath its cab was not sitting in open flames, nor were there any hot spots under the vehicle. So, what happened?

incidents.name: Chetco Bar Fire Engine Entrapment 2017
incidents.summary: The Chetco-Bar fire started on July 12, 2017 on the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest in Oregon. On August 18th an engine was working a spot fire when conditions deteriorated. "It was then evident to Larry that their egress to the cabin was cut off by the fire streaming across the 1917 road west of them. At 12:30 Larry calmly asked the helicopter if they could see any good deployment sites and the pilot said that “Nothing is adequate for a deployment site. You need to get out.” He loaded up his two crew members just as the smoke lifted enough for them to see the road, and they drove through “a tunnel of fire” to make it safely to the area of black to the east."
incidents.quote: “Do you see any good deployment sites?” Engine Boss “Nothing is adequate for a deployment site. You need to get out” Helicopter Pilot

incidents.name: Chetco Bar Fire Handwashing
incidents.summary: Rapid Lesson Sharing document highlighting sanitation and handwashing station practices at base camp during the 2017 Chetco Bar Fire in Oregon.
incidents.quote: Proper handwashing station maintenance and placement at incident base camp significantly reduced illness transmission.

incidents.name: Rice Ridge Fire Burn Injury in Tent
incidents.summary: This individual was trying to ignite a propane heater in her tent for warmth. However, evidently, the igniter was failing to strike a spark. All the while, the open propane canister was filling the tent with flammable gas. When the igniter finally did work, a flash fire occurred in the tent and caught the bedding on fire. Additionally, much of the nylon screening and various parts of the tent also melted.
incidents.quote: A verbal cry was quickly responded to by an adjacent firefighter who then saw an individual standing in the door of her tent, stamping out smoldering blankets and a sleeping bag.

incidents.name: Miller Fire Complex Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: Three firefighters were seated in the front of the vehicle at the time of the accident, Crewmembers 1 and 2 were immediately able to exit the vehicle. The Driver remained trapped in the vehicle and partially submersed in a cold stream, with his left leg pinned underneath the vehicle. The Driver directed Crewmembers 1 and 2 to call for help, however, several attempts to contact help by radio were unsuccessful. Crewmember 1 was able to walk and search for help, however, was unsuccessful in contacting two adjacent landowners. Approximately one hour after the accident, Crewmember 1 found a Heavy Equipment Boss (HEQB) assigned to the fire, who was also EMT-B qualified. Local fire district extrication team, paramedics, and multiple IMT resources responded with assistance from a local ranch owner.
incidents.quote: The engine rolled 1.5 times down a steep, approximately 30-foot-high embankment into Carberry Creek, before coming to rest on its driver side.

incidents.name: Chetco Bar Fire Entrapment 2017
incidents.summary: On August 27, 2017, intense fire behavior and snag blowdowns compromised primary egress routes for resources on the Chetco Bar Fire near Brookings, Oregon. Low RH (10-18%) and NE winds pushed fire across access roads, forcing crews to utilize secondary routes and temporary refuge areas. A Type 1 Skycrane dropped a load of water to cool the fire along the road. The engine crew talked to a strike team leader on the other end of the burning portion of road. Judging by their location dots showing in Avenza mapping, they realized they were separated by about 150 feet of fire activity. This gave the engine and tender the confidence to drive through the area immediately following the second Skycrane drop. By 1645, they had safely re-joined other division resources with no personal injury or damage to the vehicles.
incidents.quote: “You couldn’t see anything from the road but dense trees and brush. You could smell the smoke and see a little wafting in, but no way could you tell where it was coming from.”

incidents.name: Lolo Peak Fire Strep Throat Outbreak
incidents.summary: A total of seven people from the same 20-person crew had now been confirmed to have the Strep infection. The remaining 13 crew members tested negative and were not treated. Swabs from those who tested negative were sent to a lab in Missoula for more conclusive testing.
incidents.quote: The Safety Officer stressed that these crew members must remain in their camp.

incidents.name: Pleasant Fire Dozer Entrapment
incidents.summary: After a hydraulic failure on a provately owned bulldozer and a shift in fire activity the operator decided to deploy their fire shelter next to a nearby greenhouse.
incidents.quote: Operator E-7 observed increased fire behavior and deployed a fire shelter in a clearing on the west side of the greenhouse.

incidents.name: Whitewater Fire Transport Strikes Tree
incidents.summary: Seeing no opportunity to back the transport up, the operator decided they had no choice but to nose into the only available spot. The ground seemed level enough. The operator set the brake and the two headed to dinner before the kitchen closed. They returned after dinner and got ready for bed. One operator slept in the truck’s sleeper cab. Sometime between 2230 and 2300, the loaded transport rolled forward. The front driver’s side bumper and tire struck the first tree near the tents—which stopped the truck. On this transport, there is both a parking brake for the truck and one for the trailer brake. The operators involved suspect that—for some reason—only the trailer brake had been set. The trailer brake is not designedfor long-term parking.
incidents.quote: On this transport, there is both a parking brake for the truck and one for the trailer brake. The operators involved suspect that—for some reason—only the trailer brake had been set. The trailer brake is not designed for long-term parking.

incidents.name: Whitewater Fire Complex Spider Bites
incidents.summary: This fire complex’s medical units have seen an increase in spider bite issues. During the last ten days, four firefighters have experienced spider bites. Although we cannot positively identify what spider we’re dealing with—because no one has yet seen them—the locals are a great source of information when trying to identify the species. They are telling us that the culprit is most likely a hobo spider. In the fall, spiders become more aggressive when they are getting ready to reproduce. Their venom is more potent.
incidents.quote: These spider bite incidents have all advanced to a serious level due to the time lapse between being bit and coming into the Medical Unit for treatment. Yes, we all know you don't want to be taken off the line working. All the more reason to get attention earlier.

incidents.name: Los Padres NF Vehicle Accident Fatality
incidents.summary: While returning from an assignment on the Railroad Fire in the Sierra National Forest, Battalion Chief Gary Helming was killed when a Ford F-350 traveling in the opposite direction suffered a tire failure, crossed the middle of the road, and struck Chief Helming's vehicle head-on.

incidents.name: Sperry Chalet Structure Loss
incidents.summary: On August 10, 2017, a series of dry lightning storms moved across Montana and started several new fires. Among these new fires was the Sprague Fire in Glacier National Park. Over the course of the next few weeks, park management and fire resources would work to suppress the Sprague Fire and protect all threatened structures. Despite extensive protection efforts, on August 31, 2017 the Sperry Dormitory a National Historic Landmark structure, burned when the fire made a hard run up the canyon below the Dormitory.
incidents.quote: “Those firefighters are heroes, dammit. Sometimes the fire wins.”

incidents.name: Jade Creek Fire Tree Strike
incidents.summary: Prioritizing the hazard trees in the area, the Sawyer selected to cut a 15-inch DBH, 75-foot tall, fire-weakened, dead lodgepole. This tree fell as intended, but it did hit the ground with such force that it shook the other nearby dead lodgepole causing it to fall and strike the Sawyer.
incidents.quote: “Sometimes the largest hazard is not the largest tree.”

incidents.name: Liberty Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: Thirteen firefighters escaped east into the designated safety zone. Two members of the hotshot crew and the Line Safety Officer attempted to escape downhill, but found themselves surrounded by heavy smoke and fire. The three began deploying their fire shelters when a shift in the wind cleared the air long enough for them to locate an escape route, allowing them to make their way to safety without using their fire shelters. All 16 firefighters made it to safety and are uninjured.
incidents.quote: Sixteen firefighters from the hand crew, engine crew members and the Line Safety Officer found themselves caught between the main fire and emerging spot fires.

incidents.name: Pyramid Peak Fire Medical Extraction
incidents.summary: On September 3 a firefighter was struck by a limb and seriously injured on the Pyramid Peak Fire, located in a remote area of the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest. Upon notification of this serious medical incident, the Dispatch Center utilized what in Emergency Medicine is being called the “Pit Crew” or “Systems” based approach. On this incident, ground resources reported using a similar “Pit Crew” approach during their response.
incidents.quote: “It is my humble opinion that the wildland fire organization has come a long way in helping support and preparing its workforce to handle medical emergencies in the wildland arena. With that, it has to also be said that we have a long way to go.” The Primary EMT on this Incident

incidents.name: Whitewater Fire Faller Hit by Tree Top
incidents.summary: A snag was identified as a possible hazard. A crew sawyer prepared to cut it. The snag was approximately 15 inches DBH and 40 feet tall. The natural lean of the tree was toward several standing green trees with overlapping canopy. The sawyer cleared the cutting area and prepared to cut the tree. As the sawyer completed the back cut, the tree started to fall exactly as intended. As the tree committed to the fall, the sawyer took a few steps downhill away from the stump and then paused to look back to make sure that everything was going as planned. The sawyer saw the top half of the tree break and start to come back toward him. He immediately started moving along his escape route as quickly as possible. The sawyer was struck on the head and right shoulder by a five-foot section of the snag.
incidents.quote: When one’s escape route is over rough ground—or extremely steep—it’s almost as if you have to choose between turning to watch the tree fall or making sure you dont trip while traveling down your escape route.

incidents.name: Railroad Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: On September 4, 2017 at approximately 2043 hours, a medical injury occurred while working on the Railroad Fire. A firefighter, in darkness, accidently grabbed the auxiliary pump exhaust pipe which caused first degree burns to his hand and fingers and second to third degree burns to the palm of the hand. The firefighter just finished loading hose and was climbing down the apparatus.
incidents.quote: The Firefighter who was injured was not wearing gloves.

incidents.name: Chetco Bar Fire CPR Success
incidents.summary: While building a yurt on a new fire camp on the Chetco Bar East Fire in Southern Oregon, an electrical contractor named Rick suddenly collapsed. Colleagues immediately called out for help and the Incident Management Team responded instantly. The first person to arrive was Bryan, an experienced medic, who quickly assessed the situation and immediately started “Hands Only” Cardio Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR). The compressions were described as fast and deep. After two minutes of “Hands Only” CPR by Bryan, an Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) assigned to the incident, who had quickly brought an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) from his vehicle to the scene and applied the AED pads. When the AED analyzed the Rick’s heart rhythm, it did not advise a shock. “Hands Only” CPR was resumed.
incidents.quote: “I always thought the symptoms of a heart attack were only on the left side down the arm.I didn’t suspect it was a heart attack because it was on my right side.”

incidents.name: Avenue Fire Dozer Tip Over
incidents.summary: As the dozer began to cut line at the site of an old landing, everything was going well and the operator was feeling good. Once the dozer neared the break in slope, the stumps and other debris being pushed by the machine made it hard to see what was in front of him. Although this was not the first time working on steep ground, he found it difficult to judge exactly how steep the slope was—viewing it from above with all these logs, brush, and grasses obscuring his view. The dozer dropped over the edge onto a small shelf and was fully committed at this point. At that moment, the entire dozer began to tip toward the downhill side. The Dozer Operator quickly dropped the blade and angled downward in an attempt to stop the dozer from rolling over. Even so, the machine continued to tip slightly until coming to rest against a 12-inch diameter Douglas fir.
incidents.quote: “As a Dozer Boss I place trust in an operator when he tells me he is comfortable performing a given task.”

incidents.name: Uno Peak Fire Roll Call
incidents.summary: A Roll Call is a tactical pause in which everyone that is assigned to an incident is accounted for through positive communication. This Roll Call took approximately 29 minutes—from start to finish—in which all known fire line resources and incoming resources were successfully accounted for.
incidents.quote: A contractor was in a local dentist office and heard a rumor that an engine had rolled on the Uno Fire and resulted in fatalities

incidents.name: Norse Peak Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: At approximately 1600 on September 10, a firefighter (inactive medic) who was using an orange marker panel and a radio to direct bucket operations suffered burns to both hands and wrists when he was clearing the area and fell sideways into hot ash.
incidents.quote: "All hell can break loose." (Task Force Member on the potential “over-response” when a “Green” medical incident is announced on Command).

incidents.name: Jolly Mountain Fire Incident-within-an-Incident (IWI) Drill
incidents.summary: The majority of the time we make decisions and these decisions usually end in some positive manner. This can even be true when an unintended outcome occurs. A bigger question might be: “Was the positive outcome achieved for the right reasons? Or, was it just because things, luckily—this time—just worked out in our favor?” Simply put, we can have good outcomes over and over, but they may not be for the right reasons. It may be that the odds—so far—have just been in our favor.
incidents.quote: An Incident-within-an-Incident (IWI) can happen anywhere at any time. How prepared are you to deal with an IWI? Or, are you just making do when it does happen?

incidents.name: Uno Peak Fire Egress
incidents.summary: A decision was made to move the three masticators closer to the fire to aid in road brushing and line preparation. At approximately 1630, while walking the equipment closer to the fire, the larger of the two excavators had an equipment failure. The operator was unable to move the machine—that was now blocking the primary egress from the fire. It was determined that the cut-bank could be dug out and the road widened sufficiently for a standard-sized pick-up to be able to pass by. Meanwhile, farther to west on this same road, a truck pulling a trailer with a UTV also broke down—blocking the road north of the DIV G/DIV R break. This new breakdown/road block was dealt with quickly. The truck and trailer were pulled off to the side of the road.
incidents.quote: How Do You Adjust Your Plan When Your Egress has been Effectively Blocked?

incidents.name: Jolly Mountain Fire Water Tender Accident
incidents.summary: On night shift, at approximately 1845, while driving to the fire line just a short distance outside of fire camp on a county road in a semi-rural area, a cooperator Water Tender drifted to the right-hand side of this narrow road that had a minimal shoulder. The Water Tender driver said that he felt the rear tires move off of the pavement onto the gravel shoulder. Both rear tires went off the pavement, which pulled the truck into the ditch, causing it to top over and land on its side.
incidents.quote: The driver reacted according to the previous training that he had received by letting off of the accelerator and slightly applying the brakes. The driver believes that when both rear tires went off of the pavement, this action pulled the truck into the ditch.

incidents.name: Snowshoe Fire Skidgine Incident
incidents.summary: On September 11th 2017, around 1015, a squad was tasked to go to the west side of the Snowshoe Fire to mop up along the fireline. Upon arriving, they tied in with the Task Force Leader, a Skidgine Operator and an Engine Crew. Before engaging with the Skidgine the squad performed a heavy equipment safety briefing. After generating a plan of action, the Skidgine moved up the fireline to a flat section where the squad could start mopping up above the Skidgine. Once the Skidgine Operator engaged the brake system and put the front blade down, he left the cab to start the pump. Almost immediately, the Skidgine experienced a brake failure and began rolling down the fireline.
incidents.quote: The Skidgine hit several trees on the way down, finally coming to rest after uprooting a 6-8 inch DBH tree.

incidents.name: Hauser Road Engine Rollover
incidents.summary: At 1227, Captain 36 called Dispatch and reported the smoke “UTL (unable to locate) and that they were returning to station.”As the engine approached a small decline and curve in the road, the engine started to slide in the sticky clay mud. A “perfect horrible alignment” of slope, slick mud and curve in the road all lined up. Engine 36’s passenger-side front wheel slid toward the edge. Everyone braced for the expected bump into the lip of the road. However nothing was there to slow the engine’s slide to the right and the front wheel went off the road, followed by the rest of Engine 36.
