incidents.summary: The Firefighter was treated in a local hospital and released. No further information is available.
incidents.quote: Near Elko, Nevada a Shasta-Trinity National Forest Firefighter was retrieving personal belongings from the top of an engine and either fell or jumped off, breaking an ankle.

incidents.name: Trinity Fire Smokey Bear Hotshot Heat Related Illness
incidents.summary: Forest Service EMTs assisted getting the Firefighter to an ALS ambulance. The Firefighter was then driven to a local hospital. The Firefighter received multiple bags of fluid and was then released.
incidents.quote: On the Trinity Fire on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, a Smokey Bear Hotshot Crew member began showing signs of a HRI (heat-related illness)—cramping and dehydration.

incidents.name: Saber Fire Prescott IHC Member Medical Emergency
incidents.summary: Forest Service EMTs responded along with non-Forest Service EMTs. The Firefighter was then taken via ground ambulance to a hospital where the shoulder was repositioned. The firefighter was released to light duty until cleared by an orthopedist.
incidents.quote: On the Saber Fire on the Coconino NF a Prescott Hotshot Crew member slipped and dislocated his shoulder trying to catch himself.

incidents.name: Montana Training Medical Incident
incidents.summary: Upon initial assessment by crewmembers, the firefighter was unresponsive but breathing. Patient care was initiated immediately by checking vitals, removing PPE, and applying cool wet clothing to the underarms, neck and groin area.The patient was loaded into the SKED and moved by using a “leap frog” method about 150 yards at a time to the helibase. She was treated for dehydration and released from the hospital later that night.
incidents.quote: A DNRC Initial Attack Crew was conducting line construction exercises for their weekly crew training. After taking a short break (1-2 minutes) the firefighter fell to the ground.

incidents.name: Lily Lake Fire Smokejumping Accident
incidents.summary: As he fell from the tree, the jumper remembered thinking to put his feet together in preparation to do a Parachute Landing Fall (PLF); evidence of the ingrained training. When he hit the ground a log sabotaged the PLF attempt and he found himself on all fours with blood dripping through his facemask onto his arm.
incidents.quote: On the Lily Lake Fire on the Deschutes National Forest, a Smokejumper performing a letdown procedure from a tree fell and suffered a broken vertebrae due to blunt force trauma.

incidents.name: Prescribed Fire Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: Another Forest Service Firefighter who happened to also be a Registered Nurse, got the bleeding stopped and assisted in transporting the Firefighter to a waiting ambulance. The Firefighter was then taken to a hospital, received 21 staples, and was released to light duty. A full recovery is anticipated.
incidents.quote: During prep on a prescribed fire, a Firefighter working as a swamper came in contact with the chainsaw and sustained a 5-inch long cut on the upper arm.

incidents.name: Swan Lake Fire Ash Pit Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: An IHC saw team working the Swan Lake Fire was cutting hazard trees near a dozer line where another crew would be coming in to mop-up. When the swamper stepped and reached for a chunk of birch tree on the black side of the dozer line, his foot sunk into a hot ash pit, approximately 18 inches deep. As the swamper attempted to extricate himself, the sawyer stepped toward and reached for the swamper to help pull him out. They both sustained burn injuries to their lower legs caused by the hot ash.
incidents.quote: When injuries occur, we assess, stabilize, package, transport and hand-off patients to a higher level of care.

incidents.name: Southcentral Alaska Ash Pit Burn Injuries
incidents.summary: The combination of deep duff and organic soils with drought conditions creates an environment for fires to burn deep into the ground and create ash pits that may be more hazardous than those encountered in other areas of the state.
incidents.quote: The depth and heat trapped within some ash pits has taken firefighters by surprise. Firefighters may not recognize the hazard associated with these areas.

incidents.name: Verlot Hazard Tree Felling Accident
incidents.summary: The fir had been identified as a “hazard tree” during assessment performed years prior and today was the day it would be coming down. The felling operation had several complicating factors, one of which was a “green” 14-inch DBH maple with branches that were growing around the dead fir—entangling the two trees together after years of growth. As the fir began to fall and encountered the crippled maple, there was just enough resistanceto cause the fir’s brittle hinge to break and for the tree to be deflected sideways by the maple—falling in an unintended direction and striking the nearby power lines.
incidents.quote: “The fir took out the main power line for the town, crossed one lane of the road, and started a ¼ acre grass fire near the parking lot.” Sawyer

incidents.name: Woods Cabin Fire Engine Fire
incidents.summary: After deciding to hike back to the engine, the crew smelled something abnormal. Being in oil and gas county, theysuspected oil infrastructure, however, there were no locations in the immediate area. A few moments later, the Assistant alerted that the driver’s side rear tires and quarter of the truck was on fire. All indications are that the engine was parked in an area that contained a hot sagebrush stob, which eventually caused the rear tires to catch fire and spread to the vehicle.
incidents.quote: Over the years, many vehicles have burned in a similar fashion to what occurred on this incident. It is hoped that both firefighters and managers will use this report in a learning environment to prevent this all too common event. Fire managers are thankful that no one was injured during this incident.

incidents.name: Woodward Fire Tree Strike
incidents.summary: On August 27 on the Woodward Fire, part of a Type 2IA Crew was victim to a large tree falling onto them. Two of the firefighters were immobilized and transported to a nearby hospital. One firefighter was treated and released the same day, while the other firefighter was released the next day. Both are expected to make a full recovery.
incidents.quote: The Bay Laurel tree, its exposed roots and multiple trunks make it a significant hazard for burning and falling.

incidents.name: Swan Lake Fire Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: The Firefighter was assisted by Forest Service EMTs to a ground ambulance and then driven to a hospital. The Firefighter was evaluated and released.
incidents.quote: On the Swan Lake Fire on the Chugach National Forest a Beckwourth Hotshot Crewmember working as a swamper was struck by an object, possibly a stress-bound limb or a snag top (no one witnessed the event) and briefly lost conciseness.

incidents.name: White River Fire Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: A contract firefighter on the White River Fire on the Mount Hood National Forest was struck by an approximately 24-inch diameter green tree when it fell unexpectedly. The incident occurred while hiking back to vehicles, and not immediately adjacent to the fire. The firefighter received a “glancing strike” and sustained fractured ribs, sternum and spinal injury. The patient was assessed and packaged on scene by IHC and Line EMTs and transported via ground ambulance to a hospital. Two days later, the patient was still in the hospital with a liaison assigned
incidents.quote: White River Fire Hit By Tree

incidents.name: Swan Lake Fire IHC Crewmember Bee Sting
incidents.summary: The Firefighter self administered epinephrine. Forest ServiceEMTs assisted in getting the Firefighter to an ambulance and then to a hospital. The firefighter was admitted, kept for observation overnight and released the following day.
incidents.quote: An American River Hotshot Crewmember experienced an allergic reaction to a bee sting on the Swan Lake Fire on the Chugach National Forest.

incidents.name: Thorne Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: The employees were treated and transported by air ambulance to burn centers for treatment and released later that day. All three firefighters required follow up appointments and treatment, with one requiring an overnight stay for observation.
incidents.quote: On September 1, 2019, at approximately 2:50 PM, three CAL FIRE firefighters received burn injuries while fighting a wind-driven vegetation fire in Monterey County, CA.

incidents.name: Spring Coulee Fire Entrapment Fatality
incidents.summary: Assistant Chief Christian Johnson arrived in B341 (a type 6 Brush Truck) at 1615. The MAYDAY was called at 1626 and a second radio call for assistance from a separate location was made at 1655. The fire was contained at 107 acres at approximately 1730. Assistant Chief Johnson was seriously burned during the incident and succumbed to those injuries on October 2, 2019.
incidents.quote: Assistant Chief Johnson and the exterior firefighter ran toward the old cat trail at slightly different angles. In Assistant Chief Johnson’s path, hidden by vegetation, lay a substantial field of rocks and metal debris. While it is impossible to know for certain, it is thought Assistant Chief Johnson may have become entangled in the debris and was overtaken by fire.

incidents.name: SQF Complex Hit By Log
incidents.summary: The patient was initially treated by U.S. Forest Service EMTs and Line Medics and was assessed with a “Red” status. The patient was extracted via air hoist then transported via air ambulance to a hospital. A CT scan and MRI were performed with no obvious findings. The patient remains in the hospital for further observation.
incidents.quote: On the SQF Complex on the Sequoia National Forest, an Interagency Hotshot Crew firefighter was struck on the back of the head by an 8-inch diameter log, and subsequently experienced dizziness and a bad headache.

incidents.name: Country Fire Engine Burnover
incidents.summary: On September 3, 2019, at approximately 1:30 PM, resources were dispatched to a vegetation fire west of the town of Greenwood CA, within the CAL FIRE Amador - El Dorado Unit. Two local government fire personnel were transported to the hospital with minor injuries and released later the same day. The fire engine sustained major damage.
incidents.quote: During fire suppression activities, a local government fire engine was overrun by fire.

incidents.name: Lime Fire Hit By Tree
incidents.summary: The Firefighter was initially up and walking, then was degraded to condition Red, then to Yellow. Forest Service EMTs assisted and a medevac was requested. A County Hoist Helicopter extracted and transported the Firefighter to a Hospital in Medford, Ore. Evaluation indicated the Firefighter received: a fracture to the small bone on the edge of T-1, two broken ribs, a broken collar bone, bruised lungs, and minor scrapes. The Firefighter is expected to remain in an Intensive Care Unit for two days. An RLS/Safety Assistance Team is on site.
incidents.quote: A Klamath Hotshot Crewmember was struck by a tree during a felling operation on the Lime Fire on the Klamath National Forest.

incidents.name: Walker Fire Ash Pit Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The Firefighter, diagnosed with burn injuries to arms and legs, was released with a referral to a Burn Unit.
incidents.quote: A Palomar Hotshot Crewmember fell into an ash pit on the Walker Fire on the Plumas National Forest. U.S. Forest Service EMTs assisted and the Firefighter was taken to a local clinic.

incidents.name: Blacksmith Rx Heat Related Injury
incidents.summary: Municipal Fire Department medics responded and assessed the Firefighter. The Firefighter was transported via a government vehicle to a local hospital and diagnosed with a Heat Related Injury. Fluids were administered, the Firefighter was observed for several hours, then released.
incidents.quote: A Public Lands Corps Student Firefighter began vomiting and struggling to breath while working on a Prescribed Fire

incidents.name: Middle Fire Firefighters Hit By Rock
incidents.summary: Two contract Firefighters (GFP Enterprises) were hit by a rolling rock on the Middle Fire on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest. One of the Firefighters received a broken femur. The second Firefighter received head lacerations and neck injuries. The Firefighters were hoisted by a U.S. Coast Guard helicopter and flown to a hospital. The first Firefighter had surgery to repair the broken femur and is expected to be released in two or three days. The second Firefighter received seven staples and was released that evening.
incidents.quote: Two contract Firefighters (GFP Enterprises) were hit by a rolling rock on the Middle Fire.

incidents.name: Kidd Fire Retreat
incidents.summary: A Price Valley crewmember who returned to the rappel site discovered that trees torching near the site had cast a large amount of embers onto their rappel gear, and that some of the cardboard boxes holding their food, water and overnight equipment were already burning. It quickly became apparent that they were not going to be able to salvage the gear and were only putting themselves at risk by staying up there. The IC called them and told them to “ditch the gear” and said they were going to pull out.
incidents.quote: A Swiss cheese model of communication.

incidents.name: Wild Mountain Fire Engine Burnover RLS
incidents.summary: In the early morning hours of Sunday, September 6, 2020, a Brush Engine from a rural fire department responded to a wildland fire. While attacking the left flank of the fire, the engine drove into an unseen gully and became stuck. The engine was immobilized in a patch of unburned fuels surrounded by black. Eventually, the engine caught fire and was destroyed. All crewmembers were able to exit the vehicle and retreat to a safe location in the black.
incidents.quote: “It exploded…it was like a 40-foot fireball!” Duty Officer

incidents.name: Red Creek Rx Heat Related Injury
incidents.summary: . The Firefighter was taken by ambulance to a local hospital and kept overnight for observation. A full recovery is expected.
incidents.quote: A Type 2 IA Crew Firefighter was preparing a fireline on the Red Creek Prescribed Fire on the Caribou-Targhee National Forest and became short of breath, exhibiting signs of a heat related injury

incidents.name: Fork Fire Blasting Operations
incidents.summary: The Blaster and IMT implemented a thoughtful approach to blasting operations: conduct a test shot then follow up with an After Action Review to facilitate real-time evaluation and learning, and to validate blasting as a tactic to accomplish incident objectives and risk management. As each shot progressed and the AAR’s validated the tactic, field operations continued to scale up, streamline and be adjusted based on feedback from the actual result and input from those involved with operations.
incidents.quote: The Southwest Area Incident Management Team 4 used Crew 45 to blast hazard trees on five separate days, resulting in the mitigation of approximately 170-180 dead standing trees and construction or improvement of approximately 680 feet of fireline using explosives.

incidents.name: South Obenchain Fire Chainsaw Kick Back
incidents.summary: The saw’s powerhead struck the left shoulder, knocking the firefighter down into a patch of poison oak and dislocating the shoulder. The patient was initially attended to by a U.S. Forest Service EMT, then transported via agency vehicle to an Emergency Department.
incidents.quote: On the South Obenchain Fire on the Bureau of Land Management’s Medford District, an Interagency Hotshot Crew firefighter was limbing overhead with a chainsaw when it kicked-back.

incidents.name: Whiskey Fire Medical Emergency
incidents.summary: A Coconino Fuels Crew Firefighter felt ill during morning briefing on the Whiskey Fire on the Coconino National Forest. The Firefighter continued to the assigned duty and then informed Line EMTs of the ill feelings. The Firefighter was then taken by ground ambulance to a hospital where the Firefighter was evaluated and released to rest.
incidents.quote: While talking to the Line EMTs the Firefighter lost consciousness.

incidents.name: Williams Fire Infected Scratch on Knee
incidents.summary: On the Williams Fire on the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest, a Task Force Leader Trainee sustained a small scratch on the knee while moving equipment in the back of a truck. Over the next few days, the employee started experiencing pain in their knee, which became swollen and infected. The employee was examined at the Medical Unit and driven to the hospital in an agency vehicle. The patient was checked into the hospital and given IV antibiotics. A full recovery is expected.
incidents.quote: Williams Fire Infected Scratch on Knee

incidents.name: Left Hand Fire Tree Strike
incidents.summary: The Firefighter had to be extricated. This medical incident was initially reported as condition “Green”. Later, when the Firefighter complained of back pain and dizziness, the condition was updated to “Yellow”. The Firefighter was taken to a hospital in Yakima, Wash. and admitted. He was released later that day or evening.
incidents.quote: A Division Supervisor from the Fremont-Winema National Forest was in a vehicle on the Left Hand Fire near the Wenatchee National Forest when a cottonwood tree fell on the vehicle.

incidents.name: Kootenai National Forest Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: A Fuels Crew Member was cutting slash and slipped on a wet rock on the Libby Ranger District, Kootenai National Forest. The Firefighter was transported via ground ambulance to a hospital. Surgery was conducted to repair muscle tissue. The Firefighter was released the following day with an order to not put weight on the injured leg for two weeks.
incidents.quote: The chainsaw contacted the chaps and pulled the chaps away, exposing the Firefighter’s calf. The chainsaw then cut deep into the calf.

incidents.name: Mullen Fire Hit By Rock
incidents.summary: This incident occurred on the Mullen Fire on the Medicine Bow-Rout National Forests. A U.S. Forest Service firefighter was working on a spot fire, pulling hose up a steep embankment and assisted pushing on a large rock. The rock broke loose. The rock struck the firefighter and knocked the firefighter into a tree. Initial treatment was provided by an Interagency Hotshot Crew EMT. The patient was transported via ground ambulance to a hospital.
incidents.quote: Both the firefighter and rock rolled down the embankment.

incidents.name: Caples Escaped Prescribed Pile Burn
incidents.summary: The Caples understory prescribed fire was officially declared a wildfire at 1330 on October 10, 2019. After it was declared a wildfire, it became the second highest priority wildfire in the Region.
incidents.quote: My world changed as soon as I declared it a wildfire… After that I had unlimited resources.

incidents.name: Equality Volunteer Fire Department Fatality
incidents.summary: Firefighter Michael Johnston was driving the Equality Volunteer Fire Department’s 2004 GMC water tender when it overturned while responding to a brush fire.
incidents.quote: Firefighter Johnston was ejected from the truck in the single-vehicle accident and pronounced deceased at the scene from the injuries he sustained.

incidents.name: River Fire IHC Crewmember Fall
incidents.summary: A Breckenridge IHC Crewmember was mapping the fire perimeter on the River Fire near Bakersfield, Calif. The Firefighter was treated by U.S. Forest Service EMTs and then driven to a hospital in crew vehicles. The patient was treated and released.
incidents.quote: At one point, the Firefighter was side-hilling on a steep slope when the footing gave out. The Firefighter slid down and impacted the road—fracturing a fibula.

incidents.name: Martinez 3 Fire Ash Pit Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The Martinez 3 Fire started on allotted land on the area of Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indians on October 14, 2019. Resources responded to a wildfire burning in an area of heavy mulch. On October 17, 2019 the Bureau of Indian Affairs assumed command and continued suppression activity. On October 21, 2019, during suppression operations, a firefighter stepped in to an ash pit and received 2nd and 3rd degree circumferential burns to both legs below the knees. The injured firefighter was air lifted to the Arrowhead Burn Center in San Bernardino, Californiawhere they were treated and released later that evening.
incidents.quote: One (1) firefighter sustained 2nd and 3rd degree circumferential burns to both legs below the knees.

incidents.name: Arapaho Roosevelt NF PT Medical Emergency
incidents.summary: A U.S. Forest Service EMT did an assessment and directed the Firefighter to a hospital. The Firefighter was hospitalized and diagnosed with inflammation of the sack surrounding the heart. The Firefighter was released from the hospital three days later.
incidents.quote: A Firefighter had just completed physical fitness exercises and felt chest pain and pain in the left shoulder.

incidents.name: Kincade Fire Entrapment
incidents.summary: On October 25, 2019 at approximately 4:23 PM, while assigned as a Division Supervisor on the Kincade Fire, in Sonoma County, California, a CAL FIRE Fire Captain and two civilians became entrapped when their route of travel was cut off by fire. The Fire Captain defensively fired out the area and deployed a fire shelter, protecting the group from the fire’s radiant heat. During the deployment, the group needed to relocate due to the changingconditions.
incidents.quote: DIVS Trainee told DIVS1 that he heard personnel assigned to one of the Task Force engines were not wearing Nomex wildland jackets. As a result, DIVS1 began the process of locating personnel assigned to the Division to ensure all resources were wearing proper personal protective equipment.

incidents.name: Maria Fire Ash Pit Burn Injury
incidents.summary: The Firefighter was assisted by U.S. Forest Service EMTs to an ambulance that took the Firefighter to a hospital. The Firefighter was then transferred to a burn center via ambulance. The Firefighter was diagnosed with second degree burns to the calf, treated and released with orders to return to the burn center in three days.
incidents.quote: A Truckee Hotshot Crewmember stepped into an ash pit on the Maria Fire.

incidents.name: Ski Fire Helicopter Water Drop Injures
incidents.summary: The firefighter was assessed on the line by Paramedics as condition “Yellow.” The firefighter was taken via ambulance to a hospital. The Firefighter was admitted and evaluated to have bruising and contusions, and was released from the hospital late that evening.
incidents.quote: While on the Ski Fire fireline on the San Bernardino National Forest, a Big Bear Hotshot Crewmember was hit by a water drop from a helicopter.

incidents.name: Truck Damage During Pile Burning
incidents.summary: When the supervisor arrived, they attempted to pull the truck free using a winch, but were unable to do so. One of the squad members then began cutting a swath through the burning landing pile with a chainsaw to stop/slow the progression of the fire toward the truck.
incidents.quote: They then noticed that the side of the supervisor’s truck facing the fire was starting to blister and having plastic begin to melt from the radiant heat.

incidents.name: Physical Training Struck by Vehicle
incidents.summary: Forest Service Law Enforcement is currently conducting an investigation in coordination with local law enforcement. The National Forest in Florida Safety Manager is coordinating the additional accident investigations required, and will make the information known as appropriate. It is expected that the crew member will be released from the hospital soon, and the Hospital Family Liaison is coordinating to meet the family’s needs to get them home.
incidents.quote: On the evening of January 23rd, 2020, at approximately 1900 Central Time, a Forest Service Employee working with a Job Corp Fire Module was struck by a vehicle during a PT (Physical Fitness) run.

incidents.name: Round Fire Escaped Prescribed Burn
incidents.summary: An abnormally dry winter with no snow pack and readily available 1000 hour fuels aided in the escape of the piles. This specific location doesn’t represent the general weather forecast due to location and aspect. The site is much drier than the general weather forecast would indicate. The burn plan indicates that the agency administrator can exempt the need for a spot weather forecast. No such documentation exists, the burn plan does not state how that information would be recorded.
incidents.quote: Round Fire Escaped Prescribed Burn

incidents.name: Mark Twain NF Dual Wheels Engine Incident
incidents.summary: While driving my Ford F550 engine I recently had the driverside duals come off. The lugs had been checked regularly. Crew members had been asked to check them daily due to finding lugs loosened. Earlier in the day, I was driving the engine at low speeds with the windows down and heard what I thought was a wheel bearing going out. It was a clicking sound. After the tires came off, I traveled 130 yards before I could bring my engine to a complete stop. It took two full revolutions of the steering wheel to get the engine back on my side of the road. Ford vehicles use a two-piece lug nut that have a tendency to wear out due to over-tightening.
incidents.quote: Later that day while driving on the highway going approximately 45 mph, I felt the rear of the engine sway. I looked quickly in my side view mirror to see the outside dual pass the engine. It bounced through the ditch, bounced across the highway, and down the embankment. My immediate thought was that the second dual is coming off next. As I started to apply the brakes, it also came off.

incidents.name: Lakehead Prescribed Fire Firefighter Fall Broken Ankle
incidents.summary: Medical Emergency, Hand Crews, Prescribed Fire Operations
incidents.quote: Lakehead Rx Firefighter Fall Broken Ankle

incidents.name: Indianola Volunteer Fire and Rescue Fatality
incidents.summary: After returning home from a grass fire, Firefighter/EMT Donald “Donny” Lepper collapsed. He was immediately taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced deceased.

incidents.name: Baseball Escape Prescribed Fire
incidents.fire: The Upper Lake and Covelo Pile Burn prescribed fire project
incidents.summary: After initial ignition on January 30th and February 4th, 2020, the piles were patrolled periodically while a significant drying trend occurred for the remainder of February.
incidents.quote: The piles subsequently rekindled, escaped out of the initial project area and were declared a wildfire on February 25th, 2020.

incidents.name: Lion Fire COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: The preseason training that the BLM and its cooperators participated in prepared all involved to execute a safe and efficient response. There were good discussions and decisions made regarding COVID-19. The South Zone of the Northwest Colorado Fire and Aviation Management Unit made concerted efforts to limit and minimize exposure to firefighters.
incidents.quote: When working with multiple agencies, the COVID-19 mitigation measures and messages varied widely and were hard to enforce or maintain.

incidents.name: Smokejumper Physical Training Heat Related Injury
incidents.summary: Forest Service EMT administered first patient care. Ground transport was by ambulance, during which 2 liters of fluid were provided to patient en route to the medical center in Redding. The firefighter was admitted to medical center, given 4 more liters of fluid, and diagnosed with a heat-related/dehydration injury. The Firefighter was expected to be released in three days.
incidents.quote: A smokejumper doing Physical Training (4-mile run) suffered a heat-related injury/dehydration.

incidents.name: Silver King Fire COVID 19 Host Unit Mitigation
incidents.summary: Local level planning is essential, it needs to include Agency Administrators, cooperators and militia staff members who are willing to assist. Our way of doing business has changed and everyone needs to understand that response, strategies and tactics may change from previous fire seasons. The limiting factor is availability of resources and the challenge of having the capacity to support larger groups of people while adhering to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) COVID recommendations.
incidents.quote: Identify COVID-19 trigger points that will elevate the need for Type 2 or Type 1 Incident Management Teams. This is something we have never considered in the past.

incidents.name: Multiple Northwestern Fires COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: To prevent modules intermixing, engines were following well behind hand crew resources.The intermixing of resources within agency is also being intentionally avoided. For example, the IA crew module avoided intermixing with the engine personnel. Initially, physical distancing was a challenge during briefing. Feedback suggests it got better with subsequent smaller briefings and breakouts. On a positive note, this issue was identified on-the-spot and likely led to additional effort to mitigate.
incidents.quote: COVID Mitigations on the Porter Creek Fire

incidents.name: Shepard Road Fire COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: With current best management practices, adjusted work schedules, module isolation, assigned vehicle seating, and daily crewmember health monitoring, we believe we are doing everything we can to meet the intent of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the U.S. Forest Service National, Regional, and Forest guidance to mitigate exposure and spread of COVID-19.
incidents.quote: Our greatest concern is that this guidance is being strictly interpreted as mandatory, thus restricting the decision space of those on the ground.

incidents.name: Silver King Fire Heat and COVID 19
incidents.summary: Throughout the entire operation, it was agreed on by crew leadership that the primary threat to the crew’s well-being was the potential for a crew member to have a heat-related illness. Crew leadership also determined that we will occasionally find ourselves in positions where all COVID-19 mitigations cannot be met. However, as soon as the primary threat to safety is mitigated, the crew leadership is responsible for shifting back to meeting all COVID-19 mitigations that are achievable.
incidents.quote: Onsite weather at 1500 was 94 degrees with 57% humidity, which resulted in a heat index between 101 and 105 degrees—which falls into the National Weather Service Heat Index category of “Danger”.

incidents.name: 189 Fire COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: Upon arrival on the incident we noticed a large organization working the fire that included: several law enforcement vehicles, several fire department command vehicles, several volunteer engines from the surrounding communities, an ambulance, and SNF Engine 461. We did interact with SNF Engine 461 to see what intel they had prior to our arrival.
incidents.quote: An effort was made to keep our module isolated from the rest of this group for COVID concerns, having only one person obtain a briefing and assignment from the Incident Commander.

incidents.name: Holcombe Road Fire COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: RISK MANAGEMENT IDENTIFY HAZARDS (SITUATIONAL AWARENESS) ASSESS HAZARDS DEVELOP CONTROLS AND MAKE RISK DECISIONS IMPLEMENT CONTROLS
incidents.quote: COVID-19 protocol is very difficult in a wilffire environment.

incidents.name: Henry Creek Fire COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: “Virtual training is great in theory but it lacks the real content of the world outside my unit. We can train all we want using Teams, video presentations, staying at home and working virtually . . . It is like a brutal audit when you arrive on assignment. Crew cohesion and teamwork exponentially increased over a 48-hour period that we did not get during critical training (especially this year with no prescribed fire). We must respond to fires. That is our job. We need to do it with diligence and vigilance and expect the unexpected.”
incidents.quote: On April 21 at 1410, the Lolo Interagency Hotshot Crew received a call from the Missoula Dispatch Center regarding their availability to respond to the Henry Creek Fire.

incidents.name: Drumheller Fire COVID Mitigation
incidents.summary: Mitigation Measures -Gloves should be easily accessable and required for crews to wear while using Porta-Potty. Crew members will dispose glovesin garbage cans and wash hands immediately after exiting Porta-Potty. -Assign logistics personnel at Porta-Potty sites that are being used by multiple crews to disinfect all commonly touched areas of Porta-Potty and hand wash stations. -At dispersed camp site, supply Porta-Potty and hand washing station with PPE and sanitation supplies. The crew assigned to that dispersed camp site will be responsible for maintaining sanitation of their facilities.
incidents.quote: COVID-19 Observations and Concerns on the Drumheller Fire

incidents.name: Hyndman Fire Response COVID Risk
incidents.summary: The focus of this RLS is to look at the issue from a psychological and thought process based-perspective to help firefighters think about how the pandemic may affect their perceptions and reasoning.
incidents.quote: “I think for me the biggest factor to decline the assignment is the lack of direction and erring on the side of caution with all of our seasonal workforce coming on in the next two weeks. We are asking our seasonals if they have been exposed to COVID-19 or if they have been in an area where community spread is prevalent. If they have, we are going to be asking them to quarantine for 14 days.

incidents.name: Heli Rappel Training COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: Ochoco National Forest, John Day, Oregon Rappel re-certification events are typically attended by multiple crews who train together in inter-mixed groups to promote standardization and cohesion among the national rappel community. However, due to COVID-19 concerns, the plan was to have crews work through their re-certification training as isolated modules with minimal interaction from outside personnel.
incidents.quote: “Are some of these mitigations creating a larger hazard than the original hazard they were intended to mitigate?”

incidents.name: 560 Fire COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary: Together we can continue to build a body of knowledge with each passing incident so that tangible improvements can be accomplished. Combatting this outbreak has many parallels to firefighting, the way you stop the spread is by starving it of fuel and, in this case, the fuel is us. Social distancing is our fuel break.
incidents.quote: This is intended to be a short shared learning report so that we may continue to collectively improve our fire response during future pandemics.

incidents.name: Apache Sitgreaves NF PT Heat Incident
incidents.summary: A U.S. Forest Service EMT evaluated the employee, who was driven to the hospital in an agency vehicle for precautionary measures. The firefighter was released the same day. Heat exhaustion or altitude sickness was suspected. An AAR will be conducted to share information on this incident.
incidents.quote: A firefighter on a Type 2 IA crew was engaged in a 2-mile physical fitness hike and, when finished, collapsed at the crew vehicle.

incidents.name: COVID 19 Positive Test Response Huron Manistee
incidents.summary: On Thursday, April 30, one of my Zone's key overhead firefighters was notified of a positive COVID-19 test result. This employee had mostly been working from home. He did not feel the best, was looking to potentially travel out of state, so he went to his primary care doctor.
incidents.quote: I planned for my entire fire program to possibly be quarantined, pending the COVID test results—during our busiest time of the year regarding wildfire response.

incidents.name: 84 Fire COVID 19 Mitigation
incidents.summary: COVID-19 precautions and actions taken in response to a crewmember running a fever post fire.
incidents.quote: Our crewmembers self-monitor themselves daily using the Wildland Fire COVID-19 Screening Tool.

incidents.name: Basin Fire COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: Old habits die hard. The IMT noticed much more intermingling at the beginning of the incident. Over time, with consistent messaging, heavy signage around camp, and regular briefings, COVID-19 mitigations were more regularly implemented.
incidents.quote: “Be prepared to change on the fly this year, this is not a normal fire season.”

incidents.name: Florida Forest Service IMT COVID Mitigations
incidents.summary: “After two IMT deployments and a third fire which required the deployment of multiple Strike Teams, we were able to COVID test a total of 252 personnel. All of those tests came back negative. We have learned an awful lot over the last couple months, but the one thing that was most critical to us was the ability to get that testing included as part of the Demob process. It certainly made me feel a whole lot better about sending employees back to their families and coworkers in their home unit.”
incidents.quote: COVID-19 Mitigations and Lessons from Two Incident Management Teams

incidents.name: Salmon Challis NF Firefighter Fatality
incidents.summary: The day after the incident, he was hospitalized to treat a heart condition and passed away several days later from an apparent heart attack.
incidents.quote: Salmon Airbase Manager/Wildland Firefighter Eric R. Ellis complained of left arm numbness during mandated physical fitness training.

incidents.name: Humboldt Toiyabe NF Crewmember COVID 19 Exposure
incidents.summary: A single member of a Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest fire crew had a roommate who tested positive for COVID-19. This positive test became known on May 16, nearly seven days after the last direct encounter between these two individuals. During the interim, beginning May 11, the crew member was engaged in training exercises with the rest of his team at a single location. When the positive test results became known, proper notification to supervisors and the entire crew was immediate.
incidents.quote: Crew members were given enough information to make an informed decision about testing. None declined, although peer pressure may have influenced some who otherwise would have skipped the test.

incidents.name: Boggy Draw Hazard Tree Removal Limb Strike
incidents.summary: As the sawyer recalls, “The tree began to fall and was heading straight where I had intended it to go. I turned and took a few steps away. I heard and saw the tree hit the ground and come to rest. I moved a step or two back toward the tree, looked up to check for overhead hazards, and found one—with my mouth.”
incidents.quote: “I would like for those around me to use this unfortunate injury as a tool to learn and better themselves.”

incidents.name: Sawtooth Fire COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: After a COVID-19 Confirmed Contact – IC Requires Face Masks at Briefings After notification of an individual that had contact with a confirmed COVID-19 case and considering the varied adherence to recommendations, the IMT asked for all of those attending briefings to wear a cloth face cover. That briefing began with the IC sharing their reasoning and decision behind changing his Leader’s Intent. Everyone in the briefing area that morning wore a face cover and worked on maintaining social distancing.
incidents.quote: Lessons on COVID-19 Era Large Fire Briefings by the Southwest Area Type 1 IMT

incidents.name: Bush Fire PIO Lessons
incidents.summary: How to better understand and mitigate Covid 19, during Fire missions.
incidents.quote: The most important thing we do is taking care of ourselves and each other.

incidents.name: Sawtooth Fire Heat Related Injury
incidents.summary: Medics on scene of the Sawtooth Fire administered an IV and determined that the crewmember needed to go to the hospital for further evaluation. A total of five saline bags were administered. The crewmember was transported to the hospital via government vehicle by the Engine Captain with the Line Medic in the vehicle. The crewmember was held for observation and released that afternoon.
incidents.quote: An engine crewmember exhibited symptoms of Heat Stress.

incidents.name: Hotshot Crewmembers COVID 19 Positive Tests
incidents.summary: Lessons  Symptoms will vary depending on individuals, environmental factors, and severity.  Establish clear testing guidance and procedure when testing is initiated (i.e. isolate tested individuals until results are received).  Communicate with interagency leadership rather than initial ground level communication to provide additional context and follow chains-of-command.
incidents.quote: Hotshot Crewmembers COVID 19 Positive Tests

incidents.name: Miles Fire Hit By Rock
incidents.summary: A U.S. Forest Service Paramedic responded and evaluated the patient. The Superintendent then walked the firefighter off the fire and drove to a hospital. The firefighter was treated and released.
incidents.quote: On the Miles Fire on the Tonto National Forest, a Mesa Interagency Hotshot Crew member was digging line on a steep slope when a rock above dislodged and hit the firefighter, resulting in a broken finger.

incidents.name: Bucking and Limbing Boot Strike
incidents.summary: The sawyer placed his left foot up on the bole of the tree while cutting the offside branch. This sequence created an unusual footing position, which brought the sawyer’s left foot up to their waist height, under the chainsaw power head. During the cutting sequence, the chainsaw came into contact with the sawyer’s boot while running under power in mid-cut. The sawyer immediately stopped the chainsaw, ceasing operations, and reported the incident to his squad leader.
incidents.quote: I talked with the sawyer today and discussed the mishap. His reflection was super positive as to why this event happened and replied that it really came down to being in a hurry and a lapse in focus.

incidents.name: Coconino NF Limb Strike
incidents.summary: An engine crewmember was felling trees in preparation for a prescribed fire when the firefighter was struck by a tree branch. Injuries included chipped lower front teeth, facial lacerations and bruised neck and collar bone. The firefighter was given first aid and then taken by ground ambulance to a medical center, treated and released to light duty with follow-up dental treatments. The District will likely follow-up with an RLS.
incidents.quote: “I will never forget the sound of it hitting his hard hat and hearing his sigh.” Captain

incidents.name: Sheep Fire Engine Entrapment and Burnover
incidents.summary: Two members of a VFD operating a Type 6 Engine responded to a request for assistance on the Sheep Fire at 1608. The engine reached the flaming front and began direct attack, working in tandem by following a second engine. Both engines began spraying water on the flaming front, moving from north to south in the unburned fuel. The engine noticed flames coming out from under the engine. The engine became disabled and the flaming front overtook the vehicle.
incidents.quote: No anchor point was established or utilized as the both engines continued their operations.

incidents.name: Lump Gulch Fire Type 3 IMT COVID 19 Mitigation Lessons
incidents.summary: Old habits are hard to break. Entire engine crews were in the room and crew leaders brought trainees and squad leaders. This was the first large fire of the year and was also visible from the state capital, generating a lot of interest.
incidents.quote: The IMT entered the briefing room and were greeted by a large crowd.

incidents.name: New York State COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: Asymptomatic people are a major problem because there is no sign of the disease and it is therefore being spread. I worked in an ICP as an Operations Section Chief (OPSC) with someone who was asymptomatic. The entire incident management team was then tested. From that point forward, PPE was worn—treating everyone as though they had COVID-19 and were asymptomatic.
incidents.quote: “I have some Forest Rangers who were asymptomatic and suffered no ill effects. There have been others who had the worst experience of their life."

incidents.name: Mangum Fire Using the COVID 19 Screening Tool
incidents.summary: This Wildland Fire COVID-19 Screening Tool form is part of MPHAT’s interim standard operating procedure for wildland fire personnel at duty stations and wildland fire incidents. It is intended to reduce the risk of disease to sustain a viable, safe andeffective wildland fire management workforce.
incidents.quote: Cases of resources who have reasonably suspicious COVID-19 symptoms get reviewed by the Medical Secton Chief, Infections MEDL, COVID agency administrator, Forest Safety Officer, and the local Emergency Operations Center (EOC) to determine an appropriate response.

incidents.name: Wyoming Dual Wheels Engine Incident
incidents.summary: While driving 45 mph through road construction, the driver of the Type 6 Engine noticed a vibration coming from the back of the truck. The driver continued down the road, slowing down without applying the brake and pulled off to a safe location on the side of the highway. After pulling off the highway, the driver exited the engine and noticed the driver side rear dual tire was gone.
incidents.quote: This has happened before on an engine earlier this year!

incidents.name: Utah Project Work Kickback Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: A sawyer was preparing to cut down a three-inch conifer sapling. The sawyer positioned himself with his left leg forward and right leg back and proceeded to cut the base of a sapling. As the sawyer placed the tip of the running chainsaw bar next to the sapling, the tip contacted a log that was resting against the tree, which caused the chainsaw to kick back abruptly. As the saw bar kicked back, it contacted the lower portion of the sawyer’s protective chainsaw chaps. The fast-moving chain cut into the chaps, causing the chaps to be pulled quickly toward the inside of the sawyer’s lower left leg, allowing for the lower leg to become exposed to the still-moving chain.
incidents.quote: The sawyer shut down the saw, taking time to assess the situation further. The sawyer then became aware of a cut to his pants. Upon pulling up the pant leg, he noticed a two-inch horizontal cut, just above the top of the boot line.

incidents.name: Sand Creek Fire COVID 19 IMT Lessons
incidents.summary: Rocky Mountain Area Incident Management Team Black recommends an adaptive management approach to implementing the COVID-19 Response Guide. Adaptive management is a learning process, with a conscious intent of increasing the corporate knowledge of all Incident Management Teams.
incidents.quote: Sand Creek Fire COVID 19 IMT Lessons

incidents.name: Bush Fire Response and Support to Handcrew Positive COVID 19 Tests
incidents.summary: Results were received on June 26 and included seven positive results for COVID-19, with six firefighters presenting as asymptomatic. The Mesa and Maricopa County, Arizona Health Departments were notified of the test results. Follow-up testing occurred on July 1. (On July 6, as this RLS was being finalized, these test resultswere announced, indicating four additional positive COVID-19 cases. As a result, the quarantine clock was reset.)
incidents.quote: Unanticipated Complicationson the Bush Fire COVID-19 Incident

incidents.name: East Canyon Fire COVID 19 IMT Lessons
incidents.summary: • Attach “Special Covid Instructions” to the Resource Order which provides a URL to provide a single point flow of communications. • Take care of your people through your team’s COVID policy. Set the tone immediatelyupon arrival that your team’s policy is important through your actions. • Face coverings from the start. The IMT needs to set the example from day one. • Empower employees to try new ideas and support innovation. • Share the word – COVID precautions are a priority for IMT’s. • Embrace the introspective look and make positive changes to the fire team community.
incidents.quote: As every section is critically looking at their internal operations and thinking about how we can do things differently. We are finding great ideas on how we can improve fire management into the future. We really think the fire community should embrace this time of change as an opportunity.

incidents.name: Coronado NF Tire Separation Lessons
incidents.summary: While pre-positioned on severity funds, a patrol prevention unit was traveling east on Interstate 10 back to the station by himself in aFord F-350 with a utility bed. At approximately 1330, the vehicle’s tire delaminated and wrapped around the axel. When this happened, a loud cracking sound was heard along with the immediate loss of steering control, as the rear end of the truck began to swerve erratically. Steering and vehicle control was regained within a few seconds and the truck was safely steered off of the highway onto the median.
incidents.quote: A loud cracking sound was heard along with the immediate loss of steering control . . .

incidents.name: Goose Creek Fire COVID 19 Lessons
incidents.summary:  Limit the potential for COVID-19 spread within the Goose Creek incident and between incident personnel and the community:  Coordinate with the Rio Grande National Forest COVID Response IMT for current best practices and forest operating procedures.  Communicate and ensure all resources observe COVID-19 mitigations:  Use cloth face coverings when indoors or when >6’ spacing cannot be maintained—even outside, wash/sanitize hands frequently, and avoid shared surfaces.  Ensure contact tracing is immediately implementable in case of any positive or presumptive positive cases of COVID-19.
incidents.quote: Trust your gut when something doesn’t sit right.

incidents.name: COVID 19 Positive Off Unit Firefighter
incidents.summary: While on a fire assignment on the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest in Nevada this June, two firefighters from the Chattooga River Ranger District—on the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest in Georgia—were exposed to another firefighter who became sick and ultimately tested positive for COVID-19. They had been working with the Bridgeport Helitack Crew under the “Module as One” concept when they were exposed to the COVID-19 positive individual.
incidents.quote: What Happens When Your Employees from Georgia are Exposed to a Positive COVID-19 Individual During a Fire Assignment in Nevada?

incidents.name: Bighorn Fire Hit By Rock
incidents.summary: On the Bighorn Fire on the Coconino National Forest, a hotshot crew member was working as a swamper on the fireline when a crew above the Firefighter dislodged a rock. U.S. Forest Service EMTs provided initial care. The firefighter was then life-flighted to a hospital. The firefighter received 30 stitches for a facial laceration and is now stable and has been released from the hospital.
incidents.quote: The rock hit the firefighter, which caused the firefighter to fall onto an adjacent chainsaw.

incidents.name: Picture Canyon Fire Smokejumper Injury
incidents.summary: . The firefighter was taken by ambulance to a hospital and diagnosed with a dislocated shoulder and scheduled for a CT scan and further X-rays. The firefighter was expected to be released the next day.
incidents.quote: On the Picture Canyon Fire on the Comanche Cimarron National Grassland, a McCall Smokejumper received a hard landing due to a sudden gust of wind that lifted the firefighter up twice

incidents.name: Polles Fire Helicopter Accident and Fatality
incidents.summary: The Polles Fire was located approximately 11 miles west of Payson, AZ in the Mazatzal Wilderness. At approximately 1215, the Type 2, UH-1H (Huey) helicopter that was slinging in supplies for ground crews who were spiked out in the remote area, crashed, killing the pilot who was the only person on board.
incidents.quote: “The chaos slowed down when the IWI IC took command. It was such a relief for me to have someone on the ground, on the scene. Then I’m supporting the commander. There was urgency but I felt calmness coming over.”

incidents.name: Engine 644 Slides Off Road
incidents.summary: The engine bounces roughly while going over the potholes until the rear of the vehicle is bounced to the edge of the road. When the right rear tire comes into contact with the soft shoulder of the road, it sinks in and the weight of the fire engine causes the shoulder to give way. The backend of the vehicle starts to slide off the road and the momentum carries the rest of the vehicle with it.
incidents.quote: “As the engine slowly slid off the road, I had this surreal feeling of, ‘well, we are gonna roll.’”

incidents.name: Zion NP Engine Cab Fire
incidents.summary: At 1756 on July 8 a structural fire is reported through the activation of the automatic fire detection system at Zion National Park’s emergency operations center. The building is the center of emergency operations for the park—housing park dispatch, law enforcement, EMS, search and rescue, structural and wildland fire response equipment. Dispatchers in the upstairs offices smelled smoke about the time the alarms started sounding. The fire was located in the passenger compartment of the Type 6. A lithium battery is the likely cause.
incidents.quote: The fire was probably smoldering and puffing inside the cab for a while.

incidents.name: Bighorn Fire Potential Hazmat Fuel Leak
incidents.summary: A total of six 55-gallon drums had been filled with various types of fuel from the Bighorn Fire at the Supply Unit as back-haul began in early to mid-July. The fuel filled into these drums included: diesel, burn mix, gasoline, pump mix for portable pumps, and saw mix. The concern was that the damaged drum, while not leaking, would result in either a leak of flammable fuel or a fire within the Supply Unit.
incidents.quote: The concern was that the damaged drum, while not leaking, would result in either a leak of flammable fuel or a fire within the Supply Unit.

incidents.name: Numbers Fire COVID 19 Mitigation
incidents.summary: Great Basin Incident Management Team #4 (Tim Roide) was assigned to the Numbers Fire, located near Gardnerville, Nevada, from July 9 to 15, 2020. The Numbers Fire challenged all sections with the added complexity of COVID-19. To comply with State of Nevada mandates and the Wildland Fire Response Plan (WFRP), face coverings were required at the Incident Command Post (ICP).
incidents.quote: Great Basin Team #4 Type 2 Incident Management Team Numbers Fire COVID-19 Lessons Learned

incidents.name: Bitterroot Virtual Expanded Dispatch
incidents.summary: While many lessons were learned, the benefits that virtual expanded dispatch provides, scalability and redundancy in particular, were shown to greatly outweigh the challenges.
incidents.quote: Bitterroot Dispatch, along with other wildland fire dispatch offices and emergency communication centers across the country, has demonstrated the viability of the decentralized remote virtual expanded dispatch operation.

incidents.name: Remote Duty Station COVID 19 Positive
incidents.summary: On Thursday, July 16, atapproximately 10 a.m., a contracted pilot at a remote base in Alaska discovered he had lost his sense of taste and smell at breakfast. He returned to his room and notified his manager of this acute loss. The manager reported this information to the Fireline Medic on staff at the base. Exactly one month earlier, the Fire Management Officer of this remote fire protection zone based out of a small village, made some pivotal decisions that would affect the outcome of this incident. For this potential COVID-19 environment, he established a lookout, identified safety zones, identified trigger points, and communicated these to the personnel he supervised.
incidents.quote: This set of unique symptoms and travel history, combined with the Fireline Medic’s previous experience treating COVID-19, trigged the highest level of concern.

incidents.name: Bonaparte Interagency Medevac
incidents.summary: On Tuesday evening, July 21, a U.S. Forest Service firefighter at Bonaparte Mountain on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, began to feel ill while performing his duties. Recognizing the symptoms (dizziness, facial numbness, “seasickness”) being consistent with a stroke, the firefighter phoned the Northeast Washington Interagency Dispatch Center (NEWICC), reported his symptoms and requested medical assistance.
incidents.quote: The patient’s recognition of symptoms consistent with a stroke and his immediate action to call for help most likely reduced his recovery time and may have saved his life.

incidents.name: Caldwell Fire Burn Injury
incidents.summary: Initial attack resources faced active fire driven by receptive fuels and multiple thunderstorm cells. Unsecured drip torches and fuel cans were shuttled in the back of a pickup to support a firing operation. Conditions changed causing a change in strategy necessitating the repositioning of resources back through the fire area. Fire pulsed along the road and smoke obscured visibility. The occupants of the truck discovered the fuel in the bed of the pickup had caught fire. While unloading the volatile cargo a firefighter suffered a second degree burn to one leg after his pant leg caught fire.
incidents.quote: “Instinct made me think we should check the load in the back of the truck – I knew we were okay, but we may need to ditch the truck if that fuel had caught fire.”

incidents.name: July Complex COVID 19 RLS
incidents.summary: At the peak of the July Complex’s fire activity, approximately 2,000 resources were assigned to this incident—all of whom would need to be managed and guided in the proper mitigations for limiting the potential transmission of COVID-19.
incidents.quote: Managing the July Complex included the additional challenge of implementing and managing COVID-19 protocol and precautions to avoid the spread of the virus among fire personnel as well as members of the adjacent communities.

incidents.name: Badger Fire Firing Operation Near Miss
incidents.summary: On July 24, 2020, an engine responded to initial attack the Badger Fire at approximately 1730. The engine crew was assigned to conduct a firing operation from a dozer line that ascended a steep, rocky hillslope. The crew initially began firing halfway up the slope, but ceased and continued hiking towards the top of the ridge. As they were 3/4 of the way to the top, a wind shift cause fire behavior to change and fire to move towards them. They were instructed to drop their packs, and reaching the top, they were picked up and extracted from danger by engines. One engine sustained minor heat damage.
incidents.quote: Engine 1154 reported on Badger frequency “garbled…1154, fire crossed the road, gotta get out”.

incidents.name: Badger Canyon Fire Ash Pit Burn
incidents.summary: A firefighter from the Umatilla National Forest Engine Module stepped into a hot ash pit during mop-up on the Badger Canyon Fire. The firefighter sustained 1st and 2nd degree burns (less than 2 percent of body area) to the leg above the boot. The patient was evaluated and treated on scene by U.S. Forest Service EMTs, then transported via ambulance to a hospital where he was treated and released. The patient was assigned one week of light duty. The home unit is conducting an AAR.
incidents.quote: A firefighter stepped into a hot ash pit during mop-upon the Badger Canyon Fire.

incidents.name: TRMU Lightning Complex Heat Related Illness
incidents.summary: The patient was transported via ground ambulance to a local hospital where they were treated and released. A Hospital Liaison was assigned and a local AAR was conducted.
incidents.quote: On the Trinity River Management Unit (TRMU) Lightning Complex on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest, an individual from a TRMU Engine Module experienced a heat-related illness (HRI) described as dehydration/minor heat exhaustion.

incidents.name: Utah Wind Event
incidents.summary: Both the Canal Fire and Knolls Fire reacted directly to an unseasonably strong cold front pushing down from the Pacific Northwest. Dispatch logs show problematic fire behavior occurring on both incidents within three minutes of each other—at approximately 1340 on June 28.
incidents.quote: “When I saw the first Single Engine Air Tanker’s drop fly sideways, I knew it was going to be a ground game.”

incidents.name: Bishop Fire Seat Fatalities
incidents.summary: According to witnesses on the ground, as N1558W climbed, it suddenly began a left turn and collided with N8510M. Both airplanes then descended rapidly to the ground. The pilots of both airplanes were fatally injured.
incidents.quote: Witnesses in nearby firefighting aircraft stated that they heard the pilot of N1558W announce over the radio that he had retardant on his windshield and was initiating a go-around.

incidents.name: Little Soda Fire Rhabdo
incidents.summary: The patient was transported via ground ambulance to a local medical center and was admitted for treatment. A Hospital Liaison was assigned, an AAR was conducted, and a Heat-Related Illness (HRI) questionnaire will be submitted.
incidents.quote: While working on the Little Soda Fire on the Klamath National Forest, a handcrew member suffered from heat stress and was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis.

incidents.name: Pine Hollow Fire Fuel Geyser
incidents.summary: After three to five attempts to start saw, he set the saw down on its side and proceeded to check the fuel level. He held pressure down on the fuel cap. Covering the cap with his hand, as he twisted it to the “open” position, the fuel tank geyser occurred. The fuel from the tank shot upward a reported three feet and hit the Sawyer in the face and eyes. He was wearing safety glasses.Even with the safety glasses, the fuel geyser splashed fuel in both of the Sawyer’s eyes. Medical attention was given at the scene and an Incident Within an Incident (IWI) was initiated.
incidents.quote: Due to frequent training on fuel geysers and associated refueling procedures, the saw was removed from heat and ignition sources before the incident occurred. Outcomes would have been much more tragic had the fuel ignited.

incidents.name: Red Salmon Fire Bee Sting
incidents.summary: The patient was assessed on the fireline by U.S. Forest Service EMTs. Due to anaphylaxis concerns, the patient was evacuated by air. Upon arrival to the ER, the patient was stable and ambulatory and was subsequently released.
incidents.quote: While working on the Red Salmon Fire on the Six Rivers National Forest, a firefighter from the Wallowa-Whitman National Forest was stung by a bee and experienced localized swelling on the arm.

incidents.name: Bridger Teton NF Interagency Helicopter SAR COVID Mitigations
incidents.summary: ❖ For any medical this year, treat the patient as if they may have COVID-19. ❖ Incorporate precautions to be taken by EMTs responders in conversations before the incident happens. ❖ Flexible use of a “potentially exposed” pilot should be considered while COVID-19 tests are being done.
incidents.quote: Bridger-Teton Forest’s Interagency Fire Helicopter and COVID-19 Mitigations

incidents.name: Montrose Complex COVID Positive Employee Lessons
incidents.summary: There is so much guidance, direction, and information regarding COVID that it is difficult to know where to begin and to find what you need quickly. Actually reading and understanding the content of this information is often put off until the initial time that a positive case occurs. As information is updated and revised, it is difficult to keep up.
incidents.quote: Lessons from a COVID-19 Positive Employee Incident in an Interagency Environment

incidents.name: Apple Fire COVID 19 Mitigations
incidents.summary: A compilation of Lessons Learned during the Apple Fire. From the perspective of the COVID Advisor, Agency Administrator, Incident Management Team and Forest IMO.
incidents.quote: Apple Fire COVID 19 Mitigations

incidents.name: SOG Fire Rock Strike
incidents.summary: The patient was assessed, treated, and packaged on scene by U.S. Forest Service EMTs, then transported by ground ambulance to Blue Mountain Hospital in John Day, Ore. The attending physician diagnosed a skull fracture and elected to transport the patient via air ambulance to Saint Alphonsus Medical Center in Boise, Idaho. The firefighter’s anticipated release date is August 8— with a full recovery expected.
incidents.quote: While performing line construction on the BUD-2072 Incident on the Malheur National Forest, a firefighter on the Forest’s Type 2 Initial Attack Crew was struck on the head (helmet) by a large rock and sustained a 6-inch laceration.

incidents.name: Apple Fire Bucking Injury
incidents.summary: An IHC sawyer was bucking a downed tree on the Apple Fire, located on the Cal Fire Riverside Unit, when the saw bar was pinched, pulling the sawyer forward. As he was pulled, the sawyer’s face impacted a small tree, causing a lacerated septum. The patient was treated on scene by U.S. Forest Service EMTs and ambulance medics. The patient was transported to a local hospital via ground ambulance, then treated and released to full duty.
incidents.quote: Apple Fire Bucking Injury

incidents.name: Neals Hill Fire Skidgine Rollover
incidents.summary: While attempting to reposition on the hill the skidgine kicked out a large rock from its right rear tire causing it to lose balance. The operator immediately tried to use its front blade to stabilize the machine to no avail. The operator was able to safely exit the Skidgine without assistance.
incidents.quote: Witnesses described the skidgine rolling over approximately four to five timesbefore coming to rest on its side.

incidents.name: Red Salmon Fire Medevac
incidents.summary: The patient, having a history of seizures, was treated and released.
incidents.quote: A U.S. Forest Service contract firefighter experiencing seizures was flown via agency helicopter to Mercy Medical Center in Redding, Calif.

incidents.name: Red Salmon Fire Medical Emergency
incidents.summary: The patient was assessed and treated on scene by local government paramedics and was transferred by ground ambulance to a hospital in Arcata, Calif. The patient was treated and released.
incidents.quote: A firefighter from a hand crew on the Red Salmon Fire on the Six Rivers National Forest experienced seizures while at the ICP.

incidents.name: Idaho Project Work Boring Back Cut Chainsaw Cut
incidents.summary: The sawyer moved to the offside of the tree to start the boring back quarter cut. The sawyer started the chainsaw, got into a comfortable position and began their cut. The sawyer was holding the chainsaw with his left hand positioned behind the chain brake (ready to hit the brake in case of kickback from the saw), and his right hand on the trigger. The saw was turned on its left side, with the bar nuts facing the sky. Upon contact, the saw glanced off the outside of the tree and swung down and to the left, striking the sawyer on their lower left arm.
incidents.quote: Idaho Project Work Boring Back Cut Chainsaw Cut

incidents.name: Red Salmon Fire Rhabdomyolysis
incidents.summary: The patient was transferred via a Rapid Extraction Module Support (REMS) Team UTV and truck to the Medical Unit Leader (MEDL). Next, ground support transported the patient to an Emergency Department in Yreka, Calif. The patient was provided two IV bags of fluid and a series of diagnostic tests before being released back to full duty.
incidents.quote: A firefighter working as part of a chipper crew experienced swelling and numbness in the legs. The patient was assessed on scene by a U.S. Forest Service EMT and local government Paramedics and was diagnosed with Rhabdomyolysis.

incidents.name: Stagecoach Fire Fatality
incidents.summary: The patient was transported to a hospital and, later that day, died as a result of an acute medical emergency.
incidents.quote: At approximately 0230 on the Stagecoach Fire on the Sequoia National Forest, a Forest Service Administratively Determined (AD) employee in a fire support role awoke suffering from chest pains.

incidents.name: Davin Road Fire
incidents.summary: On Saturday, August 15, 2010 at approximately 1515 hours, three fire vehicles, (2 USFWS and 1 Franklin Co FD #3) were involved in a burn-over incident on the Davin Place Fire. Two Franklin Co FD#3 employees were transported to Lourdes Hospital in Pasco for smoke inhalation. One of these firefighters had 2nd degree burns to the hands. Both firefighters were treated and released the same evening. The crews had been overtaken by a fast moving grass fire as they were moving to a nearby safety zone which was identified in the black. The USFWS vehicles were able to drive through the advancing fire, but the Franklin Co FD#3 engine got stuck, the firefighters in the engine sheltered in place in the engine's cab. Once the fire front passed, they exited the engine and proceeded to extinguish any fire on the engine.

incidents.name: Heli Rappel Emergency Tie Off
incidents.summary: Once my descent stopped, I looked up at the helicopter and noticed how close it was to the trees and that I was still around 30 to 35 feet from the ground. I realized that being lowered to the ground was not a feasible option. Soon, the ship began to lift me above the tree top again and my rope (right side) became severely tangled in the left side rope. At this point, the Spotter gave me the ‘begin emergency Tie-Off’ signal.”
incidents.quote: “Everything we did just seemed to wrap more rope around the tree.” Rappel Spotter

incidents.name: Pumpkin Fire Vehicle Rollover
incidents.summary: The caravan was traveling into the morning sun and there was considerable dust being kicked up by the vehicles. The shoulders of the road were very soft in every section of the road where the grader had done work. This hazard had been communicated to personnel on the fire. The left side wheels of the pickup sank into the soft shoulder and the driver attempted to turn harder to the right. However, the shoulder gave away and the pickup began to rollover down the steep mountainside.
incidents.quote: “It just happened so fast. As we were rolling down the mountain I thought to myself: ‘I can’t believe this. I just killed my crew’.”

incidents.name: Cameron Peak Fire Support Personnel Injury
incidents.summary: A contract fire support individual on the Cameron Peak Fire on the Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests suffered an open compound fracture to the lower leg (tibia/fibula) when a crate landed on their leg while being unloaded. 9-1-1 was activated and the patient was transported to a local hospital via ambulance.
incidents.quote: A Cameron Peak Fire Support Personnel Injury suffered an open compound fracture to the lower leg.

incidents.name: P 515 Accident Investigation Warm Springs Agency
incidents.summary: A van sustained minor burn damage and a pickup truck was completely burned. The vehicles were parked next to heavy, unburned timber, along with two other vehicles belonging to a Type 2 crew. The crew was suppressing spot fires on the east side of the incident when the fire behavior increased and threatened the vehicles.
incidents.quote: Although no injuries occurred, this incident highlights how quickly fire conditions can escalate resulting hazardous conditions to personnel.

incidents.name: Ranch 2 Fire First Heat Related Injury
incidents.summary: An IHC Firefighter suffered a heat-related injury while working on the Ranch 2 Fire on the Angeles National Forest. The patient was assessed and treated by a U.S. Forest Service EMT and Line Medic, then transported to a hospital via agency helicopter and ground ambulance. The patient was treated, transported home to recover, and assigned “light duty” for the next two days.
incidents.quote: Ranch 2 Fire First IHC Heat-Related Injury

incidents.name: Kidney Lake Fire Lightning Strike
incidents.summary: This was not a direct lightning strike to either personnel. The strike happened 10-20 feet away from them. One of the firefighters was standing/walking toward a natural crevice in which the other firefighter was already positioned.
incidents.quote: “Both firefighters got struck through the ground. Both firefighters are OK. Moving downhill and taking cover.”

incidents.name: East Fork Fire Entrapment 2020
incidents.summary: During initial attack of the East Fork Fire, Utah, a trail crew member, ICT3, and three engine crew members had their primary egress cut off when winds shifted down canyon, rapidly increasing fire behavior and starting spot fires downhill from their location. They sought refuge in the creek and ran through the black to avoid the flame front. A helicopter directed them through unburned fuel to a meadow uphill from the fire where they were extracted and taken to safety.
incidents.quote: Brian told the others “No matter what happens, this guy doesn’t have a shelter and he’s getting in with one of us.” Casey texted a friend “Stuck in a fire, surrounded on all sides. Sheltering in creek. Might be ok. If something happens to me, my parents can be reached at...”

incidents.name: Frog Fire Fall from Truck at ICP
incidents.summary: The patient was transported via an agency-owned vehicle to a hospital and diagnosed with a contusion and mild concussion. The patient was treated and released to light duty. A full recovery is expected.
incidents.quote: While working at the Incident Command Post on the Frog Fire on the Mount Hood National Forest, a U.S. Forest Service employee fell from a truck when he was struck in the head by the rack from a stake side truck.

incidents.name: Pine Gulch Fire Dry Ice Outgassing
incidents.summary: The van departed ICP for the delivery. After approximately 10 minutes, the driver became short of breath and began to make involuntary quick breaths. Next, the driver reported losing cognitive ability. For instance, when the passenger told the driver to turn left, the driver indicated that the instruction was not immediately understood.The driver indicated that his condition continued to decrease. He felt an increased heart rate, was unable to concentrate, and began feeling as if he was going to pass out. The driver was about to inform the passenger that he was sick and needed to be relieved of driving. That’s when the passenger said: “I feel sick. I can’t breathe.”
incidents.quote: As of the publishing date of this RLS, the driver is under medical care for loss of cognitive abilities due to toxic carbon dioxide exposure.

incidents.name: Woodward Fire Extraction
incidents.summary: The Field Observer and firefighter started to scout the potential line later in the day. As they proceeded down the ridge line, the vegetation they encountered was thicker and more dense than they had expected. As late afternoon moved into evening, they realized that they were going to have a difficult time making it back to their vehicles before dark. At this time, fire activity increased as a result of a wind shift that brought the slope and fuels into alignment with this new wind pattern. When they called nearby Marin County Division Supervisor to provide a status of their progress, the Division Supervisorrealized that the firefighters were in a precarious situation. Within minutes, the Division Supervisor requested a local rescue helicopter from a nearby county to short-haul the firefighters off of the fireline to safety.
incidents.quote: The Interagency Emergency Extraction of Two Firefighters

incidents.name: Little Soda Fire PT Injury
incidents.summary: The patient was transported via ground ambulance to a hospital in Medford, Ore. Surgery was required, but a full recovery is expected.
incidents.quote: On the Little Soda Fire on the Klamath National Forest, a physical training injury resulted in testicular torsion.

incidents.name: Custer Gallatin NF Smokejumping Accident
incidents.summary: The smokejumper fell approximately 30 feet, landing on the buttocks. U.S. Forest Service EMTs assessed the patient on scene and suspected a spinal injury. The patient was transported via air ambulance and diagnosed at the hospital with a bulged disc. Full recovery is expected.
incidents.quote: During initial attack on the Custer-Gallatin National Forest, a smokejumper experienced a wind gust at treetop level, causing the parachute to snag a suspension line on a tree—partially collapsing the parachute.

incidents.name: Baboon Fire Dozer Tip Over
incidents.summary: A 486C Caterpillar dozer tipped over onto its side while constructing fire line on the Baboon Fire. What happened was the fire line took a dogleg upslope. There was a tree in the bottom on the dogleg. I pushed this tree over, then backed up to pick my line back up and construct line uphill. I believe that with traveling on this section of line twice broke up the rock stability underneath me. As I started to push line where I had just drove twice, the rocks and the dozer started to slide. While starting to slide, I tried to turn downhill and was unable to. I continued to slide until I slid off the rocks and with that momentum it tipped the dozer onto the side.”
incidents.quote: “While starting to slide, I tried to turn downhill and was unable to. I continued to slide until I slid off the rocks and with that momentum it tipped the dozer onto the side.”

incidents.name: Cameron Peak Fire Smoke Inhalation
incidents.summary: On the Cameron Peak Fire on the Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests, a contract hand crew member complained of chest pain radiating to arm. The patient was transported via ground ambulance to a hospital and diagnosed with smoke inhalation and altitude sickness. The patient was treated and released to light duty.
incidents.quote: Cameron Peak Fire Hand Crew Member Smoke Inhalation

incidents.name: Cameron Peak Fire COVID 19 Positive Incident
incidents.summary: This incident covers all five of the exposure events which occurred on the Cameron Peak Fire between August 24 and September 7, 2020 from the perspective of the IMT, NIMO, Regional Office, and Local Forest.
incidents.quote: "We can say, 'We care about you no matter who you work for', but it doesn't play out that way."

incidents.name: White River Fire Helicopter Accident and Fatality
incidents.summary: The helicopter had been conducting water bucket operations in support of the White River fire in Mt. Hood, National Forest. Radio communications with the helicopter pilot was lost and a second helicopter was dispatched in an effort to locate the pilot. The helicopter wreckage was later found at a designated dip site on the White River.
incidents.quote: “I heard nothing. And I called. And I called. Nothing. Then I called Columbia Cascade Dispatch and said: ‘I lost contact with 314, where are you showing him on AFF?’”

incidents.name: Bone Head Fire Insect Lodged in Throat
incidents.summary: A helitack crewmember working on the Bone Head Fire on the Idaho Panhandle National Forest, accidently swallowed a large insect which became lodged in throat, partially blocking the person’s airway. A sting/bite or irritation from the insect’s movement caused inflammation and compromised the airway. The patient quickly deteriorated—becoming near unresponsive. The patient was evaluated on scene by a U.S. Forest Service EMT, then transported via air ambulance to a hospital in Missoula, Mont.
